AI.method: UDF initializes a canonical underwater representation with 3D Gaussians in a volumetric medium field, maps it to a 4D neural voxel space with deformation and medium offset networks, and incorporates per-pixel uncertainty (from surface-view radiance ambiguity and inter-frame scene flow inconsistency) into the rendering loss.
AI.result: Experiments on controlled and in-the-wild underwater datasets show that UDF achieves high-quality 3D reconstruction and novel view synthesis.
AI.conclusion: Jointly modeling dynamic scene geometry, time-varying medium properties, and observation uncertainty enables robust underwater 3D reconstruction.

title: ROSETTA: Constructing Code-Based Reward from Unconstrained Language Preference

AI.tldr: ROSETTA uses foundation models to translate unconstrained natural language preferences into multi-stage reward functions via code generation, enabling online RL adaptation for embodied agents with an 87% average success rate.
AI.motivation: Embodied agents must align with individual human preferences, but natural language preferences are unconstrained, diverse, and dynamic, and prior methods require extensive offline training or single-task fine-grained corrections.
AI.method: The framework uses foundation models to ground and disambiguate unconstrained natural language preferences, construct multi-stage reward functions, and implement them through code generation for online reinforcement learning adaptation.
AI.result: Tested on short-horizon and long-horizon manipulation tasks with human evaluation, ROSETTA outperforms SOTA baselines and achieves an 87% average success rate and 86% human satisfaction across 116 preferences.
AI.conclusion: ROSETTA enables embodied agents to adapt online to evolving and diverse human language preferences without offline reward model training.

title: SSVPO: Effective Step-Level Credit Assignment for RL Training of Language Models

AI.tldr: SSVPO introduces Sequential Shapley Values in an insertion MDP to perform fair step-level credit assignment for RL training of language models, improving accuracy by up to 11.6% and reducing token usage by 18.1%.
AI.motivation: Outcome-based RL for LLM mathematical reasoning is inefficient due to sparse final rewards, while existing credit assignment methods struggle to fairly evaluate individual steps in partially correct reasoning chains.
AI.method: Inspired by multi-agent RL, Sequential Shapley Value Policy Optimization (SSVPO) defines an insertion MDP and computes Sequential Shapley Values by reordering reasoning steps into alternative chains, using SSV as a PPO-consistent advantage baseline and pruning zero-credit steps.
AI.result: Across 7 benchmarks, SSVPO outperforms outcome-based (RLOO, GRPO, DAPO) and credit assignment-based (VinePPO, SPO) baselines, achieving up to an 11.6% accuracy gain, 18.1% token reduction, and 1.6x reasoning efficiency improvement over vanilla methods.
AI.conclusion: SSVPO provides theoretically fair step-level credit assignment that boosts post-training LLM reasoning performance while shortening reasoning chains and reducing token budgets.

title: Frequency-Balanced Retinal Representation Learning with Mutual Information Regularization

AI.tldr: RetMAE augments masked autoencoders with a mutual-information regularizer to suppress low-frequency redundancy and emphasize diagnostically critical high-frequency structures in retinal images.
AI.motivation: Masked autoencoders (MAE) favor low-frequency content and under-encode high-frequency details where retinal pathology often manifests, limiting diagnostic performance in ophthalmic modeling.
AI.method: Within a mutual-information formulation of MAE, the Frequency-Balanced Retinal Masked Autoencoder (RetMAE) adds an MI regularizer to the reconstruction objective without altering the underlying architecture.
AI.result: RetMAE learns frequency-balanced features that surpass MAE-based retinal encoders in both quantitative and qualitative evaluations.
AI.conclusion: A frequency-oriented perspective with a simple MI-based correction addresses ViT's low-pass bias in retinal images and provides a principled foundation for ophthalmic representation learning.

title: PAC-Bayes bounds for cumulative loss in Continual Learning

AI.tldr: This paper extends PAC-Bayes bounds to continual learning, deriving general upper bounds on cumulative generalization loss and oracle bounds for Gibbs posteriors that yield non-vacuous vision bounds.
AI.motivation: Continual learning requires balancing forward transfer and forgetting, yet generally applicable upper bounds on learning plasticity and reliable risk certificates are scarce.
AI.method: The authors extend PAC-Bayes bounds from online learning and time-uniform offline learning to continual learning, deriving general cumulative generalization loss bounds for any task distribution and algorithm alongside oracle bounds for Gibbs posteriors.
AI.result: Empirical evaluations show the approach produces non-vacuous bounds on several continual learning vision problems and tight oracle bounds on linear regression tasks.
AI.conclusion: This work establishes the first general upper bound on learning plasticity for continual learning, providing formal risk certificates across arbitrary task distributions.

title: A Bayesian Nonparametric Framework for Private, Fair, and Balanced Tabular Data Synthesis

AI.tldr: This paper presents a Bayesian nonparametric conditional generative framework that enforces fairness and class balance for private tabular data synthesis, extending beyond binary protected attributes.
AI.motivation: Data synthesis in data-scarce environments risks reproducing biases and marginalizing underrepresented groups, while existing fairness-aware methods primarily focus on binary-valued sensitive attributes.
AI.method: The framework fuses a conditional generator with Bayesian nonparametric learning (BNPL), imposing fairness by minimizing mutual information between generated outcomes and non-binary protected attributes while addressing class imbalance.
AI.result: Theoretical guarantees and extensive experiments on sensitive empirical examples demonstrate scalable, privacy-preserving, and equitable tabular data generation with adequate representation of underrepresented groups.
AI.conclusion: Combining conditional generation with Bayesian nonparametric learning offers a principled and scalable solution for private, fair, and balanced tabular data synthesis.

title: Expertise Can Be Helpful for Reinforcement Learning-based Macro Placement

AI.tldr: This paper integrates EDA expert knowledge and iterative post-refinement imitation into RL-based chip macro placement, improving total negative slack by 32.53% and worst negative slack by 7.74% over the runner-up.
AI.motivation: Existing RL-based macro placement methods neglect accumulated EDA engineering expertise and optimize oversimplified proxy objectives, leading to suboptimal PPA metrics compared to expert designs.
AI.method: The framework combines Expert Knowledge Injection (dataflow guidance, periphery bias, macro grouping, I/O keepout constraints) with Expert Workflow Imitation, which iteratively updates designs based on backend PPA feedback using preference optimization.
AI.result: On the ICCAD 2015 and OpenROAD benchmarks, the method outperforms analytical, black-box optimization, and RL-based baselines, improving total negative slack by 32.53% and worst negative slack by 7.74% on average over the runner-up.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating domain expertise and expert refinement workflows into RL substantially improves timing and PPA metrics in automated chip macro placement.

title: Point-UQ: An Uncertainty-Quantification Paradigm for Point Cloud Few-Shot Class Incremental Learning

AI.tldr: Point-UQ is a training-free uncertainty-quantification paradigm for 3D few-shot class-incremental learning that dynamically arbitrates between semantic classifiers and geometric prototypes, outperforming SOTA by 4% average accuracy.
AI.motivation: Existing 3D FSCIL methods fine-tune feature representations while keeping static decision boundaries, causing a trade-off between catastrophic forgetting of base classes and overfitting to novel classes.
AI.method: Point-UQ pairs Attention-driven Adaptive Enhancement (AAE), which fuses multi-scale features to compute calibrated prediction entropy, with Uncertainty-quantification Decision Decoupling (UDD), which uses that entropy to dynamically arbitrate between semantic classifiers and geometric prototypes without retraining.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on ModelNet, ShapeNet, ScanObjectNN, and CO3D show Point-UQ outperforms state-of-the-art methods by 4% in average accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Shifting from feature fine-tuning to uncertainty-guided dynamic decision optimization enables robust base-class retention and accurate novel-class recognition in 3D FSCIL.

title: Offline Preference-Based Value Optimization

AI.tldr: Preference-based Value Optimization (PVO) solves offline preference-based RL by minimizing a value alignment loss, achieving rate-optimal O(eps^-2) sample complexity and strong empirical performance without extra preference hyperparameters.
AI.motivation: Existing offline preference-based RL algorithms either rely on computationally intractable optimization or suffer from unstable training and high performance variance.
AI.method: PVO directly optimizes the value function to align with trajectory-pair preference feedback by minimizing a novel value alignment loss, which is applicable to both value-based and actor-critic algorithms.
AI.result: PVO is proven to achieve O(eps^-2) sample complexity and consistently outperforms strong baselines across continuous control benchmarks with stable training and no extra preference hyperparameters; ablations confirm replacing TD loss with value alignment loss substantially improves learning.
AI.conclusion: PVO bridges theory and practice in offline PbRL by offering a simple, hyperparameter-free, and rate-optimal value alignment objective.

title: Sequential Information Bottleneck Fusion: Towards Robust and Generalizable Multi-Modal Brain Tumor Segmentation

AI.tldr: Sequential Multi-modal Segmentation Network (SMSN) uses an Information-Bottleneck Fusion Module for sequential multi-modal MRI fusion, improving brain tumor segmentation under missing modalities and cross-domain transfer.
AI.motivation: Parallel fusion strategies for multi-modal MRI brain tumor segmentation risk losing shared information across modalities, degrading performance when one or more modalities are missing.
AI.method: Grounded in an information-theoretic analysis showing sequential fusion yields a tighter generalization upper bound, SMSN integrates an Information-Bottleneck Fusion Module (IBFM) to sequentially extract modality-common features while reconstructing modality-specific features.
AI.result: On BRATS18 and BRATS20, SMSN consistently outperforms parallel fusion baselines across diverse missing-modality settings and transfers from BRATS20 to a brain metastasis dataset without fine-tuning.
AI.conclusion: Sequential information bottleneck fusion provides a theoretically grounded and robust approach to missing-modality multi-modal medical image segmentation and cross-domain generalization.

title: Value Matching: Scalable and Gradient-Free Reward-Guided Flow Adaptation

AI.tldr: Value Matching (VM) is an online optimal-control algorithm for reward-guided adaptation of flow and diffusion models that matches fine-tuning performance using less than 5% of the memory.
AI.motivation: Fine-tuning large flow and diffusion models via RL or optimal control incurs prohibitive memory costs, while offline Classifier Guidance suffers from limited reward expressivity and train-test distribution mismatch.
AI.method: VM learns the value function online within an optimal control setting, decoupling value network complexity from the base model, supporting non-differentiable rewards, and operating on-policy to explore high-reward regions beyond the data distribution.
AI.result: Across image generation and molecular design tasks, VM improves stability and sample efficiency over Classifier Guidance and achieves performance comparable to fine-tuning while using less than 5% of the memory.
AI.conclusion: Value Matching enables scalable, gradient-free, and memory-efficient reward-guided adaptation for large-scale flow and diffusion models.

title: Differentiable JPEG-based Input Perturbation for Knowledge Distillation Amplification via Conditional Mutual Information Maximization

AI.tldr: Differentiable JPEG-based Input Perturbation (DJIP) inserts a trainable JPEG layer before a frozen teacher network to maximize conditional mutual information, improving knowledge distillation accuracy by up to 4.11%.
AI.motivation: Maximizing conditional mutual information (CMI) improves teacher networks in knowledge distillation, but prior work requires fine-tuning large teachers or relying on inaccurate proxy objectives.
AI.method: DJIP places a plug-and-play differentiable JPEG layer before the teacher to perturb its inputs and uses an alternating optimization algorithm to learn JPEG coding parameters that directly maximize perturbed CMI without modifying the teacher.
AI.result: On CIFAR-100 and ImageNet across diverse distillers and architectures, DJIP consistently improves student accuracy by up to 4.11% while remaining lightweight and compatible with standard KD pipelines.
AI.conclusion: Input-space perturbation via differentiable JPEG coding offers an effective, teacher-agnostic way to amplify knowledge distillation.

title: PRISM: Partial-label Relational Inference with Spatial and Spectral Cues

AI.tldr: PRISM is a partial-label graph learning framework that combines spatial substructure alignment and multi-band spectral attention into a hybrid relational graph for iterative label propagation.
AI.motivation: Acquiring exact graph labels is costly, leading to partial-label graph learning where ambiguous candidate label sets hinder semantic extraction and cause overfitting to noisy labels.
AI.method: PRISM captures spatial cues via prototype-guided substructure alignment across graphs and global spectral cues via multi-frequency-band decomposition with attention, integrating both into a hybrid relational graph for candidate-constrained iterative label propagation.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets show PRISM consistently outperforms strong baselines under various label noise settings.
AI.conclusion: Combining spatial and spectral relational inference effectively mitigates label ambiguity in partial-label graph learning.

title: Paradigm Shift of GNN Explainer from Label Space to Prototypical Representation Space

AI.tldr: IDEA is a dual-stage GNN explainer optimization framework that shifts alignment from label space to a prototypical graph representation space, improving ROC-AUC by 4.45% and precision by 48.71% on average.
AI.motivation: Existing post-hoc GNN explainers align input and explanation predictions in the graph label space, which lacks structural expressiveness, and face substructure entanglement and distributional discrepancy when moving to representation space.
AI.method: IDEA operates in two stages: Structural Information Disentanglement uses a graph tokenizer with a structure-aware objective to isolate explanatory substructures into prototypes, and Explanatory Prototype Alignment aligns input and explanation distributions in that prototypical space.
AI.result: Across real-world and synthetic datasets, IDEA improves ROC-AUC by 4.45% and precision by 48.71% on average, and boosts diverse existing explainer architectures by up to 10.70%.
AI.conclusion: Optimizing GNN explainers in a disentangled prototypical representation space overcomes the structural limitations of label-space alignment and generalizes across explainer architectures.

title: Latent-Guided Reasoning: Empowering Small LLMs with Large-Model Thinking

AI.tldr: Latent-Guided Reasoning decouples high-level planning in a large model from low-level execution in a small model via latent guidance vectors, boosting small LLM reasoning accuracy by up to 13.9%.
AI.motivation: Complex reasoning in LLMs is computationally expensive because high-level cognitive planning and low-level linguistic realization are tightly coupled in large models.
AI.method: A large Implicit Thinker compresses its solution strategy into compact latent guidance vectors, which a small Explicit Executor (0.5B to 8B) uses to generate concise reasoning chains, trained with an information-theoretic dual-loss objective including reconstruction loss.
AI.result: Across 8 reasoning benchmarks, the framework substantially improves small model reasoning and generalization across 0.5B to 8B scales, boosting accuracy by up to 13.9% over standalone baselines.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling planning and execution through latent guidance offers a theoretically grounded way to transfer large-model reasoning to small LLMs with a better performance-cost trade-off.

title: MaRS: Memory-Adaptive Routing for Reliable Capacity Expansion and Knowledge Retention

AI.tldr: MaRS is a modular continual learning framework for frozen large pre-trained models that combines statistically controlled slot expansion with contrastive-distillation adaptation to balance plasticity and retention.
AI.motivation: Continual learning with frozen large pre-trained models struggles with the stability-plasticity dilemma because shallow adaptation modules are prone to catastrophic forgetting.
AI.method: MaRS (Memory-adaptive Router with Statistical control) pairs a frozen encoder, a slot-based memory router, and a lightweight classifier, using Statistically-Grounded Slot Expansion (SGSE) for controlled growth with false-alarm/delay guarantees and Dual-Stage Contrastive-Distillation Adaptation (DCDA) to integrate new slots without raw replay.
AI.result: Experiments across diverse benchmarks demonstrate that MaRS achieves state-of-the-art continual learning performance with frozen LPMs, combining adaptability, efficiency, and knowledge retention.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling representation from statistically controlled memory routing enables reliable, replay-free capacity expansion in continual learning with frozen backbones.

title: OrthoSolver: A Neural Proper Orthogonal Decomposition Solver For PDEs

AI.tldr: OrthoSolver generalizes Proper Orthogonal Decomposition to nonlinear PDEs by maximizing mutual information with orthogonality regularization, outperforming deep learning baselines on seven PDE benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Classical POD is limited by linearity and fixed snapshot bases, while purely data-driven deep learning decomposition solvers lack physical priors and suffer from modal collapse.
AI.method: Establishing that POD's energy maximization is equivalent to maximizing mutual information, OrthoSolver iteratively and adaptively extracts nonlinear basis modes by maximizing mutual information with the data field under an orthogonality regularizer to prevent mode collapse.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on seven PDE benchmarks show OrthoSolver consistently outperforms state-of-the-art deep learning baselines.
AI.conclusion: Reformulating POD from an information-theoretic perspective provides a principled nonlinear neural solver that avoids modal collapse in PDE modeling.

title: Machine Learning Research Has Outpaced Its Communication Norms

AI.tldr: An analysis of 62,628 NeurIPS, ICLR, and ICML papers against arXiv and PubMed baselines reveals declining readability, an 80% rise in sensational language, and surging acronym density that LLM judges fail to detect.
AI.motivation: Machine learning research output has grown rapidly, raising the question of whether its communication norms and readability have degraded relative to other scientific fields.
AI.method: The authors evaluate NeurIPS (30,595 papers), ICLR (16,807), and ICML (15,226) against 2.8M arXiv and 24.3M PubMed baselines using classical readability scores, writing style metrics, acronym density/reuse, LLM judge ratings, and citation counts.
AI.result: Mean Flesch Reading Ease on NeurIPS abstracts dropped from ~24 (1987) to ~8 (2025), sensational language rose ~80% (2015-2025), title acronym density reached 3.5-4.2 per 100 words (88-90% appearing <10 times), LLM judges rated recent abstracts easier to read (contradicting 14/15 classical metrics), and top-cited decile papers read easier than bottom-decile papers on 12/15 metrics.
AI.conclusion: ML venues face a measurable, citation-compounding readability decline invisible to LLM judges, motivating seven measurable writing standards proposed for venue pilots.

title: Before Explicit Patch-Level Correspondence: A Controlled Audit of Aggregation in Cross-View Assembly-State Matching

AI.tldr: Controlled audits on IKEA-Bench D1 and Assembly101 show that adding simple patch-derived frame-similarity statistics to frozen DINOv2-L global descriptors recovers most of the accuracy gain of raw-patch composites without explicit patch correspondence.
AI.motivation: Frozen visual encoders struggle on cross-view assembly-state matching, raising the question of whether discriminative evidence is missing from the representation or merely underused by clip-global descriptors.
AI.method: Under a fixed frozen-encoder, product-disjoint protocol on IKEA-Bench D1 and Assembly101, the authors compare clip-global descriptors, global features plus spatially averaged frame-centroid similarity statistics, a raw-patch composite, and a supervised PartMetric.
AI.result: With frozen DINOv2-L on IKEA-Bench D1, clip-global reaches 58.29% accuracy, global plus frame-centroid statistics reaches 64.57%, and raw-patch composite reaches 66.86%; similar point-estimate orderings appear on DINOv2-B and Assembly101 subsets, though CLIP and video-to-manual matching do not reliably reproduce the pattern.
AI.conclusion: Simple patch-derived frame statistics capture much of the benefit of finer-grained descriptors in DINOv2 cross-view assembly-state matching, while highlighting clear limits across other encoders and settings.

title: An Axiomatic Framework for Transferability Metrics with Risk-Theoretic Grounding for Source-Model Selection

AI.tldr: This paper introduces four axioms for transferability metrics, proposes the Representation-Task Alignment (RTA) score, proves a Gaussian/LDA transfer risk bound, and shows RTA and CKA induce identical rankings across tested benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing transferability metrics (LEEP, LogME, H-Score) are heuristics without formal guarantees, leaving unanswered what foundational properties any compatibility metric should satisfy.
AI.method: The authors define four axioms (monotonicity, invariance, boundedness, consistency), propose the RTA score satisfying all four, prove an excess transfer risk bound in the Gaussian/LDA setting, and show LEEP, LogME, and H-Score are special cases or relaxations that violate at least one axiom.
AI.result: Across 20 pre-trained models and 15 VTAB-1k benchmarks (300 pairs), RTA and CKA are the only metrics with positive rank correlation on every dataset, outperforming LEEP, LogME, NCE, and H-Score; however, discriminative alignment saturates in 299/300 image pairs and 28/28 NLP pairs, making RTA and CKA produce identical rankings.
AI.conclusion: The work provides CKA with an axiomatic foundation it previously lacked, while identifying non-saturated regimes as future work to realize RTA's two-component advantage.

title: Style or Strategy? Discriminating Post-Training Displacement from Its Confounds in LLM Price Negotiation

AI.tldr: Controlled tests across three open LLM lineages in bilateral price negotiation reveal that apparent post-training strategic shifts are largely confounded by output-format failures, chat-template interfaces, and fixed stylistic anchoring rather than effective strategy.
AI.motivation: When aligned LLMs negotiate differently from base models, naive comparisons are confounded by unparseable output-format failures, late-turn failures, and fixed stylistic anchoring against single opponents.
AI.method: The authors design discriminating tests for each confound and run them across three open base->SFT->DPO(->RLVR) lineages in bilateral price negotiation, alongside an interface control crossing serialization with checkpoint and an accept-timing probe at horizon k=4.
AI.result: Output-format bands differ across families, openings do not track per-seller optima, concessions show no opponent-contingent adaptation by default, serialization affects OLMo stage attribution while Tulu's preference-stage locus persists, RLVR moves behavior less than earlier stages, and aligned models show accept-timing sensitivity at k=4 that earns essentially nothing.
AI.conclusion: No tested post-training channel exhibits effective negotiation strategy in this environment, underscoring the need to separate format-controlled displacement and contingent style from true strategic adaptation.

title: Optimal Transport Feature Alignment for Cross-Domain Cell Image Classification

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an unsupervised cross-domain single-cell classification pipeline using multi-encoder foundation features, shared-class filtering, graph-regularized optimal transport, and ensemble voting, improving average accuracy by 20%.
AI.motivation: Differences in microscope hardware, illumination, staining, and media cause severe domain shifts in computational cytology, degrading single-dataset models even when cell types overlap.
AI.method: The pipeline extracts features from multiple foundation encoders, unsupervisedly identifies shared cell types between datasets to filter unmatched classes, aligns embedding spaces via graph-regularized optimal transport (OT), and classifies via ensemble voting without target-domain fine-tuning.
AI.result: Across multiple real-world cell image datasets, adding class filtering and OT improves average accuracy by +20% and yields robust performance in both fully unsupervised and low-label regimes.
AI.conclusion: Filtering non-overlapping classes before graph-regularized optimal transport alignment enables accurate, training-free cross-domain single-cell classification.

title: Pragmatic Curiosity: A Unified Framework for Hybrid Learning and Optimization via Active Inference

AI.tldr: Pragmatic Curiosity (PraC) unifies Bayesian optimization and Bayesian experimental design via active inference by trading off latent information gain against expected regret-based outcome potential.
AI.motivation: Sequential decision-making under expensive black-box evaluations often requires both reducing uncertainty and optimizing task performance, yet Bayesian optimization and Bayesian experimental design treat these goals separately.
AI.method: PraC evaluates candidate queries by balancing information gain about a task-relevant latent symbol against an expected regret potential over outcomes, parameterized by latent choice, regret encoding, and exchange strength.
AI.result: Instantiated across decision-oriented monitoring, targeted active search, and composite Bayesian optimization with unknown preferences, PraC reduces downstream decision risk, improves critical-region coverage, and jointly learns predictive and preference structures without task-specific staging rules.
AI.conclusion: Active inference provides a unified, stage-free framework for hybrid learning and optimization across diverse sequential experimental settings.

title: VideoRNG: Relightable Neural Gaussians from Generative Video Models
summary: Generating realistic 3D assets remains constrained by classical representations: surface meshes and compact physically based materials struggle to express objects whose appearance arises from fine geometry or complex light transport, while existing Gaussian-splatting generators typically bake fixed illumination into appearance. We introduce VideoRNG, a two-stage method that generates complete, relightable 3D assets from a text prompt or a single image without prescribing a mesh or analytic material model. A video generator fine-tuned from a pretrained video diffusion backbone first produces a structured RGBA turntable sequence under a known pose, camera, and illumination. A feed-forward large reconstruction model initialized from a pretrained video diffusion backbone then maps the video-VAE latent frames of selected turntable frames directly to millions of anisotropic Gaussians with learned neural appearance features. A shared directional decoder and stochastic Gaussian ray tracer turn this representation, which we call ray-traced Relightable Neural Gaussians (rtRNG), into radiance under novel viewpoints and illumination. To preserve high-frequency appearance while learning geometry, we introduce depth-anchored appearance training, and we make million-Gaussian reconstruction practical through foreground token selection and cost-aware distributed sampling. VideoRNG generates complex assets such as fur, feathers, and spider webs that can be interactively rendered, relit, and integrated into scenes.

AI.tldr: VideoRNG is a two-stage framework that generates complete, relightable 3D assets from text or a single image using ray-traced Relightable Neural Gaussians (rtRNG) without meshes or analytic material models.
AI.motivation: Classical surface meshes and compact physically based materials struggle with fine geometry and complex light transport, while existing Gaussian-splatting generators bake fixed illumination into appearance.
AI.method: A fine-tuned video diffusion generator produces a structured RGBA turntable sequence under known pose, camera, and illumination, and a feed-forward large reconstruction model maps selected video-VAE latent frames to millions of anisotropic Gaussians with neural appearance features, rendered via a shared directional decoder and stochastic Gaussian ray tracer using depth-anchored appearance training, foreground token selection, and cost-aware distributed sampling.
AI.result: VideoRNG generates complex assets such as fur, feathers, and spider webs that can be interactively rendered, relit, and integrated into scenes.
AI.conclusion: Combining generative video priors with ray-traced Relightable Neural Gaussians enables mesh-free, relightable 3D asset generation for complex geometric and optical phenomena.

title: SceneAnything: Agentic Reconstruction of Large-Scale Mesh Scenes from a Single Video
summary: Reconstructing an editable 3D scene from video requires matching visible structure while plausibly completing unseen surfaces. Agents can write scene-construction programs, but direct reconstruction attempts often produce errors in layout, scale, and lighting. We introduce SceneAnything, an automated system for reconstructing mesh scenes from real and generated videos, enabling text-to-scene construction when paired with video generation. A software harness coordinates agents, pretrained vision models, and graphics tools through an explicit reconstruction protocol. Shared camera, depth, and segmentation estimates ground component construction: a scene-owner agent plans the environment and briefs authors, who write parameterized Blender programs. A visibility- and fit-based level-of-detail rule selects the construction level, while unseen regions are completed and marked as inferred. Assembled scenes use fitted lighting and supported motion, and revisions undergo programmatic checks and independent visual comparisons. Accepted programs and lessons are reused across scenes. We evaluate on 100 scenes; subset comparisons show improved original-view fidelity over direct-agent reconstruction and higher novel-view content similarity than the compared video-to-3D methods. We will release the harness, agent instructions, reusable libraries, and scenes.

AI.tldr: SceneAnything is an automated agentic system that reconstructs editable 3D mesh scenes from real or generated videos by coordinating vision models, graphics tools, and Blender-programming agents.
AI.motivation: Reconstructing editable 3D scenes from video requires matching visible structure while plausibly completing unseen surfaces, whereas direct agent reconstruction often produces layout, scale, and lighting errors.
AI.method: A software harness coordinates a scene-owner agent and authoring agents using shared camera, depth, and segmentation estimates to write parameterized Blender programs, applying a visibility- and fit-based level-of-detail rule, marking unseen completions as inferred, fitting lighting and supported motion, and running programmatic checks and independent visual comparisons while reusing accepted programs.
AI.result: Evaluated on 100 scenes, subset comparisons show improved original-view fidelity over direct-agent reconstruction and higher novel-view content similarity than compared video-to-3D methods.
AI.conclusion: Structured multi-agent coordination with shared geometric grounding and reusable Blender libraries improves automated 3D mesh scene reconstruction from video.

title: ContextRenderer: Dynamic-Context Video Generation for Interactive Game Worlds
summary: Interactive game world models separate executable world evolution from visual generation, using video models to render engine-provided scene representations into detailed observations. During sustained gameplay, however, existing generative renderers struggle to follow changing conditions while preserving visual continuity across diverse proxies and target styles. We therefore introduce ContextRenderer, an autoregressive video diffusion framework designed for both dynamic conditioning and cross-proxy generalization. It couples Dynamic-Context Learning (DCL) for chunk-level interaction supervision with Recurrent History Compression (RHC) to follow condition updates while preserving visual continuity within a bounded token budget. Across proxy representations, Cross-Representation Flow Alignment (CRFA) connects proxy reconstruction with appearance and interaction variation through a shared high-fidelity reconstruction. WorldPrism, our interaction-centric dataset constructed from agent-built worlds, AAA gameplay, and open-source videos, supplies the corresponding renderings and chunk-level annotations for these learning tasks. Experiments on GWM-Bench and Solar-Bench show improved reconstruction and visual quality, while qualitative results demonstrate minute-long interactive rendering under changing prompts and subject references. Project page: this https URL

AI.tldr: ContextRenderer is an autoregressive video diffusion framework for interactive game worlds that improves dynamic conditioning and cross-proxy generalization, supported by the new WorldPrism dataset.
AI.motivation: Existing generative renderers for interactive game world models struggle to follow changing conditions while maintaining visual continuity across diverse proxies and target styles during sustained gameplay.
AI.method: ContextRenderer pairs Dynamic-Context Learning (DCL) for chunk-level interaction supervision with Recurrent History Compression (RHC) for bounded-budget continuity, and uses Cross-Representation Flow Alignment (CRFA) to connect proxy reconstruction with appearance and interaction variation, trained on WorldPrism (built from agent-built worlds, AAA gameplay, and open-source videos).
AI.result: Experiments on GWM-Bench and Solar-Bench show improved reconstruction and visual quality, and qualitative results demonstrate minute-long interactive rendering under changing prompts and subject references.
AI.conclusion: Combining dynamic context learning, recurrent history compression, and cross-representation flow alignment enables sustained, controllable generative rendering for interactive game worlds.

title: AGSR: Aperture-Guided Super-Resolution for Gaussian Splatting
comment: Accepted at the 2026 IEEE International Workshop on Multimedia Signal Processing (MMSP 2026). Recipient of the Best Paper Award
summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables real-time novel view synthesis, but Gaussian rasterization attenuates fine-scale scene structure through the projected covariance of each primitive. We show that contracting these projected covariances at inference time can mitigate the effective bandwidth limitation induced by finite Gaussian footprints, motivating a multi-aperture rendering framework for super-resolution. Based on this insight, we propose AGSR (Aperture-Guided Super-Resolution), a lightweight inference-time framework that progressively fuses multi-aperture renderings using uncertainty-guided feature aggregation and geometric conditioning from transmittance and depth cues. AGSR operates as a plug-in enhancement for pre-trained 3DGS models. Experiments on the Mip-NeRF 360 benchmark show that AGSR outperforms lightweight image-space super-resolution baselines, with gains increasing as the underlying Gaussian representation deteriorates. The results provide evidence that covariance contraction exposes bandwidth-sensitive structural cues attenuated by native Gaussian rasterization. AGSR achieves these improvements while maintaining real-time performance with up to 139k parameters.

AI.tldr: AGSR is a lightweight inference-time plug-in super-resolution framework for pre-trained 3D Gaussian Splatting models that contracts projected covariances to recover fine-scale scene structure.
AI.motivation: 3D Gaussian Splatting attenuates fine-scale scene structure because the projected covariance of each primitive acts as a finite-footprint bandwidth limit during rasterization.
AI.method: AGSR contracts projected covariances at inference time and progressively fuses multi-aperture renderings using uncertainty-guided feature aggregation and geometric conditioning from transmittance and depth cues.
AI.result: On the Mip-NeRF 360 benchmark, AGSR outperforms lightweight image-space super-resolution baselines, with larger gains as the underlying Gaussian representation deteriorates, while maintaining real-time performance with up to 139k parameters.
AI.conclusion: Inference-time covariance contraction exposes bandwidth-sensitive structural cues in 3DGS, enabling effective, real-time plug-in super-resolution.

title: FFGaussType: Feed-Forward Conversion of Glyph and SVG Geometry into Compact Gaussian Assets
comment: 20 pages. Project page: this https URL
summary: Immersive 3D content allows text and graphical elements, such as subtitles, annotations, and icons, to be placed inside a scene rather than displayed as flat overlays. Placed this way, they respect occlusion and perspective and take on user-assigned materials and lighting while preserving their original shapes. In Gaussian scenes, however, each new glyph or icon requires its own iterative optimization, which limits scalable content creation. We present FFGaussType, which converts extruded glyph and SVG outlines into Gaussian assets in a single forward pass. A point encoder maps anchors sampled on the known surface to a single feature plane, from which a decoder shared by all assets predicts neural Gaussians carrying surface normals. This separates geometric conversion from material and lighting choices, and the feature plane supports image and video coding for compact delivery. We construct a paired dataset of 27,221 glyph and SVG icon assets with anchors and calibrated normal and silhouette renderings, holding out font families for evaluation. Conversion from prepared anchors takes 9.1 ms per asset, at a fraction of the compute and memory of prior baselines. On unseen font families and test icons, FFGaussType achieves $1.62^\circ$ normal error and $0.985$ silhouette IoU, the best among the compared feed-forward converters, matching the fidelity that per-asset fitting needs thousands of steps to reach. The code and dataset will be released after publication.

AI.tldr: FFGaussType is a feed-forward method that converts extruded glyph and SVG outlines into compact neural Gaussian assets carrying surface normals in a single forward pass.
AI.motivation: Placing 3D text and graphical elements in Gaussian scenes previously required per-asset iterative optimization, limiting scalable content creation.
AI.method: A point encoder maps surface-sampled anchors to a single feature plane, from which a shared decoder predicts neural Gaussians with surface normals, decoupling geometry conversion from material and lighting while supporting image and video coding of the feature plane.
AI.result: Evaluated on a newly constructed dataset of 27,221 glyph and SVG icon assets with held-out font families, FFGaussType takes 9.1 ms per asset from prepared anchors and achieves 1.62 degrees normal error and 0.985 silhouette IoU on unseen fonts and test icons, outperforming compared feed-forward converters and matching per-asset fitting.
AI.conclusion: Single-pass feed-forward conversion onto a compact feature plane makes scalable, relightable 3D glyph and SVG asset creation practical for Gaussian scenes.

title: A Tutorial on Complementarity-Based Contact Models for Robotics
summary: Simulating rigid-body dynamics with contact is fundamental to robotics, from motion synthesis and control to mechanism design. Many widely used simulators rely on cone complementarity formulations, whose physical assumptions and numerical solution require substantial background. While excellent surveys, monographs, and course notes exist, they mostly address computational mechanics or computer graphics or document a single simulator. To the best of our knowledge, a self-contained pedagogical treatment for robotics, bringing these formulations and their solvers together with complete derivations and a unified notation, does not yet exist. This tutorial addresses this gap by connecting rigid-body dynamics, conic optimization, and frictional contact. In particular, we explain how complementarity conditions encode non-penetration and frictional dissipation, determining separation, sticking, and sliding without prescribed contact modes. We distinguish equivalent transcriptions from convex relaxations, showing how the latter can introduce artifacts such as lift-off and creep. We examine the existence and uniqueness of motion and contact forces, including the solver's role in selecting among multiple solutions. We then compare first-order and Newton-based methods, explain regularization and proximal strategies, and discuss trade-offs between computational cost, robustness, and physical fidelity. Connections to widely used simulators, optimal control, and differentiable simulation help readers interpret simulation results, choose suitable formulations and solvers, and develop their own contact dynamics routines.

AI.tldr: This tutorial provides a self-contained pedagogical treatment of complementarity-based contact models and their numerical solvers for rigid-body robotics simulation.
AI.motivation: Widely used robotics simulators rely on cone complementarity formulations, but existing literature is scattered across computational mechanics, computer graphics, or single-simulator documentation without a unified robotics-focused treatment.
AI.method: The tutorial connects rigid-body dynamics, conic optimization, and frictional contact, explaining complementarity conditions for non-penetration and friction, distinguishing equivalent transcriptions from convex relaxations (and artifacts like lift-off and creep), analyzing solution existence and uniqueness, and comparing first-order and Newton-based solvers with regularization and proximal strategies.
AI.result: It links these formulations and solver trade-offs directly to widely used simulators, optimal control, and differentiable simulation.
AI.conclusion: The unified notation and derivations equip robotics researchers and engineers to interpret simulation behavior, select appropriate contact models and solvers, and implement custom contact dynamics routines.

title: LLM Complexity: Towards a Computational Complexity View of Large Language Model Inference
summary: Computational complexity theory offers a principled framework for characterizing the efficiency of computational problems, and Large Language Models (LLMs) can similarly be viewed as computational systems executing a structured process of input, inference-time compute, and output. In this context, the number of generated tokens emerges as a natural and directly observable proxy for inference-time compute. However, we show that the tempting analogy between LLM token length and classical time complexity does not hold. We disprove the hypothesis that inference-time token usage aligns monotonically with classical time complexity, demonstrating a fundamental divergence grounded in how LLMs actually allocate computation during inference. To this end, we introduce LLM Complexity, a new metric designed to quantify problem complexity from the perspective of LLMs by characterizing the area bounded above by the accuracy-token curve. We find that diverse LLMs induce highly consistent task rankings under LLM Complexity, indicating that the metric captures stable notions of difficulty across models. We leverage this property to construct an easy-to-hard curriculum for supervised fine-tuning, which improves accuracy while reducing token consumption. Finally, we demonstrate that LLM Complexity generalizes to real-world tasks, producing more stable cross-model correlations than human-annotated difficulty labels.

AI.tldr: This paper disproves the monotonic alignment between LLM inference token length and classical time complexity, and introduces LLM Complexity to quantify problem difficulty from an LLM's perspective.
AI.motivation: Generated token count is often treated as a proxy for inference-time compute analogous to classical time complexity, but it is unclear whether this analogy holds for how LLMs actually allocate computation.
AI.method: The authors introduce LLM Complexity, defined as the area bounded above by the accuracy-token curve, and use it to rank tasks and construct an easy-to-hard curriculum for supervised fine-tuning.
AI.result: Diverse LLMs induce highly consistent task rankings under LLM Complexity, the easy-to-hard curriculum improves accuracy while reducing token consumption, and LLM Complexity yields more stable cross-model correlations on real-world tasks than human-annotated difficulty labels.
AI.conclusion: LLM Complexity captures model-consistent problem difficulty better than token length or human labels, offering a principled basis for curriculum design and inference-compute analysis.

title: ICARE: cross-domain text classification with incremental class-aware representation and distillation learning
summary: The rise of powerful, fine-tuned large language models (LLMs) necessitates robust natural language inference (NLI) systems. These NLI systems ideally train across various tasks, encompassing diverse concepts like sentiment analysis, news classification, and coreference resolution. However, this continual, multi-tasking approach can lead to catastrophic forgetting, where previously learned tasks are lost, especially in domains lacking specific labels. Rehearsing past examples with labels can further exacerbate this issue by causing overfitting, hindering the system's ability to classify new categories. To tackle these challenges, this research proposes ICARE, a novel framework with two key components: an instance selection module and a knowledge distillation method. The former is based on representation learning, which meticulously selects training examples to present to the NLI system. The latter, knowledge distillation with feature and logit-level transfer, facilitates knowledge transfer between tasks. This leverages pruning techniques and optimized objective functions to transfer both essential feature-level and decision-making (logit-level) knowledge, mitigating catastrophic forgetting while adapting to new patterns. Extensive evaluations on benchmark text classification datasets have demonstrated ICARE's effectiveness. The framework achieves a significant improvement in target accuracy and reduction in the ``forgetting metric''. These results solidify ICARE's ability to preserve and leverage learned knowledge across diverse tasks, ultimately enhancing the adaptability and performance of NLI systems. The source code is available at this https URL

AI.tldr: ICARE is a continual cross-domain text classification framework that mitigates catastrophic forgetting in natural language inference systems using representation-based instance selection and dual-level knowledge distillation.
AI.motivation: Continual multi-task training of fine-tuned LLMs for natural language inference causes catastrophic forgetting, while rehearsing labeled past examples can cause overfitting and hinder adaptation to new categories.
AI.method: ICARE combines a representation-learning instance selection module to choose training examples with a knowledge distillation method using pruning and optimized objectives to transfer both feature-level and decision-making (logit-level) knowledge across tasks.
AI.result: Extensive evaluations on benchmark text classification datasets show that ICARE significantly improves target accuracy and reduces the forgetting metric compared to baselines.
AI.conclusion: Pairing selective representation-based rehearsal with feature- and logit-level distillation enables NLI systems to adapt to new domains while preserving prior task knowledge.

title: TETHER: Training-Free, Elastic, ToC-Anchored Hierarchy Extraction and Recovery in Design-Driven Long Documents
summary: Converting complex documents into structured knowledge constitutes the critical infrastructure urgently required for deploying Large Language Models (LLMs) in downstream research. However, blind to the Table of Contents (ToC) as a macro-structure, existing bottom-up paradigms rely on localized visual cues, inducing heuristic fragility in high-entropy layouts where visual prominence decouples from logical depth; meanwhile, direct LLM extraction lacks spatial grounding, triggering hallucinations in long contexts. To address this, we introduce TETHER, a training-free framework that elevates the ToC from discarded noise to a vital structural prior, enabling robust adaptation across design-driven long documents. TETHER operates via a two-stage neuro-symbolic mechanism: first, it constructs a document skeleton from the raw ToC using a Large Multimodal Model (LMM) empowered by spatio-semantic constraints; second, it employs an anchor-based alignment strategy to tether content blocks to this skeleton, effectively resolving boundary ambiguities. Evaluated across a multilingual benchmark of ESG reports, product manuals, and annual reports, TETHER delivers highly precise, state-of-the-art (SOTA) zero-shot hierarchy recovery, outperforming deep hierarchical recovery models, dedicated parsers, and general-purpose LMMs. Moreover, stress tests highlight TETHER's resilience to sparse omissions and textual noise, demonstrating that its precise semantic alignment is fundamentally anchored in topological and depth fidelity. Crucially, ablations confirm the framework's architectural irreducibility, while achieving 90% token reduction and drastic speedups over end-to-end baselines, establishing a compelling equilibrium between structural precision and deployment scalability.

AI.tldr: TETHER is a training-free, two-stage neuro-symbolic framework that uses a document's Table of Contents (ToC) as a structural prior to recover hierarchies in design-driven long documents.
AI.motivation: Existing bottom-up document parsers rely on localized visual cues that fail in high-entropy layouts where visual prominence decouples from logical depth, while direct LLM extraction lacks spatial grounding and hallucinates in long contexts.
AI.method: TETHER first constructs a document skeleton from the raw ToC using a Large Multimodal Model with spatio-semantic constraints, and then uses an anchor-based alignment strategy to tether content blocks to the skeleton.
AI.result: Across a multilingual benchmark of ESG reports, product manuals, and annual reports, TETHER achieves state-of-the-art zero-shot hierarchy recovery, outperforming deep hierarchical models, dedicated parsers, and general-purpose LMMs while reducing token usage by 90% and remaining resilient to omissions and noise.
AI.conclusion: Elevating the ToC to a structural prior enables accurate, scalable, and training-free hierarchy extraction for complex long documents.

title: Physics of Language Models: Part 4.2, Canon Layers at Scale where Synthetic Pretraining Resonates in Reality
comment: Results, recipes, and code have been public since December 9, 2025 at this https URL
summary: Do standard benchmarks see the architectural differences that matter? We study it with 64 from-scratch pretraining runs of Transformers and three linear-model families at 1.3-8B parameters on 1-2T Nemotron-CC tokens, at a cost of roughly 100k USD per 8B run. In academic-scale pretraining (1.3B parameters, 100B tokens), architectural differences can all but disappear when the models are carefully tuned. Instead, at 1-2T tokens they become measurable: Canon layers, which add local token mixing, consistently improve Transformers, saving about 30% of pretraining tokens for the same MMLU accuracy at 8B. We also introduce GLA5 and GDN2, which improve gated linear attention and Gated DeltaNet with low-rank output gates. Surprisingly, with Canon, the simplest linear model, gated linear attention, matches Gated DeltaNet and outperforms Mamba2 even at 8B/1T. Therefore, the extra machinery of Gated DeltaNet and Mamba2 may do little more than mix neighboring tokens. Even at 8B/1T, however, high scores on standard benchmarks can hide weaknesses in basic in-context skills. In particular, linear models that match or beat Transformers on these benchmarks cannot, in fact, reliably retrieve information from a short 500-token context. Moreover, no model, Transformer or linear, reliably beats random guessing on arguably the simplest two-hop question, stated in a few short sentences, even at this scale. These findings $\textbf{challenge traditional architecture research}$ based primarily on standard benchmark scores. In contrast, small synthetic playgrounds, which predicted the architectural differences above at <100M parameters, can reveal what these benchmarks miss. For practitioners, one lesson is to include in-context reasoning examples in pretraining data from an early stage, rather than reserve them for later mid-training, let alone post-training.

AI.tldr: Large-scale pretraining experiments (1.3B-8B parameters, 1-2T tokens) show that Canon layers consistently improve Transformers and linear models, while standard benchmarks mask severe weaknesses in basic in-context retrieval and two-hop reasoning.
AI.motivation: Carefully tuned academic-scale pretraining (1.3B parameters, 100B tokens) can obscure architectural differences, raising the question of whether standard benchmarks capture differences that matter at scale.
AI.method: The authors conduct 64 from-scratch pretraining runs of Transformers and three linear-model families (including new GLA5 and GDN2 variants with low-rank output gates, plus Canon layers for local token mixing) at 1.3-8B parameters on 1-2T Nemotron-CC tokens, and compare findings against <100M-parameter synthetic playgrounds.
AI.result: At 8B/1-2T, Canon layers save about 30% of pretraining tokens for the same MMLU accuracy in Transformers and allow gated linear attention to match Gated DeltaNet and outperform Mamba2; however, linear models fail to reliably retrieve from a 500-token context and no model beats random guessing on a simple two-hop question.
AI.conclusion: Standard benchmarks miss critical in-context reasoning deficits that small synthetic playgrounds successfully predict, suggesting practitioners should include in-context reasoning examples early in pretraining.

title: Global Importance Estimation for KV Cache Eviction
comment: The 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026)
summary: Memory consumption of the key-value (KV) cache remains a central bottleneck for long-context LLM inference. We introduce PRKV, a training-free KV eviction method that estimates multi-hop global token importance by applying Personalized PageRank over attention-induced transition graphs. This enables importance propagation beyond recency or instantaneous attention, without modifying the model. We benchmark PRKV on long-context understanding, sparse retrieval, and chain-of-thought reasoning tasks using multiple LLM families. Under moderate to aggressive compression ratios, including up to 90%, PRKV achieves competitive task performance against established eviction baselines while reducing peak memory usage with low end-to-end overhead. These results demonstrate that multi-hop global influence estimation yields a favorable accuracy--memory trade-off for scalable long-context inference.

AI.tldr: PRKV is a training-free KV cache eviction method that applies Personalized PageRank over attention-induced transition graphs to estimate multi-hop global token importance.
AI.motivation: KV cache memory consumption is a major bottleneck for long-context LLM inference, and existing eviction methods rely on recency or instantaneous attention rather than global multi-hop importance.
AI.method: PRKV constructs attention-induced transition graphs and runs Personalized PageRank to propagate importance across tokens without modifying the underlying model.
AI.result: Across long-context understanding, sparse retrieval, and chain-of-thought reasoning benchmarks on multiple LLM families, PRKV achieves competitive accuracy against established eviction baselines under up to 90% compression while reducing peak memory usage with low end-to-end overhead.
AI.conclusion: Multi-hop global influence estimation via Personalized PageRank offers an effective, training-free accuracy-memory trade-off for scalable long-context inference.

title: HireWatch: Evaluating LLM Compliance with U.S. Employment Law Under Contextual Pressure
comment: NeurIPS 2026 Evaluation and Dataset Track. Law and AI
summary: The deployment of large language models (LLMs) in hiring pipelines is growing, yet existing evaluations generally overlook their compliance with legal rules. To fill this gap, we introduce HireWatch, an evaluation that assesses whether LLMs comply with U.S. laws that govern the questions that job candidates may be asked. We construct a 200-item bank of lawful and unlawful interview questions, whose legal classification is based on U.S. federal statutes, regulations, and agency guidance. We instruct LLMs to select questions from this bank in preparing for job interviews, across a set of various occupations and contexts, and report the fraction of unlawful questions that LLMs select. Evaluation of 18 closed and open-weight LLMs across ~100,000 trials under different types of contextual pressure reveals that LLMs' legal compliance is brittle. While LLMs generally avoid selecting unlawful questions in low-pressure contexts, legal violations increase sharply under higher pressure. Explicit prompts to comply with law can improve compliance rates, but do not altogether eliminate legal violations. We publicly release our code and data at this https URL.

AI.tldr: HireWatch is a 200-item evaluation benchmark assessing whether LLMs comply with U.S. employment law when selecting job interview questions under varying contextual pressures.
AI.motivation: Despite growing LLM deployment in hiring pipelines, existing evaluations largely overlook whether models comply with legal restrictions on interview questions.
AI.method: The authors construct a 200-item bank of lawful and unlawful interview questions grounded in U.S. federal statutes, regulations, and agency guidance, and evaluate 18 closed and open-weight LLMs across roughly 100,000 trials under different occupations and contextual pressures.
AI.result: While LLMs generally avoid unlawful questions in low-pressure contexts, legal violations increase sharply under higher contextual pressure, and explicit compliance prompts improve but do not eliminate violations.
AI.conclusion: LLM legal compliance in hiring is brittle under pressure, underscoring the need for stronger safeguards beyond prompting before deploying LLMs in employment workflows.

title: The ROI of Small Examples: Optimizing In-Context Learning Under Token Budgets
summary: In-context learning (ICL) improves large language model performance at inference time without updating model parameters. However, these gains are not free: in practical deployments, longer prompts directly increase inference cost and latency. Under a fixed token budget, prompt construction therefore becomes a resource-allocation problem. While prior work has often focused on how many examples to include in ICL, we study the complementary question of whether the available budget is better spent on a few long demonstrations or on a larger number of shorter ones. We study this aspect in question answering (QA), by organizing candidate demonstrations into length-based bins and constructing prompts from examples within the same length range under fixed budgets. Experiments on two QA benchmarks (\textit{Beat the AI} and \textit{Natural Questions}), using six instruction-tuned LLMs, show that shorter demonstrations are generally the most effective use of prompt space. This effect is especially strong on \textit{Beat the AI}, and remains visible on NQ, although gains are smaller and saturate earlier in the long-context setting. An additional natural language inference experiment on ANLI R3 finds that one of the two shorter bins performs best for five of six models, although longer demonstrations remain competitive. Overall, our results highlight demonstration granularity as an important factor in prompt design.

AI.tldr: Under fixed token budgets for in-context learning, allocating budget to a larger number of shorter demonstrations generally outperforms using a few long demonstrations.
AI.motivation: Longer prompts increase inference cost and latency, turning in-context learning (ICL) prompt construction under a fixed token budget into a resource-allocation problem between demonstration length and quantity.
AI.method: The authors bin candidate demonstrations by length and construct fixed-budget prompts from examples within the same length range, evaluating six instruction-tuned LLMs on two QA benchmarks (Beat the AI and Natural Questions) and an NLI task (ANLI R3).
AI.result: Shorter demonstrations are generally most effective on Beat the AI and Natural Questions (though gains saturate earlier in long-context NQ), and one of the two shorter bins performs best for five of six models on ANLI R3.
AI.conclusion: Demonstration granularity is a key factor in budget-constrained prompt design, favoring more, shorter examples over fewer, longer ones.

title: No-Harm-Jury A Jury-Based Multi-Dimensional Harm Evaluation Framework for Medical AI Responses
summary: We present No-Harm-Jury, a jury-based automated evaluation framework that scores AI-generated medical responses across seven conceptually distinct harm dimensions using a panel of five diverse language models as independent jurors. Responses generated by Ministral-14B on 3,000 questions drawn from PubMedQA, MedQA, and MedMCQA are scored by five jurors across dimensions of informational, social, psychological, autonomy, economic, privacy, and epistemic harm; the 151 empty responses (98 MedQA, 53 MedM- CQA) are excluded, leaving 2,849 valid samples. The median aggregation robustly suppresses individual juror biases while maintaining coverage through complementary specialisation. No existing system combines all five prop- erties of No-Harm-Jury: automated scalable evaluation, five diverse LLM jurors, robust me- dian aggregation (with a reliability-weighted extension), seven conceptually distinct harm dimensions, and application to medical QA benchmarks.

AI.tldr: No-Harm-Jury is an automated evaluation framework that uses a panel of five diverse LLM jurors and median aggregation to score medical AI responses across seven harm dimensions.
AI.motivation: Automated evaluation of medical AI responses needs scalable, multi-dimensional harm assessment that mitigates individual LLM judge biases.
AI.method: Five diverse language models independently score Ministral-14B responses on 3,000 questions from PubMedQA, MedQA, and MedMCQA (2,849 valid after excluding 151 empty responses) across informational, social, psychological, autonomy, economic, privacy, and epistemic harm, using median (and reliability-weighted) aggregation.
AI.result: Median aggregation suppresses individual juror biases while preserving coverage across the seven harm dimensions through complementary juror specialization.
AI.conclusion: No-Harm-Jury provides a scalable, bias-mitigated framework for multi-dimensional harm evaluation of medical QA systems.

title: CANDID: Candidate-Driven Intervention for Disciplined Execution in Local Computer-Use Agents
summary: We present CANDID (Candidate-Driven Intervention for Disciplined Execution), an execution-control framework designed to enhance the reliability of local computer-use agents (CUAs) in resource-constrained settings. While local CUAs feature robust baseline proficiency in single-step action prediction, they frequently fail at critical junctions due to rigid action loops or premature DONE decisions. Rather than imposing imprecise cognitive loads through textual reflection, CANDID repurposes parallel test-time scaling into a disciplined, execution-level intervention at sparse, failure-prone points. We introduce a loop-recovery mechanism to filter candidates away from repeated behaviors and a conservative, unanimous DONE gating policy that requires absolute consensus to terminate. Experiments on OSWorld demonstrate that CANDID's structural control significantly improves success rates, outperforming feedback-based alternatives with minimal execution overhead.

AI.tldr: CANDID is an execution-control framework that improves the reliability of local computer-use agents (CUAs) by using parallel test-time scaling at failure-prone steps with loop recovery and unanimous DONE gating.
AI.motivation: Local CUAs perform well on single-step actions but frequently fail in resource-constrained settings due to rigid action loops or premature DONE decisions, while textual reflection adds imprecise cognitive load.
AI.method: CANDID applies parallel test-time scaling at sparse, failure-prone points, using a loop-recovery mechanism to filter out repeated-behavior candidates and a unanimous DONE gating policy requiring consensus to terminate.
AI.result: Experiments on OSWorld show that CANDID's structural control significantly improves task success rates, outperforming feedback-based alternatives with minimal execution overhead.
AI.conclusion: Execution-level candidate filtering and consensus termination provide a lightweight, effective way to stabilize local computer-use agents.

title: Quantifying Cultural-Psychological Constructs in Four Centuries of Ottoman Court Registers
summary: Populations vary along cultural dimensions such as individualism, collectivism, and honor. But how can these dimensions be studied in historical societies for which conventional psychological data are unavailable? Here, we introduce a computational text-analytic framework for quantifying psychological constructs in 54,670 Ottoman Turkish court records from 21 Istanbul courts spanning 1513-1911 CE. We develop sentence-embedding models adapted to Ottoman legal language and extend a theory-driven, text-analytic pipeline to capture cultural variation along the dimensions of individualism, collectivism, and honor in this historical corpus. We evaluate our models through multiple methods: document retrieval, semantic textual similarity, questionnaire-item classification, and validation against expert annotations. Our adapted sentence transformer (OTA-BERTurk) achieved a Recall@1 of .843 on the test set for document retrieval, a Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR) of .806 for semantic textual similarity (meaning the best answer usually appeared as a top result), and classified questionnaire items with 89.58\% accuracy. Document-level performance varied across constructs and methods. Qualitative analysis further showed that high scores reflected historically specific legal and institutional patterns. We publicly release the models, construct representations, scoring pipeline, as well as an interactive web interface to support transparent, reproducible historical-psychological analyses of Ottoman Turkish court records spanning approximately four centuries. These computational tools enable the study of psychological variation across centuries of cultural and institutional change in a diverse empire.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a computational text-analytic framework and an adapted sentence transformer (OTA-BERTurk) to quantify individualism, collectivism, and honor across 54,670 Ottoman Turkish court records from 1513-1911 CE.
AI.motivation: Conventional psychological data are unavailable for historical societies, making it difficult to study cultural-psychological variation over centuries.
AI.method: The authors adapt sentence-embedding models to Ottoman legal language (OTA-BERTurk) and extend a theory-driven text-analytic pipeline to score 54,670 Istanbul court records (1513-1911 CE), validating via document retrieval, semantic textual similarity, questionnaire-item classification, and expert annotations.
AI.result: OTA-BERTurk achieves 0.843 Recall@1 on document retrieval, 0.806 MRR on semantic textual similarity, and 89.58% accuracy on questionnaire-item classification, with qualitative analysis linking high scores to specific legal and institutional patterns.
AI.conclusion: The released models, pipeline, and web interface enable transparent, reproducible historical-psychological analysis across four centuries of Ottoman records.

title: What the model knows but does not say: monitoring medical LLMs through verbalized thoughts
summary: Efforts to keep clinical language models safe have concentrated on what enters and leaves the model, but a manipulated model can return an answer that looks entirely ordinary. Here we show that the model's own internal state, rendered in plain language, exposes manipulations the output conceals. Using a natural-language autoencoder, we translate the activations of a multimodal LLM (Gemma-3-27B) into text and let an input-blind judge read this verbalized internal state (the thoughts channel) and the model's answer separately. Across two clinical attack objectives (omitting a pathology, covertly recommending a drug), two input modalities, and two delivery mechanisms, the thoughts channel caught the injection significantly more often than the answer in all eight injected conditions (p<0.05), while both channels held near-zero false-positive rates on clean inputs; the omission result carried over to Llama-3.3-70B. The thoughts channel also registered unsafe clinical requests as harmful while the model was still reading them, before it decided whether to refuse. None of this requires retraining: an off-the-shelf verbalizer and a general-purpose judge are enough.

AI.tldr: Translating a medical LLM's internal activations into plain-language verbalized thoughts exposes covert prompt injections and unsafe requests that are concealed in the model's final output.
AI.motivation: Clinical LLM safety efforts focus on inputs and outputs, but manipulated models can produce ordinary-looking answers that hide covert attacks such as omitting a pathology or recommending a drug.
AI.method: Using an off-the-shelf natural-language autoencoder, the authors translate activations of Gemma-3-27B (and Llama-3.3-70B for omission) into a plain-language thoughts channel and have an input-blind judge inspect the thoughts channel and final answer separately across two attack objectives, two modalities, and two delivery mechanisms.
AI.result: The thoughts channel detected injections significantly more often than the final answer in all eight injected conditions (p < 0.05) with near-zero false positives on clean inputs, and also flagged unsafe clinical requests as harmful before the model decided whether to refuse.
AI.conclusion: Monitoring verbalized internal activations without retraining provides a stronger, earlier signal for detecting covert manipulation in medical LLMs than output monitoring alone.

title: FinVeriQA: Financial Research Agents for Question Answering: Routing, Retrieval, MCP Tool Use, and Provenance-Aware Evidence Verification
comment: 15 pages, 4 figures, 11 tables. Code: this https URL
summary: Large language models (LLMs) write fluent financial analyses but miscompute ratios, recall stale prices, and route questions to the wrong tool with high confidence. We ask which component should do each job in a financial question-answering assistant, and study it with FinVeriQA, an open-source multi-agent research prototype over SEC filings and live market data: a compact typed-decision model (Laya) routes each question and screens out advice requests, Python computes every number, retrieval and tools fetch evidence, Mistral-7B writes a cited answer, a code validator checks that cited IDs exist and that numbers match computed notes, and a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server exposes the pipeline. In live experiments, Laya routed better than Mistral-7B (0.85 vs. 0.52; overall 0.86 vs. 0.68, McNemar p = 0.0003); a 12B Mistral decided no better, and DeepSeek-R1-8B decided better (0.79 vs. 0.68, p = 0.0192) but about 9.9 times more slowly. Mistral-7B computed 29% of 100 financial calculations correctly against 100% for Python, a live quote cut price error from 210% to 0.00%, and hybrid retrieval reached 76% Hit@5 on 50 filing questions. Yet in a live case study, both agent answers passed validation while describing AMD sample data under NVIDIA's and Alphabet's names. A controlled upper-bound study on the FinRank benchmark explains why: when one figure in the shared evidence is corrupted, self-consistency stays confident (agreement 0.55 to 0.59 while accuracy falls from 0.50 to 0.00), and a shared-evidence check (the kind our validator performs) catches 35% of the errors, whereas a check against the original passage catches 77% ($p = 5.96 \times 10^{-8}$); for DeepSeek-R1-8B, 68% vs. 90%. Verification must be independent of the evidence the writer saw.

AI.tldr: FinVeriQA is an open-source multi-agent financial QA prototype that separates routing, Python computation, retrieval, and citation validation, revealing that verification must be independent of the writer's shared evidence.
AI.motivation: LLMs write fluent financial analyses but frequently miscompute ratios, recall stale prices, and misroute queries, raising the question of which component should handle each role.
AI.method: FinVeriQA uses a compact typed-decision model (Laya) for routing, Python for all calculations, retrieval/tools for SEC filings and live quotes, Mistral-7B for cited answer generation, and a code validator over an MCP server; a controlled upper-bound study on FinRank tests shared-evidence versus original-passage verification.
AI.result: Laya outperformed Mistral-7B in routing (0.86 vs. 0.68 overall, p = 0.0003) and was ~9.9x faster than DeepSeek-R1-8B; Python achieved 100% calculation accuracy vs. 29% for Mistral-7B, and live quotes cut price error from 210% to 0.00%. However, on FinRank with corrupted shared evidence, shared-evidence checking caught only 35% of errors vs. 77% against the original passage (p = 5.96e-8; 68% vs. 90% for DeepSeek-R1-8B).
AI.conclusion: Decoupling computation and routing from the LLM improves financial QA accuracy, but reliable verification requires checking against original source passages rather than the writer's shared evidence.

title: Forget Freely, Grep Later: Lossless, Index-Free Memory for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
comment: 17 pages, 6 figures, 6 tables. Ziyan Yang and Taiwei Shi contributed equally
summary: Long-horizon LLM agents often exceed their context windows, forcing them to discard information that may be needed later. Existing context management strategies rely on summarization, masking, or structured memory, requiring decisions about what to preserve or how to retrieve it before future needs are known. However, these methods can introduce lossy compression, potentially discarding details needed for future tasks. To address this limitation, we introduce GrepMem, a simple, lossless, and index-free memory mechanism built on two components: an append-only plain-text log of the agent's complete history and a regular-expression search tool for on-demand recall. Unlike structured memory systems, GrepMem requires no embeddings, retrieval index, memory extraction, or additional models. We train Qwen3.5-9B with reinforcement learning under five context management strategies and evaluate on multi-question research sessions, long-stream recall, and agent-trajectory question answering. GrepMem achieves 95-97% accuracy on ContextBench, versus at most 21% for lossy baselines, and outperforms SUPO's summarization by 8.8 percentage points on BCP-Multi. GrepMem scales effectively to increasingly long input streams while remaining on the accuracy-token-cost Pareto frontier across all five evaluation tasks. Our results show that a plain-text log and grep provide a simple but competitive approach to long-horizon agent memory, without requiring complex structured memory infrastructure.

AI.tldr: GrepMem is a lossless, index-free memory mechanism for long-horizon LLM agents that pairs an append-only plain-text history log with regular-expression search for on-demand recall.
AI.motivation: Existing long-horizon context management methods rely on summarization, masking, or structured memory, which require premature decisions about what to keep and introduce lossy compression.
AI.method: GrepMem stores the agent's complete history in an append-only plain-text log and provides a regex search tool for on-demand recall without embeddings, retrieval indices, or extra models, trained with reinforcement learning on Qwen3.5-9B.
AI.result: On ContextBench, GrepMem achieves 95-97% accuracy compared to at most 21% for lossy baselines, outperforms SUPO summarization by 8.8 percentage points on BCP-Multi, and stays on the accuracy-token-cost Pareto frontier across all five evaluation tasks.
AI.conclusion: A simple plain-text log with regex search provides a competitive, lossless alternative to complex structured memory systems for long-horizon agents.

title: Blind Spots Travel, Knowledge Stays Home: What RL Inherits from an LLM Judge
comment: 31 pages, 6 figures, 27 tables. Code and data: this https URL
summary: LLM judges serve as rewards where no answer key exists, in the hope that their knowledge passes to the trained model. In 814 RL runs that teach 7-8B models to answer closed-book questions or abstain, we ask what passes. What a grader knows about single answers stays home. A wrong answer that a judge rewards is memorised for that one question. A model trained with the answer key, or with a far stronger judge, chooses which new questions to answer no better than the untrained model does by sampling 32 answers and abstaining where they disagree; the grader's knowledge adds about one corrected answer per hundred questions. What a grader believes about a kind of question travels.
