A judge that rejects eleven of the twelve correct training answers about capitals of former states teaches the model to refuse 98% of such capitals on new questions, a loss that accuracy and abstention rates do not reveal. Changing only those twelve verdicts by hand moves the refusal from 5% to 90%, even for a grader that accepts as many answers as the answer key; at that leniency, two of four judges already cost 38-42% of these capitals. The capitals are not forgotten: with "I don't know" blocked, the model answers 94% of them correctly. The grader therefore needs no knowledge of its own: rewarding the model for giving the answer that most of its own untrained samples agree on, with no labels and no judge, earns the answer key's reward and keeps the category.

AI.tldr: Across 814 RL runs on 7-8B models, LLM judges transfer their category-level blind spots rather than single-answer knowledge, whereas self-consistency over the untrained model's own samples matches the answer key without a judge.
AI.motivation: LLM judges are used as reward signals when no answer key exists, under the assumption that the judge's knowledge transfers to the trained policy.
AI.method: The authors run 814 RL experiments teaching 7-8B models to answer or abstain on closed-book questions, comparing answer-key rewards, strong LLM judges, and an untrained self-consistency reward, and testing targeted verdict flips on capitals of former states.
AI.result: Judge knowledge on single answers adds only ~1 corrected answer per 100 questions, whereas a judge rejecting 11 of 12 training answers on former-state capitals causes the model to refuse 98% of new such capitals (despite answering 94% correctly when abstention is blocked); rewarding self-consistency over 32 untrained samples matches the answer key's reward and preserves the category.
AI.conclusion: RL inherits category-level biases from LLM judges rather than factual knowledge, making label-free self-consistency a safer reward signal for closed-book abstention.

title: When Objectives and Evaluators Disagree: Evaluating Transfer for Post-hoc Demographic Framing Mitigation
summary: Post-hoc rewriting is used to reduce demographic disparities in LLM-generated text when the source model is inaccessible. A rewrite can look successful merely because it improved its own target or satisfied its selector. We study this as a transfer problem on 660 gender pairs and 1,980 age contrasts of demographic-conditioned climate messages. A rewriter proposes edits, a selection model chooses among constraint-satisfying candidates, and an independent evaluator uninvolved in either rates pairwise framing disparity. A fixed policy that always targets the message with the lower Persuasion Bias Index (PBI) transfers inconsistently across axes and outcome aggregations. An adaptive policy that proposes edits on both sides but accepts at most one significantly improves on that rule, applied to the same candidates, in seven of eight comparisons across two evaluator families, mostly by editing more pairs, not by guided direction choice, at higher preservation risk. A policy editing both messages gives the largest point reductions on fewer pairs. These two policies reduce disparity across a preservation-threshold sweep; absolute ratings vary across evaluator families and prompts. Shrinking the PBI gap increases dimension-mean disparity under both evaluator families. Mitigation should be reported as transfer across objectives, evaluators and their prompts, and editing policies.

AI.tldr: Studying post-hoc demographic framing mitigation as a transfer problem shows that adaptive and dual-side editing policies outperform fixed rules, while shrinking Persuasion Bias Index (PBI) gaps can increase dimension-mean disparity.
AI.motivation: Post-hoc rewriting to reduce demographic disparities in LLM text can appear successful simply because it satisfies its own target or selector, without transferring to independent evaluators.
AI.method: Using 660 gender pairs and 1,980 age contrasts of climate messages, a rewriter and selection model are evaluated by an independent evaluator across a fixed policy (targeting lower PBI), an adaptive single-side policy, and a both-sides policy.
AI.result: The adaptive policy significantly outperforms the fixed policy in 7 of 8 comparisons across two evaluator families (mostly by editing more pairs), while editing both messages yields the largest point reductions on fewer pairs; however, shrinking the PBI gap increases dimension-mean disparity under both evaluator families.
AI.conclusion: Post-hoc framing mitigation should be evaluated and reported as transfer across objectives, evaluators, prompts, and editing policies rather than single-metric gains.

title: LLMs Are Already Confidence-Aware Zero-Shot Classifiers
comment: 20 pages (9 pages main content), 2 figures. Code available at: this https URL
summary: Zero-shot large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as text classifiers, but their labels are only useful when we know to what extent we can trust them. We compare black-box methods (verbalised confidence and sampling) with white-box methods that read token probabilities (P(True), and multiple logit-scoring methods using constrained generation). We evaluate eleven open-weight LLMs (1B-32B parameters) on five classification datasets with 3 to 151 labels, measuring classification performance (accuracy, F1-macro), discrimination (AUROC), and calibration (ECE and Brier score). The choice of confidence method rarely impacts accuracy significantly, but logit-based scoring methods lead to much better discrimination (AUROC 0.74-0.77) than black-box methods (AUROC 0.57-0.66). Replacing labels with single-token identifiers preserves discrimination but costs 3-6 accuracy points on average. We also introduce decision-only scoring, which only scores positions where labels diverge in the prefix tree (trie). It reduces decode steps by 88-96% on the three largest label sets and performs comparably to full-label scoring. The best open-weight model-method configurations (Gemma 4 31B and Qwen 3.5 9B) are competitive with the commercial Jev 1.13.0 classifier.

AI.tldr: Logit-based white-box scoring substantially outperforms black-box confidence methods for zero-shot LLM text classification, and prefix-tree decision-only scoring cuts decode steps by 88-96%.
AI.motivation: Zero-shot LLM text classifiers are widely used, but knowing when to trust their predictions requires reliable confidence estimation across large label sets.
AI.method: The authors compare black-box methods (verbalized confidence, sampling) with white-box token-probability methods (P(True), constrained-generation logit scoring) across 11 open-weight LLMs (1B-32B) and five datasets (3 to 151 labels), and introduce decision-only scoring that scores only positions where labels diverge in a prefix tree (trie).
AI.result: Logit-based scoring achieves much higher discrimination (AUROC 0.74-0.77) than black-box methods (0.57-0.66), decision-only scoring reduces decode steps by 88-96% on the three largest label sets with comparable performance, and Gemma 4 31B and Qwen 3.5 9B rival the commercial Jev 1.13.0 classifier.
AI.conclusion: Constrained logit scoring—especially trie-based decision-only scoring—makes open-weight LLMs accurate, well-calibrated, and efficient zero-shot classifiers.

title: Enhancing Understanding of Language Models with Varied Explanations
summary: Language models are increasingly used to support human judgement in complex reasoning tasks, yet their predictions often remain difficult to interpret and validate. Explainability techniques provide insight into model decision-making, helping expose errors, failure modes, and potential bias so users can decide whether to rely on model outputs. Explanations are simplified approximations of a language model's internal workings. The goal is to obtain explanations that reflect the underlying computation as closely as possible (faithfulness), are understandable to users (plausibility), and help them achieve their intended goals (utility). Evaluation protocols are essential for assessing these dimensions. This thesis studies highlight explanations, natural language explanations, and chain-of-thought reasoning. These forms offer complementary perspectives on model behaviour and exhibit distinct strengths and limitations across tasks. Producing explanations that satisfy multiple quality dimensions remains challenging, as does evaluating them reliably across forms and settings. This thesis aims to improve people's understanding of models' decision-making processes in complex reasoning tasks. First, it proposes two evaluation frameworks for assessing highlight explanations across multiple properties and explanation types, together with a meta-evaluation framework for examining the reliability of existing faithfulness metrics for chain-of-thought explanations. Second, it proposes two techniques that generate natural language explanations designed to be faithful to the model's prediction process while remaining concise, coherent, and helpful for understanding model decisions. Finally, a study of human-AI interaction explores the roles of evidence and explanations in helping users validate model verdicts in a fact-checking setting.

AI.tldr: This thesis advances LLM explainability by introducing evaluation and meta-evaluation frameworks for highlight and chain-of-thought explanations, two techniques for faithful natural language explanations, and a human-AI fact-checking study.
AI.motivation: LLM predictions in complex reasoning tasks are hard to interpret and validate, and producing explanations that simultaneously achieve faithfulness, plausibility, and utility—and evaluating them reliably—remains challenging.
AI.method: The thesis proposes two multi-property evaluation frameworks for highlight explanations, a meta-evaluation framework for chain-of-thought faithfulness metrics, two techniques for generating concise and faithful natural language explanations, and a human-AI interaction study on fact-checking.
AI.result: The work establishes evaluation protocols across explanation forms, develops faithful natural language explanation generators, and characterizes how evidence and explanations help users validate model verdicts.
AI.conclusion: Combining rigorous faithfulness meta-evaluation with faithful explanation generation improves human understanding and validation of LLM reasoning in complex tasks.

title: Incorporating argumentation frameworks for LLM decision-making: Task-specific design and evaluation
summary: Argumentation frameworks (AFs) provide explicit, formal mechanisms for representing and resolving conflicts and thus have been incorporated into large language model (LLM) decision-making. The benefits vary and depend on how arguments and their relations are constructed, evaluated, and incorporated into the decision process. {We abstract a workflow consisting of four stages based on existing argumentation-augmented methods} and investigate their design choices over tasks of debate-based decision-making and retrieval-based fact verification. Our evaluation with recent LLMs shows that existing methods do not consistently improve performance across the considered tasks. Motivated by this observation, we develop two task-specific methods. The first is called Qnt-Arg, which organizes arguments around the original speakers in debate materials and aggregates model-estimated argument strengths and candidate-answer priors under gradual semantics. The second is Qlt-Arg that uses credibility estimates to establish preferences between conflicting evidence items and applies grounded semantics to select acceptable evidence for subsequent LLM inference. We examine the roles of generative and decision models within the two methods. In the debate setting, Qnt-Arg consistently outperforms other argumentation-augmented methods across matched configurations; Qlt-Arg improves retrieval-based fact-verification performance compared with the baselines. These findings demonstrate the value of combining formal argumentation and LLM while highlighting the importance of aligning with tasks in argumentation construction, model selection, and the role of formal semantic reasoning.

AI.tldr: Evaluating argumentation frameworks (AFs) in LLM decision-making reveals inconsistent gains from existing methods and motivates two task-specific designs, Qnt-Arg for debate and Qlt-Arg for fact verification.
AI.motivation: Although argumentation frameworks offer formal conflict resolution for LLMs, existing argumentation-augmented methods do not consistently improve performance across tasks.
AI.method: The authors abstract a four-stage argumentation workflow and develop Qnt-Arg (which organizes arguments by speaker and aggregates model-estimated strengths and priors under gradual semantics) for debate, and Qlt-Arg (which uses credibility estimates and grounded semantics to filter conflicting evidence) for fact verification.
AI.result: In matched configurations, Qnt-Arg consistently outperforms other argumentation-augmented methods on debate-based decision-making, while Qlt-Arg improves retrieval-based fact-verification performance over baselines.
AI.conclusion: Aligning argumentation structure, formal semantics, and model roles to the specific task is essential for realizing the benefits of formal argumentation in LLM decision-making.

title: ChronoDossier: Long-Form Personas as Temporal Memory Representations
comment: 28 pages, 4 figures, 32 tables. Under review at ICLR 2027. Code and data: this https URL
summary: Long-horizon agents rely on stored records to recover a person's state as facts change. Reliable answers depend on how facts are recorded, retrieved, and presented to the reader. We treat a long-form persona dossier as a memory representation of a known latent state, an invariant identity plus a timeline of facts, routines, and decision rules tied to life phases. We present ChronoDossier, a benchmark of 311 synthetic dossiers of 1k-10k words written by seven generators from dated timelines. Intrinsic metrics evaluate the records against their intended states; extrinsic metrics test recovery by five readers on a seeded 32-persona GPT-5.1 panel balanced across lengths (520 rated turns per condition). The linked states, records, evidence packets, and answers support tests of construction and evidence delivery. In a contextual-stress control, tag-scoped writer inputs remove detected out-of-scope anchor copying. Frozen questions authored on staged dossiers transfer less reliably to one-pass dossiers of the same states. In matched evidence controls, whole sections repair 29 of 32 GPT-5.1 and 25 of 30 Sonnet 4.6 failures labeled as packaging, compared with 2 of 8 and 1 of 8 answer-formation failures. Attribution uses separate key-based and key-free support measures, with model disagreements retained. Length remains confounded with persona and question composition; the observed between-bucket widening depends on excerpt construction. The benchmark supports offline evaluation against known facts. Memory acquisition from interaction and validation against real users remain outside its scope.

AI.tldr: ChronoDossier is a benchmark of 311 synthetic long-form persona dossiers (1k-10k words) designed to evaluate how temporal memory representation and evidence packaging affect state recovery in long-horizon agents.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon agents rely on stored records to recover changing personal states, but it is unclear how record construction, retrieval, and evidence presentation affect answer reliability.
AI.method: Seven generators write 311 dated-timeline dossiers (1k-10k words) evaluated intrinsically against latent states and extrinsically by five readers on a 32-persona GPT-5.1 panel (520 rated turns per condition), with matched evidence controls and key-based/key-free attribution.
AI.result: Tag-scoped writer inputs eliminate out-of-scope anchor copying, frozen questions transfer poorly from staged to one-pass dossiers, and providing whole sections repairs 29/32 GPT-5.1 and 25/30 Sonnet 4.6 packaging failures (versus 2/8 and 1/8 answer-formation failures).
AI.conclusion: ChronoDossier isolates construction and packaging bottlenecks in temporal memory recovery, showing that whole-section evidence delivery resolves most packaging errors.

title: Evolve Where It Matters: Coverage-Guided Self-Evolution of Agent Skills
summary: Agent skills package procedural knowledge as natural-language instructions, and a skill helps only when its instructions are correct and properly followed by the agent. Self-evolving agents revise their own skills from the runs they make, but existing methods judge each run as a whole, by its outcome or by where it went wrong, and cannot tell whether a failure comes from a wrong instruction or from one the agent did not follow. Instruction-level coverage was introduced to test skills and labels each instruction of a run as follow, not-follow, or not covered, which separates these causes. We leverage it for skill self-evolution with SkillPlumber, a framework in which an agent evolves its own skills where coverage shows they fall short. A persistent root cause analysis agent turns each label into a revision question and checks each revision against the next run, while a maintainer distills investigations across tasks into a shared strategy library. Across three benchmarks and three executors, SkillPlumber solves 64.7% to 70.5% of the tasks, 25.6 to 30.4 percentage points higher than the initial skill and 8.7 to 14.0 percentage points higher than the strongest baseline, and removing coverage reduces recovered failures by 20.8% on SkillsBench with GPT-5.5.

AI.tldr: SkillPlumber is a coverage-guided self-evolution framework that revises agent skills at instruction-level failure points, improving task success by 25.6 to 30.4 percentage points over initial skills.
AI.motivation: Existing self-evolving agents judge runs as a whole and cannot distinguish whether a failure stems from a wrong skill instruction or an instruction the agent failed to follow.
AI.method: SkillPlumber uses instruction-level coverage labels (follow, not-follow, not covered) to guide a persistent root-cause analysis agent that turns each label into a revision question verified on the next run, while a maintainer distills findings into a shared strategy library.
AI.result: Across three benchmarks and three executors, SkillPlumber solves 64.7% to 70.5% of tasks (25.6-30.4 percentage points above initial skills and 8.7-14.0 points above the strongest baseline), and removing coverage drops recovered failures by 20.8% on SkillsBench with GPT-5.5.
AI.conclusion: Grounding skill self-evolution in instruction-level coverage enables targeted, verifiable revisions that substantially outperform outcome-only evolution.

title: RoCoKV: Accelerating LLM Inference Serving through Uncertainty and Redundancy Aware KV Cache Compression
summary: KV cache compression is critical for large reasoning models, where most of the cost comes from long generated reasoning traces rather than the input prompt. These traces often contain redundant and low-utility tokens due to looping, self-verification, and corrections. However, such tokens may still receive high attention scores, making it difficult to remove them without harming the reasoning process. We propose RoCoKV, a KV cache compression method designed for large reasoning models. RoCoKV introduces two key components. First, uncertainty-guided adaptive pruning adjusts the compression strength based on the model's confidence, allocating more memory during uncertain phases and applying stronger pruning when the model is confident. Second, redundancy-aware token selection reduces the impact of tokens that are highly similar to recent reasoning content, encouraging the model to retain more informative and diverse tokens. Beyond the algorithm, we co-design RoCoKV with the serving stack: we develop fused three-phase CUDA decode kernels and integrate them into vLLM as a drop-in plugin that preserves its paged KV layout and CUDA graph capture, turning algorithmic savings into real end-to-end speedups. Extensive experiments across three reasoning benchmarks and two reasoning models demonstrate that RoCoKV consistently improves reasoning accuracy under constrained KV cache budgets, achieving higher accuracy compared to state-of-the-art KV cache compression methods. For DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B in vLLM, RoCoKV achieves a 1.27X speedup and 38% higher throughput on AIME25, the most challenging evaluated reasoning benchmark, and a 1.43X speedup and 45% higher throughput on the long synthetic benchmark, compared with Full-KV.

AI.tldr: RoCoKV is an uncertainty- and redundancy-aware KV cache compression method co-designed with fused vLLM CUDA decode kernels to accelerate large reasoning models.
AI.motivation: Large reasoning models generate long traces with redundant looping and self-verification tokens that still receive high attention scores, making standard KV cache eviction harmful to reasoning accuracy.
AI.method: RoCoKV combines uncertainty-guided adaptive pruning (retaining more memory during uncertain phases) with redundancy-aware token selection (suppressing tokens similar to recent content), integrated into vLLM via fused three-phase CUDA decode kernels preserving paged KV layout and CUDA graph capture.
AI.result: Across three reasoning benchmarks and two models, RoCoKV outperforms state-of-the-art KV compression baselines in accuracy, and on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B in vLLM achieves 1.27x speedup (38% higher throughput) on AIME25 and 1.43x speedup (45% higher throughput) on a long synthetic benchmark versus Full-KV.
AI.conclusion: Co-designing uncertainty- and redundancy-aware KV compression with paged-attention CUDA kernels turns memory savings into real end-to-end serving speedups for reasoning models.

title: PAIR-MED: Policy-reward Alternation for Iterative Refinement in Multilingual Medical Reasoning
summary: Large language models demonstrate strong medical question-answering capabilities, yet reasoning performance remains uneven across languages. Process reward models (PRMs) provide step-level feedback for improving reasoning, but a fixed PRM may become increasingly misaligned with the trajectory distribution of an evolving policy during reinforcement learning, thereby reducing the reliability of its supervision. We propose a policy--reward alternating training framework that jointly adapts a medical PRM and optimizes a multilingual reasoning policy. Following supervised initialization, the current policy generates multilingual trajectories to update the PRM, which then provides process-level rewards for the next policy update. Medical step supervision maintains the PRM's medical foundation, while process, outcome, and language-related rewards guide policy learning. We develop multilingual medical PRMs (PAIR-PRM) and reasoning models (PAIR-MED) at 8B and 9B scales across 12 languages. On the medical subsets of Global-MMLU and MMLU-ProX, our models improve average accuracy by 3.01--7.47% over their corresponding Qwen backbones. On CUREMED-BENCH, PAIR-MED-9B improves the joint language consistency and logical accuracy metric by 12.88% and 7.45% over baselines for in-domain and out-of-domain languages. Further analyses examine PRM adaptation, multilingual reasoning quality, and the contributions of individual training components.

AI.tldr: PAIR-MED is a policy-reward alternating training framework that jointly adapts a multilingual medical process reward model (PAIR-PRM) and a reasoning policy, improving accuracy across 12 languages.
AI.motivation: LLM medical reasoning varies widely across languages, and a fixed process reward model (PRM) becomes misaligned with an evolving policy's trajectory distribution during reinforcement learning.
AI.method: After supervised initialization, the policy generates multilingual trajectories to update PAIR-PRM (anchored by medical step supervision), which then supplies process, outcome, and language rewards for the next policy update at 8B and 9B scales across 12 languages.
AI.result: On Global-MMLU and MMLU-ProX medical subsets, PAIR-MED improves average accuracy by 3.01-7.47% over Qwen backbones, and PAIR-MED-9B improves joint language consistency and logical accuracy on CUREMED-BENCH by 12.88% (in-domain) and 7.45% (out-of-domain).
AI.conclusion: Alternating policy and PRM updates prevents reward-policy misalignment and strengthens multilingual medical reasoning.

title: PILAPS: A Bilingual Benchmark for Evaluating Pragmatic Inference across Phenomena and Settings
summary: Recent work reports strong pragmatic performance by large language models (LLMs) in English, yet whether this performance generalises across languages and evaluation settings remains unclear. This question is increasingly important as LLMs are deployed across languages, cultures, and conversational contexts. In this paper, we first introduce PILAPS, a bilingual English/Mandarin Chinese benchmark covering eight pragmatic phenomena across purpose-written and dialogue-derived items, with both culturally adapted and independently sourced data. We then evaluate eight LLMs from four families across a range of model sizes and prompting strategies. Our results reveal substantial variation across models and pragmatic phenomena: open-source models continue to struggle particularly with humour, while cross-linguistic performance varies with model origin. Our error analysis shows that, compared with human participants, models are more prone to literal interpretations in conversational contexts. Theory-of-Mind prompting lowers the literal share of errors, whereas Chain-of-Thought prompting slightly raises it. Together, these findings demonstrate that strong pragmatic performance in one evaluation setting does not necessarily generalise across languages or conversational contexts.

AI.tldr: PILAPS is a bilingual English/Mandarin Chinese benchmark of eight pragmatic phenomena showing that LLM pragmatic performance does not reliably generalize across languages, models, or conversational settings.
AI.motivation: Strong English pragmatic scores on existing benchmarks leave unclear whether LLMs generalize pragmatics across languages, cultures, and conversational contexts.
AI.method: The authors build PILAPS from purpose-written and dialogue-derived items (both culturally adapted and independently sourced) across eight pragmatic phenomena and evaluate eight LLMs from four families under multiple prompting strategies.
AI.result: Open-source models struggle especially with humour, cross-linguistic performance depends on model origin, models make more literal errors than humans in dialogue (reduced by Theory-of-Mind prompting but slightly increased by Chain-of-Thought).
AI.conclusion: Pragmatic competence in one language or setting does not guarantee cross-lingual or conversational generalization, highlighting the need for culturally and contextually diverse evaluations.

title: DRVEXO-4B-Unified: Design and Evaluation of a Modular Speech-Vision System
summary: We present DRVEXO-4B-Unified, a modular multimodal assistant built around a 4B language backbone. A self-contained checkpoint combines text, image, and speech inputs with reference-conditioned speech output and structured interaction. A temporal residual connector adapts acoustic sequences to the language interface; explicit text boundaries support incremental speech synthesis; and three task-conditioned scoring heads rank supplied action candidates alongside generative tool calls. These interfaces connect conversation to application-defined choices while leaving action authorization to the application. The system obtains 74.22% on all 900 MMMU validation questions, exceeding the published validation scores of Gemma 3 4B IT and InternVL3.5-4B without test-time scaling. Strict prompt-level IFEval accuracy is 82.26% and MATH-500 accuracy is 89.40%, above the original Qwen3-4B non-thinking report's 81.2% and 84.8%, respectively. On NVIDIA GB10, the model achieves a speech-synthesis first-chunk latency of 390 ms. For concurrent text generation, a growth-aware admission policy completes a 128-answer batch at 594.41 output tokens/s, including filling and draining, without preemptions. We plan to release the model weights and accompanying code under Apache License 2.0, retaining applicable third-party terms.

AI.tldr: DRVEXO-4B-Unified is a modular 4B speech-vision-text assistant with reference-conditioned speech output, incremental synthesis, and task-conditioned action-scoring heads.
AI.motivation: Building compact multimodal assistants that combine speech, vision, and text with low-latency speech synthesis and structured application interaction requires unified, efficient interfaces.
AI.method: Built on a 4B language backbone, DRVEXO-4B-Unified uses a temporal residual connector for acoustic sequences, explicit text boundaries for incremental speech synthesis, three task-conditioned scoring heads to rank action candidates alongside tool calls, and a growth-aware admission policy for concurrent text generation.
AI.result: It achieves 74.22% on all 900 MMMU validation questions (beating Gemma 3 4B IT and InternVL3.5-4B without test-time scaling), 82.26% on IFEval, 89.40% on MATH-500, 390 ms speech first-chunk latency on NVIDIA GB10, and 594.41 output tokens/s for a 128-answer batch without preemptions.
AI.conclusion: Modular acoustic-language interfaces and task-conditioned scoring heads enable a 4B multimodal assistant to deliver strong reasoning, low-latency speech, and high-throughput serving.

title: MATE: Mobile Agent Trustworthy Execution for Safe and Efficient Mobile Control
summary: Mobile agents on personal smartphones can affect private data, payments, settings, and the foreground screen. We present MATE (Mobile Agent Trustworthy Execution), an execution-layer system that controls the boundary between agent action proposals and device effects without modifying the underlying model. MATE represents each UI primitive as a structured action record that combines the instruction, target app, screen context, primitive, and action fields. Runtime Guardrail (RG) maps this record to an allow, block, or user-approval decision; Predefined Task Routing (PTR) serves recurring requests through verified routes with post-execution screen checks; and a floating interface keeps execution in a compact overlay. On MobileSafetyBench, MATE raises high-risk blocking from 29.7% to 97.0% under GPT-4o. On AndroidWorld, it reduces LLM calls by up to 6x and raises recurring-use task success to 95.7%.

AI.tldr: MATE is an execution-layer guardrail and task-routing system for mobile agents that raises high-risk action blocking to 97.0% and reduces LLM calls by up to 6x without modifying the underlying model.
AI.motivation: Mobile agents on personal smartphones can trigger risky actions affecting private data, payments, and settings, while recurring tasks incur unnecessary LLM calls.
AI.method: MATE represents UI primitives as structured action records, using a Runtime Guardrail (RG) to allow, block, or request user approval, Predefined Task Routing (PTR) to execute recurring requests via verified routes with post-execution screen checks, and a compact floating overlay UI.
AI.result: On MobileSafetyBench under GPT-4o, MATE increases high-risk blocking from 29.7% to 97.0%, and on AndroidWorld it cuts LLM calls by up to 6x while raising recurring-use task success to 95.7%.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling safety enforcement and recurring-route execution into an execution layer makes mobile agents substantially safer and more efficient without model retraining.

title: The Coverage Selection Gap: Ranking, Not Generation, Limits LLM Rubric Construction
summary: Task-specific rubrics are increasingly used to evaluate open-ended language-model outputs, yet constructing comprehensive evaluation criteria from complex source documents remains challenging. We study automatic rubric construction in professional mergers and acquisitions (M&A) due diligence, where evaluation criteria must be inferred from task instructions and supporting documents without access to an expert-authored reference rubric. We introduce a multi-axis generation framework that explores complementary structural and free-form views of the source evidence to construct a broad pool of candidate evaluation criteria. To distinguish failures of criterion discovery from failures of candidate selection, we introduce the coverage-selection gap, which measures the difference between reference-free ranking and a reference-informed greedy diagnostic under a fixed selection budget. Developed on 16 tasks and evaluated on four held-out tasks, our framework achieves 0.876 macro recall against senior-authored reference rubrics under an LLM-based criterion-equivalence protocol. Ablation studies further show that introducing new structural search axes improves recall by 6-10 percentage points, whereas increasing generation volume along existing search directions yields at most 1.5 points. These findings suggest that, once a high-coverage candidate pool has been constructed, effective reference-free selection becomes a substantial bottleneck in document-grounded rubric construction.

AI.tldr: Studying automatic rubric construction in M&A due diligence reveals that once a multi-axis candidate pool is generated, reference-free candidate selection—not generation—is the primary bottleneck.
AI.motivation: Constructing task-specific evaluation rubrics from complex source documents without an expert reference rubric is challenging, and it is unclear whether failures stem from criterion discovery or selection.
AI.method: The authors propose a multi-axis generation framework combining structural and free-form views of source evidence and define the coverage-selection gap between reference-free ranking and a reference-informed greedy diagnostic under a fixed budget, evaluated on 16 development and 4 held-out M&A due diligence tasks.
AI.result: The framework reaches 0.876 macro recall against senior-authored reference rubrics, and ablations show new structural search axes improve recall by 6-10 percentage points versus at most 1.5 points from higher generation volume along existing axes.
AI.conclusion: Improving document-grounded rubric construction requires better reference-free ranking and selection methods rather than simply generating more candidates.

title: AutoRAGBench: A Benchmark for LLM Agents Automating RAG System Development
summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is a well-established paradigm for augmenting large language models (LLMs) with information retrieved from external corpora. However, developing effective RAG systems requires substantial engineering effort and iterative experimentation, as effective design choices vary across tasks and domains. With rapid advances in LLM agent capabilities, we ask how well these agents can autonomously build RAG systems and how effectively they can improve them through iteration. In this paper, we propose AutoRAGBench, the first benchmark to evaluate how well LLM agents develop RAG systems from scratch in an open code space. It comprises nine RAG system development tasks. For each task, agents build RAG systems from scratch without starter code or prescribed strategies, under a six-hour budget on a single H800 GPU. They analyze task data, implement RAG pipelines, and iteratively refine their designs based on experimental feedback. We evaluate nine agent configurations and analyze both the effectiveness of the resulting RAG systems and their development trajectories. GPT-6.1 Sol with Codex CLI achieves the highest average score of 56.1. The composite Human-SOTA baseline averages 44.4. These results show that LLM agents can automate effective RAG system development. When starting from a human-designed system on each of seven tasks, GPT-6.1 Sol with Codex CLI improves the score by 16.6 points on average.

AI.tldr: AutoRAGBench is a nine-task benchmark evaluating how well LLM agents autonomously build and iteratively refine RAG systems from scratch in an open code space, where top agents surpass a composite Human-SOTA baseline.
AI.motivation: Developing effective RAG systems requires substantial engineering and iterative experimentation, but no benchmark previously measured LLM agents' ability to automate end-to-end RAG development from scratch.
AI.method: Agents receive nine RAG development tasks with no starter code or prescribed strategies under a six-hour single-H800-GPU budget, analyzing data, implementing pipelines, and iterating on experimental feedback across nine evaluated agent configurations.
AI.result: GPT-6.1 Sol with Codex CLI achieves the highest average score of 56.1 versus 44.4 for the composite Human-SOTA baseline, and starting from a human-designed system on seven tasks improves scores by 16.6 points on average.
AI.conclusion: Autonomous LLM agents can design and iteratively optimize competitive RAG systems from scratch, outperforming human-designed baselines.

title: Rubric Semantics or Numerical Priors? Auditing Scale-Direction Bias in LLM Judges
summary: Recent benchmark evaluations increasingly rely on Large Language Models (LLMs) as automatic judges. This paradigm assumes LLMs evaluate based on the rubric's semantic meaning rather than its numeric scale. We question this assumption by introducing semantic faithfulness: the principle that semantically equivalent rubrics must yield consistent scores. To quantify this, we propose a scale-reversal probe that inverts score anchors without altering evaluation criteria. Furthermore, we introduce floor normalization to calibrate reversal disagreement against intrinsic model variability, enabling fair cross-model comparisons. Experiments across five meta-evaluation benchmarks with seven diverse LLM judges spanning open-weight and proprietary models reveal widespread violations of semantic faithfulness, showing that raw reversal agreement alone is misleading. Finally, we demonstrate that bidirectional anchor averaging reduces dependence on any single anchor direction without compromising alignment with human judgments. Our findings emphasize that trustworthy LLM judges must reliably follow rubric semantics, not just correlate with human ratings.

AI.tldr: Auditing LLM judges with a scale-reversal probe and floor normalization reveals widespread violations of semantic faithfulness, which bidirectional anchor averaging mitigates.
AI.motivation: LLM-as-a-judge evaluations assume judges score according to rubric semantics rather than numeric scale direction, but this assumption has not been systematically tested.
AI.method: The authors introduce semantic faithfulness, a scale-reversal probe that inverts score anchors without changing criteria, floor normalization to calibrate disagreement against intrinsic model variability, and bidirectional anchor averaging, tested across five meta-evaluation benchmarks and seven diverse LLM judges.
AI.result: All tested judges exhibit widespread violations of semantic faithfulness that raw reversal agreement masks, whereas bidirectional anchor averaging reduces anchor-direction dependence without hurting human-judgment alignment.
AI.conclusion: Trustworthy LLM judges require auditing for scale-direction bias and using bidirectional anchor averaging rather than relying solely on human correlation.

title: TRAC: Efficient Diffusion Language Models for Machine Translation via Length-Aware Decoding
summary: Machine translation with large language models requires both high translation quality and low generation latency. Accelerating translation while preserving quality is therefore essential for practical deployment. Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) can generate tokens at arbitrary target positions through iterative denoising, offering a new paradigm for parallel translation beyond sequential autoregressive decoding. However, existing methods still incur redundant computation: fixed target generation lengths waste computation on unused positions, while confidence-only commitment delays medium-confidence tokens whose predictions have largely stabilized. To address these issues, we propose TRAC, a training-free adaptive decoding method for diffusion machine translation. TRAC adapts the target generation length using source length and translation direction, with a conservative fallback to the maximum length for empty or unusually short outputs. It preserves high-confidence commitment while identifying temporally stable medium-confidence tokens for early commitment using cross-step top-1 persistence and approximate Jensen-Shannon divergence over Top-$K$ distributions. On bidirectional Chinese-English translation across FLORES-200, WMT23, and NTREX-128, TRAC reduces model forward calls by 24.9% to 36.8% and achieves sentence-level generation speedups of 1.91 to 2.19 times over Fast-dLLM, with only a 0.02-point decrease in macro-average COMET. These results demonstrate that adaptive generation lengths and stability-aware token commitment improve the efficiency of diffusion machine translation.

AI.tldr: TRAC is a training-free adaptive decoding method for diffusion machine translation that adjusts target length and commits stable medium-confidence tokens early, achieving 1.91-2.19x speedups over Fast-dLLM.
AI.motivation: Diffusion large language models enable parallel machine translation, but fixed target generation lengths waste compute and confidence-only commitment delays medium-confidence tokens whose predictions have already stabilized.
AI.method: TRAC adapts target generation length from source length and translation direction (with a max-length fallback for empty or short outputs) and commits temporally stable medium-confidence tokens early using cross-step top-1 persistence and approximate Jensen-Shannon divergence over Top-K distributions.
AI.result: On bidirectional Chinese-English translation across FLORES-200, WMT23, and NTREX-128, TRAC cuts model forward calls by 24.9% to 36.8% and speeds up sentence-level generation by 1.91x to 2.19x over Fast-dLLM with only a 0.02-point drop in macro-average COMET.
AI.conclusion: Length-aware generation and stability-based early token commitment substantially accelerate diffusion machine translation without sacrificing translation quality.

title: ColorRef: Calibrating Verbal Feedback for Color Revision
summary: People rarely specify an exact color when asking someone to revise a design: they might say \textit{a little darker} or \textit{more blue} after seeing a proposal. A language-model assistant must then infer not only which way to change the color, but how far. We study this distinction with \textsc{ColorRef}, a color reference game in which a model guesses a color from a description and a teacher, knowing a recorded target hidden from the guesser, supplies verbal corrections. On 1{,}000 crowd-sourced description--target pairs, three rounds of deterministic oracle feedback reduce mean target distance from 42.33 to 22.15 $\Delta E_{76}$. However, those corrections provide additional information, and improvement alone does not establish well-calibrated feedback following. A controlled Qwen3-14B diagnostic reveals a more specific failure: following a requested direction and ordering graded phrases do not guarantee a suitable step size; strong modifiers can induce excessive changes. We therefore measure each receiver's typical response to \textit{a little}, \textit{somewhat}, and \textit{much} on separate colors and select wording matched to its observed steps. On 128 held-out starting colors, calibration reduces one-step mean error from 12.36 to 6.86 for Qwen3-14B and from 11.06 to 5.89 for Gemma 4 12B against a fixed graded-wording rule. The benefit is concentrated on large corrections, with many unchanged cases and no consistent increase in threshold success. Our findings show that following the direction of feedback is not the same as making an appropriately sized revision.

AI.tldr: ColorRef is a color-revision game showing that LLMs often misjudge revision step sizes despite following direction, and calibrating graded wording to each model's observed step sizes roughly halves one-step error.
AI.motivation: In iterative design revision, users give relative verbal feedback (e.g., "a little darker"), requiring models to infer both direction and magnitude, yet improvement over rounds does not prove calibrated step sizing.
AI.method: Using 1,000 crowd-sourced description-target pairs in ColorRef, the authors diagnose Qwen3-14B's step sizes for "a little", "somewhat", and "much", and calibrate wording selection to each receiver's measured response on 128 held-out starting colors.
AI.result: Three rounds of oracle feedback reduce mean target distance from 42.33 to 22.15 Delta E76, while step-size calibration cuts one-step mean error from 12.36 to 6.86 for Qwen3-14B and from 11.06 to 5.89 for Gemma 4 12B (concentrated on large corrections, without consistent threshold-success gains).
AI.conclusion: Following verbal feedback direction is distinct from calibrating revision magnitude, and receiver-specific wording calibration substantially reduces one-step color-revision error.

title: FoodReact-AR: Learning Audience Reactions that Zero-Shot LLMs Miss in Arabic Food-Insecurity Discourse
summary: Facebook reactions record how an audience received a post, a signal absent from the post's text. We treat the six differentiated reactions on 74,241 Arabic food-insecurity posts from public Facebook pages (2020-2024) as compositions, apply a centered log-ratio transformation, and cluster them into four audience profiles: Solidarity (Love-dominant), Dismissal (Haha-dominant), Grief (Sad-dominant), and a flat Ambivalent profile. Dismissal peaks in 2022 (22.3%), the year of the wheat price shock, and grief in 2024 (14.0%), during the Gaza food emergency; a page-clustered GEE confirms both shifts (odds ratios 2.18 and 1.34), and they survive minimum-reaction filtering, alternative zero replacements and clustering methods, and bootstrap resampling. We then test whether the profiles can be predicted without reactions. A zero-shot Arabic LLM recovers Grief for 83.8% of posts but Dismissal for only 3.4%, and in a matched ablation, it shows the reaction percentages do not help. A simple classifier trained on the reaction-derived labels and tested on unseen pages recovers dismissal for 60.0% (macro-F1 0.56 against 0.43), mainly from mentions of officials and institutions. Derisive audience responses are thus learnable from text, yet a zero-shot LLM misses them. We release the corpus, LLM, and human annotation layers, and an evaluation protocol as FoodReact-AR.

AI.tldr: FoodReact-AR is an Arabic food-insecurity Facebook corpus and evaluation protocol showing that zero-shot LLMs miss derisive audience reactions (3.4% recall) that a simple supervised classifier recovers at 60.0%.
AI.motivation: Social media reactions capture audience reception absent from post text, and it is unclear whether zero-shot LLMs can infer these reaction profiles from text alone.
AI.method: The authors apply centered log-ratio clustering to six Facebook reaction types across 74,241 Arabic food-insecurity posts (2020-2024) to derive four profiles (Solidarity, Dismissal, Grief, Ambivalent), verify temporal shifts with page-clustered GEE, and compare a zero-shot Arabic LLM against a simple supervised classifier on unseen pages.
AI.result: Dismissal peaks in 2022 (22.3%) and Grief in 2024 (14.0%); the zero-shot LLM recovers Grief at 83.8% but Dismissal at only 3.4%, whereas the supervised classifier recovers Dismissal at 60.0% (macro-F1 0.56 vs. 0.43), mainly from mentions of officials and institutions.
AI.conclusion: Derisive audience reactions in Arabic food-insecurity discourse are learnable from text cues but systematically missed by zero-shot LLMs.

title: From Geographic Memory to Spatial Generalization in Large Language Models
summary: Large language models (LLMs) can associate places with geographic descriptions, but recovering an observed association does not establish an ability to generalize across geographic space. We distinguish geospatial memory, the recovery of location--description associations observed during training, from spatial generalization, the prediction of descriptions for locations in unobserved regions. We investigate whether continuous location representations improve this generalization and encourage geographic knowledge to become spatially organized within an LLM. We frame this organization as a latent spatial field: a learned mapping from locations to descriptions connected through spatial dependencies. Building on a continuous spatial encoder, we project location representations into the model's embedding space and supply them as spatial tokens. We evaluate the resulting models on two newly curated geo-text benchmarks for Los Angeles and London using two complementary assessments. Geospatial captioning tests both memory and spatial generalization by generating descriptions at observed locations and at locations beyond the spatial coverage of the training observations. A separate geospatial grounding model tests whether generated location--description pairs provide useful additional supervision for mapping text to geographic space. Across multiple LLM families, continuous location representations improve captioning at unobserved locations relative to textual coordinates, while their generated descriptions yield modest but consistent improvements in downstream grounding. Layer-wise probing and representation clustering provide additional evidence consistent with spatially organized geographic representations. Together, these findings show the value of evaluating spatial generalization separately from memory and of incorporating continuous spatial representations into language models.

AI.tldr: Projecting continuous spatial encoder representations into LLMs as spatial tokens improves spatial generalization to unobserved geographic locations over textual coordinates.
AI.motivation: LLMs can memorize observed location-description pairs, but recovering training associations does not establish spatial generalization to unobserved regions.
AI.method: Framing geographic knowledge as a latent spatial field, the authors project continuous spatial encoder outputs into an LLM's embedding space as spatial tokens and evaluate geospatial captioning and downstream grounding on new Los Angeles and London geo-text benchmarks.
AI.result: Across multiple LLM families, continuous spatial tokens improve captioning at unobserved locations over textual coordinates, yield modest consistent gains in downstream grounding, and show spatially organized representations under layer-wise probing and clustering.
AI.conclusion: Separating spatial generalization from geospatial memory reveals that continuous spatial representations help LLMs organize and generalize geographic knowledge.

title: STARK: Moving towards Personalized Agents That Truly Learn and Remember
summary: Long-term memory is essential for personalized agentic systems that interact with users over long time periods, yet current architectures only capture what happened while leaving the reasoning of why it happened to be derived later by underlying LLMs.%, and silo knowledge within individual users. These events can, however, convey not only what a user experienced but also how that experience shaped their behavioral patterns. We introduce STARK, a dual-graph memory architecture which treats these events not just as nodes but also as edges between behavioral insights. STARK maintains an Episodic Graph which records interactions as temporally, causally, and semantically linked episodes; and an Insight Graph which represents LLM-extracted behavioral signals scored by how many events support them, connected by the very events that led to them. At inference, behavioral knowledge is retrieved directly from insight nodes grounded by event-as-edges, eliminating repeated episodic traversal. The event-as-edge structure also naturally enables projecting the knowledge graph into a relational embedding space where cross-user transfer becomes possible under shared contextual circumstances, allowing the system to infer missing insights for cold-start users. Evaluations show that STARK improves by 1.48 judge score on LongMemEval information extraction and 0.93 on LoCoMo open domain questions over state of the art. On the public LongLaMP abstract-generation benchmark, cross-user transfer improves open-ended judge scores by 0.7 points and ROUGE-L by 3 at 5% graph sparsity.

AI.tldr: STARK is a dual-graph memory architecture that represents user events as both episodic nodes and edges between behavioral insights, enabling direct insight retrieval and cross-user transfer for cold-start personalization.
AI.motivation: Existing personalized agent memory systems record what happened but leave reasoning about why it happened to repeated LLM traversal over siloed user episodes.
AI.method: STARK pairs an Episodic Graph of temporally, causally, and semantically linked episodes with an Insight Graph of LLM-extracted behavioral signals connected by the events that caused them, projecting the graph into a relational embedding space for cross-user transfer.
AI.result: STARK improves judge scores by 1.48 on LongMemEval information extraction and 0.93 on LoCoMo open-domain questions over state of the art, and cross-user transfer on LongLaMP improves open-ended judge scores by 0.7 and ROUGE-L by 3 at 5% graph sparsity.
AI.conclusion: Modeling events as edges between behavioral insights eliminates repeated episodic traversal and enables effective cross-user personalization for cold-start users.

title: VR-SparseQuant: Accurate FP4 Quantization with 2:4 Sparsity on Vera Rubin
summary: In recent years, GPUs have incorporated increasingly specialized support for low-precision computation, from Hopper's FP8 to Blackwell's FP4 Tensor Cores. Precision formats have evolved alongside this hardware, from MXFP4 and NVFP4 on Blackwell to E2M1 FP4 with direct UE5M3 block scaling on Vera Rubin, which we term as $\boldsymbol{VRFP4}$. These advances help serve larger language models at lower cost, but four-bit activation quantization can substantially degrade model quality. We introduce VR-SparseQuant, which uses Vera Rubin's elementwise 2:4 sparsity to recover accuracy while retaining native FP4 execution. By allowing two sparse streams to overlap, we use the same FP4 value budget as dense quantization to refine activations with larger errors. Offline scale-ratio calibration avoids runtime search, while a shared-weight GEMM accumulates both streams efficiently. On Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B, VR-SparseQuant reduces WikiText-2 perplexity from $\boldsymbol{6.85}$ to $\boldsymbol{5.57}$ versus dense RTN W4A4. Including activation preparation, our native Rubin kernels for VRFP4 achieve up to $\boldsymbol{3.1\times}$ GEMM and $\boldsymbol{2.7\times}$ MoE speedup over BF16. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study of adaptive activation quantization using Vera Rubin's elementwise 2:4 structured sparse FP4 instructions.

AI.tldr: VR-SparseQuant leverages Vera Rubin's elementwise 2:4 structured sparsity to recover four-bit activation quantization accuracy while achieving up to 3.1x GEMM and 2.7x MoE speedups over BF16.
AI.motivation: Four-bit activation quantization (such as Vera Rubin's VRFP4) lowers LLM serving cost but can substantially degrade model quality.
AI.method: VR-SparseQuant uses two overlapping 2:4 sparse streams within the same FP4 value budget to refine high-error activations, paired with offline scale-ratio calibration and a shared-weight GEMM kernel on Vera Rubin.
AI.result: On Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B, VR-SparseQuant reduces WikiText-2 perplexity from 6.85 to 5.57 compared to dense RTN W4A4, and native Rubin VRFP4 kernels achieve up to 3.1x GEMM and 2.7x MoE speedup over BF16 including activation preparation.
AI.conclusion: Exploiting hardware 2:4 structured sparse FP4 instructions enables accurate, native-speed W4A4 LLM inference on Vera Rubin GPUs.

title: Verification Behavior Across Five Qwen2.5-Instruct Checkpoints
comment: 10 pages, 1 figure. Includes English translations of the experiment prompts and the behavioral rating rubric. AI language models were used for behavioral ratings and to assist manuscript preparation
summary: We evaluate five Qwen2.5-Instruct checkpoints (0.5B to 32B) under four prompting conditions using three fixed tasks per information condition and five generations per task. Two AI raters scored 600 trajectories. Under the coordinated instruction, both raters recorded strict declarations of insufficiency in 11/15 cases at 7B, 0/15 at 14B, and 5/15 at 32B. The runner sent a standard follow-up when a request detector fired. The three checkpoints received at least one follow-up in 15, 12, and 15 cases, respectively. On information-sufficient tasks at 3B through 32B, scored format markers appeared in 60/60 protocol trajectories and 0/60 baseline trajectories. After adjudication, 1/60 in each condition met the diagnostic-execution criterion (H3). Across all checkpoints and prompts, 7/300 information-sufficient trajectories met H3 after adjudication, all on the same task. The prespecified upward transition did not occur in this run. The results separate visible structure, diagnostic execution, and persistence after a request for evidence.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates five Qwen2.5-Instruct checkpoints (0.5B to 32B) across four prompting conditions to separate visible format structure, diagnostic execution, and persistence after evidence requests. None of the checkpoints showed the prespecified upward transition, and only 7 of 300 information-sufficient trajectories met the diagnostic-execution criterion after adjudication.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations need to distinguish between superficial adherence to visible formatting protocols, actual diagnostic execution, and how models persist after receiving follow-up requests for evidence.
AI.method: The authors test five Qwen2.5-Instruct checkpoints (0.5B to 32B) under four prompting conditions using three fixed tasks per information condition and five generations per task, with two AI raters scoring 600 trajectories and a runner sending standard follow-ups when a request detector fires.
AI.result: Under coordinated instructions, both raters recorded strict declarations of insufficiency in 11/15 cases at 7B, 0/15 at 14B, and 5/15 at 32B, with at least one follow-up sent in 15, 12, and 15 cases respectively. On information-sufficient tasks from 3B to 32B, format markers appeared in 60/60 protocol trajectories and 0/60 baseline trajectories, yet only 1/60 in each condition (and 7/300 overall on a single task) met the diagnostic-execution criterion (H3).
AI.conclusion: Visible protocol formatting does not guarantee diagnostic execution, and the expected capability transition across model scales did not occur in this evaluation.

title: Closing Performance Gap for Diffusion Language Models under Low Inference Budgets
summary: Diffusion language models offer an architectural route to low-budget generation by updating multiple tokens in parallel, which can reduce the number of sequential decoding steps relative to token-by-token autoregressive decoding. However, realizing this advantage at low budgets is challenging, as generation quality often declines when the number of denoising and refinement steps is reduced. Editable diffusion models address this quality loss through post-draft refinement, but useful intermediate results may still be lost before final submission. We introduce CaRR (Commitment-aware Refinement and Recovery), a training-free framework which improves submission quality from a fixed editable checkpoint through updated-context refill and trajectory-based recovery within its existing forward schedule. Token Commitment Remasking (TCR) remasks selected native pure replacements and refills them on the next scheduled edit forward using the updated context. Submission Commitment Recovery (SCR) uses the resulting refinement trajectory to recover supported candidates when the final response does not satisfy task-specific output requirements. Both modules operate within the native mask/edit schedule without additional backbone forwards. Experiments on code generation and mathematical reasoning show consistent gains in average accuracy over native ME-DLM across four inference budgets, with the largest gains under tight budgets. At one-eighth of the full scheduled forward budget, CaRR improves the six-metric average accuracy by 7.44 pp, including gains of 11.37 and 10.05 on MBPP and MBPP+.

AI.tldr: The authors introduce CaRR, a training-free framework that improves editable diffusion language model quality under low inference budgets without adding backbone forward passes. At one-eighth of the full forward budget, CaRR improves six-metric average accuracy by 7.44 percentage points over native ME-DLM.
AI.motivation: Diffusion language models enable parallel token updates for low-budget generation, but reducing denoising and refinement steps degrades quality, and editable diffusion models can still lose useful intermediate results before final submission.
AI.method: CaRR (Commitment-aware Refinement and Recovery) adds two training-free modules within the native mask/edit forward schedule: Token Commitment Remasking (TCR), which remasks selected native pure replacements for refilling with updated context, and Submission Commitment Recovery (SCR), which uses the refinement trajectory to recover supported candidates when the final output fails task requirements.
AI.result: On code generation and mathematical reasoning across four inference budgets, CaRR consistently outperforms native ME-DLM in average accuracy, with the largest gains under tight budgets. At one-eighth of the full scheduled forward budget, CaRR improves six-metric average accuracy by 7.44 percentage points, including gains of 11.37 on MBPP and 10.05 on MBPP+.
AI.conclusion: Trajectory-based recovery and context-updated remasking within the existing forward schedule effectively close the performance gap of diffusion language models under tight inference budgets.

title: Language models represent more about emphasis than they can tell you
summary: Prosodic prominence can largely be predicted from the words of a sentence, but part of it depends on how the speaker reads it. We study how much of prominence language models recover from text, whether they can report it when asked, and what the speech signal adds. On read English speech labelled for word-level prominence, we compare frozen and fine-tuned text models, prompted large language models (LLMs) and speech models on the same words. All text models end within about one point of each other, at best 68.8% on the 3-way task, and largely make the same errors. With the prompts we tested, LLMs do no better than a word-majority baseline, even with 500 examples. Linear probes find more in their representations. Speech models reach 84.7%. We argue that text determines only part of prominence, and that the rest has to be heard. LLMs encode what the text determines, but prompting does not bring it out: they represent more about where the emphasis falls than they tell you.

AI.tldr: This study investigates how much prosodic prominence language models recover from text versus what requires the speech signal. While linear probes find prominence information in LLM representations, prompted LLMs perform no better than a word-majority baseline, and speech models substantially outperform all text models.
AI.motivation: Prosodic prominence depends partly on wording and partly on how a speaker reads a sentence, raising the question of how much prominence text models encode, whether LLMs can report it when prompted, and what acoustic information adds.
AI.method: The authors compare frozen and fine-tuned text models, prompted LLMs (with up to 500 examples), linear probes on LLM representations, and speech models on read English speech labeled for word-level prominence.
AI.result: All text models plateau within one point of each other at best 68.8% on the 3-way task and make similar errors, while prompted LLMs do not beat a word-majority baseline even with 500 examples. Linear probes extract more prominence signal from LLM representations, and speech models reach 84.7%.
AI.conclusion: Text determines only part of prosodic prominence, and while LLMs represent more about emphasis than prompting can elicit, acoustic speech signals are needed for full prominence prediction.

title: Efficient and Robust Drafting with Multi-Token Prediction
summary: Speculative decoding has emerged as a critical technique for accelerating Large Language Model (LLM) inference by decoupling generation into a drafting phase and a parallel verification phase. A crucial challenge is therefore designing a drafter that is both lightweight and accurate enough to approximate the predictions of the target model. We present a highly optimized Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) architecture that extends existing backbone LLMs to efficiently produce high-quality drafts. Built around a single shared drafting head, our approach features three core architectural optimizations: target activation injection to anchor semantic planning, zero-copy KV-cache cross-attention to bypass prefill compute and reduce memory overhead, and an efficient clustered vocabulary projection to reduce the cost of full-vocabulary decoding. Testing these improvements with the Gemma 4 model family, our G-MTP shows out-of-the-box speedups for both large server-side setups (up to 3.1$\times$) and smaller models targeting memory-constrained on-device environments (up to 2.3$\times$ on H100 and up to 2.2$\times$ on a smartphone GPU). In addition, we present parameter-efficient fine-tuning recipes for G-MTP that keep the drafter aligned with the backbone LLM under domain shift, requiring up to 1.83$\times$ fewer target forward passes than tuning only the backbone.

AI.tldr: The authors present an optimized Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) drafting architecture for speculative decoding that achieves up to 3.1x speedups on Gemma 4 models. It combines target activation injection, zero-copy KV-cache cross-attention, and clustered vocabulary projection.
AI.motivation: Speculative decoding requires a drafter that is both lightweight and accurate enough to approximate the target model's predictions without introducing heavy prefill or vocabulary-decoding overhead.
AI.method: Built around a single shared drafting head, the G-MTP architecture incorporates target activation injection to anchor semantic planning, zero-copy KV-cache cross-attention to bypass prefill compute and reduce memory overhead, and clustered vocabulary projection to cut full-vocabulary decoding costs, alongside parameter-efficient fine-tuning recipes for domain shift.
AI.result: Evaluated on the Gemma 4 model family, G-MTP achieves out-of-the-box speedups of up to 3.1x in large server-side setups, up to 2.3x on H100 for smaller models, and up to 2.2x on a smartphone GPU. Its fine-tuning recipes require up to 1.83x fewer target forward passes than tuning only the backbone under domain shift.
AI.conclusion: Architectural optimizations to shared-head MTP drafters enable fast, memory-efficient speculative decoding across both server and on-device environments while remaining adaptable to domain shifts.

title: TableRoute: Capability-Aware Routing for Scalable Table Question Answering
summary: Table question answering with large language models remains difficult to scale: tables range from compact to million-token sizes, while questions require precise grounding of columns, values, and computations. Existing methods often specialize in a fixed inference strategy, which is brittle across different table scales and model capabilities. Full-table reading is efficient for compact inputs but suffers from irrelevant context. Table reduction helps long inputs but depends on reliable evidence localization, while execution is required when tables exceed the model context window and remains sensitive to schema and value grounding errors. We propose TableRoute, a capability-aware routing framework with evidence-conditioned inference for scalable TableQA. TableRoute first generates validated question--table evidence and identifies the required operations, then routes each instance among these three strategies according to serialized table length and calibrated estimates of how reliably the base model handles these operations. The validated evidence supports the selected route by grounding columns, values, and conditions. Across WikiTQ, WTQ-L, BirdQA, and TableBench, TableRoute consistently improves accuracy through complementary routing and evidence conditioning across table scales, while reducing online token cost. Code will be made available upon publication.

AI.tldr: TableRoute is a capability-aware routing framework for TableQA that dynamically selects between full-table reading, table reduction, and execution based on table length and model capability estimates. It improves accuracy while reducing online token cost across four TableQA benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing TableQA methods rely on a fixed inference strategy, which is brittle across tables ranging from compact to million-token sizes and sensitive to irrelevant context, localization errors, or schema grounding failures.
AI.method: TableRoute first generates validated question-table evidence and identifies required operations, then routes each instance among full-table reading, table reduction, and execution using serialized table length and calibrated estimates of the base model's reliability on those operations, with the validated evidence grounding the selected route.
AI.result: Across WikiTQ, WTQ-L, BirdQA, and TableBench, TableRoute consistently improves accuracy through complementary routing and evidence conditioning across table scales while reducing online token cost.
AI.conclusion: Capability-aware routing combined with validated evidence conditioning provides a scalable and cost-effective solution for TableQA across diverse table sizes.

title: HALTT: A HAte Lexicon Through Time
summary: Automated hate speech detection degrades over time as everyday vocabulary is weaponized into covert slurs while retaining original benign meanings (polysemy retention). Existing lexical semantic change detection (LSCD) frameworks struggle with this phenomenon due to a lack of standardized, sense-delineated diachronic resources. We propose a multi-stage framework to construct and validate a diachronic lexicon of semantically shifted hate speech terms. Filtering > 20,000 candidates, our pipeline combines historical (1770-1964) and modern (2001-2024) corpus frequency grounding, masked definition-level scoring to mitigate LLM temporal bias, and a dual-persona reasoning prompt paradigm. We release HALTT, a grounded lexicon of 19 polysemous terms with literal and derogatory senses, analyze shift typologies, and establish evaluation protocols for downstream diachronic benchmarking.

AI.tldr: The authors introduce a multi-stage framework to build HALTT, a diachronic lexicon of 19 polysemous hate speech terms that retain benign literal meanings while acquiring covert derogatory senses over time.
AI.motivation: Automated hate speech detection degrades as everyday words are weaponized into covert slurs while keeping their original meanings, and existing lexical semantic change detection frameworks lack standardized, sense-delineated diachronic resources.
AI.method: Filtering over 20,000 candidates, the pipeline combines historical (1770-1964) and modern (2001-2024) corpus frequency grounding, masked definition-level scoring to mitigate LLM temporal bias, and a dual-persona reasoning prompt paradigm.
AI.result: The authors release HALTT, a grounded lexicon of 19 polysemous terms with both literal and derogatory senses, alongside an analysis of shift typologies and evaluation protocols for downstream diachronic benchmarking.
AI.conclusion: HALTT provides a sense-delineated diachronic resource and evaluation protocol to support research on covert, semantically shifted hate speech.

title: Verifiable Logic in Medical LLMs: A Critical Review of Agentic Clinical Reasoning Optimization and Neuro-Symbolic Grounding
summary: Clinical large language models are usually judged by whether the final answer is right. Yet a model can reach a fluent, plausible output through invalid reasoning that static benchmarks do not detect, and confident hallucination, causally invalid inference, and spurious demographic shortcuts can pass conventional evaluation. This critical review covers four paradigms in turn: how clinical hallucination arises and why static metrics miss it; the agentic hallucination cascade, in which multi-agent and tool-augmented systems propagate and amplify early reasoning errors; process reward modeling as step-level supervision; and neuro-symbolic grounding, in which formal logic engines, ontology reasoners, and knowledge graphs place verifiable constraints on neural output. Within their encoded domains, systems with symbolic veto layers offer guarantees that hold relative to their encoded knowledge, and they report large gains on the safety measures they use. These results come from single studies, mostly in simulated or small-sample settings, and are not directly comparable with neural baselines. Process reward models remain bounded by the statistics of their training data. We propose a conceptual framework that maps each agentic failure mode to a symbolic intervention point, and we argue that clinical AI safety depends substantially on system architecture. Because current regulation emphasizes performance and does not require verification of reasoning steps, we argue that responsible certification should also audit reasoning trajectories alongside accuracy on static benchmarks.

AI.tldr: This critical review examines four paradigms for clinical LLM reasoning reliability, arguing that static accuracy benchmarks miss invalid reasoning and that responsible clinical AI certification must audit reasoning trajectories alongside final answers.
AI.motivation: Clinical LLMs can produce fluent, correct-looking answers via invalid reasoning, confident hallucinations, or demographic shortcuts that static benchmarks fail to detect, and multi-agent systems can amplify these errors.
AI.method: The authors review clinical hallucination mechanisms, agentic hallucination cascades, process reward modeling, and neuro-symbolic grounding (formal logic engines, ontology reasoners, knowledge graphs), and propose a conceptual framework mapping agentic failure modes to symbolic intervention points.
AI.result: Systems with symbolic veto layers provide guarantees relative to their encoded knowledge and report large gains on their chosen safety measures, though these come from single, mostly simulated or small-sample studies not directly comparable to neural baselines, while process reward models remain bounded by training data statistics.
AI.conclusion: Clinical AI safety depends heavily on system architecture, and regulatory certification should audit reasoning trajectories rather than relying solely on static benchmark accuracy.

title: The Linguistic Structure of Dependency-Conditioned Embeddings
summary: Dependency-based distributional models capture syntactically informed lexical similarities, but the geometric organisation of dependency-conditioned lexical representations remains underexplored. We investigate the global and local geometry of lemma-dependency relation embeddings using four representations trained on WikiText-103: two count-based PPMI configurations and two Skip-Gram with Negative Sampling (SGNS) configurations. At the global level, we analyse dependency-relation centroids, control for lexical identity through within-lemma centring, and examine their alignment with part-of-speech (POS) distributions. At the local level, we evaluate cross-relation geometric consistency, cross-method agreement, lexical similarity, and polysemous usages. Results show that global geometry is structured strongly by context POS across all representations. Locally, broader lexical similarity structures are partially preserved across dependency relations, while immediate neighbourhoods vary substantially, highlighting different usages. PPMI-based representations exhibit greater cross-relation consistency than SGNS-based representations, with cross-method agreement varying by relation. These findings reveal systematic linguistic organisation at multiple geometric scales and its sensitivity to representation choices.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes the global and local geometric organization of dependency-conditioned lexical embeddings trained on WikiText-103, finding that global geometry aligns with part-of-speech distributions and PPMI representations show greater cross-relation consistency than SGNS.
AI.motivation: Although dependency-based distributional models capture syntactically informed lexical similarities, the geometric organization of dependency-conditioned lexical representations remains underexplored.
AI.method: The authors train four representations on WikiText-103 (two count-based PPMI and two SGNS configurations) and analyze global dependency-relation centroids (controlling for lexical identity via within-lemma centering and comparing to POS distributions) as well as local cross-relation consistency, cross-method agreement, lexical similarity, and polysemous usages.
AI.result: Global geometry is strongly structured by context POS across all representations; locally, broader lexical similarity structures are partially preserved across dependency relations while immediate neighborhoods vary substantially. PPMI-based representations exhibit greater cross-relation consistency than SGNS-based ones, with cross-method agreement varying by relation.
AI.conclusion: Dependency-conditioned embeddings exhibit systematic linguistic organization across multiple geometric scales that is sensitive to the underlying representation method.

title: Many Solutions, One Answer: Search Order Shapes the Default Solutions of Language Models
summary: When a constraint puzzle has several correct answers, language models tend to give the same this http URL study four open-weight models from three families on symbolic puzzles and multi-solution ZebraLogic variants with exactly known solution this http URL samples concentrate on one default solution far beyond uniform sampling, and different models often share this http URL models usually produce even rarely sampled solutions when added clues uniquely identify this http URL held-out symbolic puzzles, we compare visiting entities in name order with visiting those with the fewest initial candidates first. Both searches try values in the stated order. Where their pre-specified predictions differ, the latter matches a larger share of responses in all four models, by 26 to 40 percentage this http URL the stated value order or specifying a search order shifts responses towards the solution that the new order favours, on both testbeds. Randomising the presentation or supplying a random search order raises breadth (the effective share of solutions in use) by 26 to 42 percentage points on the symbolic task and 11 to 26 on ZebraLogic.
