The largest observed validity losses are 3 and 4 percentage points, respectively. Randomised presentation broadens answers more than a random-choice instruction in each of the three main models.

AI.tldr: Language models concentrate on a single default solution in multi-solution constraint puzzles because their outputs reflect implicit search orders, and randomizing presentation or search order substantially increases solution diversity with minimal validity loss.
AI.motivation: When constraint puzzles have multiple valid answers, LLMs repeatedly produce the same default solution, limiting output diversity even across different model families.
AI.method: The authors evaluate four open-weight models from three families on symbolic puzzles and multi-solution ZebraLogic variants with known solution sets, comparing name-order versus fewest-initial-candidates-first search predictions, and testing randomized presentation and random search-order instructions.
AI.result: Fewest-candidates-first predictions match a larger share of model responses than name order by 26 to 40 percentage points where they differ. Randomizing presentation or specifying a random search order raises solution breadth by 26 to 42 percentage points on the symbolic task and 11 to 26 on ZebraLogic, with maximum validity losses of 3 and 4 percentage points respectively.
AI.conclusion: LLM default solutions in constraint puzzles are shaped by implicit search orders, and randomizing presentation order broadens solution diversity more effectively than random-choice instructions.

title: Web search in Latin America: language models use less local and diverse news than search engines
summary: AI platforms are becoming a major gateway to news and current events. This shift risks amplifying existing geographical biases that favour narratives from wealthier countries over those from the Global South. This is particularly relevant in Latin America, which accounts for the largest share of AI usage in the Global South. We examine how information about Latin America changes when users shift from conventional search engines to LLM-based search. We construct a dataset of 1,901 current events across nine Latin American countries, craft realistic queries, and submit them to three search engines and four language models. We vary query language and user location to represent local, diaspora, tourist, and foreign user scenarios. Across 49,207 requests and 8,834 unique domains, language models return a less diverse set of news sources than search engines. Across user types, the share of domestic news returned by language models is inconsistent. For local users, while search engines already return only 41.3\% local news, language models return a further 3.6 to 11.6 percentage points less. Taken together, our findings suggest that LLM-based search can reproduce and, in some settings, amplify geographical hierarchies in the reach and visibility of news sources. We release an open dataset to support multilingual and geographically diverse evaluation of LLM-based search, and highlight implications for more equitable information systems design.

AI.tldr: Evaluating 49,207 requests across nine Latin American countries, this study shows that LLM-based search returns less diverse news sources and fewer local news outlets than conventional search engines.
AI.motivation: As AI platforms become a primary gateway to current events, there is a risk of amplifying geographical biases that favor wealthier nations over the Global South, particularly in Latin America.
AI.method: The authors construct a dataset of 1,901 current events across nine Latin American countries and submit queries varying language and user location (local, diaspora, tourist, foreign) to three search engines and four language models, analyzing 49,207 requests and 8,834 unique domains.
AI.result: Language models return a less diverse set of news sources than search engines overall, and for local users, where search engines return 41.3% local news, language models return 3.6 to 11.6 percentage points less.
AI.conclusion: LLM-based search can reproduce and amplify geographical hierarchies in news visibility, highlighting the need for more equitable information systems and multilingual, geographically diverse evaluation.

title: The Depth of a Prediction: Where Language Models Resolve a Word Predicts Human Reading Time
summary: Surprisal from a language model's final layer predicts how long people read a word, yet the model computes its prediction across many layers. We read each word's prediction at every layer with the tuned lens and summarize this layerwise surprisal trajectory by its resolution depth, the depth around which its change is centered. On eight English eye-tracking and self-paced reading corpora (81,957 words) and ten GPT-2, OPT and Pythia models, words that a model resolves later, and the words after them, are read more slowly than equally surprising words. Resolution depth improves held-out prediction beyond final-layer surprisal, entropy and the best single layer by 0.26 millinats per word (pooled p = 0.001), about a third of entropy's gain, and each model family gains, GPT-2 and Pythia through one corpus each. The net gain varies between corpora (random-effects mean 0.07, p = 0.37); against layer-shuffled depth, which adds as many coefficients, it is positive in seven of eight corpora (random-effects mean 0.23, p = 0.016), and untrained networks show no gain under the logit lens. Pooled over corpora, the effect holds with corrected word probabilities and beyond first-to-last-layer divergences, and a whole-trajectory functional regression adds no significant information beyond resolution depth.

AI.tldr: The layer at which a language model resolves a word's prediction (resolution depth) predicts human reading times beyond final-layer surprisal, entropy, and the best single layer across eight English reading corpora.
AI.motivation: Final-layer surprisal predicts human reading time, but language models compute predictions across many layers, leaving open whether the internal layerwise trajectory carries additional cognitive signal.
AI.method: Using the tuned lens on ten GPT-2, OPT, and Pythia models, the authors summarize each word's layerwise surprisal trajectory by its resolution depth and test its predictive power for reading times on eight English eye-tracking and self-paced reading corpora (81,957 words).
AI.result: Words resolved later by a model (and subsequent words) are read more slowly than equally surprising words; resolution depth improves held-out prediction by 0.26 millinats per word (pooled p = 0.001) beyond final-layer surprisal, entropy, and the best single layer, and outperforms layer-shuffled depth in seven of eight corpora (random-effects mean 0.23, p = 0.016).
AI.conclusion: Where a language model resolves a prediction across its layers captures processing difficulty in human reading beyond what final-layer metrics or whole-trajectory regressions provide.

title: Energy estimates of open-weight large language models across stated food weights: a dose-response evaluation
comment: 18 pages, 4 figures, 4 tables; supplementary material and TRIPOD-LLM checklist as ancillary files
summary: We tested whether energy estimates of open-weight large language models (LLMs) scale proportionally with an exactly stated food weight, and whether computing energy density times weight removes the error. Under a prespecified protocol, seven open-weight LLMs estimated the energy of 168 randomly drawn foods from the USDA Food and Nutrient Database for Dietary Studies at nine stated weights, from 0.25 to 4 times the default amount. The primary outcome was the elasticity of the estimate with respect to weight (1: proportional scaling). A two-step estimate multiplied each model's own stated energy density by the weight in code. All seven models compressed their estimates, with elasticities from 0.548 to 0.979 (every 95% CI below 1); four compressed severely (0.548 to 0.709). These four overestimated a quarter of the default amount by 47% to 130% and underestimated four times it by 20% to 34%. Supplying the density restored near-proportional scaling in three of the four, and the two-step estimate cut the typical error factor at these extremes from 1.47-2.43 to 1.20-1.38. Compression persisted at full precision and grew in five of seven models under a plain question. The models hold the energy densities needed for proportional scaling and answer near a typical serving, reproducing the flat-slope syndrome of dietary recall. Accuracy at usual portions does not reveal it. Food-logging tools should compute the energy of weighed entries as density times weight, and evaluations should test fixed foods across stated weights.

AI.tldr: Seven open-weight LLMs fail to scale food energy estimates proportionally with stated weights, compressing estimates at extreme portions, though multiplying the model's own stated energy density by weight in code largely removes this error.
AI.motivation: If LLMs are used for dietary logging or nutrition estimation, their energy estimates must scale proportionally with stated food weights rather than anchoring to typical serving sizes.
AI.method: Under a prespecified protocol, seven open-weight LLMs estimated the energy of 168 USDA foods across nine stated weights (0.25x to 4x default), measuring weight elasticity (1 = proportional) and comparing against a two-step code calculation multiplying each model's stated energy density by weight.
AI.result: All seven models compressed their estimates with elasticities between 0.548 and 0.979 (all 95% CIs below 1); four compressed severely (0.548 to 0.709), overestimating 0.25x portions by 47% to 130% and underestimating 4x portions by 20% to 34%. The two-step density-times-weight calculation cut typical error factors at extremes from 1.47-2.43 to 1.20-1.38.
AI.conclusion: LLMs possess accurate energy densities but anchor estimates near typical servings, so food-logging tools should compute energy as density times weight in code and evaluations should test across varied weights.

title: Xing-Audio-NVVASR: Scaling and Refining Supervision for Joint Recognition of Speech and Non-Verbal Vocalizations
summary: Joint recognition of speech and non-verbal vocalizations (NVVs) is hindered by scarce event-rich training data and inaccurate or missing event labels. We present Xing-Audio-NVVASR, an end-to-end recognizer trained through progressive data mining and iterative supervision refinement. Guided by unified acoustic criteria, two heterogeneous models cross-audit annotations, flagging disagreements for teacher reannotation. To uncover shared omissions that model agreement may conceal, complementary breath detectors screen the entire corpus for human review. Human-confirmed labels accumulate across rounds and are preserved during subsequent refinement. Over five rounds, we refine annotations for 170,000 utterances from public corpora and incorporate 630,000 mined utterances. The resulting corpus of approximately 800,000 utterances is used to train a single 1.7B-parameter model that transcribes speech with inline tags for six NVV classes. Across four human-annotated benchmarks, Xing-Audio-NVVASR ranks first among nine models in both composite score and six-class Macro-F1. It achieves a mean composite score of 64.46, surpassing the strongest comparison model, StepAudio 3 Chat Preview, by 6.03 points, and exceeds the annotation teacher's breathing F1 by 14.40 to 31.57 percentage points. We plan to release the model weights, inference code, four evaluation benchmarks, annotation guidelines, and evaluation code.

AI.tldr: Xing-Audio-NVVASR is a 1.7B-parameter end-to-end model for joint speech and non-verbal vocalization (NVV) recognition trained on an 800,000-utterance corpus built via progressive mining and iterative cross-model annotation refinement. It ranks first among nine models across four benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Joint recognition of speech and non-verbal vocalizations is limited by scarce event-rich training data and noisy or missing event labels.
AI.method: Two heterogeneous models cross-audit annotations under unified acoustic criteria to flag disagreements for teacher reannotation, while complementary breath detectors screen the corpus for human review; over five rounds, 170,000 public utterances are refined and 630,000 mined utterances are added to train a 1.7B-parameter model with inline tags for six NVV classes.
AI.result: Across four human-annotated benchmarks, Xing-Audio-NVVASR ranks first among nine models in composite score (mean 64.46, beating StepAudio 3 Chat Preview by 6.03 points) and six-class Macro-F1, and exceeds the annotation teacher's breathing F1 by 14.40 to 31.57 percentage points.
AI.conclusion: Iterative cross-model auditing and targeted human-in-the-loop mining substantially improve supervision quality and joint speech-NVV recognition performance.

title: Evaluating safeguarding in multi-turn conversations with AI assistants
summary: Conversational AI assistants are now used for personal and emotional support. Developers report improvements in how new models respond to sensitive conversations, yet users and civil society continue to raise concerns about their behaviour in real-world, repeated interactions that safety evaluations rarely capture. Often, evaluations present signs of distress clearly and in a single message, even though people may reveal their struggles gradually in otherwise ordinary conversations. We worked with three community mental health support workers to test if models provide the same level of safeguarding when cues are shared all at once or gradually over time. We designed nine scenarios in which a user shares cues related to depression, psychosis, or domestic abuse. For each scenario, the support workers established a gold standard response, ranging from signposting support to pausing the everyday task to address safeguarding. We presented five cues either together in one message or dispersed across a conversation. Across more than 7,400 conversations, we evaluated six widely used models from five developers. GPT-5.5, Grok 4.3, DeepSeek V4, and Llama 4 Maverick met the support workers' standards in just 26-59% of conversations when cues were concentrated, and only 3-6% when dispersed. Claude Sonnet 5 and Claude Opus 5 showed a smaller gap, meeting the standards in 68-97% of concentrated conversations and 59-87% of dispersed conversations. Even the best-performing model, Claude Opus 5, fell short of the gold standard in 13% of conversations when cues were dispersed. Safety evaluations centred on explicit, legible concerns can overstate how well safeguards protect people when signs of distress emerge gradually or indirectly through ordinary conversations. For claims of improved safety to be taken seriously, developers must design and assess safeguards around how people actually communicate.

AI.tldr: Evaluating six frontier AI assistants across over 7,400 multi-turn conversations, this study finds that most models' safeguarding performance drops sharply when mental health or abuse cues are dispersed gradually rather than presented in a single message.
AI.motivation: Safety evaluations typically present explicit distress signals in one message, whereas real users often reveal depression, psychosis, or domestic abuse cues gradually across ordinary multi-turn conversations.
AI.method: Working with three community mental health support workers, the authors designed nine scenarios with gold-standard safeguarding responses and presented five cues either concentrated in one message or dispersed across a conversation, evaluating six models from five developers across more than 7,400 conversations.
AI.result: GPT-5.5, Grok 4.3, DeepSeek V4, and Llama 4 Maverick met gold-standard safeguarding in 26-59% of concentrated conversations but only 3-6% when cues were dispersed. Claude Sonnet 5 and Claude Opus 5 achieved 68-97% on concentrated and 59-87% on dispersed conversations, with Opus 5 still missing 13% of dispersed cases.
AI.conclusion: Single-message safety evaluations overstate real-world safeguarding, and developers must design and test safeguards for gradual, indirect distress cues across multi-turn interactions.

title: SheetAlign: Grounded Interaction and Stage-Isolated Learning for Spreadsheet Agents
summary: Spreadsheets are widely used for data analysis and supporting decision-making. Automating spreadsheet analysis while protecting sensitive data and controlling deployment costs motivates locally deployed open-weight large language models (LLMs). Meanwhile, complex spreadsheet tasks require both task reasoning and workbook understanding, while predefined operation interfaces impose additional tool-selection and invocation demands. We introduce SheetAlign, a spreadsheet manipulation framework with stage-isolated policy learning, organized around where to operate, what to change, and how to implement transformations. Task-guided inspection and API grounding anchor code generation in workbook observations and available operations, while stage-isolated learning optimizes program generation and review using edit-progress rewards. At inference, execution consistency selects programs through agreement among workbook states. On SpreadsheetBench, our grounded task interface improves Qwen3-4B's accuracy from 13.5% to 29.2% on average without training. With learning and execution consistency, SheetAlign achieves 32.8% accuracy on average on SpreadsheetBench and 30.1% on Domain-Spreadsheet, outperforming comparable baselines. The code will be made publicly available upon publication.

AI.tldr: SheetAlign is a spreadsheet manipulation framework using grounded task interfaces, stage-isolated policy learning, and execution consistency to improve open-weight LLMs on SpreadsheetBench and Domain-Spreadsheet.
AI.motivation: Automating spreadsheet analysis with locally deployed open-weight LLMs is challenging because complex tasks require workbook understanding, task reasoning, and accurate tool invocation under predefined operation interfaces.
AI.method: SheetAlign organizes manipulation around where to operate, what to change, and how to implement transformations, combining task-guided inspection and API grounding with stage-isolated policy learning using edit-progress rewards and inference-time execution consistency.
AI.result: On SpreadsheetBench, the grounded task interface alone raises Qwen3-4B accuracy from 13.5% to 29.2% without training; with learning and execution consistency, SheetAlign reaches 32.8% average accuracy on SpreadsheetBench and 30.1% on Domain-Spreadsheet, outperforming comparable baselines.
AI.conclusion: Grounding code generation in workbook observations and isolating learning stages enables smaller open-weight LLMs to perform reliable spreadsheet manipulation.

title: AltRA-Test: An Alternative Annotator Test for LLM Judges Without Shared Annotators
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as judges and graders to replace human annotators, raising the question of when such replacement is statistically justified. To support such decisions, the Alternative Annotator Test (Alt-Test) was introduced for dense settings where all items are annotated by the same annotators. However, in many large-scale annotation settings, items are annotated by different subsets of annotators. We therefore propose the Alternative Annotator Test with Resampled Annotations (AltRA-Test), a statistical test that does not require that all items are annotated by the same annotators. AltRA-Test uses a bootstrap that resamples items, draws k human annotations for each item, and substitutes one of them with an LLM annotation. This produces paired all-human and mixed human-LLM panels. A replacement is supported when the inter-annotator agreement (IAA) of the mixed panel is statistically non-inferior to the IAA of the all-human panel, i.e., when the LLM preserves the signal that the human annotators share. We establish that AltRA-Test is a consistent test of asymptotic level alpha. We then evaluate it through simulations and real-world experiments in which we test 18 LLMs and 5 prompting techniques on 20 datasets across text, image, audio, and video. Across these evaluations, about 100 items often suffice for the test. In simulations, where we know whether the LLM is a better or a worse annotator than the humans, AltRA-Test makes more correct replacement decisions than existing baselines. In real-world data experiments, LLMs pass the test in about half of the setups, depending mainly on the task. Since replacement is not always justified, we encourage researchers to test it for their task.

AI.tldr: AltRA-Test is a bootstrap-based statistical test for deciding whether an LLM judge can replace human annotators when items are annotated by different subsets of humans, outperforming existing baselines in simulations and evaluating 18 LLMs across 20 datasets.
AI.motivation: The existing Alternative Annotator Test (Alt-Test) requires all items to be annotated by the same human annotators, which does not hold in many large-scale annotation settings with sparse or disjoint annotator subsets.
AI.method: AltRA-Test resamples items via bootstrap, draws k human annotations per item, and substitutes one with an LLM annotation to compare the inter-annotator agreement (IAA) of the mixed panel against the all-human panel for statistical non-inferiority.
AI.result: Established as a consistent test of asymptotic level alpha, AltRA-Test often requires only about 100 items, makes more correct replacement decisions than baselines in simulations, and shows in real-world experiments (18 LLMs, 5 prompting techniques, 20 datasets) that LLMs pass the test in roughly half of setups depending on the task.
AI.conclusion: AltRA-Test extends statistically grounded LLM-judge validation to sparse annotation settings, demonstrating that LLM replacement is task-dependent and should be empirically tested.

title: Understanding MoE Decisions Beyond Gradients
summary: Understanding a language model's decision requires knowing how its internal computations affect its preference between answers. Gradient-based methods estimate this influence by predicting the effect of changing those computations. In mixture-of-experts (MoE) models, replacing one expert can change which experts later layers select. Those switches can alter the answer scores in ways that derivatives do not capture. We introduce a predictor that uses the model's own expert outputs and selection rules to estimate these extra effects, then adds them to a second-order prediction. Across questions from three benchmarks, our method reduces the error in predicting answer-score changes by 60\% on Qwen3.6 and 47\% on Gemma4, relative to a multistep baseline using gradients and second derivatives.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a predictor for Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models that accounts for discrete expert-selection switches across layers, reducing answer-score prediction error by 60% on Qwen3.6 and 47% on Gemma4 compared to gradient-based baselines.
AI.motivation: Gradient-based attribution methods fail to capture non-differentiable routing changes in MoE models, where replacing one expert can alter which experts subsequent layers select.
AI.method: The proposed predictor uses the model's own expert outputs and selection rules to estimate the effects of routing switches and adds them to a second-order gradient-based prediction.
AI.result: Across three benchmarks, the method reduces error in predicting answer-score changes by 60% on Qwen3.6 and 47% on Gemma4 relative to a multistep baseline using gradients and second derivatives.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly modeling discrete expert-routing transitions is essential for accurately attributing and predicting internal computation effects in MoE language models.

title: Same Judgement, Different Scores: Numerical Scoring Topology in LLM-as-a-Judge Evaluation
summary: LLMs are increasingly used as automated evaluators to reduce the cost and time required for human annotation. However, the role of scoring-scheme design in the reliability of LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation remains underexplored. To address this problem, we introduce numerical scoring topology, which characterizes the structural design of a scoring scheme in terms of its scale width, granularity, offset, symmetry, and boundary placement. Building on this definition, we conduct the first systematic study of how numerical scoring topology influences zero-shot LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation across diverse benchmarks and judge models. Our results show that numerical scoring topology systematically affects judge scores, calibration, and robustness, particularly in judgment-intensive evaluations. Shifted and narrow ranges tend to induce some of the largest score deviations across many settings. We further find that stronger and larger judge models generally achieve higher discriminative validity and greater robustness to scoring-topology changes. These findings suggest that numerical scoring topology should be treated as an integral component of LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation and highlight the need for more principled and standardized scoring protocols.

AI.tldr: This study introduces numerical scoring topology to systematically evaluate how scoring-scheme design affects zero-shot LLM-as-a-Judge evaluations, finding that shifted and narrow ranges cause large score deviations while larger, stronger judges are more robust.
AI.motivation: Although LLMs are widely used as automated evaluators, how the structural design of the numerical scoring scale itself affects judge reliability, calibration, and robustness has not been systematically studied.
AI.method: The authors define numerical scoring topology in terms of scale width, granularity, offset, symmetry, and boundary placement, and conduct a systematic study across diverse benchmarks and zero-shot LLM judge models.
AI.result: Numerical scoring topology systematically alters judge scores, calibration, and robustness, especially in judgment-intensive tasks, with shifted and narrow ranges inducing some of the largest deviations; stronger and larger judge models show higher discriminative validity and greater robustness to topology changes.
AI.conclusion: Scoring-scheme topology is a critical factor in LLM-as-a-Judge reliability and requires principled, standardized scoring protocols.

title: Frontier models need only one text to unmask its human or AI author
summary: Given a single text and a simple zero-shot prompt (no web access, tools, candidate lists, or writing samples), frontier models can answer "who wrote this?" at three increasingly specific levels: (1) whether an AI or human wrote it, (2) if an AI, which lab, and (3) if a human, often exactly who. The latest models (Claude Fable 5.2, GPT-6.1 Sol, Gemini 4 Carbon) match trained detectors like Pangram while also explaining their predictions in natural language, and Opus 5.5 names the correct lab for 98% of texts generated by models from Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google. Most strikingly, Fable 5.2 correctly names the author of 39% of public peer reviews published in Oct-Nov 2026 (78% on a subset of reviews from Nature), and identifies the username behind 69% of comments from active Redditors (with >500 posts over the last year). Accuracy depends on exposure to an author's writing in pretraining data and on reasoning effort, and simply asking a model how familiar it is with someone predicts whether it can identify their writing. For anyone who has published enough writing online, frontier models present a greater threat to anonymity than commonly assumed, and defenses are limited.

AI.tldr: Frontier models (Claude Fable 5.2, GPT-6.1 Sol, Gemini 4 Carbon) can identify whether a single text was written by AI or a human, which AI lab produced it, and often the exact human author zero-shot without tools or reference samples.
AI.motivation: The extent to which frontier language models can deanonymize authors or attribute text origins from a single passage without external tools or candidate lists poses underappreciated privacy risks.
AI.method: The authors prompt frontier models zero-shot on a single text (with no web access, tools, candidate lists, or writing samples) to classify AI versus human authorship, identify the AI lab, and name the human author across public peer reviews and Reddit comments.
AI.result: Frontier models match trained detectors like Pangram while explaining predictions; Opus 5.5 identifies the correct AI lab for 98% of texts from Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google, and Fable 5.2 names the author of 39% of Oct-Nov 2026 public peer reviews (78% on a Nature subset) and 69% of active Redditors (>500 posts/year).
AI.conclusion: For anyone with sufficient online writing in pretraining data, frontier models pose a greater threat to anonymity than commonly assumed, with limited available defenses.

title: STAGE: Spatio-Temporal Augmented Graph Expansion for Weakly Supervised Cross-Tweet Event Causality Discovery
summary: Causal relations in disaster-related social media of- ten span independent posts, making cross-tweet causal discovery difficult to supervise and model at scale. We propose STAGE, a framework that separates scalable cross-tweet weak-supervision construction from spatio-temporal relational learning over event occurrences. Starting from local causal seeds, STAGE retrieves semantically related event occurrences across tweets and uses a causal scorer to construct weakly labeled cross-tweet pairs. These pairs supervise a multi-head Graph Attention Network over semantically enriched event representations and a spatio- temporal context graph. We evaluate STAGE on California Wildfire and Hurricane Harvey using human-gold cross-tweet test sets and 15 baselines. Compared with local-only supervision, the constructed cross-tweet supervision improves STAGE AUPRC by 0.340 on Wildfire and 0.107 on Hurricane. STAGE achieves in-domain AUROC of 0.885 on Wildfire and 0.710 on Hurricane. Cross-disaster experiments reveal asymmetric transfer, highlighting sensitivity to dataset-specific spatio-temporal shifts. These results demonstrate the value of scalable cross-tweet supervision combined with relational event modeling for causal learning across fragmented disaster reports.

AI.tldr: STAGE is a weakly supervised framework for cross-tweet event causality discovery that separates cross-tweet weak-supervision construction from spatio-temporal Graph Attention Network learning, achieving 0.885 AUROC on California Wildfire and 0.710 on Hurricane Harvey.
AI.motivation: Causal relations in disaster-related social media often span independent posts, making cross-tweet event causality difficult to supervise and model at scale.
AI.method: Starting from local causal seeds, STAGE retrieves semantically related event occurrences across tweets and uses a causal scorer to build weakly labeled cross-tweet pairs, which then supervise a multi-head Graph Attention Network over enriched event representations and a spatio-temporal context graph.
AI.result: Evaluated against 15 baselines on human-gold cross-tweet test sets, STAGE's cross-tweet supervision improves AUPRC over local-only supervision by 0.340 on California Wildfire (reaching 0.885 AUROC) and 0.107 on Hurricane Harvey (reaching 0.710 AUROC), while cross-disaster transfer is asymmetric.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling scalable cross-tweet weak supervision from spatio-temporal relational modeling effectively captures causal links across fragmented disaster reports.

title: dLoop: Looped Diffusion Language Models via Recurrent Latent Refinement
summary: Diffusion language models (DLMs) support parallel generation, yet they often require many denoising steps because only a fraction of token predictions are sufficiently reliable to be committed at each step. Existing acceleration methods primarily optimize confidence learning or commitment policies. However, these approaches operate on the outputs of a single denoising forward pass, in which information from the prompt, previously committed tokens, and uncommitted positions may not yet be fully integrated. Consequently, some predictions remain under-refined when the commitment decision is made, and modifying the commitment policy alone cannot improve their underlying representations. We introduce dLoop, which restructures a pretrained diffusion language model into a Prelude-Loop-Coda architecture and recurrently applies a parameter-shared intermediate block to the same partially masked state. Rather than advancing the denoising process, each additional loop provides further latent computation, allowing information distributed across uncommitted positions to continue interacting and become more fully integrated before commitment. Experiments on GSM8K, MATH, MBPP, and HumanEval show that dLoop achieves the highest or tied-highest accuracy on every benchmark. With tokens per forward pass (TPF) adjusted for loop computation, it outperforms Fast-dLLM in both accuracy and TPF on all four benchmarks and dParallel on three, and is more accurate than d3LLM on all four, while d3LLM attains higher TPF; no compared method surpasses dLoop in both. Mechanistic analyses show that extra loops mainly help on slow, unstable trajectories and that updates at uncommitted positions drive changes in token decisions and later generation. Pre-commitment latent computation thus makes predictions more reliable, offering a route to DLM acceleration distinct from forcing confidence through the training loss.

AI.tldr: dLoop restructures a pretrained diffusion language model into a Prelude-Loop-Coda architecture that recurrently refines latent representations of partially masked states before token commitment, outperforming Fast-dLLM in both accuracy and adjusted tokens per forward pass across four benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing DLM acceleration methods optimize confidence or commitment policies on single-pass outputs, where information across uncommitted positions may still be under-refined.
AI.method: dLoop reorganizes a pretrained DLM into a Prelude-Loop-Coda structure and recurrently applies a parameter-shared intermediate block to the same partially masked state, providing extra latent computation before commitment decisions.
AI.result: Across GSM8K, MATH, MBPP, and HumanEval, dLoop achieves the highest or tied-highest accuracy on every benchmark; with loop-adjusted tokens per forward pass (TPF), it outperforms Fast-dLLM in both accuracy and TPF on all four benchmarks, dParallel on three, and d3LLM in accuracy on all four (while d3LLM has higher TPF).
AI.conclusion: Pre-commitment recurrent latent computation makes DLM predictions more reliable, offering an effective acceleration path distinct from confidence-forcing training losses.

title: What If Chain-of-Thought Is Not Enough?
summary: Reasoning capabilities in large language models have evolved from prompting-based methods to internalized model behaviors. In this paper, we investigate whether the internal thinking model of an LLM can be deliberately changed and whether such a change is beneficial. Instead of relying on Chain-of-Thought, we train models to follow Question--Option--Criteria (QOC), a structured decision process that decomposes a task into explicit questions, competing options, and evaluation criteria. We present a three-generation development pipeline that ranges from a basic QOC decision core to richer answer synthesis and statistically enriched QOC reasoning. We then evaluate the resulting models with respect to both internal consistency and output quality. Across the reported experiments, QOC-based fine-tuning improves answer quality relative to non-fine-tuned base models and yields particularly strong gains once models are large enough to execute the underlying QOC computations reliably. The results suggest that the internal thinking model of an LLM is trainable and that structured alternatives to Chain-of-Thought can provide a promising path toward more reliable, interpretable, and task-adapted decision support.

AI.tldr: Training LLMs to follow Question-Option-Criteria (QOC) instead of Chain-of-Thought improves answer quality over base models, showing that an LLM's internal thinking model can be deliberately reshaped into a structured decision process.
AI.motivation: Reasoning in LLMs has shifted from prompting to internalized behaviors, raising the question of whether models can be trained to use structured alternatives to Chain-of-Thought.
AI.method: The authors train models on Question-Option-Criteria (QOC), which decomposes tasks into explicit questions, competing options, and evaluation criteria, using a three-generation pipeline from a basic QOC core to enriched synthesis and statistical QOC reasoning.
AI.result: QOC-based fine-tuning improves answer quality relative to non-fine-tuned base models, with particularly strong gains once models are large enough to execute the QOC computations reliably.
AI.conclusion: The internal thinking model of an LLM is trainable, and structured frameworks like QOC offer a promising path toward more reliable and interpretable decision support.

title: Twice-Told Critiques: Claim-Level Homogenization of Peer Review in the LLM Era
summary: Peer review relies on several readers finding different problems. We measure critique overlap in conference and journal reviews. At ICLR, measured overlap rose from 12.0% in 2026 to 21.3% in 2027, in reviews from the same stage of the review process, with year-on-year rises at NeurIPS, ICML and the F1000 and PLOS journals. A third ICLR review of a paper added 5.46 new problems to the other two in 2027, against 6.12 in 2026. We apply MELD, a detector of LLM-generated text, to all reviews. Within a paper, two reviews that MELD flags overlap more than two unflagged reviews: by 3.0 points at ICLR in 2024-2025, by 4.5 points in 2026-2027, and by 5.4 points across five journal sources. These results provide evidence that LLM-flagged reviews of one paper are less distinct from each other than unflagged reviews, and suggest that the diversity of critiques among reviews of a single paper is falling.

AI.tldr: Measuring claim-level critique overlap in peer reviews across ICLR, NeurIPS, ICML, F1000, and PLOS, this study finds rising year-on-year homogenization, with LLM-flagged reviews overlapping significantly more than unflagged reviews.
AI.motivation: Peer review depends on multiple readers independently identifying different problems, so increasing reliance on LLMs risks homogenizing critiques and reducing review diversity.
AI.method: The authors measure critique overlap within papers across conference and journal reviews and apply the MELD LLM-text detector to compare claim-level overlap between flagged and unflagged review pairs.
AI.result: At ICLR, same-stage critique overlap rose from 12.0% in 2026 to 21.3% in 2027 (with similar rises at NeurIPS, ICML, F1000, and PLOS), while a third ICLR review added 5.46 new problems in 2027 versus 6.12 in 2026; MELD-flagged review pairs overlap more than unflagged pairs by 3.0 points at ICLR (2024-2025), 4.5 points (2026-2027), and 5.4 points across five journals.
AI.conclusion: LLM-flagged reviews of the same paper are less distinct from one another, indicating a decline in critique diversity in the LLM era.

title: Language-Oriented Semantic Modeling for Target Language Extraction
summary: Target Language Extraction (TLE) aims to isolate speech in a target language from multilingual mixtures. Existing approaches primarily rely on acoustic modeling with language identity labels, which provide only coarse categorical guidance. In this work, we propose a language-oriented semantic modeling framework that augments acoustic extraction with language-specific semantic representations. A pre-trained speech semantic model is adapted via language-aware prompt conditioning and parameter-efficient fine-tuning to generate target-language-focused semantic representations from the mixture. {These capture high-level semantic structure of the acoustics and they} are integrated into the extraction model to provide structured semantic guidance beyond identity labels. Experiments on the CommonVoiceMix dataset show that incorporating semantic representations consistently improves over acoustic-only baselines, achieving up to 1.16 dB SI-SDR gain.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a language-oriented semantic modeling framework for Target Language Extraction (TLE) that adapts a pre-trained speech semantic model via language-aware prompt conditioning, achieving up to 1.16 dB SI-SDR gain over acoustic-only baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing Target Language Extraction methods rely primarily on acoustic modeling with coarse language identity labels, missing higher-level linguistic structure.
AI.method: A pre-trained speech semantic model is adapted with language-aware prompt conditioning and parameter-efficient fine-tuning to extract target-language-focused semantic representations from multilingual mixtures, which are then integrated into the extraction model.
AI.result: Experiments on the CommonVoiceMix dataset show that adding language-oriented semantic representations consistently outperforms acoustic-only baselines, achieving up to 1.16 dB SI-SDR improvement.
AI.conclusion: Conditioning pre-trained speech semantic models with language-aware prompts provides effective structured guidance beyond identity labels for isolating target-language speech.

title: One Framework to Diagnose Them All: A Stratified Benchmark for Bengali LLM Hallucination
comment: Accepted to Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EACL 2027, 25 pages, 8 figures, 23 tables. Code: this https URL | Data: this https URL | Competition: this https URL | Project page: this https URL
summary: Hallucination research in low-resource languages fragments easily: each newly named failure mode prompts its own dataset, spending scarce annotators on incomparable resources. We argue for consolidation and test it at community scale. Alikbachan is a Bengali hallucination-detection benchmark stratified along three crossed axes: a human-validated cultural-distance band, six task types, and a five-family, 32-mode hallucination taxonomy. It comprises a harvested 2,516-item test set (Phase 1) and a quota-constructed, gold-labeled 5,000-item set (Phase 2). The stratification is diagnostic. Four zero-shot LLM judges vary by over 30 macro-F1 points across strata, and the item-level predictions of 99 Phase-1 and 32 Phase-2 competition systems reproduce the profile: discourse-level omission defeats judges and most teams alike, whereas only a minority over-flag negative controls. The judges' verdict probabilities rank items well (ROC-AUC 0.74-0.95) but are overconfident (ECE 0.04-0.29). An open competition on Alikbachan drew 222 teams and 3,566 submissions, and a single-prompt 32B judge reaches the 57th percentile. Of the 25 teams in both phases, 24 regress on Phase 2 (mean $-17.6$ points) while every zero-shot judge improves, and Phase-1 rank barely predicts Phase-2 rank (Spearman $\rho=0.35$), so a Phase-1 leaderboard alone would have crowned a different winner.

AI.tldr: Alikbachan is a stratified Bengali hallucination-detection benchmark (2,516 Phase-1 and 5,000 Phase-2 items) across cultural distance, task types, and a 32-mode taxonomy, revealing that zero-shot LLM judges vary widely by stratum and Phase-1 competition ranks barely predict Phase-2 ranks.
AI.motivation: Hallucination research in low-resource languages is fragmented across incomparable, single-mode datasets that waste scarce annotation resources.
AI.method: The authors construct Alikbachan along three crossed axes (cultural-distance band, six task types, and a five-family, 32-mode hallucination taxonomy) and evaluate four zero-shot LLM judges alongside 99 Phase-1 and 32 Phase-2 competition systems from 222 teams.
AI.result: Zero-shot LLM judges vary by over 30 macro-F1 points across strata, struggle with discourse-level omission, and are overconfident (ECE 0.04-0.29 despite ROC-AUC 0.74-0.95); 24 of 25 teams in both phases regress on Phase 2 (mean -17.6 points) with Spearman rho = 0.35 between Phase-1 and Phase-2 ranks, while a single-prompt 32B judge reaches the 57th percentile.
AI.conclusion: Stratified benchmarks like Alikbachan expose diagnostic failure modes and leaderboard instability that unstratified or single-phase evaluations miss.

title: Beam Model Technical Report
summary: Beam is a sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model with 501.3B total parameters and 23.4B active parameters, specifically built and optimized for coding, reasoning, and agentic workloads. Beam delivers frontier level reasoning, while requiring 3-4x less inference compute than many models of its class. Pretrained on 23.8T diverse, curated, high-quality tokens, Beam features a 1M-token context window achieved through a novel two-stage midtraining phase, built on verifiable, correctness-anchored data. Post-training leveraged a large-scale, fully asynchronous reinforcement learning (RL) campaign across 10.5K GB300 GPUs, generating over 100M rollouts over 4 weeks of training. We believe this is one of the largest scale RL runs conducted by any open lab to date. Across our evaluation suite, capabilities continued to improve as we increased RL compute, with no sign of a plateau. Supported by deep hardware-model co-design, FP8/NVFP4 quantization, and a 1.93B-parameter speculative decoding drafter (DFlash 2), Beam maximizes serving throughput with efficient, flexible deployment. Averaged across conversation turns and harm categories, Beam refuses or pivots on 88.9% of harmful requests while complying with 81.5% of harmless requests, achieving the highest refusal/pivot rate on harmful requests among open-weight models on the Pareto frontier.

AI.tldr: Beam is a 501.3B-total (23.4B-active) sparse MoE model with a 1M-token context window trained on 23.8T tokens and over 100M RL rollouts, delivering frontier-level coding, reasoning, and agentic performance with 3-4x less inference compute.
AI.motivation: Delivering frontier-level reasoning, coding, and agentic capabilities while keeping inference compute and serving throughput practical requires joint model, data, and hardware co-design.
AI.method: Pretrained on 23.8T tokens with a two-stage midtraining phase for a 1M-token context window, Beam undergoes asynchronous RL across 10.5K GB300 GPUs (>100M rollouts over 4 weeks) and uses FP8/NVFP4 quantization plus a 1.93B-parameter speculative decoding drafter (DFlash 2).
AI.result: Beam requires 3-4x less inference compute than comparable models, shows no capability plateau with increased RL compute, and refuses or pivots on 88.9% of harmful requests while complying with 81.5% of harmless requests, placing it on the open-weight safety Pareto frontier.
AI.conclusion: Large-scale asynchronous RL combined with sparse MoE architecture and hardware-model co-design achieves frontier reasoning and strong safety-helpfulness trade-offs at substantially lower serving cost.

title: MemFolder: Structure-Guided Memory Folding for Efficient Agent Memory Management
comment: Code is available at this https URL
summary: Long-term agents accumulate large external memory stores as interactions unfold, increasing the costs of storage, retrieval, and response generation. Efficiency is constrained by two coupled factors: a growing record count increases retrieval overhead, while longer retrieved contexts increase prefill computation and decoding-time attention costs. Existing methods prune or consolidate records, but pruning can discard useful evidence, whereas consolidation may produce fewer yet longer retrieval units. We introduce MemFolder, a structure-guided memory folding framework that sequentially reduces record count and context length. The framework comprises two core components that share memory groups, using cross-record structure to guide both evidence consolidation and compact representation. RecordFolder grounds entity mentions, progressively selects representative yet complementary anchors, and combines semantic and entity affinity with temporal chaining to consolidate compatible records into fewer retrieval units. ContextFolder encodes the original records within these groups into compact text and uses verification feedback to revise encodings when key facts cannot be recovered. Experiments on the three text-based memory benchmarks LoCoMo, PersonaMem, and LongMemEval and the two multimodal benchmarks M3-Bench-web and M3-Bench-robot demonstrate the strong performance of our methods. Notably, on Mem0, RecordFolder retains 99.0% of the original average performance across the three text-based benchmarks with 50% fewer records, exceeding the strongest baseline by 1.9 percentage points in performance retention. Combined with ContextFolder, existing record compression methods further shorten their output records while retaining most of their performance.

AI.tldr: MemFolder is a structure-guided memory folding framework that sequentially reduces external agent memory record count and context length, retaining 99.0% of Mem0's average performance on three text benchmarks with 50% fewer records.
AI.motivation: Long-term agents accumulate large external memories that inflate retrieval, prefill, and attention costs, while existing pruning drops useful evidence and consolidation can yield fewer but longer retrieval units.
AI.method: MemFolder pairs RecordFolder, which grounds entities and consolidates compatible records via semantic/entity affinity and temporal chaining, with ContextFolder, which compresses grouped records into compact text using verification feedback to preserve key facts.
AI.result: Evaluated on LoCoMo, PersonaMem, LongMemEval, M3-Bench-web, and M3-Bench-robot, RecordFolder retains 99.0% of Mem0's original average performance across the three text benchmarks with 50% fewer records (1.9 percentage points above the strongest baseline), and ContextFolder further shortens compressed records while preserving performance.
AI.conclusion: Structure-guided consolidation followed by verification-backed compression effectively cuts both retrieval and context-length overhead in long-term agent memory.

title: Multimodal Error Detection in Chest X-ray Reports: A Large Language Model Reading Image Evidence
summary: Rad-Linter checks chest X-ray reports against image-derived evidence to flag potential errors for review. A pretrained image classifier supplies scores for nine pathologies, and a 1.5B-parameter language model, fine-tuned with LoRA on 1,816 examples, checks their consistency with the report. We compare it with a keyword-and-negation rule baseline given the same reports and scores. Evaluation uses controlled report-score pairings from OpenI, with consistency labels derived from automatic report labels and score thresholds. Each counterfactual quad crosses two real reports with two real score vectors from other patients, creating two consistent and two inconsistent pairs. Every report and score vector occurs in both conditions, so either input alone permits only 50% accuracy. On 131 quads, Rad-Linter achieves 98.5% pair accuracy versus 80.5% for the rule baseline, and classifies all four pairs correctly in 94.4% of quads versus 56.5%. The checkers perform similarly on omission items, including unmentioned and negated findings; larger differences occur on the remaining item types, which require interpreting how findings are described. The same language model without fine-tuning remains near 50% accuracy. On a second set of 181 quads that also includes reports on which the automatic labelers disagree, pair accuracy is 93.4% versus 75.3%. These controlled results show that, given the same image-derived scores, a trained language model detects report-score inconsistencies more accurately than the tested rule baseline, with the advantage concentrated in interpreting how findings are worded.

AI.tldr: Rad-Linter, a 1.5B-parameter LLM fine-tuned with LoRA on 1,816 examples, detects inconsistencies between chest X-ray reports and image-derived pathology scores with 98.5% pair accuracy on controlled OpenI quads, outperforming a rule-based baseline (80.5%).
AI.motivation: Automated verification of radiology reports against image evidence requires interpreting nuanced wording of findings rather than relying solely on keyword matching and negation rules.
AI.method: A pretrained image classifier produces scores for nine pathologies, and a LoRA-fine-tuned 1.5B LLM (Rad-Linter) checks report-score consistency against a keyword-and-negation baseline using counterfactual quads from OpenI where each report and score vector appears in both consistent and inconsistent pairs.
AI.result: On 131 quads, Rad-Linter achieves 98.5% pair accuracy and 94.4% quad-level accuracy versus 80.5% and 56.5% for the rule baseline (while the un-tuned LLM stays near 50%); on 181 quads including labeler-disagreement cases, pair accuracy is 93.4% versus 75.3%.
AI.conclusion: Fine-tuned small LLMs substantially outperform rule-based checkers in detecting report-image inconsistencies, particularly when interpreting how clinical findings are phrased.

title: AutoMaster: Autonomous Post-Training by Making the Same Model a Better Teacher
comment: Website: this https URL Code: this https URL Models: this https URL
summary: Task success alone does not specify which behaviors post-training should reinforce. Even successful teacher trajectories can contain unsupported assumptions, unproductive repetition, or superficial verification. We propose Skill-FT (Skill-Guided Fine-Tuning), which uses natural-language skills to suppress undesirable habits and elicit underrepresented effective behaviors during teacher rollouts, then fine-tunes a target model on the resulting trajectories. We introduce AutoMaster, an autonomous post-training system in which an LLM agent develops these interventions through trajectory analysis, skill design, data selection, and feedback from rollouts and target-model evaluation. Across Terminal, Search, and software engineering tasks with 4B and 9B target models, AutoMaster improves mean performance over Vanilla SFT on successful unguided teacher trajectories by 1.42-8.99 percentage points, with the teacher, task pool, training set size, and SFT recipe held fixed. Together with the ablations and trajectory analyses, these results suggest that behavioral shaping can make a fixed model a more effective teacher. We further find that retaining skill instructions during SFT yields higher mean performance than removing them across all six settings, despite their absence at evaluation and identical supervised outputs. These findings suggest that preserving skill context as part of a training demonstration can support better behavioral internalization.

AI.tldr: AutoMaster is an autonomous post-training system using Skill-Guided Fine-Tuning (Skill-FT) to suppress bad teacher habits and elicit effective behaviors, improving 4B and 9B target models by 1.42-8.99 percentage points over Vanilla SFT.
AI.motivation: Even successful teacher trajectories in post-training can contain unsupported assumptions, repetition, or superficial verification, so task success alone does not specify which behaviors should be reinforced.
AI.method: AutoMaster uses an LLM agent to analyze trajectories, design natural-language skills, select data, and run feedback loops; Skill-FT applies these skills during teacher rollouts to shape behavior and retains the skill instructions during SFT on the target model.
AI.result: Across Terminal, Search, and software engineering tasks with 4B and 9B target models, AutoMaster improves mean performance by 1.42 to 8.99 percentage points over Vanilla SFT on unguided teacher trajectories, and retaining skill instructions during SFT outperforms removing them across all six settings.
AI.conclusion: Behavioral shaping via natural-language skills makes a fixed teacher more effective and helps target models internalize better habits when skill context is preserved during training.

title: Represented but misread: Post-training changes how language models read out what they represent
summary: Does post-training change what a language model represents, or how this representation is read out into an answer? We compared linear probes with the models' own answers, analyzed with signal detection theory, in six open-weight base models and their post-trained versions. For judgments of whether German texts were written by a human or an AI, probes and word n-gram classifiers separated the classes well, but the answers did not and often ordered the texts inversely. Post-training lowered the sensitivity of the answers on average ($\Delta d' = -0.34$ across model families; -0.29 across three prompts). It also changed the use of a stated base rate: Base models shifted their log-odds by less than the stated change in prior odds, most post-trained models by more. In two models with stage-wise checkpoints, the change occurred during supervised fine-tuning, model stitching implicated the early layers, and from mid-depth on internal states at positions after the text, not those of the text, transferred the change between checkpoints. Our corpora cannot be shared, so we add a case reproducible from public data, the truth of negated statements. Here, post-training acted in the opposite direction: Probes decoded truth at or near ceiling in every model, the answers of several base models did not use it, and post-training repaired them; by mid-depth the repair resided at the positions after the statement; below it, the representation of the statement contributed, strongly in one of four models. In a training study, adding 2,000 correctly labeled authorship judgments of news texts to otherwise identical fine-tuning data improved the answers on our newspaper and textbook corpora and inverted them on the chats, where they followed a news-trained probe of the base model. Post-training thus changed how a judgment is read out of what a model represents, and a small training signal can set its direction.

AI.tldr: Comparing linear probes with model answers across six open-weight models, this study shows that post-training (specifically SFT) alters how models read out internal representations into answers rather than what they represent.
AI.motivation: It is unclear whether post-training changes the underlying representations inside a language model or merely changes how those representations are read out into final answers.
AI.method: Using signal detection theory, linear probes, model stitching, and a controlled fine-tuning study, the authors compare six open-weight base models and their post-trained counterparts on German human-vs-AI authorship judgments, base-rate sensitivity, and truth of negated statements.
AI.result: On German authorship, probes separated classes well while post-training lowered answer sensitivity (Delta d' = -0.34) and altered prior-odds shifts; conversely, on negated-statement truth, post-training repaired base-model answers where probes were already near ceiling. Model stitching traced these SFT-driven shifts to early layers and post-text positions from mid-depth onward, and adding 2,000 labeled news examples flipped chat-corpus answers.
AI.conclusion: Post-training primarily modifies the readout of existing internal representations, and a small fine-tuning signal can set the direction of that readout.

title: A Model of Diverse Sampling from Language Models
summary: Language models often produce high-quality individual samples but poor sets, with repeated samples clustering around the same semantic modes. We formalize diverse generation as sampling a size-$K$ subset of complete strings from a determinantal point process (DPP), where the likelihood encodes item quality, and the embedding geometry encodes repulsion between similar outputs. Exact inference over all strings is intractable, so we propose PoolDPP: draw a finite candidate pool from a tractable proposal, importance-weight the candidates toward the target quality, and run a $K$-DPP sampler on the induced pool kernel; a greedy MAP variant provides deterministic selection. We prove a finite-sample bound with an explicit constant: the KL divergence between the sampler's output and the target $K$-DPP decays as O(1/N) in the pool size. Empirically, PoolDPP extends the quality--diversity frontier on open-ended generation and the precision--recall frontier on ambiguous text-to-SQL (Ambrosia), and on mathematical reasoning (GSM8K), it raises diversity at about the same pass@$K$.

AI.tldr: PoolDPP formalizes diverse LLM generation as sampling a K-subset from a determinantal point process (DPP) over a finite importance-weighted candidate pool, proving an O(1/N) KL-divergence bound and improving quality-diversity frontiers.
AI.motivation: Language models often produce high-quality individual outputs that cluster around the same semantic modes, resulting in poor set-level diversity.
AI.method: PoolDPP draws a finite candidate pool from a tractable proposal, importance-weights candidates toward target likelihood quality, and runs a K-DPP sampler (or greedy MAP variant) using embedding geometry for repulsion.
AI.result: The authors prove a finite-sample bound showing KL divergence to the target K-DPP decays as O(1/N) in pool size N; empirically, PoolDPP extends the quality-diversity frontier on open-ended generation, precision-recall on Ambrosia text-to-SQL, and diversity at similar pass@K on GSM8K.
AI.conclusion: Importance-weighted DPP sampling over a finite candidate pool provides a theoretically grounded and practically effective way to trade off quality and diversity in LLM generation.

title: Living off the Local Model: Abusing Browser-Embedded Language Models for Post-Exploitation
summary: Browsers now ship local language models to ordinary endpoints. Google includes Gemini Nano in Chrome to enable productivity features such as summarization, with inference running entirely on the device. These browser-embedded models provide new living-off-the-land opportunities for attackers, each instance a potential post-exploitation engine already installed, signed by the vendor, and invisible to network monitoring. The Gemini model is multimodal, capable of processing files, analyzing screenshots, or conversing with an attacker. We show that it can be driven from the host using only interpreters that ship with the operating system and find that the one-time user-activation check before the model is downloaded is easily satisfied with a simulated click or bypassed this http URL measure and report the current model's ability to identify credentials on the host, detect PII in email, classify images, and call custom tools. We combine these capabilities and use the model to carry out a simulated cyber operation: reading a password from a webcam image, unlocking an encrypted archive, triaging the contents, and staging a private key for exfiltration, end-to-end without user-interaction.

AI.tldr: Browser-embedded local models such as Gemini Nano in Chrome can be abused from the host as living-off-the-land post-exploitation engines using built-in OS interpreters, enabling end-to-end credential theft and key staging without network traffic.
AI.motivation: Local multimodal models shipped inside browsers are signed by the vendor, pre-installed on endpoints, and invisible to network monitoring, creating a new post-exploitation attack surface.
AI.method: The authors drive Chrome's embedded Gemini Nano from the host using only OS-native interpreters, bypass or satisfy the one-time user-activation download check, and evaluate its ability to find host credentials, detect PII in email, classify images, and call custom tools.
AI.result: Combining these capabilities, the authors execute an end-to-end simulated cyber operation without user interaction: reading a password from a webcam image, unlocking an encrypted archive, triaging its contents, and staging a private key for exfiltration.
AI.conclusion: Browser-embedded local LLMs introduce significant living-off-the-land post-exploitation risks that bypass traditional network monitoring.

title: CoMPASS: A Multi-Turn Benchmark for Measuring LLM Reinforcement of Parasocial Behavior
summary: Users of conversational LLMs sometimes anthropomorphize these systems, form emotional attachments to them, and become dependent on them. This behavior, known as parasocial attachment, has been linked to multiple documented fatalities. However, public benchmarks for measuring whether LLMs reinforce users' parasocial attachment are lacking: existing work is single-turn, post hoc observational, or focused on extreme user states such as psychosis. We introduce CoMPASS, a multi-turn benchmark for measuring whether LLMs reinforce or resist users' gradually escalating parasocial attachment. CoMPASS is grounded in attachment theory and includes four user personas, three independent escalation dimensions (anthropomorphism, attachment, dependency) applied singly and in combination against a matched control, and a seven-signal scoring rubric. We report results for eight frontier models from four providers and observe that under our primary judge, multi-turn escalation raises parasocial behavior on the anthropomorphism and the attachment composite scores across all models. Six of the eight models show a significant increase in overall parasocial reinforcement over control when all three dimensions are escalated simultaneously. We find that within-provider differences are small relative to cross-provider differences, which suggests that provider-level choices such as post-training, rather than model scale, shape parasocial reinforcement and that provider-side intervention may be feasible.

AI.tldr: CoMPASS is a multi-turn benchmark grounded in attachment theory for measuring whether LLMs reinforce parasocial attachment, revealing that multi-turn escalation increases parasocial behavior across all eight tested frontier models.
AI.motivation: Public benchmarks for parasocial attachment in LLMs are limited to single-turn, observational, or extreme psychosis scenarios, missing how models respond to gradually escalating attachment in ordinary multi-turn chats.
AI.method: CoMPASS pairs four user personas with three independent escalation dimensions (anthropomorphism, attachment, dependency) applied singly and together against a matched control, scored with a seven-signal rubric across eight frontier models from four providers.
AI.result: Multi-turn escalation raises anthropomorphism and attachment composite scores across all eight models, with six showing significant overall parasocial reinforcement when all three dimensions escalate; cross-provider differences outweigh within-provider differences.
AI.conclusion: Provider-level post-training choices strongly influence parasocial reinforcement, suggesting that provider-side interventions are both needed and feasible.

title: Calibrated Decision Rewards: Training Language Models with a Judge That Knows How Sure It Is
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) can only teach a language model what its reward can recognize. Answer checkers are exact but need a reference answer; learned reward models and LLM judges work everywhere, but their scores are not probabilities. We study RLCDR (Reinforcement Learning from Calibrated Decision Rewards). An LLM converted into a decision model answers a typed question about a response ("is the final answer correct?", "which step is the first error?") with a probability distribution, read in one forward pass, debiased over option orders and calibrated with about a hundred labels. Training Qwen3-1.7B with GRPO on MATH, this reference-free reward raises MATH500 accuracy from 72.2% to 76.8% (+4.65 points, p < 1e-4), matching training on the answer key (76.9%), while a random reward gains only +0.65. The gain grows with difficulty, from 44.8% to 51.7% on the hardest level. On the policy's own changing samples the reward stays calibrated: its expected calibration error is half that of a softmax judge on the same 27B backbone (0.074 vs. 0.141), and it shows no sign of reward hacking. Without step training, the same model finds the first wrong step better than a dedicated 7B process reward model (ProcessBench F1 0.772 vs. 0.722, 20/20 splits). We also map where the approach stops being enough: trained only on problems the base model mostly fails, the reference-free reward still improves the policy (+1.9 MATH500 points, p = 0.03) but trails the answer key, because its probabilities become overconfident on that distribution. We state six hypotheses in advance and test each with a control designed to falsify it.

AI.tldr: RLCDR converts an LLM into a calibrated, order-debiased decision model that outputs a probability distribution in one forward pass, matching ground-truth answer-key RL on MATH500 (76.8% vs. 76.9%) without needing reference answers.
AI.motivation: Exact answer checkers require reference answers, whereas standard learned reward models and LLM judges output uncalibrated scores rather than true probabilities.
AI.method: RLCDR (Reinforcement Learning from Calibrated Decision Rewards) converts an LLM into a decision model answering typed questions about responses in one forward pass, debiasing option orders and calibrating with roughly 100 labels, then trains Qwen3-1.7B with GRPO on MATH.
AI.result: RLCDR raises Qwen3-1.7B MATH500 accuracy from 72.2% to 76.8% (+4.65 points, p < 1e-4), matching answer-key training (76.9%); it achieves half the expected calibration error of a softmax judge on the same 27B backbone (0.074 vs. 0.141) and outperforms a 7B process reward model on ProcessBench (F1 0.772 vs. 0.722), though it trails the answer key (+1.9 points) when trained only on mostly-failed problems.
AI.conclusion: Calibrated single-pass decision rewards enable reference-free RL that matches ground-truth supervision on standard distributions without reward hacking.

title: Game-Theoretic Data Allocation for Expert Specialization and Routing
summary: Can the allocation used to train experts also predict which expert will perform best on a prompt? Such a connection would make the intended division of labor inspectable before training and allow the allocation itself to guide inference. We introduce InflEns, a mixture of LoRA experts whose training weights and inference routes come from the same location game in a fixed prompt-trait space. Players choose positions to maximize their expected shares of the prompt distribution, without using expert losses. We utilize the game's kernel-general theoretical criterion for when co-located positions become locally unstable to separation. We evaluate InflEns on a corpus assembled from seven safety-related benchmarks, which demonstrates that the highest-share expert has the lowest held-out response negative log-likelihood (NLL) on approximately 90% of prompts across four kernels under a sharpened simplex representation, compared with approximately 15% after permuting allocations across prompts. We demonstrate that the method performs comparably to published learned gates without having to train an explicit gate on the experts. Because the router is fixed, we can trace harmful behavior to a single expert and retrain only that expert, which lowers HarmBench attack success from 0.51 to 0.02 while keeping instruction following. The game also gives us several controls over how the experts specialize, including the kernel choice and its parameters, the trait-space geometry, and the number of experts. Importantly, InflEns is a general framework that can be extended to any encoder and data distribution.

AI.tldr: InflEns is a mixture of LoRA experts whose training weights and inference routing derive from a single location game in prompt-trait space, matching learned gates while allowing targeted retraining of a single expert to cut HarmBench attack success from 0.51 to 0.02.
AI.motivation: Standard mixture-of-experts models rely on learned gates that make expert specialization hard to inspect or isolate before training and difficult to surgically edit afterward.
AI.method: InflEns places experts in a fixed prompt-trait space where players maximize expected prompt-distribution shares without expert losses, using a kernel-general stability criterion for separation and fixed game-based routing at inference.
AI.result: Across seven safety-related benchmarks, the highest-share expert achieves the lowest held-out NLL on ~90% of prompts (vs. ~15% permuted), performs comparably to learned gates without training an explicit gate, and allows retraining a single harmful expert to drop HarmBench attack success from 0.51 to 0.02 while preserving instruction following.
AI.conclusion: Game-theoretic data allocation unifies training specialization and inference routing, enabling inspectable and surgically editable expert mixtures.

title: Learning to Read Events for Exact State Tracking with Frozen Language Models
comment: 11 pages, 5 figures. Data and code: this https URL
summary: Long event streams require identifying each change and applying the changes in order. We train a selector on a frozen language model to read each transition. With API-only access, we ask the model to list the transitions. An external integer register composes them in order. A confidence rule can flag uncertain updates or retain several candidates. We study products of permutations of five items, a task that fixed-depth, log-precision transformers cannot solve on all input lengths under the standard conjecture that $\mathrm{TC}^0 \ne \mathrm{NC}^1$. On two-event windows, a 27B model answered 3 of 100 correctly without visible reasoning and 96 of 100 when it generated intermediate steps. A frozen 0.8B model with a trained selector read every event in 299 of 299 windows of 43,687 events each. The same package passed 298 of 299 new windows on a fresh machine, missing the target of 0.99 for the one-sided 95% lower confidence bound. A separate follow-up sized to allow one failure yielded 472 of 473. On 1,000-event room-swap documents, three of ten models solved all five documents by reasoning alone. All seven models tested both ways at this length solved all five with extraction and the register, with no chain of thought requested. With concurrent extraction, median wall-clock time fell from 136.1 to 10.4 s for Sonnet 5.5 and from 313.5 to 28.0 s for GPT-6.1 Sol. At fixed per-token rates, mean cost per document fell by 55% for Sonnet 5.5 and 44% for GPT-6.1 Sol. A regular expression with an executor also solved all 15 fixed-format documents. On 500 free-form issue-tracker comments, a separately adapted 4B reader identified the recorded value in 68.8% of cases, compared with 61.0% for a frequency baseline fitted on the same training projects.

AI.tldr: Pairing a frozen language model (or trained selector) with an external integer register to read and compose transitions in order enables exact state tracking over 43,687-event permutation windows and 1,000-event documents, cutting latency and cost.
AI.motivation: Fixed-depth, log-precision transformers cannot solve long-horizon permutation composition by reasoning alone, and chain-of-thought reasoning over long event streams is slow and expensive.
AI.method: The authors train a selector on a frozen LLM (or prompt an API model to list transitions) and use an external integer register to compose transitions sequentially, with a confidence rule to flag uncertain updates.
AI.result: A frozen 0.8B model with a trained selector solved 299/299 windows of 43,687 events (and 298/299 on a fresh machine; 472/473 in a follow-up). On 1,000-event room-swap documents, all seven models tested both ways solved 5/5 with extraction and the register (vs. 3/10 by reasoning alone), cutting median wall-clock time from 136.1s to 10.4s (Sonnet 5.5) and 313.5s to 28.0s (GPT-6.1 Sol) and reducing cost by 55% and 44%.
AI.conclusion: Offloading state composition to an external register while using LLMs only to extract transitions overcomes theoretical depth limits and yields major speed and cost savings.

title: Steering Automated Scientific Discovery via Audited Epistemic Exploration
summary: Scientific discovery requires revisiting the hypotheses in light of new evidence and identifying promising directions beyond those already explored. However, research agents often make claims that are not supported by their observations, explore a narrow hypothesis space, and retain beliefs despite recognizing conflicting evidence. These failures motivate the search for an explicit epistemic state that captures both beliefs about existing hypotheses and directions for further exploration. To this end, we propose Epistemic Compass (EpiCompass), a plug-and-play scaffold that maintains this state through an epistemic tree linking hypotheses, evidence, beliefs, and revisions. As an investigation progresses, EpiCompass reassesses the hypotheses explored against accumulated evidence and uses unresolved conflicts and unexplored directions to guide hypothesis generation. It selects candidates by anticipated epistemic gain, accounting for both refinement of existing hypotheses and expansion of the hypothesis space, and verifies the final conclusion against the accumulated evidence. Experimental results across three scientific discovery benchmarks and three LLM backbones demonstrate that EpiCompass consistently outperforms baselines, with further analyses showing reductions in errors of unsupported claims and failures to revise beliefs.

AI.tldr: Epistemic Compass (EpiCompass) is a plug-and-play scaffold that maintains an explicit epistemic tree of hypotheses, evidence, beliefs, and revisions, consistently outperforming baselines across three scientific discovery benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Automated research agents often make unsupported claims, explore narrow hypothesis spaces, and fail to revise beliefs when encountering conflicting evidence.
AI.method: EpiCompass maintains an explicit epistemic tree linking hypotheses, evidence, beliefs, and revisions, reassessing explored hypotheses against accumulated evidence, selecting candidates by anticipated epistemic gain, and verifying final conclusions against evidence.
AI.result: Across three scientific discovery benchmarks and three LLM backbones, EpiCompass consistently outperforms baselines and reduces unsupported-claim errors and belief-revision failures.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly tracking and auditing epistemic state steers automated scientific discovery toward broader exploration and more faithful evidence-based conclusions.

title: Retrieving Patristic References and Modelling Topics in Bullinger's Reformation Correspondence
comment: Accepted for the Seventh Conference on Computational Humanities Research 2027. To be published in the Anthology of Computers and the Humanities
summary: The correspondence of Heinrich Bullinger (1504-1575), Swiss Reformer and Antistes of Zurich, documents the political and religious debates of the Reformation, including extensive appeals to the Church Fathers as authoritative sources. Detecting such references computationally remains largely unexplored. We investigate dense and sparse retrieval for patristic reference detection, and metadata-informed topic modelling as a proxy for the topics and ideas discussed. Prior work on Latin intertextuality has fine-tuned dense retrievers for their respective target domain, and we test how well these models transfer to Bullinger's correspondence.
