We compare lexical (BM25), dense (bi-encoders), and hybrid methods on explicit and implicit references. A Latin encoder fine-tuned on biblical reuse performs best among the bi-encoders (82%, Recall@20 on explicit and 16% on implicit references), while BM25 outperforms dense approaches on explicit citations (94%, R@20). Because BM25 and dense retrieval recover disjoint sets of implicit references, fusing their rankings raises implicit R@20 to 22%, close to cross-encoder reranking of the same candidates (26%) but without its inference cost. For topic modelling, we extend FASTopic with a seed-guided loss function and editorial abstract embeddings. Measurable coherence gains over the baseline remain minimal, but qualitative and temporal analysis shows that some topics track documented historical events. However, dominant topic weights barely exceed a uniform distribution, making topics unusable to inform retrieval. A pilot application of LLM-based concept induction (LLooM) further points towards a more human-interpretable alternative. Together, these results present a first approach to retrieving patristic references and modelling fine-grained topics in Bullinger's correspondence.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the first computational study of patristic reference retrieval and topic modeling on Heinrich Bullinger's Reformation correspondence, finding that hybrid BM25-dense fusion improves implicit reference recall (22% R@20) while FASTopic topics are too uniform to aid retrieval.
AI.motivation: Detecting explicit and implicit appeals to Church Fathers and modeling fine-grained topics in Bullinger's 16th-century correspondence remains largely unexplored computationally.
AI.method: The authors compare BM25, fine-tuned Latin bi-encoders, hybrid rank fusion, and cross-encoder reranking on explicit and implicit patristic references, and extend FASTopic with a seed-guided loss and editorial abstract embeddings alongside a pilot of LLM concept induction (LLooM).
AI.result: BM25 achieves 94% Recall@20 on explicit citations, while a biblically fine-tuned Latin bi-encoder reaches 82% explicit and 16% implicit R@20; fusing BM25 and dense rankings raises implicit R@20 to 22% (near cross-encoder reranking at 26% without its cost). Extended FASTopic shows minimal coherence gains and near-uniform topic weights, whereas LLooM yields more interpretable concepts.
AI.conclusion: Lexical-dense fusion effectively captures disjoint explicit and implicit patristic references, while LLM-based concept induction offers a promising alternative to topic modeling for historical correspondence.

title: Pro$^2$ Agent: Scientific Problem Probing for Autonomous AI R&D
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents can now autonomously conduct AI research by writing code and running experiments. They typically do so by iteratively optimizing a codebase, while ignoring the problem structure behind the task. This formulation is effective on simpler tasks, but on difficult problems it often gets stuck in the wrong solution region because the agent never explicitly represents its understanding of the problem. We introduce Pro$^2$ Agent, which shifts the primary state of autonomous AI research from a codebase state to a Problem State: an explicit structure of what problems prevent success and which solutions are likely to address them. Pro$^2$ Agent initializes the Problem State through comprehensive analysis of available resources and constraints. It then performs targeted research to relate the identified problems to candidate solutions. Through controlled hypothesis testing, the agent updates the importance of a suspected problem or the benefit brought by a candidate solution. On the complete MLE-Bench, Pro$^2$ Agent matches the best reported medal rate (70.7%) under the standard 24-hour budget and reaches 76.0% with a 48-hour budget, the highest medal rate reported on the complete benchmark. It also achieves competitive performance on PostTrainBench. In addition, it produces research notes for each task that make the research process transparent and reusable by human researchers.

AI.tldr: Pro^2 Agent shifts autonomous AI R&D from optimizing a codebase state to maintaining an explicit Problem State, achieving a 76.0% medal rate on the complete MLE-Bench under a 48-hour budget.
AI.motivation: Autonomous AI R&D agents that iteratively edit code without explicitly modeling the underlying problem structure often get stuck in suboptimal solution regions on difficult tasks.
AI.method: Pro^2 Agent initializes an explicit Problem State from available resources and constraints, maps identified problems to candidate solutions via targeted research, and updates problem importance and solution benefits through controlled hypothesis testing while generating reusable research notes.
AI.result: On the complete MLE-Bench, Pro^2 Agent matches the best reported medal rate (70.7%) within 24 hours and reaches 76.0% within 48 hours (the highest reported on the complete benchmark), while also performing competitively on PostTrainBench.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly representing and probing the Problem State enables autonomous R&D agents to solve complex tasks more effectively and transparently.

title: When Should a Voice Agent Speak? End-of-Turn Detection in Turkish
summary: A voice agent that waits for a fixed silence before replying either interrupts users who pause mid-utterance or responds late to users who have finished. This study examines the decision at the onset of silence, using turn ends and turn-internal pauses extracted from the Real-TurnTurk corpus of Turkish dyadic video calls. A fine-tuned Turkish TurnGPT model, a zero-shot Turkish language model and a deployed multilingual detector are compared, together with voice-activity timing and facial features, under recording-disjoint and speaker-disjoint evaluation with paired cluster bootstrap tests. On held-out recordings, the fine-tuned model separates turn ends from pauses better than both text baselines and is the best calibrated of the three. Timing features of the current speaker are similarly informative, and their combination with the fine-tuned text score gives the best timing-based results; with logistic regression, this combination also outperforms the same combination with either text baseline. In a latency simulation, adding the text score to a silence timeout shortens the mean response delay at the same interruption rate. On automatic Whisper transcripts, the fine-tuned model retains its advantage over the zero-shot model.

AI.tldr: Evaluating end-of-turn detection at silence onset on the Turkish Real-TurnTurk corpus, this study shows that a fine-tuned Turkish TurnGPT model outperforms zero-shot and multilingual baselines and shortens response delay when combined with timing features.
AI.motivation: Voice agents using a fixed silence timeout either interrupt users mid-utterance or respond too late, requiring accurate end-of-turn prediction at the onset of silence.
AI.method: Using turn ends and turn-internal pauses from Turkish dyadic video calls (Real-TurnTurk), the authors compare a fine-tuned Turkish TurnGPT, a zero-shot Turkish LLM, and a deployed multilingual detector alongside voice-activity timing and facial features under recording-disjoint and speaker-disjoint evaluation.
AI.result: On held-out recordings, fine-tuned TurnGPT separates turn ends from pauses better and is better calibrated than both text baselines (even on Whisper transcripts), and combining its text score with speaker timing features via logistic regression yields the best timing-based results and shorter simulated response delays at the same interruption rate.
AI.conclusion: Fine-tuned language-specific turn-taking models combined with speaker timing cues substantially improve end-of-turn detection and latency in Turkish voice agents.

title: LM-based Personalized Travel Planner
summary: Effective travel planning requires handling multiple information sources, managing constraints, and tailoring recommendations to user preferences. While LLMs have introduced dynamic, context-aware decision-making, single-agent models often struggle with complex multi-step reasoning, constraint adherence, and modular execution. To overcome these limitations, we propose a hierarchical multi-agent framework where a supervising chatbot agent coordinates specialized agents for schedule validation, user query formulation, real-time data retrieval, and constraint-aware itinerary generation. By integrating LLM reasoning, external APIs, and iterative refinement mechanisms based on a deterministic, multi-dimensional scoring framework, our approach ensures adaptability, efficiency, and personalization. Evaluations on the well-known TravelPlanner benchmark demonstrate improvements in Budget Constraint planning by 10\%, wider constraints set-based planning by 25\%, and personalized planning results by 45\%. compared to the ReAct baseline. Our code is available at this https URL

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a hierarchical multi-agent LLM framework for personalized travel planning that coordinates specialized sub-agents and outperforms the ReAct baseline on TravelPlanner.
AI.motivation: Single-agent LLM models struggle with complex multi-step reasoning, constraint adherence, and modular execution when handling multiple information sources and user preferences in travel planning.
AI.method: A supervising chatbot agent coordinates specialized agents for schedule validation, user query formulation, real-time data retrieval, and constraint-aware itinerary generation, integrating LLM reasoning, external APIs, and iterative refinement via a deterministic multi-dimensional scoring framework.
AI.result: On the TravelPlanner benchmark, the framework improves Budget Constraint planning by 10%, wider constraints set-based planning by 25%, and personalized planning by 45% compared to the ReAct baseline.
AI.conclusion: Hierarchical multi-agent coordination with deterministic scoring and API integration enables more adaptable, efficient, and personalized travel planning than single-agent baselines.

title: COVERAGE-TRACE: Source-Side Counterfactual Tracing for Detecting Omissions in LLM Summaries
summary: Omissions are difficult to verify because missing information leaves no output span to inspect: a summary may be factually supported while still excluding a decision, qualification, quantity, or condition needed to preserve the source's meaning. We introduce COVERAGE-TRACE, a source-side counterfactual framework that evaluates omission as dependence on a designated atomic source fact. It replaces only the target fact with type-matched alternatives, holds the candidate summary fixed, and measures the resulting change in its teacher-forced, length-normalized likelihood. A summary covering the target should respond more strongly than one omitting it, while aggregation across multiple counterfactuals reduces sensitivity to replacement choice. We evaluate COVERAGE-TRACE on 80 matched covered--omitted QMSum pairs spanning several fact types and four open-weight models. Multi-CF achieves 0.764--0.825 AUROC, compared with 0.640 for the strongest evaluated text-only baseline. On Falcon-7B, targeted interventions achieve 0.779 AUROC, whereas shuffling counterfactual assignments reduces performance to 0.533; target deletion is effective while unrelated deletion is not. However, adjustment for meaning-preserving paraphrases reduces AUROC to 0.591--0.624. COVERAGE-TRACE therefore provides a practical, complementary signal of target-specific source--summary dependence, but not a wording-invariant semantic coverage probability. These results establish source-side intervention as a promising approach to omission detection while identifying semantic invariance as the central remaining challenge.

AI.tldr: The authors introduce COVERAGE-TRACE, a source-side counterfactual tracing framework that detects omissions in LLM summaries by measuring how teacher-forced summary likelihood changes when atomic source facts are replaced.
AI.motivation: Omissions in summaries leave no output span to inspect, making them hard to verify because a summary can be factually supported while still excluding critical decisions, qualifications, quantities, or conditions.
AI.method: COVERAGE-TRACE replaces a designated atomic source fact with type-matched counterfactual alternatives while holding the candidate summary fixed, measuring the change in teacher-forced length-normalized likelihood and aggregating across multiple counterfactuals.
AI.result: Evaluated on 80 matched covered-omitted QMSum pairs across four open-weight models, Multi-CF achieves 0.764-0.825 AUROC versus 0.640 for the strongest text-only baseline, though adjusting for meaning-preserving paraphrases drops AUROC to 0.591-0.624.
AI.conclusion: Source-side counterfactual intervention provides a practical, complementary signal for omission detection, while achieving wording-invariant semantic coverage remains the central challenge.

title: Generative News Recommendation Reproduces Popularity: A Memorization-Based Analysis
comment: The 11th International Workshop on Application of Big Data for Computational Social Science (ABCSS2026 @ IEEE BigData 2026)
summary: Text-based generative recommenders can go beyond ranking existing items by directly generating item titles or other textual representations. In the news domain, this raises a societal concern that models may repeatedly surface already popular articles and thereby narrow the diversity of information to which users are exposed. We investigate training-data memorization as one mechanism behind this concentration. Using approximately 20 million browsing sessions from a Japanese news service, we continually trained an instruction-tuned Llama 3 8B model to generate the next article title in a session. The generated-title distribution was more concentrated and less diverse than the distribution of titles observed in the browsing logs. Frequently repeated target titles exhibited greater verbatim and approximate memorization, and more strongly memorized titles were generated in response to a wider range of prompts. These findings support a pathway in which popularity in behavioral logs becomes repeated training text, is preferentially memorized, and is subsequently reproduced by a generative recommender. An exploratory target-level deduplication condition reduced both memorization and output concentration, while substantially reducing the training-set size and recommendation accuracy. Our results suggest that popularity bias in generative recommendation may arise not only from user preferences or ranking objectives, but also from the model's tendency to reproduce frequently encountered strings, with important implications for information diversity on news platforms.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates popularity bias in text-based generative news recommendation and finds that models reproduce popular articles because frequently repeated target titles in training logs are preferentially memorized.
AI.motivation: Text-based generative recommenders can surface already popular news articles and narrow user information diversity, but the role of training-data memorization in driving this concentration is unclear.
AI.method: The authors continually trained an instruction-tuned Llama 3 8B model on approximately 20 million Japanese news browsing sessions to generate the next article title, and tested an exploratory target-level deduplication condition.
AI.result: The generated-title distribution was more concentrated and less diverse than the browsing logs, with frequently repeated titles showing stronger verbatim and approximate memorization and appearing across more prompts; target-level deduplication reduced memorization and concentration but substantially reduced training-set size and recommendation accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Popularity bias in generative news recommendation stems not only from user preferences or ranking objectives but also from memorizing and reproducing frequent training strings.

title: SEAF: Selective Semantic Enrichment and Visual Evidence Fusion for Multimodal Sarcasm Detection
summary: Multimodal sarcasm detection requires textual, visual, and contextual evidence, particularly when multiple images provide complementary cues. Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can generate auxiliary information from a post's text and images, but their outputs may mix useful background knowledge with redundant visual descriptions. We propose SEAF, a dual-branch framework for selective semantic enrichment and visual evidence fusion. SEAF assigns generated fields to distinct roles: entity background enriches semantic input, while image descriptions supply alignment statistics. The semantic branch combines the original post text, background from a frozen MLLM, and optical character recognition (OCR) text. The aligned visual branch combines global and local visual features with statistics of cross-modal and inter-image similarity. Text-Anchored Smoothed Aggregation (TASA) weights images by their similarity to the original post text while preserving contributions from images with low literal similarity. Summing the branch classification scores integrates contextual semantics with visual evidence. Experiments on the multi-image MMSD3.0 benchmark show that SEAF outperforms all compared methods.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes SEAF, a dual-branch framework for multimodal sarcasm detection that separates MLLM-generated entity background and image descriptions into semantic enrichment and visual alignment roles, outperforming baselines on MMSD3.0.
AI.motivation: MLLMs can generate auxiliary information for multimodal sarcasm detection, but their outputs often mix useful background knowledge with redundant visual descriptions.
AI.method: SEAF combines original post text, frozen MLLM entity background, and OCR text in a semantic branch, while an aligned visual branch pairs global/local visual features with cross-modal and inter-image similarity statistics using Text-Anchored Smoothed Aggregation (TASA), summing both branch scores.
AI.result: Experiments on the multi-image MMSD3.0 benchmark show that SEAF outperforms all compared methods.
AI.conclusion: Assigning MLLM-generated outputs to distinct semantic and visual-alignment roles effectively integrates contextual semantics with multi-image visual evidence for sarcasm detection.

title: PosteriorBench: Evaluating Behavior Posterior Sampling in Language Models
summary: Rare language model behaviors can be difficult to study because obtaining them through ordinary sampling can require a very large number of samples. This motivates the behavior posterior sampling problem: given a language model and a behavior of interest, is there an algorithm that efficiently samples from the model's distribution over transcripts that exhibit this behavior? We introduce PosteriorBench, a benchmark for comparing algorithms by their compute cost and by how close their samples are to the true posterior in forward and reverse KL divergence. PosteriorBench contains 21 tasks on Qwen3.5-0.8B with behavior probabilities from $10^{-5}$ to $10^{-1}$, each with exact posterior samples from a corpus of one billion labeled responses. We find that no method we evaluate is both efficient and faithful: simple methods like prompting are cheap but plateau at a high KL divergence from the posterior, fine-tuning on posterior samples is often cost-prohibitive, and several training methods from prior work do not perform better. Building a posterior sampler that can cheaply approximate the true posterior remains an open problem, and we hope PosteriorBench can measure progress towards this objective. Code and data are available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The authors introduce PosteriorBench, a benchmark for evaluating behavior posterior sampling algorithms in language models, and find that no tested method is both compute-efficient and faithful to the true posterior.
AI.motivation: Studying rare language model behaviors via ordinary sampling requires prohibitively many samples, motivating algorithms that sample from the behavior posterior, yet no standardized benchmark exists to compare their efficiency and fidelity.
AI.method: PosteriorBench comprises 21 tasks on Qwen3.5-0.8B with behavior probabilities from 10^-5 to 10^-1, each paired with exact posterior samples from one billion labeled responses, evaluating methods by compute cost and forward/reverse KL divergence.
AI.result: Across evaluated approaches, prompting is cheap but plateaus at high KL divergence, fine-tuning on posterior samples is often cost-prohibitive, and several prior training methods fail to perform better.
AI.conclusion: Building a posterior sampler that cheaply approximates the true behavior posterior remains an open problem that PosteriorBench is designed to measure.

title: RouteVerify: Routing Interventions for Step-Level Verification in Mixture-of-Experts Models
comment: 38 pages, 5 figures. Code: this https URL
summary: Routing states in mixture-of-experts (MoE) models can distinguish correct from erroneous reasoning steps. If changing routing also changes a model's step-level verification judgment, it is tempting to conclude that the judgment follows what routing encodes. We test this inference with RouteVerify, a controlled intervention study that replaces selected internal activations from one solution trace with activations from another, while keeping the evaluated input unchanged. Across nine MoE checkpoints, we compare three intervention interfaces: router logits, MoE outputs, and post-MoE residual states. We vary the layers and token positions at which activations are replaced. We measure changes in a verification margin that quantifies the model's preference for INCORRECT over CORRECT. We also evaluate the same input with activations from correct versus erroneous steps to test whether the resulting judgment depends on the source step's correctness. We report four linked results. First, probes on router logits separate correct from erroneous steps in eight checkpoints (AUROC 0.80-0.88). Second, replacing router logits across all routed layers changes the judgment in all nine checkpoints, and by more than a norm-matched random replacement. Third, this change rarely depends on whether the source step is correct. At one layer, routing from erroneous steps and from correct steps produces indistinguishable margins in all nine checkpoints. Under all-layer routing, their difference is resolved and positive in only one. Fourth, the same difference is positive for local residual replacements in eight of nine checkpoints, so the measure does detect such dependence where it exists. Correctness is therefore readable from routing, and routing replacements move the judgment, but the movement rarely follows correctness.

AI.tldr: RouteVerify tests whether Mixture-of-Experts routing states causally drive step-level verification judgments and finds that while routing encodes correctness and routing interventions shift judgments, the shift rarely depends on source-step correctness.
AI.motivation: Because MoE routing states can distinguish correct from erroneous reasoning steps and altering routing changes verification judgments, it is tempting to infer that judgments follow what routing encodes, which requires causal testing.
AI.method: Across nine MoE checkpoints, RouteVerify replaces router logits, MoE outputs, or post-MoE residual states from one solution trace with those from correct versus erroneous steps while keeping the input fixed, measuring changes in verification margin.
AI.result: Router-logit probes separate correct from erroneous steps in eight checkpoints (AUROC 0.80-0.88) and all-layer router-logit replacement shifts judgments in all nine checkpoints, yet single-layer routing from correct vs. erroneous steps yields indistinguishable margins in all nine checkpoints and all-layer routing differs positively in only one, whereas local residual replacements show positive dependence in eight of nine checkpoints.
AI.conclusion: Step correctness is readable from MoE routing and routing interventions move verification judgments, but the movement rarely follows the correctness encoded in routing.

title: What Does Anti-Hallucination Training Buy? Saying Less, Cheap Pruning, and the Rest
summary: Preference training is the standard recipe for reducing object hallucination in vision-language models, and each new method reports a lower CHAIR score. We ask what that reduction consists of. Every trained system is compared with its base model's caption truncated to the same object recall, which removes the part of the gain that comes from saying less; the remainder is compared with what a deliberately weak, frozen, eleven-feature post-hoc probe fitted on 500 annotated images can reproduce. All criteria were specified in the analysis code and frozen before the outputs they judge existed. For eight public methods on LLaVA-1.5-7B, the probe reproduces at least two thirds of what training removes beyond saying less for 7 of 8 methods on COCO, 8 of 8 on AMBER and 6 of 8 on Object HalBench, with RLAIF-V the consistent exception; a later public method released for both LLaVA-1.5 and Qwen2.5-VL (SENTINEL) meets the same bar on both. On our own DPO checkpoints the accounting holds on Qwen2.5-VL but fails on InternVL2.5 on COCO (2 of 4 training designs). At matched recall, the base model plus the probe beats truncation for 8 of 9 LLaVA-1.5 systems on COCO and 9 of 9 on AMBER, on the two newer backbones, and when realized as actual sentence deletion. The same measure prices training signals: DPO on the model's own samples labelled by the probe or by an object-level CLIP score recovers 0.70 and 0.87 of the beyond-brevity gain of ground-truth-labelled DPO on Qwen2.5-VL (the probe 0.73 on InternVL2.5), both beat length-matched random labels, and CLIP labels buy more than probe labels on COCO. Human judgements show that the sentences the probe deletes are wrong more often than those truncation would delete; a human check of the CHAIR evaluator's precision falls below our pre-set bar, which we report as a limitation.

AI.tldr: This paper decomposes object hallucination reductions from preference training in vision-language models and shows that beyond saying less, a weak eleven-feature post-hoc probe reproduces at least two-thirds of the remaining gain for most methods.
AI.motivation: Preference training methods report lower CHAIR hallucination scores, but it is unclear how much of the improvement comes simply from generating shorter captions versus genuine hallucination reduction.
AI.method: Each trained model is compared against its base model truncated to matched object recall, and the remaining gain is benchmarked against a frozen eleven-feature post-hoc probe fitted on 500 annotated images; the authors also test DPO trained on probe or object-level CLIP labels.
AI.result: For eight public methods on LLaVA-1.5-7B, the probe reproduces at least two-thirds of the beyond-brevity gain on 7/8 methods on COCO, 8/8 on AMBER, and 6/8 on Object HalBench (with RLAIF-V as the exception); DPO with probe or CLIP labels recovers 0.70 and 0.87 of ground-truth DPO's beyond-brevity gain on Qwen2.5-VL.
AI.conclusion: Much of the anti-hallucination gain from preference training beyond brevity can be matched by a simple post-hoc probe, though human checks also reveal limitations in CHAIR evaluator precision.

title: Anchor and Check: Deterministic Cross-Prompt, Cross-Model Reconciliation for Auditable LLM Decisions
summary: Pipelines that let a large language model (LLM) make discrete decisions need to know which decisions they may act on unattended, and a record that explains each one. We study a small, fully specified reconciliation contract: commit the target model's greedy answer (the anchor), draw one or two greedy checks that reach the answer by a different route (an alternate prompt, or a model from another family), and let a pure function return one of five outcomes, of which only Agree is acted on. On 48,000 model-item evaluations over 6,000 questions, with every method given access to verbalized confidence as a tie-breaker, the main finding concerns where calls come from: pooling another family's samples raises semantic entropy's AUROC by 1.7 to 4.0 points at every budget, and a same-model temperature check is the weakest design. As complete pipelines, the point estimates of the three-call contract and pooled semantic entropy over 3 or 5 samples differ by less than one point, with intervals containing zero. As detectors of the anchor's errors, the contract is ahead of pooled entropy with 3 and 5 samples under both tie-breaker conventions; with 10 samples the point estimates differ by less than one point and the sign depends on the convention. Under the strict Agree gate it automates 70% of items and still acts on 16% of errors. What the contract adds is a fixed committed answer, an explicit outcome and a decision replayable from its record; generation itself was not reproducible on the hosted API.

AI.tldr: The authors evaluate a deterministic cross-prompt, cross-model reconciliation contract for auditable discrete LLM decisions and show that cross-family checks boost error detection while providing a replayable decision record.
AI.motivation: Automated LLM decision pipelines need to know which discrete decisions can be acted on unattended and require an auditable record explaining each decision.
AI.method: The contract commits the target model's greedy answer as an anchor, draws one or two greedy checks via an alternate prompt or a model from another family, and applies a pure function returning five outcomes where only Agree is acted on.
AI.result: Across 48,000 model-item evaluations over 6,000 questions, pooling another family's samples raises semantic entropy AUROC by 1.7 to 4.0 points at every budget, the three-call contract matches pooled semantic entropy over 3 or 5 samples within one point, and the Agree gate automates 70% of items while acting on 16% of errors.
AI.conclusion: Cross-family checking improves error detection over same-model temperature checks, and the reconciliation contract adds a fixed committed answer and replayable decision record.

title: One Schedule Does Not Fit All: Adaptive Inference Schedules for Diffusion Language Models
summary: Diffusion language models typically use a fixed denoising schedule across workloads. We show that the cheapest schedule that preserves quality depends on the task, model, and sampler. We propose Task-Calibrated Denoising Allocation (TCDA), a deployment rule with an explicit error guarantee. Given candidate samplers, paired calibration data, a utility tolerance, and guardrails against degeneration, TCDA uses simultaneous one-sided bootstrap bounds to certify which candidates meet both the utility and guardrail criteria. It deploys the cheapest certified candidate or falls back to the full schedule. The probability of deploying an infeasible schedule is asymptotically at most alpha. Candidates include early prefix decoding, state-reusing continuation, reduced time grids, and confidence-threshold decoding. Across seven datasets and two model families, TCDA certifies reductions in denoiser evaluations by factors of 3.4 on XSum and 2.0 on WMT14 for ELF-B; 8.0 on WMT14 and 4.1 on GSM8K for LLaDA-8B; and 1.33 on OpenWebText for both ELF-M and ELF-L. A validation protocol fixed before generation confirmed every selection on fresh seeds. Across 500 calibration splits, false certification remained below 2% in every setting at a nominal level of 5%. Certified schedules vary across tasks and model scales. Trajectory measurements suggest that when decoded tokens commit is more informative for schedule selection than the remaining latent discretization error. We also find that the ELF reference sampler draws its time grid at random, so reproducible schedule comparisons for unconditional generation require fixing the grid.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Task-Calibrated Denoising Allocation (TCDA), a statistically certified rule for selecting the cheapest adaptive inference schedule in diffusion language models, achieving up to 8.0x denoiser evaluation reductions.
AI.motivation: Diffusion language models typically use a fixed denoising schedule across all workloads, even though the cheapest quality-preserving schedule varies by task, model, and sampler.
AI.method: Given candidate samplers, paired calibration data, a utility tolerance, and degeneration guardrails, TCDA uses simultaneous one-sided bootstrap bounds to certify candidates and deploys the cheapest certified schedule or falls back to the full schedule, with asymptotic error probability at most alpha.
AI.result: Across seven datasets and two model families, TCDA certifies denoiser evaluation reductions of 3.4x on XSum and 2.0x on WMT14 for ELF-B, 8.0x on WMT14 and 4.1x on GSM8K for LLaDA-8B, and 1.33x on OpenWebText for ELF-M and ELF-L, with false certification below 2% at a 5% nominal level.
AI.conclusion: Certified adaptive schedule selection substantially reduces diffusion language model inference cost while controlling quality degradation, and token commitment timing is more informative than latent discretization error.

title: When Sounds Turn Heads: Recovering Event Timing That Audio LLMs Fail to Say
summary: Audio LLMs can know when a queried sound occurs but fail to say it. We find a few attention heads that track the queried sound: they shift when the query changes, follow the sound when it moves, and removing or blocking them often hurts the model's timestamps. Yet the answer does not express what they track. Intervals read directly from these heads outperform the model's original answer and recover events that its timestamps miss. To bring this timing into the answer, we introduce head-guided decoding, which needs no training. It keeps the model's decision on whether the sound is present and rescores its candidate timestamps with a prior from these heads. Heads selected on development data transfer unchanged to new recordings and free-text queries, where head-guided decoding improves the timestamps of three audio LLMs, scores above their head readout on every benchmark, and, in most settings, outperforms random-head guidance. On recordings released after the models were trained, head-guided decoding raises mIoU from 0.07-0.36 to 0.48-0.56. These results suggest that poor temporal answers in audio LLMs partly reflect a failure to say rather than to hear, and that the model's own attention can close part of this gap.

AI.tldr: The authors discover attention heads in audio LLMs that track queried sound timing even when the model's text answer misses it, and introduce training-free head-guided decoding to recover accurate timestamps.
AI.motivation: Audio LLMs often fail to output accurate event timestamps in their text responses, leaving unclear whether they fail to perceive the timing or fail to express it.
AI.method: Head-guided decoding identifies attention heads that track queried sounds on development data and, without training, rescores candidate timestamps using a prior from these heads while keeping the model's sound-presence decision.
AI.result: Across three audio LLMs, head-guided decoding outperforms both the original model answers and direct head readouts on every benchmark, raising mIoU on post-training recordings from 0.07-0.36 to 0.48-0.56.
AI.conclusion: Poor temporal answers in audio LLMs partly reflect a failure to express rather than to hear, and internal attention heads can be used at decoding time to narrow this gap.

title: Policy Improvement-Guided Replay for Continual Reinforcement Learning
summary: Continual reinforcement learning (CRL) requires models to acquire new capabilities while retaining performance on previous tasks. A stability-oriented perspective common in conventional continual learning emphasizes knowledge preservation and interference mitigation. Complementing this perspective, we revisit CRL for vision-language models through policy improvement, a fundamental principle of RL, to preserve acquired performance gains. Using the performance difference lemma, we characterize historical performance changes through the current policy's expected advantages on historical task distributions, motivating replay of historical prompts with the current policy. To allocate limited replay memory, we propose Contrastive Likelihood Replay (CoLiR), which contrasts likelihood gains on correct responses from the final task policy with likelihood reductions on incorrect responses from the initial policy. Our analysis links correct-response likelihood gains to reference-policy advantages under an idealized KL-regularized optimal update and provides an endogenous-reward interpretation for general policy updates. CoLiR estimates scores from finite training rollouts and cached log-likelihoods, selects prompts at task boundaries, and replays them uniformly during subsequent training, with KL regularization restricted to replayed prompts. Memory construction only requires a small amount of additional cross-policy scoring but no additional response generation. Across three Qwen3-VL model sizes on MRCL, CoLiR achieves the highest mean final accuracy and mean task accuracy among the compared methods while maintaining competitive new-task performance.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Contrastive Likelihood Replay (CoLiR) for continual reinforcement learning in vision-language models, selecting historical prompts that maximize policy-improvement retention and achieving top accuracy on MRCL.
AI.motivation: Conventional continual learning focuses on stability and interference mitigation, whereas continual reinforcement learning also needs to preserve acquired policy-improvement gains under limited replay memory.
AI.method: Motivated by the performance difference lemma, CoLiR scores prompts at task boundaries by contrasting likelihood gains on correct responses from the final task policy against likelihood reductions on incorrect responses from the initial policy, then replays selected prompts uniformly with restricted KL regularization.
AI.result: Across three Qwen3-VL model sizes on MRCL, CoLiR achieves the highest mean final accuracy and mean task accuracy among compared methods while maintaining competitive new-task performance without extra response generation.
AI.conclusion: Grounding replay selection in policy improvement and contrastive likelihoods effectively preserves prior RL gains in continual VLM training.

title: Complete-SVD: A Functional Norm Approach to Low-Rank LLM Compression
summary: Post-training low-rank compression of neural networks must not only approximate the original weights but also preserve the model's input-output behavior. Recent output-aware methods measure the compression error beyond the compressed layer, at the model output, weighting logit changes by the observed next token or by the model's predicted probabilities. We propose Complete-SVD, a method for large language models that minimizes the $L_2$ distance between the logits of the original and compressed models, weighting all logit changes equally. Linearizing the network around the original weights, together with a Kronecker-factored approximation, reduces this objective to a weighted SVD with a closed-form solution. Its output-side factor is intractable to compute; we estimate it without bias from random probes, at a cost of $K$ backward passes per sequence, independent of vocabulary size and sequence length. At matched settings with uniform ranks and WikiText-2 calibration, Complete-SVD achieves the lowest C4 and PTB perplexity in every setting, and at ratio 0.7 under LEMS rank allocation. Replacing the $L_2$ distance by the Kullback-Leibler divergence (KL-SVD), with the same estimation framework, lowers calibration perplexity in most settings and raises downstream accuracy, but raises cross-corpus perplexity. Complete-SVD also improves IFEval instruction-following accuracy over the strongest prior output-aware methods throughout.

AI.tldr: The authors introduce Complete-SVD, a low-rank LLM compression method that minimizes the unweighted L2 distance between original and compressed model logits via an unbiased probe-based Kronecker-factored approximation.
AI.motivation: Existing output-aware low-rank compression methods weight logit changes by observed next tokens or predicted probabilities rather than preserving the full output logit distribution equally.
AI.method: Complete-SVD linearizes the network around original weights and uses a Kronecker-factored approximation to reduce L2 logit preservation to a weighted SVD, estimating the intractable output-side factor without bias using random probes in K backward passes per sequence; a KL-divergence variant (KL-SVD) is also studied.
AI.result: With uniform ranks and WikiText-2 calibration, Complete-SVD achieves the lowest C4 and PTB perplexity in every setting and at ratio 0.7 under LEMS rank allocation, while also improving IFEval instruction-following accuracy over prior output-aware methods.
AI.conclusion: Minimizing unweighted L2 logit distance via probe-estimated weighted SVD better preserves general language modeling and instruction-following capabilities under low-rank compression.

title: RL Can Only Reinforce What It Sees Succeed
summary: When a familiar rule stops working, an agent has to weigh what pre-training taught it against what it now observes. We ask how outcome-reward reinforcement learning (RL) changes this balance, in a puzzle world where both sides are known: small language models trained from scratch on games played by a Bayesian player, so that the prior and the right answer are exact. Base models hedge as their corpus did, and RL turns that hedging into decisions, in whichever direction the reward favours. But RL can only reinforce what it sees succeed. When the right action is rare, each run either learns it everywhere or not at all, and which runs take off is predicted before training by one count: the expected number of groups of attempts in which the action wins. About 35 such groups give even odds. The count holds for new and repeated problems and for groups of 4 to 256 attempts, and across learning rates, optimizers, GRPO variants and model sizes from 1.3M to 85M parameters, which move the threshold but not what is counted.

AI.tldr: Studying small language models on a Bayesian puzzle game, this paper shows that outcome-reward RL can only reinforce rare correct actions it sees succeed, with training takeoff predicted by a single count of winning attempt groups.
AI.motivation: When a familiar rule stops working, it is unclear how outcome-reward reinforcement learning shifts an agent from its pre-training prior toward new observations, especially when the right action is rare.
AI.method: The authors train small language models (1.3M to 85M parameters) from scratch on games played by a Bayesian player where both the prior and ground-truth answer are exact, then apply outcome-reward RL across varied group sizes, learning rates, optimizers, and GRPO variants.
AI.result: Base models hedge like the corpus while RL turns hedging into decisions, and when the right action is rare, runs either learn it everywhere or not at all; takeoff is predicted before training by the expected number of attempt groups in which the action wins, with about 35 winning groups giving even odds.
AI.conclusion: Outcome-reward RL cannot amplify behaviors it does not observe succeeding, and a simple pre-training count of winning groups governs whether rare-action learning takes off.

title: Can World Models Predict Rice Growth? Toward Agricultural World Models
summary: World models can imagine how a physical scene evolves over the next few seconds, but growers need to know how a crop will develop over weeks to months: will this rice plant have headed a month from now, and how will it look at harvest? We introduce agricultural world modeling, the task of predicting how the same plant will look at a requested horizon of days to months, from one photo of it, its cultivar, and its camera view. In preliminary analysis, even state-of-the-art image generators get this wrong: they often grow the plant too little or give it the color and form of the wrong growth stage. We argue that they do not work out the plant's developmental state, which the photo reveals only indirectly. We therefore propose AgroWM, which reasons about development before it draws growth. Its reasoning module, PhenoClock, works out the current growth stage, predicts the future one, and writes a Growth Script with numeric targets for height, plant area, and color; its generation module, the Rooted Renderer, then edits the photo to follow this script, adding new organs and colors to the photographed plant. Because pixel scores can prefer an unchanged copy of the photo, we instead check each forecast's traits and developmental timing against the plant's own later photos. On rice, 54.6% of the forecasts of AgroWM are matched to the target stage (Stage R@1), against 34.8% for GPT Image 2.5, 24.0% for Qwen Image 2.1, and 47.4% for the strongest domain-specific baseline, the same backbone fine-tuned without Growth Scripts; 9 to 20 weeks ahead, it still reaches 46.4%, against 35.7% for that baseline. On maize, a crop with a different body plan and stage scale, the same design again scores best on all four measures.

AI.tldr: The authors introduce agricultural world modeling and propose AgroWM, which predicts plant developmental stages and numeric growth targets before editing a single crop photo to forecast its appearance weeks to months ahead.
AI.motivation: Existing world models and image generators fail to forecast how a crop will look weeks or months later because they do not infer the plant's underlying developmental state from a single photo.
AI.method: AgroWM pairs PhenoClock, which infers the current growth stage, predicts the future stage, and outputs a Growth Script with numeric targets for height, area, and color, with the Rooted Renderer, which edits the input photo to match the script.
AI.result: On rice, 54.6% of AgroWM forecasts match the target stage (Stage R@1) versus 34.8% for GPT Image 2.5, 24.0% for Qwen Image 2.1, and 47.4% for a fine-tuned backbone without Growth Scripts (46.4% vs. 35.7% at 9-20 weeks ahead), and AgroWM also scores best on all four measures on maize.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly reasoning about developmental stages and numeric growth targets before rendering enables accurate long-horizon agricultural forecasting across crop species.

title: Learning to Think with Images Faithfully via Adaptive Data Selection
summary: Thinking with images (TwI) empowers vision-language models (VLMs) to overcome perceptual bottlenecks by actively cropping and zooming into fine-grained visual details, promising both higher accuracy and interpretable, region-grounded reasoning. However, our analysis shows that the improved accuracy of TwI models does not guarantee faithful tool use; they frequently invoke tools without actually relying on the zoomed region, undermining the reliability of tool-assisted reasoning. We trace this unfaithful behaviour to the training data: when questions are answerable without zooming, the model can answer correctly while ignoring the returned evidence, and this problem is exacerbated during training as the model becomes better at answering without tools. To keep zooming useful throughout training, we adapt the training data to the model's evolving capability and train on questions where correct zoomed evidence can still help the model answer correctly. This selection is supported by a data synthesis pipeline that localises small objects and constructs verifiable questions about their fine details, and complemented by an adaptiveness reward that favours tool-free answers when zooming is unnecessary. The experimental results show that our method substantially improves reasoning faithfulness and achieves state-of-the-art performance on visual search benchmarks (+11.6% on V*, +7.9% on HR-Bench 4K, and +9.4% on HR-Bench 8K). On multimodal hallucination benchmarks, our model also outperforms the compared TwI baselines. These results suggest that improving TwI faithfulness does not sacrifice accuracy and that both can be learnt from the right training data without directly supervising the reasoning process.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses unfaithful tool use in Thinking with Images (TwI) VLMs by adapting training data to the model's evolving capability and adding an adaptiveness reward, achieving state-of-the-art visual search results.
AI.motivation: TwI models often invoke crop-and-zoom tools without actually using the zoomed evidence, because training on questions answerable without zooming teaches the model to ignore tool outputs as its base capability grows.
AI.method: The authors synthesize verifiable fine-detail questions around localized small objects, dynamically select training examples where zoomed evidence still helps the current model answer correctly, and apply an adaptiveness reward favoring tool-free answers when zooming is unnecessary.
AI.result: The method substantially improves reasoning faithfulness and achieves state-of-the-art performance on visual search benchmarks (+11.6% on V*, +7.9% on HR-Bench 4K, and +9.4% on HR-Bench 8K), while also outperforming TwI baselines on multimodal hallucination benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Adapting training data to the model's evolving tool-free capability improves both TwI faithfulness and accuracy without requiring direct supervision of the reasoning process.

title: TwinLab-Bench: Evaluating AI Scientists in Agentic Twins of Real Labs
comment: this https URL contains tasks and code. 33 pages, 6 figures, 14 tables. LLM-agent benchmark for autonomous experimental design in digital twins of real labs (physics, chemistry, wet-lab biology, materials, engineering). 13 agents evaluated: Claude Fable 5.2 45.0, Opus 5.5 40.2, GPT-6.1-sol 31.7, plus DeepSeek, Qwen, Kimi, GLM and others
summary: AI agents are increasingly expected to act as AI scientists, which requires three increasingly open abilities: carrying out a given computational workflow correctly, choosing the next measurements from a given design space, and designing their own experiments. Existing benchmarks mainly evaluate the first two abilities, in a terminal or in a closed loop that selects from predefined candidates. Evaluating the third ability requires reliably executing an experiment that an agent designs, with readings grounded in a real laboratory. We introduce TwinLab-Bench, which evaluates AI scientists on self-designed experiments in 52 tasks from laboratories in the physical sciences, the life sciences, and engineering. The benchmark supports more than 100 experimental action types, and the agent's report is scored by comparison with a hidden answer taken from real laboratory records. Each task has its own TwinLab agent, an agent that serves as the environment and executes the experiments that the tested agent designs, reading the raw materials of the laboratory and calling calculators that are built from its records. Compared with a language model that sees only the task description, the TwinLab agent almost eliminates readings that deviate from the real records and inconsistent answers to a repeated request, and closed-book probes control for answers recalled from memory. We find that these tasks remain hard for frontier models: the strongest, Claude Fable 5.2, averages a score of only 45.0, and we conduct an empirical study of where it fails.

AI.tldr: The authors introduce TwinLab-Bench, a benchmark of 52 real-lab tasks where AI scientists design their own experiments executed by TwinLab environment agents, showing frontier models still struggle with an average score of 45.0.
AI.motivation: Existing AI scientist benchmarks mainly test executing given workflows or selecting from predefined candidates, rather than evaluating an agent's ability to design its own experiments grounded in real laboratory records.
AI.method: TwinLab-Bench spans 52 tasks across physical sciences, life sciences, and engineering with over 100 experimental action types; each task uses a TwinLab agent that executes self-designed experiments using raw lab materials and calculators, scoring reports against hidden real-lab answers.
AI.result: Compared to a task-description-only LM, the TwinLab agent nearly eliminates non-record-grounded readings and inconsistent repeated answers, and the strongest tested model, Claude Fable 5.2, averages only 45.0.
AI.conclusion: Grounding self-designed experiments in agentic twins of real laboratories exposes major gaps in frontier AI scientists' experimental design capabilities.

title: BADAS-3.0: Real-Time Driving Perception and Planning from One Camera
summary: We ask how far a driving model can get with one camera and real-time latency. BADAS-3.0 is a 1B-parameter video encoder with four small heads. From two seconds of one forward camera, it predicts the current speed, the metric path just driven, a collision-risk score and six candidate futures over 6.4 seconds, in under 50 ms. Given the car's current speed, BADAS-3.0 has 44% lower minADE$_6$ over five trajectory benchmarks than the 34B Alpamayo 2 Super, which reads six cameras and runs over 100x slower. The gain comes from camera rigs that neither model was trained on. On the rig they share, the two are on par. Existing benchmarks are mostly nominal driving, so we add two open-loop safety benchmarks, one of real dashcam collisions and near-misses and one of Euro NCAP scenarios. On both, BADAS-3.0 has a higher pass rate than every published planner we tested.

AI.tldr: BADAS-3.0 is a 1B-parameter single-camera driving model that predicts speed, driven path, collision risk, and six future trajectories in under 50 ms, outperforming a 34B six-camera planner on cross-rig benchmarks.
AI.motivation: It remains an open question how far a real-time driving perception and planning model can go using only a single forward camera.
AI.method: BADAS-3.0 uses a 1B-parameter video encoder with four lightweight heads taking two seconds of forward-camera video to predict current speed, metric path, collision risk, and six 6.4-second future trajectories in under 50 ms.
AI.result: Given current speed, BADAS-3.0 achieves 44% lower minADE_6 across five trajectory benchmarks than the 34B six-camera Alpamayo 2 Super (which runs over 100x slower) due to better generalization to unseen camera rigs, and achieves the highest pass rate on two new open-loop safety benchmarks (real dashcam collisions/near-misses and Euro NCAP).
AI.conclusion: A compact single-camera video model can achieve real-time latency, strong cross-rig generalization, and higher open-loop safety pass rates than much larger multi-camera planners.

title: HiSA: Sparsifying the Hidden Dimension of RoPE Attention in LLMs
summary: Attention in large language models (LLMs) scores every query against every key with a full dot product. We investigate whether this dot product must be computed completely for attention to be effective. We propose Hidden Sparse Attention (HiSA), which keeps the query and key projections intact but only computes a partial dot product, following a static, parameter-free rule set by the token positions: attention becomes sparse in the hidden (feature) dimension, an axis much less explored than token sparsity, rather than over tokens as in almost all sparse attention methods. Based on the structure of rotary position embeddings (RoPE), we decompose keys and queries into parts which can be omitted when computing attention. By training LLMs from scratch with HiSA, we find that this partial dot product does not hurt but improves performance compared with the complete product while computing only about a third of the query-key products. During inference HiSA improves decoding speed and shrinks memory footprint. We also extend HiSA to FlashAttention-3 kernels for training and inference. Finally, we motivate our approach by showing that dense attention learns to suppress the attention score parts that HiSA drops. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The authors propose Hidden Sparse Attention (HiSA), which sparsifies the hidden feature dimension of RoPE attention using a static position-based rule, improving LLM performance while computing only about a third of query-key products.
AI.motivation: Nearly all sparse attention methods sparsify over tokens rather than the hidden feature dimension, leaving open whether full query-key dot products are needed for effective attention.
AI.method: Exploiting the structure of rotary position embeddings (RoPE), HiSA keeps query and key projections intact but computes a partial dot product according to a static, parameter-free rule determined by token positions, and extends FlashAttention-3 kernels for training and inference.
AI.result: Training LLMs from scratch with HiSA improves performance over full dot-product attention while computing roughly one-third of query-key products, and speeds up decoding while reducing memory footprint during inference.
AI.conclusion: Sparsifying the hidden dimension of RoPE attention removes score components that dense attention learns to suppress, yielding both better performance and faster, lighter inference.

title: Democratizing Cross-Project Knowledge for Transforming Water Governance and Climate Resilience: an Agentic AI Ecosystem
comment: 8 pages, 2 figures. Accepted at WDSA/CCWI 2026. Proceedings publication pending
summary: EU-funded projects produce extensive evidence in the form of deliverables, reports, and case studies. However, this knowledge is typically scattered across projects and document structures, making it difficult to locate relevant, contextual information when making decisions. This paper introduces an Agentic AI Ecosystem that consolidates heterogeneous project documentation into a domain-aware knowledge base and provides adaptive access through an agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation pipeline. Documents from three EU-funded projects (IMPETUS, NATALIE, and InnWater) are reconstructed into hierarchical section trees and indexed with structured metadata. Retrieval is supported by two domain-specific embedding models fine-tuned on domain data (water and climate). On top of this knowledge base, a ReAct-style controller iteratively orchestrates retrieval actions by allocating retrieval budget across domain collections and accumulating evidence until a stopping criterion is met. In a retrieval benchmark over the corpus, the proposed approach improves Mean Reciprocal Rank by 26.7% (relative) compared to a single-domain embedding baseline, indicating more consistent retrieval of relevant evidence to support cross-project knowledge synthesis and climate-resilient decision-making.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an Agentic AI Ecosystem combining a hierarchical, domain-embedded knowledge base with a ReAct-style retrieval controller for cross-project water governance and climate resilience, improving MRR by 26.7%.
AI.motivation: Evidence from EU-funded water and climate projects is scattered across heterogeneous deliverables and reports, making it hard for decision-makers to locate relevant contextual information.
AI.method: Documents from three EU projects (IMPETUS, NATALIE, InnWater) are parsed into hierarchical section trees with structured metadata, indexed with two fine-tuned domain embedding models (water and climate), and queried by a ReAct-style controller that allocates retrieval budgets iteratively until a stopping criterion is met.
AI.result: On a retrieval benchmark over the project corpus, the ecosystem improves Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR) by 26.7% relative to a single-domain embedding baseline.
AI.conclusion: Combining hierarchical document structuring, domain-specific embeddings, and agentic budget-aware retrieval enables more consistent cross-project evidence synthesis for climate-resilient decision-making.

title: GLiDE: A Fast, Calibrated Decision Model Distilled from Reasoning Teachers
summary: Decision models enable fast, confidence-aware decisions by scoring candidate answers in a single forward pass, without generating text or intermediate reasoning. Yet reasoning can substantially improve decision quality, raising the question of whether its benefits can be retained without the cost of generating it. We investigate this question with \textbf{GLiDE}, a family of decision models spanning 0.4B to 27B parameters. Building on Qwen hybrid language models, GLiDE enables bidirectional interactions between the context, question, and candidate answers by removing causal masking from full-attention layers. To transfer reasoning capabilities into single-pass inference, we combine soft-target distillation from multiple teachers, including a reasoning model, with progressive post-training on diverse decision tasks. We further explore parameter-free recurrent depth to increase inference-time computation without generating tokens. Across five model sizes, GLiDE lies on the performance--parameter Pareto frontier of the Hugging Face \DI{}, with each model outperforming evaluated alternatives of equal or smaller size. \dmtwo{} (27B) achieves a hidden-set score of 71.52, with an expected calibration error of 2.0\% and a median latency of 92.9\,ms on a single GPU. Further checkpoint averaging and parameter-free recurrent depth yield GLiDE~27B, which reaches 73.37 with an expected calibration error of 2.1\%.

AI.tldr: The authors introduce GLiDE, a family of single-pass bidirectional decision models (0.4B-27B) distilled from reasoning teachers that achieve state-of-the-art calibrated decision performance with sub-100ms latency.
AI.motivation: Single-pass decision models offer fast, confidence-aware scoring without generating tokens, but it is unclear whether they can retain the decision quality of slower reasoning models.
AI.method: Built on Qwen hybrid language models with causal masking removed from full-attention layers, GLiDE combines soft-target distillation from multiple teachers (including a reasoning model), progressive post-training, checkpoint averaging, and parameter-free recurrent depth.
AI.result: Across five sizes, GLiDE lies on the Hugging Face Decision Index Pareto frontier, with the 27B base model scoring 71.52 (2.0% ECE, 92.9 ms median latency on one GPU) and checkpoint averaging plus recurrent depth raising the score to 73.37 (2.1% ECE).
AI.conclusion: Bidirectional single-pass architectures distilled from reasoning teachers can match or exceed larger alternatives on calibrated decision-making without token-generation overhead.

title: Hybrid Retrieval for Government Scheme Search in English and Marathi
summary: Retrieving government schemes requires matching citizens' information needs to formal administrative descriptions, often across languages and terminology. We present a bilingual search system for Maharashtra government schemes and public services that combines BM25 retrieval with sentence-embedding similarity through equal-weight score fusion. The system indexes aligned English-Marathi scheme descriptions and supports multilingual, Marathi-focused, and translation-mediated semantic configurations. Evaluation on manually curated bilingual queries compares BM25, dense retrieval, and hybrid retrieval using IndicSBERT and MahaSBERT. BM25 provides a strong baseline with a mean reciprocal rank (MRR) of 0.864. Hybrid retrieval increases MRR to 0.872 with IndicSBERT and 0.879 with MahaSBERT, whereas the corresponding dense-only systems achieve 0.663 and 0.655. MahaSBERT-based fusion also increases precision from 0.781 to 0.808 while matching BM25 recall at 0.946. These results support the complementary use of lexical and semantic signals in this collection, while showing that improvements over a strong lexical baseline are modest and metric-dependent. The study provides an application-focused analysis of hybrid retrieval for bilingual public-service information access.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates hybrid BM25 and dense sentence-embedding retrieval for bilingual English-Marathi government scheme search, finding modest MRR and precision gains over a strong BM25 baseline.
AI.motivation: Matching citizens' queries to formal administrative descriptions of government schemes across languages and terminology is challenging for purely lexical or purely dense retrieval.
AI.method: The authors build a bilingual search system over aligned English-Marathi Maharashtra government scheme descriptions using equal-weight score fusion of BM25 and sentence embeddings from IndicSBERT or MahaSBERT.
AI.result: On manually curated bilingual queries, BM25 achieves 0.864 MRR, while hybrid fusion raises MRR to 0.872 (IndicSBERT) and 0.879 (MahaSBERT) compared to 0.663 and 0.655 for dense-only models; MahaSBERT fusion also improves precision from 0.781 to 0.808 at matched 0.946 recall.
AI.conclusion: Lexical and semantic signals are complementary for bilingual public-service search, though gains over a strong BM25 baseline are modest and metric-dependent.

title: AgentRoboCritic: Understanding the Capability of Frontier Agents on Direct Robot Control
comment: 28 pages. Project page: this https URL
summary: Frontier multimodal language agents such as GPT-6 Astra have demonstrated strong capabilities in controlling robots directly via low-level numerical actions without high-level primitives. However, existing benchmarks report only episode-level success rates, which show neither how these agents succeed nor where they fail. In this paper, we present a systematic action-level analysis of frontier agents on direct robot control across 12 manipulation benchmarks. We introduce AgentRoboCritic, an intent-grounded critique framework in which the policy agent states a local intent alongside each action, and a critic evaluates the action's outcome and failure mode against this intent. Our action-level analysis demonstrates the promising capabilities of frontier agents on direct robot control, including closed-loop recovery from local execution failures, reliable semantic grounding across diverse scenes, and strong zero-shot manipulation without task-specific adaptation. It also identifies their current limitations, including task-relevant physical execution bottlenecks such as grasping and alignment, and uneven recovery across failure modes. Finally, we validate our critic on a 400-action human-annotated benchmark and release a dataset of 12,844 annotated actions alongside a fine-tuned open-source critic, Muse-Glimmer-30B, whose failure-mode accuracy rises from 32.58% to 74.24%, enabling low-cost action-level analysis.

AI.tldr: The authors introduce AgentRoboCritic, an intent-grounded action-level critique framework across 12 manipulation benchmarks, revealing both strong zero-shot control and physical execution bottlenecks in frontier multimodal agents.
AI.motivation: Existing direct robot control benchmarks report only episode-level success rates, obscuring how frontier multimodal agents succeed or where their low-level actions fail.
AI.method: In AgentRoboCritic, the policy agent states a local intent alongside each low-level numerical action, and a critic evaluates the action's outcome and failure mode against that intent; the authors also release a 12,844-action dataset and fine-tune Muse-Glimmer-30B as a critic.
AI.result: Action-level analysis across 12 manipulation benchmarks shows reliable semantic grounding and closed-loop recovery alongside physical execution bottlenecks in grasping and alignment; fine-tuning Muse-Glimmer-30B raises failure-mode accuracy from 32.58% to 74.24% on a 400-action human-annotated benchmark.
AI.conclusion: Intent-grounded action-level critique enables low-cost diagnosis of frontier robot control agents, pinpointing physical execution and recovery gaps hidden by episode-level metrics.

title: EgoPass-Bench: Identifying Objects That May Affect the Wearer's Passage in Egocentric Video
summary: Understanding an egocentric environment requires reasoning about how surrounding entities affect the observer's actions. Existing evaluations of multimodal foundation models (MFMs) examine observer localization, motion trajectories, and action feasibility, but leave the discovery and interpretation of evolving observer-entity interactions insufficiently assessed. We introduce EgoPass-Bench, a benchmark for observer-relative interaction understanding in real-world egocentric video. EgoPass-Bench comprises 284 manually reviewed evaluation clips recorded using Ray-Ban Meta (Gen 2) smart glasses and 2,201 distinct questions across five tasks assessing motion perception, interaction judgments about specified entities, and relevant-entity discovery without target cues. Our evaluation of eight frame-based and six native-video configurations reveals a pronounced discrepancy between motion perception and interaction understanding. The strongest evaluated model, GPT-6 Astra, correctly recognizes object motion in 91.37% of 394 comparisons involving the same targets, but correctly identifies changes in passage constraints in only 66.50%. Across all 574 entity-discovery questions, it trails the two-person human baseline by $23.65 \pm 7.45$ percentage points (paired 95% CI), while exceeding the always-empty baseline (36.76%) by at least 18.9 percentage points. Further analysis reveals frequent inclusion of entities that neither pose a plausible physical conflict nor constrain passage, showing that accurate motion recognition does not ensure reliable relevant-entity discovery.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces EgoPass-Bench for evaluating observer-relative passage-constraint understanding in egocentric video, showing that even the strongest MFM trails humans by 23.65 percentage points on entity discovery.
AI.motivation: Existing egocentric video benchmarks assess motion and action feasibility but inadequately evaluate how multimodal foundation models discover and interpret evolving observer-entity passage constraints.
AI.method: EgoPass-Bench contains 284 manually reviewed clips recorded on Ray-Ban Meta (Gen 2) smart glasses and 2,201 questions across five tasks covering motion perception, interaction judgments, and relevant-entity discovery without target cues, evaluated on eight frame-based and six native-video configurations.
AI.result: The strongest model, GPT-6 Astra, recognizes object motion in 91.37% of 394 comparisons but identifies passage-constraint changes in only 66.50%, and trails the two-person human baseline by 23.65 +/- 7.45 percentage points across 574 entity-discovery questions.
AI.conclusion: Accurate motion recognition in egocentric video does not guarantee reliable discovery of entities that physically constrain the wearer's passage.

title: Closing the Analyze-to-Design Gap: An Authorization-Bounded Agent for Self-Driving Laboratories
summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) agents are increasingly integrated into self-driving laboratories (SDLs) to plan experiments and interpret results. However, analytical reasoning alone does not make a laboratory autonomous: autonomy in an SDL is achievable only when the agent can be trusted to act on physical hardware unsupervised and knows when to defer to a human. Here, we present an architecture that integrates an agent at the Analyze-Design interface of the Design-Make-Test-Analyze (DMTA) cycle, enabling agent-driven measurement selection and data interpretation while ensuring that state-changing operations are authorized, validated, and auditable. We demonstrate this architecture on a liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) instrument in an oxidant-screening campaign for synthesizing an organic dye. Within human-defined campaign limits, the agent submitted measurement jobs, interpreted mass spectrometry (MS) and diode-array detection (DAD) data, flagged failed experiments, and produced an oxidant ranking. This ranking matched that obtained from scripted peak integration, and organic chemists confirmed the agent's spectral interpretations and failure assignments. In a simulated environment that replays the archived LC-MS data, where the agent chose which wells to inject under varying injection limits, it measured the highest-yielding condition at about its seventh injection, against 14.5 on average for a random order, and identified it in every campaign with a limit of eight or more injections. An agent can therefore close the analysis-to-design gap while its actions stay bounded and verifiable, which is a step toward greater autonomy for SDLs.

AI.tldr: The authors present an authorization-bounded agent architecture at the Analyze-Design interface of a self-driving laboratory, demonstrating safe, auditable LC-MS oxidant screening that finds the top condition in roughly half the injections of random search.
AI.motivation: Autonomy in self-driving laboratories requires not only analytical reasoning but also ensuring that physical hardware actions are authorized, validated, auditable, and bounded by human-defined limits.
AI.method: The architecture integrates an AI agent at the Analyze-Design interface of the DMTA cycle on an LC-MS instrument, allowing it to submit measurement jobs, interpret MS and DAD spectra, flag failures, and rank oxidants within human-defined campaign limits.
AI.result: The agent's oxidant ranking matched scripted peak integration and chemists verified its spectral interpretations; in archived LC-MS replay simulations, it found the highest-yielding condition at around its seventh injection (versus 14.5 for random order) and succeeded in every campaign with a limit of eight or more injections.
AI.conclusion: Bounding agent actions with explicit authorization and validation closes the analyze-to-design gap safely for physical self-driving laboratories.

title: Infer3D: Inverse Generative Modeling Enables Robust 3D Reconstruction
comment: 23 pages, 12 figures, 15 tables. Includes references and appendices. Project page: this https URL
summary: Humans can understand the 3D structure of scenes even from highly unfamiliar or extreme viewpoints. Cognitive science suggests this generalization stems from a top-down generative inference strategy. In contrast, state-of-the-art 3D reconstruction neural networks typically rely on amortized, feedforward inference. While fast, this pattern-matching approach degrades when faced with out-of-distribution (OOD) scene conditions unseen during training. Inspired by the generative nature of human vision, we propose Infer3D, an inverse generative modeling framework that recovers the latent variables of a generative model to best match the monocular input. To prevent degenerate flat outputs, we couple the generative image prior with a frozen 3D lifting network that constrains the optimization space to a valid, multi-view-consistent 3D manifold. Across a variety of controlled synthetic and real-world tasks, Infer3D demonstrates superior OOD reconstruction accuracy compared to feedforward networks trained on equal or larger datasets. Furthermore, mirroring how human perception requires more time to process confusing stimuli, we introduce an adaptive inference strategy that expends more test-time compute on ambiguous OOD examples while efficiently routing in-distribution inputs. Project website: this https URL

AI.tldr: Infer3D proposes an inverse generative modeling framework for monocular 3D reconstruction that optimizes generative latents constrained by a frozen 3D lifting network, outperforming feedforward baselines on out-of-distribution scenes.
AI.motivation: Feedforward 3D reconstruction networks are fast but degrade under out-of-distribution (OOD) scene conditions and extreme viewpoints unseen during training.
AI.method: Infer3D recovers the latent variables of a generative image model to match the monocular input while coupling it with a frozen 3D lifting network to constrain optimization to a multi-view-consistent 3D manifold, paired with an adaptive inference strategy that allocates more test-time compute to ambiguous OOD inputs.
AI.result: Across controlled synthetic and real-world tasks, Infer3D achieves superior OOD reconstruction accuracy compared to feedforward networks trained on equal or larger datasets.
AI.conclusion: Top-down inverse generative inference constrained by a 3D manifold and adaptive test-time compute provides a more robust path to OOD 3D reconstruction than purely feedforward pattern matching.

title: VisAlloc: Allocating Visual Supervision for On-Policy Self-Distillation
summary: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) offers a promising approach to improving visual reasoning in multimodal large language models (MLLMs). However, not all samples benefit equally from privileged visual guidance, and uniform token supervision can dilute visually grounded signals. We propose VisAlloc, a dual-level framework combining sample-level visual filtering with token-level counterfactual reweighting. A fixed paired-teacher filter retains samples answered correctly from an evidence-centered positive crop but incorrectly from a spatially displaced negative crop. At the token level, both EMA teachers score the same student-generated response, and their absolute log-probability differences measure view sensitivity. Additional supervision targets tokens admitted by sensitivity or teacher-distribution disagreement, with shared frozen-prior, template-bigram, and student--teacher divergence gates. Inverse-frequency redistribution preserves the total additional weight within each micro-batch, while the positive teacher remains the sole distillation target. Inference requires only the full-image student. Across eight benchmarks, our 4B and 9B models achieve macro-averages of 81.44 and 84.92, outperforming Vision-OPD reproductions by 0.97 and 0.52 points, respectively. Code on GitHub: this https URL

AI.tldr: VisAlloc improves on-policy self-distillation for MLLMs via sample-level visual filtering and token-level counterfactual reweighting, achieving 81.44 (4B) and 84.92 (9B) macro-averages across eight benchmarks.
AI.motivation: In on-policy self-distillation for multimodal LLMs, not all samples benefit from privileged visual guidance and uniform token supervision dilutes visually grounded learning signals.
AI.method: A fixed paired-teacher filter retains samples answered correctly from an evidence-centered positive crop but incorrectly from a displaced negative crop; at the token level, EMA teachers score student responses to reweight view-sensitive or teacher-disagreement tokens under divergence gates while keeping the positive teacher as the sole target.
AI.result: Across eight benchmarks, VisAlloc's 4B and 9B models achieve macro-averages of 81.44 and 84.92, outperforming Vision-OPD reproductions by 0.97 and 0.52 points, respectively, while requiring only the full-image student at inference.
AI.conclusion: Allocating visual supervision at both sample and token levels sharpens visually grounded distillation in MLLMs without adding inference overhead.

title: Do Deep Stereo Models Learn Shape Priors?
summary: Localizing object boundaries is important for embodied visual systems, since small boundary errors can change the inferred geometry of physical surfaces. We study whether deep stereo models produce boundaries consistent with simple shape priors when local image and disparity cues are weak. We create a synthetic stereo dataset consisting of objects drawn from a highly constrained family of shapes, with randomized depth, slant, color and texture.
