Despite the simplicity of this shape space, we find that several state-of-the-art stereo models retain systematic boundary errors, even when finetuned or trained from scratch on the dataset. We then introduce a simple generative stereo model that jointly predicts disparity and a distance field representing object boundaries. The model improves boundary localization and produces contours that adhere more closely to the underlying shape space. These results expose limitations in the boundary predictions of current stereo architectures when local evidence is weak, and motivate further study of whether generative models can better combine regional grouping evidence with global geometric structure.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that state-of-the-art deep stereo models retain systematic object-boundary errors even on simple synthetic shapes, and introduces a generative stereo model that improves boundary localization.
AI.motivation: Accurate object boundary localization is critical for embodied visual systems, yet it is unclear whether deep stereo models learn simple shape priors when local image and disparity cues are weak.
AI.method: The authors build a synthetic stereo dataset of simple shapes with randomized depth, slant, color, and texture to evaluate existing stereo models, and propose a simple generative stereo model that jointly predicts disparity and a boundary distance field.
AI.result: Existing state-of-the-art stereo models exhibit systematic boundary errors even when fine-tuned or trained from scratch on the synthetic dataset, whereas the joint generative model improves boundary localization and produces contours closer to the true shape space.
AI.conclusion: Current stereo architectures struggle to combine regional grouping with global geometry under weak local evidence, motivating generative approaches to boundary-aware stereo.

title: TALD: Transferability-Aware Logit Disentanglement for Cross-Modal Knowledge Distillation
summary: Cross-modal knowledge distillation can incur negative transfer when source-modality supervision conflicts with the target modality's discriminative characteristics. We propose TALD, a two-stage framework for Transferability-Aware Logit Disentanglement in class-aligned logit space. Guided by task-dependent self-benefiting and cross-modal exclusivity criteria, a Residual Disentangler decomposes logits from a teacher and an independently trained target-modality reference student into modality-general and modality-specific components. A Sample-Adaptive Modulator regulates decomposition constraints and sample-specific fusion weights. The learned modality-general components are then adaptively fused to supervise the final student. Across five benchmarks spanning vision, audio, and text, TALD achieves the largest mean accuracy gain and highest positive-transfer frequency among the compared methods. Across ten transfer directions with five runs each, TALD improves over training without distillation in 84% of evaluations, compared with at most 70% for the baselines, while offering a favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off. We plan to release the code.

AI.tldr: TALD is a two-stage cross-modal knowledge distillation framework that disentangles modality-general from modality-specific logits, achieving the highest mean accuracy gain and 84% positive-transfer rate across five benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Cross-modal knowledge distillation often suffers from negative transfer when source-modality supervision conflicts with the target modality's discriminative characteristics.
AI.method: Guided by self-benefiting and cross-modal exclusivity criteria, TALD uses a Residual Disentangler to split teacher and target-reference student logits into modality-general and modality-specific components, regulated by a Sample-Adaptive Modulator that fuses modality-general components to supervise the final student.
AI.result: Across five benchmarks spanning vision, audio, and text (ten transfer directions), TALD achieves the largest mean accuracy gain and improves over no-distillation training in 84% of evaluations, compared to at most 70% for baselines.
AI.conclusion: Disentangling and adaptively fusing modality-general logit components mitigates negative transfer in cross-modal knowledge distillation.

title: CoRelate: Coordinated Human-Object Motion Synthesis through Interaction Relations
summary: Human-object motion synthesis requires coordinated human participation as objects move toward specified goals. However, reaching object targets does not ensure that contact is established and maintained, while adjustments that improve contact may interfere with task completion. We introduce CoRelate, a diffusion framework that coordinates full-body human-object motion through explicit interaction relations and task feedback for rigid and articulated objects. We represent intended participation through hand-part relations that specify the participating hand, its part-relative reference position, and participation interval. These relations serve both as generation conditions and as references for measuring interaction realization. At each denoising step, a temporal refiner trained jointly with the generator combines relation deviations, task residuals, and motion features from the current prediction to jointly update human and object motion across the sequence. After generation, temporal motion correction addresses remaining contact failures by optimizing local motion segments while preserving object trajectories and protected human motion. Experiments demonstrate improved object-goal satisfaction, contact F1, and complete interaction success over the evaluated baselines. Ablation studies support the benefits of relation conditioning and the complementary roles of task and relation feedback.

AI.tldr: CoRelate is a diffusion framework for coordinated human-object motion synthesis that uses explicit hand-part interaction relations and a joint temporal refiner, improving goal satisfaction, contact F1, and interaction success.
AI.motivation: In human-object motion synthesis, reaching object targets does not guarantee proper contact, while enforcing contact can interfere with task completion.
AI.method: CoRelate conditions diffusion generation on hand-part relations (participating hand, part-relative reference position, participation interval), applies a jointly trained temporal refiner at each denoising step using relation deviations and task residuals, and performs post-generation temporal motion correction.
AI.result: Experiments on rigid and articulated objects show improved object-goal satisfaction, contact F1, and complete interaction success over evaluated baselines, with ablations confirming the complementary roles of task and relation feedback.
AI.conclusion: Explicit hand-part interaction relations combined with step-wise task and relation feedback effectively coordinate full-body human and object motion.

title: What a Calibrated Probability Hides: Belief-Level Post-Training for Decision Models
summary: A calibrated decision model can predict how often each answer is chosen. The same prediction can reflect disagreement among people who are confident in their choices or uncertainty among people who share a belief. Disagreement calls for identifying whose perspective applies, while uncertainty calls for gathering more evidence. Standard post-training scores a single prediction against one observed choice at a time, learning the pooled distribution without distinguishing these two sources of uncertainty. We introduce Belief-Grouped Policy Optimization (BGPO). The policy proposes a list of beliefs, estimates their prevalence, and predicts a choice distribution for each. During training, BGPO uses Bayes' rule to estimate how likely each belief was to generate an observed choice. These estimates weight the choice's contribution to each belief's log-score reward. To discover rare beliefs, the policy also proposes lists after seeing a few observed choices and retains them only if they predict held-out choices well. At inference, the policy uses only the question and combines the belief-specific distributions by prevalence to produce a calibrated aggregate prediction. On benchmarks covering opinions, conversation safety, emotions elicited by artwork, and photo aesthetics, BGPO achieves the lowest conditional, worst-group, and overall Jensen-Shannon divergence across model initializations. It improves conditional divergence on both text and image tasks. On a synthetic image task with known beliefs, BGPO recovers the underlying groups more accurately than baselines trained with belief labels.

AI.tldr: The authors introduce Belief-Grouped Policy Optimization (BGPO), which models latent belief groups and their prevalence rather than pooled choice distributions, achieving the lowest Jensen-Shannon divergence across four subjective benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Standard post-training learns a pooled choice distribution that cannot distinguish disagreement among confident groups from shared uncertainty, which require different downstream actions.
AI.method: BGPO proposes a list of beliefs, estimates their prevalence, and predicts a choice distribution per belief; during training it uses Bayes' rule to weight each belief's log-score reward by its likelihood of generating an observed choice, and discovers rare beliefs from few-shot observations.
AI.result: Across benchmarks on opinions, conversation safety, artwork emotions, and photo aesthetics, BGPO achieves the lowest conditional, worst-group, and overall Jensen-Shannon divergence, and recovers underlying groups more accurately than belief-labeled baselines on a synthetic image task.
AI.conclusion: Modeling latent belief groups via Bayesian reward weighting separates population disagreement from individual uncertainty and improves calibrated decision-making.

title: MV-JEPA: Post-Training Video Encoders for Cross-View Understanding
summary: JEPA-based video encoders learn strong representations for video and image understanding through prediction in latent space. However, their standard pretraining predicts features within individual images or video clips, without explicitly exploiting paired camera views of the same object or moment. Consequently, the learned representations may not reliably support matching across different camera viewpoints. To solve this problem, we introduce multi-view predictive post-training to strengthen cross-view instance and temporal correspondence while retaining independent single-view inference. A shared encoder processes masked context views independently, and a training-time predictor jointly predicts latent tokens for masked context regions and a fully held-out view. We alternate cross-view prediction with single-view masked prediction on general image and video data to help retain the encoder's pretrained capabilities. After only 9,000 post-training updates on a single GPU, MV-JEPA improves cross-view instance retrieval and coarse cross-camera moment retrieval on various datasets, with further gains in zero-shot action-phase retrieval and frozen-feature classification on AE2. Frozen-probe evaluations further indicate that post-training largely preserves motion recognition, image recognition, and dense semantic segmentation performance on the evaluated benchmarks. Together, these results demonstrate that multi-view predictive post-training can strengthen instance and coarse temporal correspondence in JEPA video encoders without modifying the encoder architecture or single-view inference interface.

AI.tldr: MV-JEPA introduces multi-view predictive post-training for JEPA video encoders, strengthening cross-view instance and temporal correspondence in 9,000 single-GPU updates while preserving single-view inference.
AI.motivation: Standard JEPA video pretraining predicts features within single images or clips, leaving learned representations weak at matching objects or moments across different camera viewpoints.
AI.method: A shared encoder processes masked context views independently while a training-time predictor jointly predicts latent tokens for masked context regions and a held-out view, alternating with single-view masked prediction on general data to retain pretrained capabilities.
AI.result: After 9,000 post-training updates on one GPU, MV-JEPA improves cross-view instance retrieval, coarse cross-camera moment retrieval, zero-shot action-phase retrieval, and frozen-feature classification on AE2, while largely preserving motion, image, and dense segmentation probe performance.
AI.conclusion: Multi-view predictive post-training efficiently adds cross-view correspondence to JEPA video encoders without altering the encoder architecture or single-view inference interface.

title: Phantom Success, Silent Failure: Auditing the Success Checkers of Simulated Manipulation Benchmarks
summary: Simulated manipulation benchmarks measure policy performance using hand-written success checkers that label each episode as a success or failure. Passing an expert demonstration shows that a checker accepts one way of completing the task. Learned policies, however, may stop after partial progress or complete the task in a different way. A checker may then accept an incomplete execution (phantom success) or reject an execution that satisfies the instruction (silent failure). In this paper, we introduce SimAudit, an LLM-based pipeline that audits success checkers against task instructions. SimAudit analyzes the instruction and checker code to identify scenarios where the two may disagree, recreates those scenarios in simulation, and runs the original checker. Multi-view renderings are then used to verify whether the observed behavior satisfies the instruction. Across RoboTwin 2.0, RoboCasa365, and RoboDojo, 183 simulated test cases produced the predicted checker verdict. Visual verification and deduplication yielded 61 distinct defects across 49 tasks, including 40 phantom successes and 21 silent failures. Most defects in RoboCasa365 accepted incomplete executions, most in RoboDojo rejected valid executions, and both error types were common in RoboTwin 2.0. These findings suggest that validating success checkers requires testing both incomplete executions and valid alternatives to expert demonstrations, and motivate more rigorous evaluation protocols for future benchmarks.

AI.tldr: SimAudit is an LLM-based pipeline that audits hand-written success checkers in simulated manipulation benchmarks, uncovering 61 distinct phantom-success and silent-failure defects across 49 tasks.
AI.motivation: Hand-written success checkers in simulated manipulation benchmarks are typically validated only on expert demonstrations, leaving them prone to accepting incomplete runs (phantom success) or rejecting valid alternative executions (silent failure).
AI.method: SimAudit uses an LLM to analyze task instructions and checker code for potential disagreements, recreates those scenarios in simulation, runs the original checker, and verifies behavior via multi-view renderings.
AI.result: Across RoboTwin 2.0, RoboCasa365, and RoboDojo, 183 simulated test cases yielded 61 distinct defects across 49 tasks (40 phantom successes and 21 silent failures), with RoboCasa365 dominated by phantom successes and RoboDojo by silent failures.
AI.conclusion: Auditing success checkers requires testing both incomplete executions and valid non-expert alternatives to ensure reliable benchmark evaluation.

title: Identity World Model: Recognizing People in an Imagined Latent World
summary: Whole-body human recognition has advanced rapidly with large vision models. However, existing methods remain fragile under real-world variations, as they tie identity to transient cues such as clothing, texture, pose, or viewpoint. We argue that a robust recognizer should not merely learn to ignore these cues, but imagine how a person would be represented if they changed. To this end, we propose IDWorld, an identity world model: just as a latent world model predicts the features of a scene after an action, IDWorld predicts how a person would be represented under a changed condition. In a single forward pass, IDWorld imagines these counterfactual features under shared canonical conditions, such as the same outfit, a fixed view, or a bare silhouette, without rendering any pixels. Compared with explicit imagination in pixels, this latent imagination keeps nearly the same accuracy while being over 11x faster, at 5.9 ms per frame. Since each imagined condition has its own strengths, IDWorld then fuses them adaptively, weighting each condition for every probe-gallery pair. Extensive experiments show that IDWorld achieves state-of-the-art results on CCPG and CCGR-MINI, outperforms the compared methods on MEVID, and generalizes best to CASIA-B* and SUSTech1K, with the best mAP on CCVID. These results suggest identity world models offer a simple yet effective path to robust recognition. Code will be released.

AI.tldr: IDWorld is an identity world model for whole-body human recognition that imagines counterfactual person representations under canonical conditions in latent space, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy at 5.9 ms per frame.
AI.motivation: Whole-body human recognition models remain fragile to clothing, texture, pose, and viewpoint changes because they tie identity to transient visual cues.
AI.method: In a single forward pass without pixel rendering, IDWorld predicts counterfactual latent features of a person under shared canonical conditions (same outfit, fixed view, or bare silhouette) and adaptively fuses them per probe-gallery pair.
AI.result: IDWorld achieves state-of-the-art results on CCPG and CCGR-MINI, outperforms compared methods on MEVID, generalizes best to CASIA-B* and SUSTech1K, and obtains the best mAP on CCVID, while running over 11x faster than pixel-space imagination at 5.9 ms per frame.
AI.conclusion: Latent-space identity world modeling offers a fast, effective path to human recognition invariant to transient appearance and viewpoint changes.

title: Recurrent Vision Language Models Solve the Shell Game
summary: Tracking a hidden object through a video is effortless for humans, yet it remains a bottleneck for vision language models (VLMs). In the shell game, where a ball is hidden under one of several identical cups that are then swapped, VLMs that answer directly stay near chance, thinking models fail on long games, and fine-tuning learns only the lengths it has seen. We argue that the limit is serial computation: each swap must be composed with the last result, and a VLM of fixed depth has only a fixed number of state transitions for it. To address this, we propose RecurrentVLM, which makes every attention layer of a pretrained VLM recur over time by computing the keys and values of finished frame groups from the layer's own output. With a single answer token, RecurrentVLM reaches 100% on VET-Bench and 99.6% on MET-Bench, and 99% on 50-swap games after training on at most 30 swaps. We also observe several interesting phenomena: length generalization emerges suddenly at an aha moment; without recurrence, each swap costs an attention layer; the ball's state forms in the first four attention layers; and recurrence keeps the latest state at the cost of details of earlier moments. These results suggest that recurrent VLMs are a potential solution for tracking the states of unobserved objects in video. Code will be released.

AI.tldr: RecurrentVLM makes every attention layer of a pretrained VLM recur over time to solve hidden-object tracking in the shell game, reaching 100% on VET-Bench and 99% on 50-swap games after training on at most 30 swaps.
AI.motivation: Standard and thinking VLMs fail at tracking hidden objects through long shell-game sequences because fixed-depth models have only a fixed number of serial state transitions.
AI.method: RecurrentVLM turns every attention layer of a pretrained VLM into a recurrent layer over time by computing keys and values of finished frame groups from the layer's own output.
AI.result: Using a single answer token, RecurrentVLM reaches 100% on VET-Bench, 99.6% on MET-Bench, and 99% on 50-swap games after training on at most 30 swaps, with length generalization emerging suddenly during training.
AI.conclusion: Layer-wise temporal recurrence overcomes fixed-depth serial computation bottlenecks in VLMs, enabling length-generalizable tracking of unobserved object states in video.

title: Beyond Restoration: Content-Degradation Factor Unfolding for Real-World Concealed Object Segmentation
summary: Reliable visual perception under degradation requires distinguishing task-relevant content from degradation-induced variations, especially in concealed object segmentation (COS), where foreground cues are inherently weak. The central challenge is not merely improving visibility, but identifying reliable content evidence amid degradation-induced variations. RGB-space segmentation often entangles content and degradation cues, while restoration-based methods primarily focus on image recovery and task interaction. This motivates explicit factorization to distinguish content evidence from degradation effects and assess its reliability. Retinex provides a spatially aligned basis for this separation but remains illumination-centric. We therefore extend it to content-degradation formation with task-asymmetric factor roles. The Factor Unfolding Network (FUN) uses the content factor R as the sole source of direct semantic evidence for segmentation, while the degradation factor L captures degradation-related variations and generates a spatial reliability map to calibrate this evidence. A unified energy couples observation formation with reliability-weighted foreground-background separation, and its alternating updates yield a coarse-to-fine network without clean-image supervision. In this way, FUN factorizes degradation for perception rather than removing it. Extensive experiments across clean and degraded conditions and diverse segmentation tasks demonstrate robust performance and generalization. Code will be released.

AI.tldr: The Factor Unfolding Network (FUN) extends Retinex to content-degradation factorization for real-world concealed object segmentation without clean-image supervision, improving robustness across clean and degraded scenes.
AI.motivation: Concealed object segmentation under real-world degradation struggles because RGB segmentation entangles content and degradation cues while restoration-based methods focus on image recovery rather than task evidence.
AI.method: FUN unfolds a unified energy into a coarse-to-fine network where a content factor R provides direct semantic evidence for segmentation and a degradation factor L generates a spatial reliability map to calibrate that evidence without clean-image supervision.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across clean and degraded conditions and diverse segmentation tasks demonstrate robust performance and generalization.
AI.conclusion: Factorizing degradation to calibrate perception rather than removing it provides an effective, clean-supervision-free approach to degraded concealed object segmentation.

title: Branch Caching After Step Distillation in Four- and Eight-Step Image Generators
summary: Can a distilled image generator save time by reusing features between its few remaining denoising steps? We study a fixed branch cache that replaces selected attention and MLP evaluations while preserving the student's noise schedule. One full trajectory and one raw-cache trajectory from the same initial noise supply a scalar correction for each branch type and reuse position. At $1024^2$, one internal reuse reduces four-step Qwen-Image-Lightning denoising time from 1.279 to 0.977 seconds. Three reuses yield $1.51\times$ speedup on eight-step Lightning and $1.53\times$ on eight-step Hyper-FLUX. We evaluate image quality on all 200 DrawBench prompts. With the reuse positions held fixed, correction improves mean same-seed image fidelity over raw reuse by 0.66 and 0.87 dB on the two Lightning students. On Hyper-FLUX the PSNR difference is 0.01 dB, while LPIPS improves from 0.1625 to 0.1546. These results measure the effect of branch caching and correction while retaining each student's original sampling grid.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates fixed branch caching with trajectory-derived scalar corrections in four- and eight-step distilled image generators, achieving up to 1.53x speedup while improving or preserving image fidelity.
AI.motivation: It is unclear whether few-step distilled image generators can further reduce denoising latency by reusing attention and MLP features across their remaining steps without breaking their noise schedules.
AI.method: A fixed branch cache replaces selected attention and MLP evaluations while preserving the student's noise schedule, using one full trajectory and one raw-cache trajectory from the same initial noise to fit a scalar correction per branch type and reuse position.
AI.result: At 1024x1024, one internal reuse cuts four-step Qwen-Image-Lightning time from 1.279 s to 0.977 s, while three reuses yield 1.51x speedup on eight-step Lightning and 1.53x on eight-step Hyper-FLUX; on 200 DrawBench prompts, correction improves mean same-seed PSNR by 0.66 and 0.87 dB over raw reuse on Lightning and improves Hyper-FLUX LPIPS from 0.1625 to 0.1546.
AI.conclusion: Scalar-corrected branch caching meaningfully accelerates four- and eight-step distilled image generators while maintaining or improving fidelity on their original sampling grids.

title: Keel: A Frontier Model Teaches a Vision-Language Model by Rewriting Its Weights
summary: Can a frontier model repair a vision-language model (VLM) by rewriting its weights? Small reasoning VLMs such as Qwen3.5 need such a repair: in thinking mode they fall into loops on many image questions, repeating themselves until the token limit, spending the whole budget and losing the answer. The usual remedies act on the decoding, leaving the looping model as it was, or must be told what to change. Yet the cause is written in the weights. Keel, the first agentic weight-editing method for VLMs on image tasks, finds and removes it there. Told only the symptom, an editor, a frontier multimodal LLM acting as an agent, locates the cause, edits the weights and tests them, with a failure census and instruments showing it the failing images and where the VLM attends; among several editors, the harness keeps only edits that clearly reduce the failure without lowering accuracy on questions no editor saw. The repair needs no training, keeps the model's size and per-token cost, and applies to already-edited weights. The editors expose where the loops live: from the original weights, independent editors on both models trace them to the attention outputs of the middle layers, and the smaller VLM stops consulting the image inside a loop. On Qwen3.5-0.8B and Qwen3.5-2B, across six image benchmarks from visual mathematics to GUI grounding, the edit removes most loops on every benchmark and shortens answers, and the edited models are significantly more accurate than the thinking models on average; the larger one gains most on GUI grounding, a task absent from the practice questions. Because the repair lives in the weights, it combines with budget forcing where held-out questions favor it: on the best available weights, Keel has the best average accuracy on both models, significantly above every training-free baseline we compare on the larger one.

AI.tldr: Keel is an agentic weight-editing method where a frontier multimodal LLM diagnoses and repairs repetition loops in smaller reasoning VLMs without training, improving accuracy across six image benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Small reasoning VLMs such as Qwen3.5 frequently fall into repetition loops in thinking mode until hitting the token limit, and existing decoding-time fixes leave the underlying weight cause intact.
AI.method: Given only the failure symptom, a frontier MLLM agent uses a failure census and attention/image inspection tools to locate the cause in the weights, edits them, and keeps only edits that reduce loops without hurting held-out accuracy.
AI.result: Independent editors trace loops to middle-layer attention outputs where the VLM stops attending to the image; on Qwen3.5-0.8B and Qwen3.5-2B across six image benchmarks, Keel removes most loops, shortens answers, and improves average accuracy without training or extra inference cost.
AI.conclusion: Agentic weight editing by frontier models can diagnose and permanently repair behavioral failure modes in smaller VLMs while preserving model size and per-token cost.

title: Real Cameras are Radiometric
summary: We propose the radiometric camera, a model that lifts any central geometric camera model to a radiometric one. The lifted model keeps the projection of the geometric model and adds a finite aperture, a free-form focus surface and a generic vignetting function. We calibrate it by inverse rendering directly on the relative irradiance of the sensor, from the same images of standard calibration targets used in geometric calibration. Geometric calibration absorbs the bias of its feature detections. The proposed radiometric calibration uses no features, and our radiometric cameras have lower reprojection errors on held-out test sets. The focus surface extends defocus modeling from the thin lens to any central camera, and we use it in a first multi-view radiometric reconstruction, which recovers the in-focus reflectance of a texture from defocused images. The vignetting is estimated jointly and accurately reproduces a flat field measured through a diffuser. Because every standard camera model lifts to a radiometric one, the radiometric camera naturally and directly extends generative scene models beyond multi-view geometry to multi-view radiometric ones, where phenomena such as lighting and attenuation can be accurately estimated.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes the radiometric camera, lifting any central geometric camera model with a finite aperture, free-form focus surface, and vignetting calibrated via feature-free inverse rendering.
AI.motivation: Standard geometric camera calibration relies on feature detections that introduce bias and ignores radiometric phenomena such as defocus and vignetting.
AI.method: The radiometric camera preserves the central geometric projection while adding a finite aperture, a free-form focus surface, and a generic vignetting function, calibrated by inverse rendering directly on sensor relative irradiance from standard calibration target images.
AI.result: Feature-free radiometric calibration achieves lower reprojection errors on held-out test sets, recovers in-focus texture reflectance from defocused multi-view images, and accurately reproduces diffuser-measured flat-field vignetting.
AI.conclusion: Lifting central geometric cameras to radiometric ones unifies geometric and radiometric calibration and extends multi-view scene modeling to lighting and attenuation.

title: Accord: Universal Online Metric Localization and Dense Mapping from one Camera and an IMU
summary: Dense metric mapping from a single camera and IMU remains challenging: visual-inertial odometry (VIO) provides metric motion but sparse geometry, whereas feed-forward depth models predict dense structure without ensuring metric scale. We present Accord, which constructs an accurate online dense metric map from any camera with an IMU. A VIO filter publishes metric poses, a depth foundation model conditioned on them predicts depth for short keyframe windows, and a factor graph fuses the resulting submaps. Recent work has explored several approaches to this problem. What is essential is the multi-view agreement (Accord), which is considered in SLAM as a source of geometric self-consistency. Accord anchors each keyframe window to metric 3D points triangulated from the filter poses, then exploits bidirectional dense depth agreement between co-visible images to estimate and correct per-image scale errors while preserving the metric scale established by the anchors. Context keyframes further improve depth prediction, and the resulting submaps are fused in a factor graph. We evaluate a single mapping configuration across five public camera-IMU setups and a new Phone-rig/GoPro dataset. With nothing tuned per dataset/setup and every map aligned only by Accord's own trajectory, Accord achieves consistently best/second-best mean F-score at 5 cm on every platform. Accord is open-source along with the phone-rig dataset for the benefit of the research community

AI.tldr: Accord is an online dense metric mapping system from a single camera and IMU that uses multi-view depth agreement anchored to VIO points, achieving top-two 5 cm F-scores across five public setups and a new phone-rig dataset.
AI.motivation: Single-camera VIO provides metric poses but sparse geometry, whereas feed-forward depth models produce dense structure without reliable metric scale.
AI.method: Accord anchors short keyframe windows to metric 3D points triangulated from VIO filter poses, uses bidirectional dense depth agreement between co-visible images to correct per-image scale errors, and fuses the resulting submaps in a factor graph.
AI.result: Using a single untuned configuration across five public camera-IMU setups and a new Phone-rig/GoPro dataset, Accord achieves consistently best or second-best mean F-score at 5 cm on every platform.
AI.conclusion: Exploiting multi-view dense depth agreement anchored to VIO poses enables universal, online dense metric mapping from any camera-IMU setup without per-dataset tuning.

title: Persistent Identity in Person Tracking: Online Enrollment and Registered Recognition
comment: 7 pages, 2 figures, 7 tables. An earlier version of this paper was submitted to an IEEE conference
summary: We extend PoseTReID with online appearance-bank matching (Gallery) and a residual-conflict guard for registered SVM recognition. All methods use supplied ground-truth (GT) person boxes. We average all-box assessment IDF1/HOTA equally across videos. On six SportsMOT clips, StrongSORT leads standalone trackers (79.44/84.72%) and exceeds both Gallery variants. Over eleven videos, Gallery AIN (83.29/85.44%) and COPE (84.66/86.38%) exceed standalone trackers with complete results. This lead depends on two retrospectively added GTA development compilations and is absent on the original nine videos. Registered SVMs lead both cohorts among complete results, with AIN at 95.72/94.82% over eleven videos. They use every GT crop from approximately 20% of frames, including future appearances. On MOT20-03, registered AIN reached 96.80% IDF1 and assigned the correct enrolled name to 90.72% of assessment GT observations. Gallery and standalone trackers receive no per-video labelled enrollment. Both identity routes restore identities across internal title cards, but Gallery trails SORT on three videos (four in HOTA) and both SVMs trail SORT on MOT16-04/MOT20-03. Under six-clip persistent-only scoring, native Gallery gains 2.39 percentage points in mean IDF1 over a matched control, with lower correct-P coverage and 5.02 times as many encoder attempts. Pose gating is mixed; the guard's metric effect is not isolated.

AI.tldr: This paper extends PoseTReID with online appearance-bank matching (Gallery) and registered SVM recognition, showing that registered SVMs lead overall while Gallery gains depend on dataset composition and add encoder cost.
AI.motivation: Maintaining persistent person identity across tracking interruptions requires comparing online appearance-bank enrollment against registered recognition under ground-truth person boxes.
AI.method: The authors evaluate two Gallery variants (AIN, COPE) and registered SVMs (trained on ~20% of frames including future appearances) with a residual-conflict guard across SportsMOT, MOT16, MOT20, and GTA compilations using IDF1 and HOTA.
AI.result: Over eleven videos, registered AIN leads at 95.72/94.82% IDF1/HOTA and Gallery AIN/COPE reach 83.29/85.44% and 84.66/86.38%, though Gallery's lead over standalone trackers disappears without two retrospectively added GTA compilations and trails StrongSORT on six SportsMOT clips (79.44/84.72%); native Gallery gains 2.39 points in six-clip persistent-only IDF1 at 5.02x encoder attempts.
AI.conclusion: Registered SVMs provide strong persistent identity when enrolled crops are available, whereas online Gallery matching offers modest persistent-only gains with notable computational overhead and dataset sensitivity.

title: CalibCache: Cache-to-Full Feature Dynamics Calibration for Diffusion Transformers
summary: Diffusion Transformers generate high-quality images, but iterative sampling remains computationally expensive. Feature caching reduces the number of full network evaluations, yet its approximation error can become more severe under short sampling schedules, where fewer full-compute steps and a coarser sampling grid can make history-based extrapolation less reliable. In this paper, we propose CalibCache, a lightweight offline calibration method that corrects systematic discrepancies between cached and full-compute feature dynamics. Specifically, CalibCache calibrates feature acceleration, defined as the second-order finite difference across sampling steps. Using only a single pair of full-compute and naive-cache trajectories at each setting, CalibCache fits scalar acceleration maps offline by centered least squares. These maps are then applied during sampling without additional full-network evaluations or online optimization. Across FLUX.1-dev and Qwen-Image on DrawBench and DiT-XL/2 on ImageNet-256, CalibCache consistently improves fidelity or generation quality over TaylorSeer under 20-step sampling at cache intervals $N=3,4,5$. At $N=5$, it reduces FLUX.1-dev LPIPS from $0.563$ to $0.429$ while achieving a $2.86\times$ denoising speedup over full-compute sampling, and lowers DiT-XL/2 FID from $16.39$ to $10.37$ relative to TaylorSeer.

AI.tldr: CalibCache is a lightweight offline calibration method for Diffusion Transformers that corrects systematic discrepancies between cached and full-compute feature dynamics, improving generation quality under short sampling schedules.
AI.motivation: Feature caching speeds up Diffusion Transformer sampling, but approximation errors become severe under short sampling schedules where fewer full-compute steps and coarser grids make history-based extrapolation unreliable.
AI.method: CalibCache calibrates feature acceleration (the second-order finite difference across sampling steps) by fitting scalar acceleration maps offline via centered least squares using a single pair of full-compute and naive-cache trajectories per setting, then applying them during sampling without extra full-network evaluations or online optimization.
AI.result: Across FLUX.1-dev and Qwen-Image on DrawBench and DiT-XL/2 on ImageNet-256 under 20-step sampling at cache intervals N=3,4,5, CalibCache consistently outperforms TaylorSeer; at N=5, it reduces FLUX.1-dev LPIPS from 0.563 to 0.429 with a 2.86x denoising speedup over full-compute sampling, and lowers DiT-XL/2 FID from 16.39 to 10.37 relative to TaylorSeer.
AI.conclusion: Offline calibration of feature acceleration effectively mitigates caching errors in Diffusion Transformers under short schedules without adding inference overhead.

title: ScaleDiag: Diagnosing the Limits of Test-Time Scaling in GUI Grounding
comment: Accepted by ICDM@D2AI 2026 Best Paper Award
summary: GUI grounding maps a screenshot and a natural language instruction to the coordinates of the intended interface element. Existing approaches improve grounding through visual scaling, instruction scaling, and sampling scaling, yet it remains unclear which grounding bottlenecks these strategies address and where their gains saturate. To address this gap, we introduce ScaleDiag, a controlled diagnostic framework that isolates the effects of visual input, instruction information, and prediction sampling on GUI grounding by independently varying target scale and surrounding context, target-specific information and auxiliary descriptions, and candidate coverage and selection, respectively. We evaluate ScaleDiag across five benchmarks and up to eight vision-language models and find that each scaling strategy operates within a much narrower regime than commonly assumed. (1) Visual scaling is governed by target occupancy rather than a fixed crop ratio, with full-screen errors typically rescued once the target occupies only 0.32% of the cropped view, while further zooming eventually becomes harmful. (2) Instruction scaling is driven by information that identifies the target rather than description richness itself, as even ground-truth-derived attributes such as color, size, and shape are often neutral or harmful, while appearance and spatial descriptions account for over 90% of the achievable gain. (3) Repeated sampling exposes a different limitation, as correct coordinates are frequently generated but remain difficult to select, leaving 5.1--11.0 points of oracle headroom while geometric consensus provides almost no improvement. Together, these results show that test-time scaling is constrained by distinct operating regimes rather than benefiting monotonically from more visual focus, richer instructions, or additional samples. Our code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: ScaleDiag is a controlled diagnostic framework that evaluates visual, instruction, and sampling scaling in GUI grounding, revealing that each strategy operates within a narrow regime rather than scaling monotonically.
AI.motivation: Existing GUI grounding methods rely on visual, instruction, and sampling scaling, but it remains unclear which bottlenecks each strategy addresses and where gains saturate.
AI.method: ScaleDiag isolates the effects of visual input (target scale and surrounding context), instruction information (target-specific vs. auxiliary descriptions), and prediction sampling (candidate coverage and selection) across five benchmarks and up to eight vision-language models.
AI.result: Visual scaling is governed by target occupancy, rescuing full-screen errors once the target occupies 0.32% of the cropped view before further zooming becomes harmful; instruction scaling depends on target-identifying appearance and spatial descriptions (>90% of achievable gain) while ground-truth attributes like color, size, and shape are often neutral or harmful; repeated sampling leaves 5.1 to 11.0 points of oracle headroom with geometric consensus offering almost no improvement.
AI.conclusion: Test-time scaling in GUI grounding is constrained by distinct operating regimes, showing that more visual focus, richer descriptions, or additional samples do not monotonically improve performance.

title: VoxForge: A Unified Foundation Model for Dense 3D Features Across MRI, CT and PET
comment: 34 pages (8-page main paper, references, and 23-page supplementary material), 7 figures. Rushil Anirudh and Jayaraman J. Thiagarajan contributed equally
summary: A unified 3D medical foundation model promises reusable, frozen features that serve a wide variety of tasks such as segmentation, classification and registration on MRI, CT and PET as well as specialist models do. Generalist models still need separate backbones for localized and global tasks, specialist models are confined to a single modality, with the concern that spanning modalities under-emphasizes fine anatomy, and both typically rely on end-to-end fine-tuning to be competitive. We present VoxForge, a single encoder that integrates recent advances in 3D architecture, self-distillation and cross-modal curricula to learn transferable features from permissively licensed MRI and CT volumes. We evaluate it strictly frozen, the test a reusable foundation model must pass, against state-of-the-art generalist and specialist models on segmentation, classification and registration across MRI and CT, and on PET, which it never sees. VoxForge has the best or tied-best average rank in every task group, serves localized and global tasks across modalities at the level of state-of-the-art specialists, and is extremely label-efficient, matching top-performing models on TotalSegmentator CT with a tenth of the labels.

AI.tldr: VoxForge is a unified, frozen 3D medical foundation encoder trained on MRI and CT volumes that matches specialist models across segmentation, classification, and registration on MRI, CT, and unseen PET.
AI.motivation: Existing generalist 3D medical models still require separate backbones for localized and global tasks, specialist models are limited to single modalities, and both typically depend on end-to-end fine-tuning to be competitive.
AI.method: VoxForge integrates 3D architectural advances, self-distillation, and cross-modal curricula to learn transferable features from permissively licensed MRI and CT volumes, and is evaluated strictly frozen across localized and global tasks.
AI.result: Evaluated strictly frozen against state-of-the-art generalist and specialist models on segmentation, classification, and registration across MRI, CT, and unseen PET, VoxForge achieves the best or tied-best average rank in every task group and matches top models on TotalSegmentator CT using one-tenth of the labels.
AI.conclusion: A single frozen 3D foundation encoder can effectively serve diverse localized and global medical imaging tasks across modalities, including unseen PET, with high label efficiency.

title: MoGloss: Joint Motion and Pseudo-Gloss Pretraining for American Sign Language Understanding
comment: 15 pages, 4 figures. Project page: this https URL
summary: Sign language translation and recognition have been shown to benefit from various pretraining approaches. We propose a novel two-stage pretraining approach for the motion encoder, which first learns to reconstruct masked motion, followed by joint masked prediction of pseudo-gloss units and motion. Pseudo-glosses serve as an intermediate structured representation of natural language text and are obtained from the captions by a large language model. We curate a corpus of about 1,100 hours of American Sign Language from five public datasets, estimate 2D pose for all clips and define an evaluation protocol. We then reproduce state-of-the-art translation methods and evaluate them using the same train and test splits. We propose a translation model built on our pretraining strategy, and this model outperforms the previous state-of-the-art methods Uni-Sign and SHuBERT, as well as the YouTube-ASL baseline, on the How2Sign, ASL STEM Wiki and OpenASL datasets. Furthermore, the gain from the joint pretraining using motion and pseudo-gloss grows as translation data shrinks. A classifier built on the same encoder also achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on ASL Citizen isolated sign recognition and outperforms our reproduction of Uni-Sign on WLASL2000.

AI.tldr: MoGloss is a two-stage motion encoder pretraining strategy combining masked motion reconstruction and joint masked prediction of motion and LLM-generated pseudo-glosses, achieving state-of-the-art ASL translation and recognition.
AI.motivation: Sign language translation and recognition benefit from pretraining, but need better ways to align motion representations with structured linguistic units across large-scale corpora.
AI.method: The authors curate an ~1,100-hour American Sign Language corpus from five public datasets with estimated 2D poses, pretrain a motion encoder first via masked motion reconstruction and then via joint masked prediction of motion and LLM-derived pseudo-glosses, and build downstream translation and classification models.
AI.result: On How2Sign, ASL STEM Wiki, and OpenASL, the proposed translation model outperforms Uni-Sign, SHuBERT, and the YouTube-ASL baseline, with larger gains as translation data shrinks; a classifier on the same encoder achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on ASL Citizen and outperforms Uni-Sign on WLASL2000.
AI.conclusion: Joint pretraining with motion and LLM-generated pseudo-glosses provides strong, data-efficient representations for both sign language translation and isolated sign recognition.

title: Search or Scoring? Diagnosing Why Visual World-Model Planners Fail
comment: 43 pages, 10 figures, 30 tables; supplementary material included
summary: Visual world models such as DINO-WM and JEPA-WM plan with an optimizer that searches for actions whose predicted outcome has the lowest cost, its distance to a goal image. A plan can thus fail in two ways: the optimizer never tries a good action that the cost would prefer (a search failure), or the cost, computed on predictions, ranks a bad action first (a scoring failure). The two need different remedies, more search or a better model, but a planner does not record which one occurred. We tell them apart by executing the optimizer's candidates, scoring a known solution with the planner's own cost, and comparing costs on predicted and real outcomes. An error model explains when each arises and so how to use retrieved demonstration windows (DemoProp): start the search from them (a warm start) when prediction errors are small, and average them without the model when large errors make the optimizer pick overrated actions. Across four simulated environments and three world models, on short tasks whose goals the planner can represent, PushT and Wall fail mostly by search, while Metaworld and RoboCasa fail by scoring because the cost, sound on real outcomes (AUROC 0.94 on Metaworld), is at chance on predictions (0.54). The diagnosis tells which remedy pays off: a four times larger search lowers the real-outcome cost only where failures come from search (clearly for DINO-WM), and where they come from scoring, averaging the windows without the model solves 127 of 168 new Metaworld tasks, against at most 87 when the model chooses among them. Within PushT, degrading only the model flips which use is better, and our rule, frozen in advance, follows the flip and solves 678 of 960 new episodes, against 530 for the best fixed use.

AI.tldr: This paper diagnoses whether visual world-model planners fail due to search or scoring errors and introduces a rule for using retrieved demonstration windows (DemoProp) accordingly.
AI.motivation: Visual world-model planners can fail either because the optimizer never tries a good action (search failure) or because the cost function on predicted outcomes ranks a bad action first (scoring failure), yet planners do not record which occurred.
AI.method: The authors distinguish failure modes by executing optimizer candidates, scoring known solutions with the planner's cost, and comparing costs on predicted versus real outcomes; they propose using retrieved demonstration windows to warm-start search when prediction errors are small, and averaging them without the model when large errors cause overrated actions.
AI.result: Across four simulated environments and three world models (including DINO-WM and JEPA-WM), PushT and Wall fail mostly by search while Metaworld and RoboCasa fail by scoring (cost AUROC 0.94 on real outcomes vs. 0.54 on predictions); a 4x larger search helps only on search failures, whereas model-free window averaging solves 127 of 168 new Metaworld tasks (vs. at most 87 with model selection), and the frozen rule solves 678 of 960 PushT episodes (vs. 530 for the best fixed use).
AI.conclusion: Separating search from scoring failures enables targeted remedies and dictates whether retrieved demonstrations should warm-start model-based search or bypass the world model.

title: Fold the Loop: Decoding-Time KV Memory for Looped Vision-Language Models
summary: Looped vision-language models (VLMs) deepen visual reasoning by repeatedly applying weight-tied modules. However, their decoding memory grows with recurrent depth and limits the image size and batch size that fit in a fixed memory budget. Each recurrent step produces its own key-value (KV) states, so the cache holds several copies of the same image. We find that, after an exact prefill, earlier steps still need access to visual information but can reuse the final visual KV within the same module. We propose FoldCache, which compresses visual KV along the recurrent axis while preserving the full prefill computation. FoldCache partitions recurrent steps within each module into groups and retains the final visual KV of each group for its members to share during decoding. Sharing stays within module boundaries, while question and answer KV remain separate for each step. The grouping granularity controls the degree of compression, and folding can be combined with token eviction and quantization to further reduce memory use. On LoopVL, FoldCache approximately halves prefix KV memory while matching full-cache accuracy on five open-ended benchmarks. These memory savings support batch sizes up to 1.7 times those of a full cache under the same GPU memory budget, and up to 2.6 times with the more aggressive FoldCache-Lite.

AI.tldr: FoldCache compresses decoding-time visual KV memory in looped vision-language models by sharing the final visual KV across grouped recurrent steps within each module, halving prefix KV memory without losing accuracy.
AI.motivation: Looped vision-language models repeatedly apply weight-tied modules to deepen visual reasoning, but each recurrent step stores its own copy of visual KV states, causing decoding memory to grow with recurrent depth and limiting batch and image sizes.
AI.method: FoldCache preserves exact prefill computation, partitions recurrent steps within each module into groups, and retains only the final visual KV of each group for its members to share during decoding while keeping question and answer KV separate per step.
AI.result: On LoopVL across five open-ended benchmarks, FoldCache roughly halves prefix KV memory while matching full-cache accuracy, enabling batch sizes up to 1.7x larger (and up to 2.6x with FoldCache-Lite) under the same GPU memory budget.
AI.conclusion: Folding visual KV states along the recurrent axis within module boundaries substantially reduces memory overhead in looped VLMs while preserving reasoning accuracy.

title: A Unified Framework for Image Manipulation Localization Under Multi-Type Weak Supervision
summary: Existing weakly supervised image manipulation localization (IML) methods typically rely on annotation-specific training strategies, hindering the joint use of diverse annotations within a single model. This limits the scale of usable training data and constrains further progress. We propose UniIML, a teacher-student framework that maps diverse weak annotations into a unified representation to guide the Segment Anything Model (SAM) in generating multiple candidate masks. However, SAM is designed for general-purpose segmentation and has limited sensitivity to manipulation traces; its predicted quality scores alone may therefore fail to reliably identify the candidate that best delineates the manipulated region. We introduce Ordinal Safe Consensus (OSC), which first filters candidates using trusted weak-annotation constraints encoded in the unified representation. It then ranks the remaining candidates separately by consistency with weak annotations, SAM-predicted quality scores, and cross-view stability, aggregating these rankings for an initial selection. To assess how changes in the evaluation criteria affect candidate selection, OSC repeats ranking and selection while omitting one criterion at a time. The most frequently selected candidate is adopted as the final mask, and its relative selection frequency quantifies selection stability. We construct soft pseudo-labels from the selected candidate's predicted probabilities and estimate pixel-level supervision weights based on selection stability, pixel-level agreement among candidates, and predictive certainty. The student receives direct supervision in regions defined by weak annotations and learns from soft pseudo-labels elsewhere through reliability-weighted distillation, enabling unified training across weak annotation types. Experiments show that UniIML achieves superior average performance compared with state-of-the-art IML methods.

AI.tldr: UniIML is a unified teacher-student framework for weakly supervised image manipulation localization that converts diverse weak annotations into a shared representation to guide SAM and distills reliable pseudo-labels.
AI.motivation: Existing weakly supervised image manipulation localization methods use annotation-specific training strategies, preventing joint training across diverse weak annotation types and limiting usable training data.
AI.method: UniIML maps diverse weak annotations into a unified representation to prompt SAM for candidate masks, introduces Ordinal Safe Consensus (OSC) to filter and rank candidates by annotation consistency, SAM quality, and cross-view stability while estimating selection stability, and trains a student via direct weak supervision plus reliability-weighted distillation of soft pseudo-labels.
AI.result: Experiments demonstrate that UniIML achieves superior average performance compared with state-of-the-art image manipulation localization methods.
AI.conclusion: Unifying diverse weak annotations with consensus-based candidate selection and reliability-weighted distillation enables effective, scalable weakly supervised image manipulation localization.

title: Text Lives in the Guidance: Preventing Silent Text Rewriting in Cached Diffusion Transformers
summary: Diffusion transformers (DiTs) now render long, legible text in images, and feature caching is a standard way to accelerate them. Caches are judged by image-level metrics, which do not check whether the rendered text is still correct. We find that caching silently rewrites this text. On Z-Image, TaylorSeer at 2.9x fewer FLOPs lowers word accuracy from 62% to 46%, while ImageReward and CLIP Score barely change. Sampling with fewer steps at the same compute keeps almost all of this text, so the loss comes from how the cache predicts the skipped steps. Decomposing the cache error along classifier-free guidance (CFG), we trace this loss mainly to the guidance term, the difference between the conditional and unconditional predictions, which caches extrapolate worst on text. Correcting the guidance inside the text alone recovers most of the lost text. We therefore propose GuideCache, which recomputes both CFG branches only on the tokens with the largest predicted guidance error, using the guidance terms that the cache already stores. At 2.4x fewer FLOPs, GuideCache restores full-compute prompt fidelity on Z-Image and Qwen-Image, and on Z-Image it renders text as well as or better than ToCa, TeaCache, and FasterCache while staying much closer to the full model's output. GuideCache works with caches of any order, and on top of fewer sampling steps it keeps more text than step reduction at a higher speedup. These results suggest that acceleration methods for text-rendering models should be evaluated on the text they render.

AI.tldr: GuideCache prevents feature caching from silently corrupting rendered text in Diffusion Transformers by selectively recomputing classifier-free guidance branches on tokens with the largest predicted guidance error.
AI.motivation: Feature caching accelerates text-rendering Diffusion Transformers, but standard image-level metrics miss silent text corruption; on Z-Image, TaylorSeer at 2.9x fewer FLOPs drops word accuracy from 62% to 46% while ImageReward and CLIP Score barely change.
AI.method: Decomposing cache error along classifier-free guidance (CFG) reveals that the guidance term is extrapolated worst on text; GuideCache uses cached guidance terms to identify tokens with the largest predicted guidance error and recomputes both CFG branches only on those tokens.
AI.result: At 2.4x fewer FLOPs, GuideCache restores full-compute prompt fidelity on Z-Image and Qwen-Image, renders text as well as or better than ToCa, TeaCache, and FasterCache on Z-Image while staying closer to the full model output, and preserves more text than step reduction at a higher speedup.
AI.conclusion: Caching acceleration for text-rendering diffusion models must be evaluated on text fidelity, and targeted CFG recomputation effectively preserves legible text.

title: Zero to Four Views: Unified Panorama Generation and Preference RL for Unobserved Regions
summary: Panoramas can serve as shared scene backgrounds for multi-shot video generation, but most existing panorama generators take text alone or a single input image. We present a single model that generates a full equirectangular panorama from a text caption and K in {0,...,4} perspective conditioning views taken by a four-camera rig at one viewpoint. We fine-tune a pretrained text-to-image rectified-flow transformer in two stages. In the first stage, each conditioning view is appended to the token sequence together with the ID of its camera slot, and the number of views varies during training, so one set of weights serves every input setting. In the second stage, we improve the region not covered by any conditioning view. Supervised training computes its loss on noisy latents of the ground truth and never scores a panorama the model has generated and decoded, so we propose Uncovered-Region GRPO (UR-GRPO), a reinforcement-learning recipe that rewards the candidates a vision-language model prefers in pairwise comparisons on crops around this region. Because the slot ID alone does not tell the model which way the rig points, we also offer an optional variant that writes each view's camera direction into its position encoding, which lets the user decide where each view appears in the output. With one conditioning view, our model outperforms the previous state of the art, 360Anything, trained on the same data and evaluated with the same code, on Laval Indoor and gives mixed results on an indoor subset of SUN360; the second stage improves the results for every number of conditioning views.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a unified rectified-flow transformer that generates full equirectangular panoramas from text and 0 to 4 perspective camera views, enhanced by a vision-language preference RL stage for unobserved regions.
AI.motivation: Most existing panorama generators accept only text or a single input image, and supervised latent training never scores decoded panoramas in regions not covered by conditioning views.
AI.method: A pretrained text-to-image rectified-flow transformer is fine-tuned in two stages: first appending varying numbers (0 to 4) of conditioning views with camera slot IDs (and optional directional position encodings), and second applying Uncovered-Region GRPO (UR-GRPO) using pairwise VLM preferences on crops around unobserved regions.
AI.result: With one conditioning view, the model outperforms 360Anything on Laval Indoor under identical training data and evaluation code, shows mixed results on an indoor SUN360 subset, and improves across all view counts after the UR-GRPO stage.
AI.conclusion: Variable-view conditioning combined with VLM-guided preference RL on uncovered regions enables flexible, higher-quality multi-view panorama generation within a single model.

title: HOPD: Historical On-Policy Distillation for SAR MLLM Continual Learning
summary: Continual SAR interpretation requires multimodal large language models to learn incoming sources while retaining earlier task abilities. This is difficult when acquisition and geographic shifts alter visual evidence, regionally concentrated categories bias answers, and historical images are scarce. We address this problem with Historical On-Policy Distillation (HOPD), which reuses source-acquisition LoRA states as persistent teachers for one evolving student. Archiving each state before consolidation preserves a stable source reference. The teachers supervise student-generated prefixes, transferring historical behavior to the student's changing generation contexts. To enrich sparse replay, original-view teachers guide augmented historical student views while preserving spatial coordinates. This knowledge is consolidated into a single deployed adapter that requires no source identity. On SARVQA-CL, our source-incremental evaluation protocol, HOPD achieves the highest final mean score of 54.51 among the compared methods, exceeding the strongest baseline by 2.96 points. It also improves the final source-macro score in every evaluated task over shared-memory Replay-SFT, with gains across source orders. These results support source-acquisition history as supervision for retaining earlier task performance during continual SAR adaptation. Code and data: this https URL.

AI.tldr: HOPD is a continual learning method for SAR multimodal LLMs that archives source-acquisition LoRA states as persistent teachers to perform on-policy distillation on student-generated prefixes and augmented historical views.
AI.motivation: Continual SAR interpretation suffers from forgetting when acquisition and geographic shifts alter visual evidence, regional category concentrations bias answers, and historical images are scarce.
AI.method: Historical On-Policy Distillation (HOPD) archives each source-acquisition LoRA state before consolidation as a persistent teacher that supervises student-generated prefixes and guides augmented historical student views while preserving spatial coordinates, consolidating knowledge into a single adapter requiring no source identity.
AI.result: On the SARVQA-CL source-incremental protocol, HOPD achieves the highest final mean score of 54.51 (exceeding the strongest baseline by 2.96 points) and improves final source-macro scores across every evaluated task and source order over shared-memory Replay-SFT.
AI.conclusion: Using archived source-acquisition LoRA states as on-policy teachers effectively mitigates catastrophic forgetting during continual SAR MLLM adaptation without needing source identities at inference.

title: Decision Boundaries Matter: Graph-Regularized Residual Adaptation for Cross-Domain Fake Image Detection
summary: Despite learning transferable features, fake image detectors may struggle on unseen domains due to mismatched decision boundaries. Our analysis shows that features extracted by the frozen forensic encoder remain discriminative, but the source-trained decision boundary does not fully exploit this information. However, correcting this boundary without source data or target labels remains challenging, as unreliable source predictions may lead to incorrect adaptation. To address this issue, we propose Graph-Regularized Residual Adaptation (GraRA), which refines the source decision boundary using only unlabeled target data. To determine which classifier directions to update, GraRA constructs a compact residual subspace from uncertainty-weighted target features and keeps it orthogonal to the source classification direction. To guide these updates, it uses source-score anchors to generate soft labels through target-graph diffusion, while neighborhood consistency regularizes residual learning within the constrained subspace. The learned correction is merged into the source classifier, requiring only 32 optimized coefficients and no additional inference branches. On diverse unseen OpenMMSec domains, GraRA achieves 84.36\% accuracy and 91.34\% AUC, improving over the source detector by 4.33 and 3.50 percentage points, respectively. Further analysis shows that reliable source predictions and locally consistent neighborhoods help guide residual learning, allowing GraRA to correct ranking errors that a simple threshold shift cannot address. \textcolor{cvprblue}{Code will be made publicly available.

AI.tldr: GraRA refines the decision boundary of a frozen fake-image detector on unseen domains using only unlabeled target data by optimizing a compact, orthogonal residual subspace via target-graph diffusion.
AI.motivation: Fake-image detectors often fail on unseen domains due to mismatched decision boundaries even when frozen forensic features remain discriminative, and adapting without source data or target labels risks reinforcing unreliable source predictions.
AI.method: Graph-Regularized Residual Adaptation (GraRA) constructs a compact residual subspace from uncertainty-weighted target features orthogonal to the source classification direction, generates soft labels via target-graph diffusion from source-score anchors, regularizes with neighborhood consistency, and merges 32 learned coefficients into the source classifier.
AI.result: On unseen OpenMMSec domains, GraRA achieves 84.36% accuracy and 91.34% AUC, improving over the source detector by 4.33 and 3.50 percentage points, respectively, while correcting ranking errors that threshold shifts cannot fix.
AI.conclusion: Unlabeled target-graph diffusion within an orthogonal residual subspace provides lightweight, effective cross-domain adaptation for fake-image detection without source data or extra inference branches.

title: Watertight Mesh Optimization of Textured Objects
summary: When reconstructing high-quality 3D assets from images, existing approaches often excel at one objective while compromising another, and frequently overlook the intrinsic quality of the reconstructed surfaces. We present MODL, a framework that jointly optimizes geometry and view-dependent appearance directly on a watertight triangle mesh. Our approach combines Laplacian-preconditioned optimization for smooth vertex updates with curvature-adaptive remeshing to preserve fine details and well-shaped triangles. The triangle mesh is optimized subject to multi-view normalized cross-correlation constraints, but without segmentation, geometric supervision or alpha-blending. Evaluations on object reconstruction datasets demonstrate that MODL achieves competitive novel-view synthesis while producing geometrically accurate models with superior intrinsic mesh quality. Our results highlight the potential of direct mesh optimization to unify photorealistic rendering, geometric reconstruction, and practical 3D asset creation.

AI.tldr: MODL is a direct mesh optimization framework that jointly refines geometry and view-dependent appearance on a watertight triangle mesh using Laplacian preconditioning and curvature-adaptive remeshing.
AI.motivation: Existing 3D reconstruction methods from images often trade off geometric accuracy against rendering quality and frequently neglect the intrinsic triangle quality of the reconstructed surface.
AI.method: MODL jointly optimizes geometry and view-dependent appearance directly on a watertight triangle mesh under multi-view normalized cross-correlation constraints—without segmentation, geometric supervision, or alpha-blending—by combining Laplacian-preconditioned vertex updates with curvature-adaptive remeshing.
AI.result: Evaluations on object reconstruction datasets show that MODL achieves competitive novel-view synthesis alongside accurate geometry and superior intrinsic mesh quality.
AI.conclusion: Direct watertight mesh optimization can unify photorealistic rendering, accurate geometric reconstruction, and high-quality 3D asset creation.

title: MIR-Depth: Multi-Range Refinement for Single-View RGB-D Depth Completion of Transparent Objects
summary: Recovering accurate visible-surface depth from a single RGB-D image and an object mask is essential for robotic grasping and manipulation of transparent objects. Specular reflections cause missing depth, while refraction corrupts nonzero returns with background depth, making raw measurements unreliable as surface anchors. Under a fixed sampling budget, refining an initial single-view prediction within a single search interval either misses large refraction offsets or sacrifices fine local resolution. To resolve this single-view trade-off, MIR-Depth constructs Coordinate-Aware Multi-Range Hypotheses: a 3D-aggregated global inverse-depth volume and depth-axis-filtered pixel-wise local volumes around a prior-guided initial depth. Selective Recurrent Refinement then introduces out-of-bounds lookup masking and validity-masked softmax fusion to iteratively update inverse depth from these volumes using a multi-scale ConvGRU. Finally, Spatially Gated Correction applies a learned per-pixel spatial gate to the full-resolution residual, preserving accurate initial geometry without imposing raw sensor readings as hard constraints. Experiments on TransCG, TODD, TRansPose, ClearPose, and HouseCat6D show that MIR-Depth achieves lower error than ReMake, DFNet, BP-Net, and PSD. Real-robot evaluations confirm accurate surface geometry for 6-DoF grasp pose prediction. Code and pretrained models will be publicly available.

AI.tldr: MIR-Depth is a single-view RGB-D depth completion method for transparent objects that combines multi-range inverse-depth hypotheses, selective recurrent refinement, and spatially gated residual correction.
AI.motivation: Specular reflections and background refraction corrupt raw RGB-D depth on transparent objects, and single-interval refinement under a fixed sampling budget either misses large refraction offsets or loses fine local resolution.
AI.method: MIR-Depth builds Coordinate-Aware Multi-Range Hypotheses (a 3D-aggregated global inverse-depth volume and depth-axis-filtered local volumes around a prior-guided initial depth), updates inverse depth via Selective Recurrent Refinement (out-of-bounds masking, validity-masked softmax fusion, and multi-scale ConvGRU), and applies Spatially Gated Correction to preserve accurate initial geometry.
AI.result: On TransCG, TODD, TRansPose, ClearPose, and HouseCat6D, MIR-Depth achieves lower depth error than ReMake, DFNet, BP-Net, and PSD, and real-robot experiments confirm accurate surface geometry for 6-DoF grasp pose prediction.
AI.conclusion: Multi-range inverse-depth refinement with selective gating effectively resolves refraction and reflection artifacts in single-view transparent-object depth completion.

title: Bilateral Evidence Selection and Reasoning for Mammography Vision--Language Models
summary: Medical vision--language models (VLMs) often need to identify small, subtle lesions within high-resolution images containing extensive normal anatomy and redundant visual information. Visual-token compression improves efficiency, but preserving salient regions alone can discard the context needed for diagnostic interpretation. This context can extend across images: in bilateral mammography, the opposite breast provides a patient-specific anatomical reference. Yet retaining such evidence does not ensure that the model uses it effectively. We propose Bilateral Evidence Selection and Reasoning (BESR), which connects evidence preservation with comparative assessment through a bilateral-guided token selector and a bilateral reward. Under a shared token budget, the selector jointly prioritizes lesion appearance and its local and bilateral context, while the reward encourages assessments that benefit from the preserved comparison. Experiments on a bilateral dataset constructed from CBIS-DDSM and on VinDr-Mammo demonstrate improved evidence retention and diagnostic performance under constrained visual-token budgets. Inference benchmarking further shows reduced prefill latency.

AI.tldr: BESR improves mammography vision-language models under tight visual-token budgets by jointly selecting lesion and bilateral reference tokens and training with a bilateral comparative reward.
AI.motivation: Visual-token compression in medical VLMs can discard cross-image anatomical context—such as the opposite breast in bilateral mammography—and simply retaining context does not guarantee the model uses it for comparative reasoning.
AI.method: Bilateral Evidence Selection and Reasoning (BESR) pairs a bilateral-guided token selector (prioritizing lesion appearance, local context, and bilateral reference under a shared token budget) with a bilateral reward that encourages assessments benefiting from the preserved comparison.
AI.result: Experiments on a bilateral dataset derived from CBIS-DDSM and on VinDr-Mammo show improved evidence retention, higher diagnostic performance under constrained token budgets, and reduced prefill latency.
AI.conclusion: Coupling bilateral-aware token selection with comparative reasoning rewards enables accurate, lower-latency mammography VLMs.

title: DiLE: Discrimination-Aware Latent-Space Learning for Universal Multimodal Embeddings
summary: Multimodal large language models have greatly improved input understanding in universal multimodal embedding models. However, this understanding does not ensure that their embeddings preserve the evidence needed to distinguish relevant items from confusable alternatives. To preserve essential discriminative evidence in embeddings, this paper proposes DiLE, a discrimination-aware latent-space learning framework that combines task guidance with on-policy retrieval feedback. Specifically, a few learnable queries are used to encode task-relevant information in a compact latent space. Reasoning instructions and auxiliary answer-generation supervision shape these representations to support both task understanding and retrieval discrimination. To address task-specific discriminative needs, we design shared-private expert adaptation that integrates cross-task knowledge sharing with task-specific representation learning. Building on this, the on-policy hard-negative distillation is introduced: the student retrieves confusable candidates, and a reverse KL divergence objective aligns its embedding-based similarity distribution with the teacher's fine-grained relevance distribution over these candidates. Candidates are periodically refreshed using updated student snapshots, tying teacher supervision to the student's evolving retrieval behavior and confusions. Across four model configurations that span two backbone generations, DiLE achieves state-of-the-art performance on MMEB-v2, UVRB, and MRMR, demonstrating its effectiveness across modalities and tasks.

AI.tldr: DiLE is a latent-space learning framework for universal multimodal embeddings that combines task-guided queries, shared-private expert adaptation, and on-policy hard-negative distillation to preserve fine-grained discriminative evidence.
AI.motivation: MLLM-based universal embedding models have strong input understanding, but their embeddings often fail to retain the discriminative evidence needed to separate relevant items from confusable alternatives.
AI.method: DiLE encodes task-relevant information into learnable queries using reasoning instructions and auxiliary answer-generation supervision, applies shared-private expert adaptation for cross-task sharing and task-specific needs, and uses on-policy hard-negative distillation with reverse KL divergence against a teacher over periodically refreshed student-retrieved candidates.
AI.result: Across four model configurations spanning two backbone generations, DiLE achieves state-of-the-art performance on MMEB-v2, UVRB, and MRMR across diverse modalities and tasks.
AI.conclusion: Combining task-guided latent queries with on-policy hard-negative distillation effectively preserves discriminative evidence in universal multimodal embeddings.

title: Raptor: Rejection-aware Adaptive Tree based on Speculative Decoding
summary: Tree-structured speculative decoding accelerates vision-language models (VLMs) by verifying multiple candidate continuations in parallel. However, long visual contexts increase the cost of speculative computation, making candidate coverage and redundant expansion important considerations beyond tree topology adaptation.
