We propose Raptor, a training-free framework that uses rejection feedback to jointly regulate candidate coverage and drafting effort. Our key insight is that acceptance length alone cannot distinguish insufficient candidate coverage from excessive deep expansion, and these conditions require different allocation decisions. Raptor therefore extracts complementary rejection-aware signals to characterize speculative progress, frontier coverage, and redundant expansion. These signals jointly guide bounded, momentum-smoothed updates of tree depth, branching width, and drafting budget, together with execution control that limits unnecessary drafting and progressively restores expansion when appropriate. Extensive experiments with two VLMs across seven multimodal benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of Raptor, achieving up to 2.39x average speedup over autoregressive decoding.

AI.tldr: Raptor is a training-free tree-structured speculative decoding framework for VLMs that uses rejection feedback to dynamically balance candidate coverage and drafting depth.
AI.motivation: Long visual contexts increase speculative verification costs in VLMs, and acceptance length alone cannot distinguish insufficient candidate coverage from excessive deep expansion.
AI.method: Raptor extracts rejection-aware signals characterizing speculative progress, frontier coverage, and redundant expansion to perform bounded, momentum-smoothed updates of tree depth, branching width, and drafting budget, alongside execution control that limits unnecessary drafting.
AI.result: Across two VLMs and seven multimodal benchmarks, Raptor achieves up to a 2.39x average speedup over standard autoregressive decoding.
AI.conclusion: Rejection-aware regulation of tree topology and drafting effort enables efficient, training-free speculative decoding for vision-language models.

title: Wearable Logo, Silent Hijack: Stealthy Cross-Modal Semantic Attacks on Visible--Infrared Vision-Language Models
summary: Logos appear naturally on clothing and daily necessities, where their recognizable shapes and semantic associations make them familiar visual cues. This familiarity helps them blend into real-world environments and remain visually inconspicuous. We ask whether an existing logo can serve as a carrier for coordinated targeted semantic attacks on visible-infrared (VIS-IR) vision-language models (VLMs) without changing its original outline. This setting requires expressive adversarial variation within a fixed shape while accounting for different appearance characteristics and model responses across modalities. We propose Logo-guided Semantic Attack (LoSA), a score-based black-box framework that optimizes a logo's interior appearance and placement while preserving its silhouette. LoSA uses a contour field and low-frequency graph spectral modes to structure the interior color layout, a frozen appearance adapter to couple VIS and IR appearances, and particle swarm optimization to jointly optimize shared design parameters. Experiments across four datasets demonstrate that LoSA consistently outperforms the evaluated baselines in simultaneous Top-1 targeted success. Cross-architecture experiments, visual naturalness ratings, and captioning/VQA transfer analyses further characterize its effectiveness and limitations. These findings reveal that familiar visual symbols from real-world environments can serve as shape-preserving carriers for coordinated targeted semantic attacks across imaging modalities.

AI.tldr: LoSA is a score-based black-box attack that turns wearable logos into stealthy, shape-preserving adversarial carriers against visible-infrared (VIS-IR) vision-language models.
AI.motivation: Existing physical attacks often alter object silhouettes or fail to coordinate across visible and infrared modalities, whereas familiar logos on clothing offer a naturally inconspicuous carrier if their outline is preserved.
AI.method: Logo-guided Semantic Attack (LoSA) parameterizes a logo's interior appearance using a contour field and low-frequency graph spectral modes, couples VIS and IR appearances through a frozen appearance adapter, and optimizes placement and interior layout via particle swarm optimization.
AI.result: Across four datasets, LoSA consistently outperforms evaluated baselines in simultaneous Top-1 targeted attack success, with cross-architecture, naturalness, and captioning/VQA transfer analyses characterizing its behavior.
AI.conclusion: Familiar real-world logos can be optimized within fixed silhouettes to execute coordinated cross-modal semantic attacks on VIS-IR VLMs.

title: VisualTalk-Bench: Evaluating Question-Driven Avatar-Led Video Explanations
summary: Advances in video generation and avatar synthesis enable new ways to answer user questions through visual explanations. This task requires a system to formulate a correct answer, translate relevant information into visual material, and deliver the explanation through an avatar's speech and actions. Existing benchmarks rarely assess whether avatars point to the visual content being discussed. We introduce VisualTalk-Bench for question-driven avatar-led video explanations in finance and Chinese and English education. It includes 800 curated reference videos and 100 independent evaluation requests, assessing Content Factuality, Speech-Visual Consistency, Visual Quality, Motion Smoothness, and Avatar-Content Pointing. Yet end-to-end video generators often struggle to align gestures with specific visual targets. To explore this challenge, we develop Avatar-O Agent, a modular reference implementation with explicit interaction planning. Experiments across six agents show that factual precision and visual quality do not guarantee accurate pointing. A 26-participant study comparing four agents finds that Avatar-O Agent receives the highest average ratings for visual guidance, perceived pointing accuracy, and explanation effectiveness. We will release the data and code.

AI.tldr: VisualTalk-Bench is a benchmark for question-driven avatar-led video explanations, and Avatar-O Agent is a modular reference agent with explicit interaction planning that improves avatar pointing and visual guidance.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks for avatar-led video explanations rarely evaluate whether avatars accurately point to the visual content they discuss, and end-to-end video generators struggle to align gestures with visual targets.
AI.method: The authors introduce VisualTalk-Bench (800 reference videos and 100 evaluation requests in finance and Chinese/English education) measuring Content Factuality, Speech-Visual Consistency, Visual Quality, Motion Smoothness, and Avatar-Content Pointing, and build Avatar-O Agent with explicit interaction planning.
AI.result: Experiments across six agents show that factual accuracy and visual quality do not guarantee accurate pointing, while a 26-participant study comparing four agents gives Avatar-O Agent the highest ratings for visual guidance, perceived pointing accuracy, and explanation effectiveness.
AI.conclusion: Explicit interaction planning is essential for aligning avatar gestures with visual content in question-driven video explanations.

title: Beyond Resemblance: Image Fusion Reimagined
summary: Image fusion often lacks ground-truth fused images, forcing existing deep methods to indirectly define fusion objectives by requiring the fused image to simultaneously resemble multiple source images. However, the distinct imaging characteristics of different modalities can impose competing constraints on the fused result, potentially limiting the effective integration of their complementary information. To address this long-standing challenge facing the image fusion community, we propose ApexFuse, a novel generative image fusion paradigm that moves beyond source-resemblance constraints toward learning a general distribution of high-quality scene representations. Specifically, we develop a human-LMM-in-the-loop pipeline that leverages large multimodal generative models and iterative human feedback to translate abstract fusion objectives into reliable visual references, thereby defining the target distribution of ideal fusion outcomes. Through target-distribution-guided adaptation, we transfer the rich generative priors of pretrained FLUX to image fusion, enabling high-quality scene reconstruction conditioned on multimodal observations. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ApexFuse harmoniously integrates salient thermal targets, natural colors, and fine textures, achieving superior visual quality as well as semantic segmentation and object detection performance over previous source-resemblance methods. Moreover, ApexFuse exhibits remarkable cross-task generalization, extending from infrared-visible fusion to multi-exposure fusion, multi-focus fusion, and visible-depth fusion without additional fine-tuning.

AI.tldr: ApexFuse is a generative image fusion paradigm that replaces source-resemblance objectives with target-distribution-guided adaptation of pretrained FLUX, improving visual quality and downstream perception across multiple fusion tasks.
AI.motivation: Lacking ground-truth fused images, existing deep fusion methods force outputs to resemble multiple source images simultaneously, creating competing modality constraints that limit complementary information integration.
AI.method: ApexFuse uses a human-LMM-in-the-loop pipeline to generate reliable visual references defining an ideal fusion target distribution, then adapts pretrained FLUX via target-distribution-guided training conditioned on multimodal observations.
AI.result: ApexFuse integrates thermal targets, natural colors, and fine textures to outperform source-resemblance methods in visual quality, semantic segmentation, and object detection, and generalizes zero-shot from infrared-visible fusion to multi-exposure, multi-focus, and visible-depth fusion.
AI.conclusion: Moving from source-resemblance constraints to target-distribution-guided generative adaptation enables higher-quality, cross-task generalizable image fusion.

title: Lossless Latent Diffusion Models
summary: We study the problem of training image diffusion models while preserving pixel-exact reconstruction. Prior works typically address this problem by directly modeling images in pixel space, requiring modifications to the diffusion training objective or model architecture. In this work, we introduce a different paradigm: rather than modifying diffusion models, we construct a lossless transformation that maps pixels into a representation more amenable to diffusion modeling. We term our approach the Lossless Latent Diffusion Model (LLDM). We construct LLDM using residual latent transformation and uneven latent scaling, and explain its effectiveness through a proposed metric, semantic rank priority (SRP). Empirically, LLDM substantially outperforms prior pixel-space diffusion models in generation quality and even surpasses several widely used lossy VAEs. Furthermore, we show that SRP is strongly correlated with downstream generative performance.

AI.tldr: Lossless Latent Diffusion Models (LLDMs) map pixels into a lossless latent representation via residual latent transformation and uneven latent scaling, outperforming pixel-space diffusion models and several lossy VAEs.
AI.motivation: Training diffusion models with pixel-exact reconstruction typically requires modeling directly in pixel space and modifying the diffusion objective or architecture.
AI.method: LLDM applies a lossless transformation—combining residual latent transformation and uneven latent scaling—to map pixels into a diffusion-friendly representation without altering the diffusion model itself, and introduces semantic rank priority (SRP) to explain its effectiveness.
AI.result: Empirically, LLDM substantially outperforms prior pixel-space diffusion models in generation quality, surpasses several widely used lossy VAEs, and shows that SRP correlates strongly with downstream generative performance.
AI.conclusion: Lossless latent transformations offer an effective alternative to pixel-space diffusion for achieving both pixel-exact reconstruction and strong generation quality.

title: CANDOR: Contrastive Self-Denoising Rewards for Label-Free Text-to-Image Post-Training
summary: Post-training text-to-image generators with reinforcement learning usually relies on external reward models that need annotated preferences or auxiliary evaluators and are prone to reward hacking. We show that the generator's own denoising accuracy, used by a recent intrinsic reward, is a poor proxy for prompt fidelity. Within a same-prompt group, this absolute self-confidence is dominated by image complexity and ranks correct samples above incorrect ones near chance. We introduce CANDOR (Contrastive Alignment from Null-referenced Denoising lOg-Ratio), the log-ratio of unconditional to conditional denoising errors under shared noise probes, which measures how much the prompt helps the model denoise its own sample. It cancels prompt-independent difficulty that scales both errors and ranks the better of two same-prompt samples higher in 60% and 63% of pairs on compositional generation and text rendering. As the only Flow-GRPO reward for a flow-matching model, CANDOR improves text rendering, aesthetic and human-preference scores over the base model and a prior absolute self-confidence reward, with text-rendering and preference gains that stronger classifier-free guidance does not reproduce. On public Flow-GRPO adapters trained on external rewards, CANDOR further raises PickScore and ImageReward, so it can complement those rewards. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: CANDOR is a label-free intrinsic reward for text-to-image RL post-training based on the log-ratio of unconditional to conditional denoising errors, outperforming absolute self-confidence rewards.
AI.motivation: External reward models for text-to-image RL require annotated preferences and risk reward hacking, while prior intrinsic rewards based on absolute denoising accuracy are dominated by image complexity and rank same-prompt samples near chance.
AI.method: CANDOR (Contrastive Alignment from Null-referenced Denoising lOg-Ratio) computes the log-ratio of unconditional to conditional denoising errors under shared noise probes to cancel prompt-independent difficulty, and is used as a Flow-GRPO reward.
AI.result: CANDOR ranks the better of two same-prompt samples higher in 60% of compositional generation pairs and 63% of text-rendering pairs; as the sole Flow-GRPO reward, it improves text rendering, aesthetics, and preference scores over the base model and absolute self-confidence, and further boosts PickScore and ImageReward on public external-reward adapters.
AI.conclusion: Measuring how much a prompt reduces denoising error relative to an unconditional baseline provides a reliable, label-free intrinsic reward for text-to-image post-training.

title: RemoteVLPG: How to Obtain a Specific VLM for Language-Guided Path Generation on Remote Sensing Images?
summary: We study how to obtain a task-specific Vision-Language Model (VLM) for language-guided path generation between start and end points on remote sensing images. We explore this question from three aspects. First, we implement three widely used architectural approaches and compare their performance. Second, we design a scalable method for constructing pre-training data and build an effective pre-training dataset with a degree of diversity. Methods trained on this dataset achieve promising zero-shot performance. Third, we construct three benchmarks that support stratified evaluation and design three metrics for path generation. We investigate this problem through extensive experiments. The results show that the zero-shot performance of methods trained on the constructed pre-training dataset can exceed that of some advanced commercial VLMs. Code and Dataset can be available at this https URL

AI.tldr: RemoteVLPG investigates how to build a task-specific VLM for language-guided path generation on remote sensing images, introducing a scalable pre-training dataset, three benchmarks, and three evaluation metrics.
AI.motivation: Obtaining a specialized VLM for language-guided path generation between start and end points on remote sensing images lacks standardized architectures, diverse pre-training data, and stratified evaluation protocols.
AI.method: The authors compare three architectural approaches, design a scalable method to construct a diverse pre-training dataset, and establish three stratified benchmarks with three path-generation metrics.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show that models trained on the constructed pre-training dataset achieve strong zero-shot performance that exceeds some advanced commercial VLMs.
AI.conclusion: Scalable, diverse pre-training data enables specialized open VLMs to surpass commercial models in zero-shot remote sensing path generation.

title: ActMem: From Latent Memory Reasoning to Grounded Robotic Action
comment: 17 pages, 11 figures, 6 tables. Code and checkpoints: this https URL
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have shown promising results in real-world long-horizon manipulation, where memory plays a crucial role. However, existing memory-augmented VLAs either retrieve past observations without reasoning about what they imply, or reason over the full history in a shared context where it crowds out current perception. Cognitive science treats them as distinct systems: memory reconstructs past experience to decide what to do, while perception guides how to act. We therefore propose ActMem, an in-context memory framework that decouples memory reasoning from perceptual grounding within a single vision-language backbone. Built on a vision-language model with native video understanding, ActMem infers the current subtask from a timestamped interaction history and keeps the hidden states formed during this inference as a Latent Memory Chain-of-Thought (Memory CoT), which conditions a flow-matching action expert. Perception Attention further lets the expert attend directly to the current view. To keep inference fast under long histories, Efficient Memory CoT Inference reuses computation across consecutive decisions without changing the output. ActMem achieves 71.1% task success and 80.8% completion success on RoboMemArena, surpassing the strongest baseline by 7.5 and 8.7 percentage points, and 73.8% average success on MIKASA-Robo, the best among all compared methods. In the real world, it reaches 68.8% average success on exogenous, endogenous, and traceless memory tasks, 10.0 percentage points above the strongest memory-augmented VLA. Code and checkpoints will be released at this https URL and this https URL.

AI.tldr: ActMem is an in-context memory framework for Vision-Language-Action models that decouples latent memory reasoning from perceptual grounding, achieving state-of-the-art long-horizon robotic manipulation.
AI.motivation: Existing memory-augmented VLAs either retrieve past observations without reasoning or reason over full histories in a shared context that crowds out current perception.
AI.method: Built on a video-capable VLM, ActMem infers the current subtask from timestamped history and stores the resulting hidden states as a Latent Memory Chain-of-Thought (Memory CoT) to condition a flow-matching action expert, while Perception Attention attends directly to the current view and Efficient Memory CoT Inference reuses computation across steps.
AI.result: ActMem achieves 71.1% task success and 80.8% completion success on RoboMemArena (+7.5 and +8.7 points over the strongest baseline), 73.8% average success on MIKASA-Robo, and 68.8% real-world average success (+10.0 points over the strongest memory-augmented VLA).
AI.conclusion: Decoupling latent memory reasoning from direct perceptual grounding within a single VLM backbone substantially improves long-horizon robotic manipulation.

title: A Wolf in Sheep's Pixels: Visual Camouflage Attacks via HDR Gain Maps
summary: An image can pass automated safety checks while showing harmful content to its human viewer. We introduce DRJanus, a visual camouflage attack that exploits the gap between standard dynamic range (SDR) processing and high dynamic range (HDR) display. Automated systems often read only an image's SDR base, whereas HDR viewers reconstruct its appearance using an auxiliary gain map. DRJanus inverts this reconstruction to embed two independently chosen color images in a single JPEG, without querying or optimizing against the target model. It preserves the chosen SDR base exactly and reconstructs HDR targets at an average PSNR of 43.03 dB across 400 images. On a benchmark of 100 sexual-content images, DRJanus evades detection by all six tested commercial moderation services and nine vision-language models. Across five agents, each evaluated on 120 task cases per threat setting, attack success ranges from 31.67% to 100% for moderation evasion and from 95% to 100% for task manipulation. We also explore cross-view consistency checks as a mitigation. These findings expose a gap in visual trust: securing what a machine reads does not secure what a user sees. A demo is available at this https URL

AI.tldr: DRJanus is a visual camouflage attack that exploits the gap between SDR processing and HDR gain-map reconstruction to hide harmful content in a single JPEG that evades automated moderation while remaining visible to human viewers.
AI.motivation: Automated safety systems typically inspect only an image's SDR base, whereas HDR displays reconstruct appearance using an auxiliary gain map, creating an unguarded visual trust gap.
AI.method: DRJanus inverts HDR gain-map reconstruction to embed two independently chosen color images into one JPEG without querying or optimizing against target models, preserving the SDR base exactly.
AI.result: Across 400 images, DRJanus reconstructs HDR targets at 43.03 dB average PSNR; on 100 sexual-content images, it evades all six tested commercial moderation services and nine VLMs, achieving 31.67% to 100% moderation evasion and 95% to 100% task manipulation across five agents (120 cases each).
AI.conclusion: Securing what automated systems read in SDR does not secure what users see on HDR displays, highlighting the need for cross-view consistency checks.

title: TuringPAI: A Foundation for On-Device Physical AI
summary: Physical AI requires models that understand spatial relationships and dynamic environments and translate observations into actions under limited onboard compute. We present TuringPAI, a family of models for on-device Physical AI comprising TuringPAI-VL for shared vision-language understanding, TuringPAI-Drive for autonomous driving, and TuringPAI-Embodied for robotic manipulation. TuringPAI-VL is a 0.65B model built on HybridViT-MLQ, which combines convolutional local aggregation with Transformer-based global modeling. Multi-scale Latent Queries integrate spatial features and observation history within the same visual Transformer, providing a compact, structured interface to the language model. Training combines general vision-language data with geometric, cross-view, and temporal supervision. TuringPAI-VL supports general multimodal understanding and improves quantitative geometric perception over Qwen2-VL-2B, while providing a shared initialization for the two downstream VLA models. For autonomous driving, TuringPAI-Drive maintains all evaluated ADE/FDE metrics within 1.2\% of a full-token HybridViT baseline using the MLQ interface and achieves comparable aggregate scores in an in-house simulation evaluation. Using XPeng Native Runtime (XNRT) on a single NVIDIA Orin-X SoC, TuringPAI-Drive generates trajectories at 12\,Hz in on-vehicle operation. For robotic manipulation, TuringPAI-Embodied achieves a 96.8\% average success rate across the four LIBERO suites. These results demonstrate a shared vision-language foundation for driving and robotic manipulation under practical on-device constraints.

AI.tldr: TuringPAI is a family of compact models for on-device Physical AI built on a shared 0.65B HybridViT-MLQ vision-language foundation, enabling real-time autonomous driving at 12 Hz on Orin-X and 96.8% success on LIBERO robotic manipulation.
AI.motivation: Physical AI requires spatial and dynamic understanding under strict onboard compute constraints, where a shared foundation must support both driving and robotic manipulation.
AI.method: TuringPAI-VL (0.65B) uses HybridViT-MLQ (combining convolutional local aggregation, global Transformer modeling, and Multi-scale Latent Queries) trained with general VLM data plus geometric, cross-view, and temporal supervision, serving as a shared initialization for TuringPAI-Drive and TuringPAI-Embodied.
AI.result: TuringPAI-VL outperforms Qwen2-VL-2B on quantitative geometric perception; TuringPAI-Drive keeps ADE/FDE within 1.2% of a full-token HybridViT baseline and runs at 12 Hz on a single NVIDIA Orin-X SoC; TuringPAI-Embodied achieves a 96.8% average success rate across the four LIBERO suites.
AI.conclusion: A compact, shared vision-language foundation with multi-scale latent queries can power both autonomous driving and robotic manipulation under practical on-device constraints.

title: SegAnyFruit: Learning Generalizable and Edge Deployable Fruit Instance Segmentation at Scale
summary: Deploying fruit instance segmentation in real agricultural settings requires generalizing across unseen species, orchards, and imaging conditions under strict onboard compute and annotation budgets. We introduce SegAnyFruit (SAF), a data construction and progressive training framework that distills foundation-model priors into lightweight, prompt-free segmenters. SAF combines generic mask pre-training, broad mid-training on automatically annotated web imagery from our curated WebFruits dataset, and human-verified agricultural refinement post-training on PaperFruits, together spanning 733K images and 9.66M whole-fruit masks across 165 fruit types. Across seven benchmarks, zero-shot SAF-RF-DETR-XL reaches 69.06 average mask AP50:95 (+4.76 over SAM 3) while remaining deployable on edge devices. SAF initialization also boosts few-shot to full-shot adaptation across five agricultural domains while mitigating catastrophic forgetting. Finally, we systematically analyze training stages, data scale, model capacity, and generative augmentation, and validate our pipeline's transferability to underwater, cell, and human segmentation. We will release our datasets, code, and SAF models.

AI.tldr: SegAnyFruit (SAF) is a data construction and progressive training framework that distills foundation-model priors into lightweight, prompt-free fruit instance segmenters, achieving 69.06 zero-shot mask AP50:95.
AI.motivation: Agricultural fruit instance segmentation must generalize across unseen species, orchards, and imaging conditions under strict onboard compute and annotation budgets.
AI.method: SAF combines generic mask pre-training, broad mid-training on automatically annotated WebFruits imagery, and human-verified refinement on PaperFruits (totaling 733K images and 9.66M masks across 165 fruit types) to train lightweight segmenters.
AI.result: Across seven benchmarks, zero-shot SAF-RF-DETR-XL reaches 69.06 average mask AP50:95 (+4.76 over SAM 3) while remaining edge-deployable; SAF initialization also improves few-shot to full-shot adaptation across five agricultural domains, mitigates forgetting, and transfers to underwater, cell, and human segmentation.
AI.conclusion: Progressive distillation from foundation models onto curated web and agricultural data yields generalizable, edge-deployable instance segmenters.

title: TAP: Tapping the Discriminative Potential of Frozen Representations for Class-Incremental Learning
comment: 10 pages, 3 figures. Code is included as an ancillary file
summary: Pre-trained models provide transferable representations for class-incremental learning (CIL). However, sequentially adapting these representations introduces optimization costs and may disrupt old-class feature structure. This motivates us to explore whether the discriminative potential of these representations can be further exploited by continually accumulating class information while keeping the encoders frozen. To this end, we propose TAP, a new and novel framework for tapping the discriminative potential of frozen representations in class-incremental learning. It accumulates visual and semantic class information in the frozen CLIP embedding space with only lightweight optimization. TAP comprises three modules: class-conditional visual distribution modeling, class-adaptive semantic calibration, and visual-semantic posterior fusion. The first module retains class means and within-class scatters, combining class-specific and shared covariances to stabilize distribution estimation. The second module learns class-specific weights over text templates from current-task images, adapting text representations to downstream classes. The third module combines the visual and semantic posteriors through a weighted product of experts for prediction over all seen classes without retaining images from previous tasks. Across nine datasets under two incremental protocols, TAP achieves state-of-the-art performance, attaining the highest average incremental and final-stage accuracies among the compared methods. The code is provided as an ancillary file.

AI.tldr: TAP is a class-incremental learning framework that keeps CLIP encoders frozen and accumulates class-conditional visual distributions, calibrated text templates, and posterior fusion without storing old images.
AI.motivation: Sequentially adapting pre-trained representations in class-incremental learning incurs optimization costs and risks disrupting old-class feature structures.
AI.method: TAP operates in the frozen CLIP embedding space via three modules: class-conditional visual distribution modeling (retaining class means and combining class-specific and shared covariances), class-adaptive semantic calibration (learning class-specific weights over text templates), and visual-semantic posterior fusion via a weighted product of experts.
AI.result: Across nine datasets under two incremental protocols, TAP achieves state-of-the-art average incremental and final-stage accuracies among compared methods without retaining previous-task images.
AI.conclusion: Lightweight accumulation of visual distributions and calibrated semantic posteriors in frozen CLIP space is an effective, rehearsal-free strategy for class-incremental learning.

title: PRIO: Pre-trained Representation for Interactive Objects in 4D Worlds
summary: 3D worlds can now be captured, reconstructed, and generated at scale, yet the objects in them stay still: a pressed pillow does not compress, and a pulled door does not swing. Bringing these objects into interactive 4D world models requires a representation of how they can move, deform, and respond physically to user actions in real time. We present PRIO, a pre-trained representation for interactive objects. Given static geometry, PRIO predicts an object-specific configuration space in a single forward pass. This space provides generalized coordinates for Lagrangian mechanics, allowing physical laws and user actions to govern motion. Configurations are linear in these coordinates, allowing the quantities needed by the dynamics to be precomputed. Dynamics then run at interactive rates without further network inference. Pre-trained on diverse 4D trajectories, PRIO learns priors over object configurations that generalize to unseen shapes. It supports meshes, point clouds, and 3D Gaussians, bringing objects in reconstructed and generated scenes into interaction. We demonstrate its use in real-to-sim workflows and robot manipulation. In addition, compared with existing 4D generation methods, PRIO generates dynamics faster and follows user actions more faithfully.

AI.tldr: PRIO is a pre-trained object representation that predicts a linear configuration space from static 3D geometry in a single forward pass, enabling real-time, physically governed 4D object interaction.
AI.motivation: Existing 3D reconstructions and generated worlds are static and cannot deform or respond physically to user actions in real time.
AI.method: Pre-trained on diverse 4D trajectories, PRIO predicts an object-specific configuration space in one forward pass from static meshes, point clouds, or 3D Gaussians; because configurations are linear in these generalized coordinates, Lagrangian dynamics quantities are precomputed so interactive simulation runs without further network inference.
AI.result: PRIO generalizes to unseen shapes, supports real-to-sim workflows and robot manipulation, and generates dynamics faster and more faithfully to user actions than existing 4D generation methods.
AI.conclusion: Predicting linear generalized coordinates for Lagrangian mechanics bridges static 3D assets and real-time interactive 4D worlds.

title: Carry the Fine Print: Budget-Aware Visual Token Compression for Document OCR
comment: 11 pages; supplementary material is included as an ancillary file
summary: Visual token compression often treats salience or similarity as a proxy for transcription importance. Complete document OCR breaks this assumption: small symbols and repeated entries can be indispensable to the transcript despite being visually inconspicuous. We present Select and Compensate, a two-stage framework built on a simple idea: choosing where to retain a token need not determine all the evidence it carries. Selection combines adaptive encoding resolution with global importance and local contrast to choose which tokens to retain as anchors. Compensation enriches these anchors with nearby discarded content and its relative position, without adding tokens. The OCR backbone remains frozen, and native coordinates and structural tokens are preserved. We evaluate complete page transcription across five backbones on OmniDocBench and document reconstruction on MPDocBench. With half the original visual tokens, our input-adapted configuration reaches 95.42 OmniDocBench Overall on Ovis versus 96.09 for the uncompressed model, and paired evaluations show gains over simply reducing the input resolution on both benchmarks. With the original input grid, our method stays within 0.17 points of the uncompressed model at 75% retention and exceeds a learned global selector by 4.70 points at 25%. On a fixed 200-page Ovis workload at the same 50% visual-token budget, only 3 of its outputs hit the length limit, versus 30-34 for the evaluated RTPrune, DivPrune, and HiPrune adaptations, and it finishes the batch 35-40% sooner. Code will be made publicly available.

AI.tldr: Select and Compensate is a two-stage visual token compression framework for document OCR that retains anchor tokens via adaptive resolution and local contrast, then enriches them with nearby discarded content.
AI.motivation: Standard visual token compression relies on salience or similarity, which drops visually inconspicuous small symbols and repeated entries that are critical for complete document OCR.
AI.method: Keeping the OCR backbone frozen, the Selection stage combines adaptive encoding resolution with global importance and local contrast to pick anchor tokens, while the Compensation stage enriches anchors with nearby discarded content and relative positions without adding tokens.
AI.result: On OmniDocBench with 50% visual tokens, the input-adapted Ovis configuration reaches 95.42 Overall (vs. 96.09 uncompressed); with the original grid, it stays within 0.17 points at 75% retention and beats a learned global selector by 4.70 points at 25%; on a 200-page Ovis workload at 50% budget, only 3 outputs hit the length limit (vs. 30-34 for RTPrune, DivPrune, and HiPrune) and batch runtime is 35-40% faster.
AI.conclusion: Compensating retained anchor tokens with nearby discarded content preserves fine-grained transcription accuracy under aggressive visual token budgets.

title: Persona Lenses: What Makes a Vision-Language Model See Through Its Persona's Eyes?
comment: 29 pages, 9 figures, 14 tables, including supplementary material
summary: Vision-language models have been used to simulate where a user looks on a web page. However, a persona in the prompt reaches the simulated gaze only partly. We measure this reach as the difference in one model's gaze between two MatrAIx personas that differ in a single attribute. We introduce persona lenses, which place the persona between the model and the page: a text lens (a two-step prompt in which the model first writes what the persona would look at), a pixel lens (marks on the region matching the persona's interests) and a weight lens (a dwell reward gated to keep the scanpath natural). Using Qwen3-VL (4B and 32B) and Qwen3.5-9B on generated and live pages, we compare the lenses with one another and with scale, the 32B model with no lens. It has been confirmed that the text lens separates the personas strongly but is not robust to profile changes that should not move gaze. The pixel lens separates the personas less but is unaffected by attributes unrelated to gaze. At 4B and 9B, the weight lens separates the personas on interests held out from training, with no extra step on a new page. The 32B model separates the personas with the base prompt alone. Therefore, the choice of a lens depends on cost and model size.

AI.tldr: Persona Lenses studies how text, pixel, and weight lenses steer VLMs to simulate persona-specific web gaze, finding that optimal lens choice depends on model size and robustness requirements.
AI.motivation: Prompting a VLM with a user persona only partially shifts its simulated web-page gaze toward that persona's interests.
AI.method: The authors measure gaze separation between MatrAIx personas differing in a single attribute across Qwen3-VL (4B, 32B) and Qwen3.5-9B, comparing a text lens (two-step interest verbalization), a pixel lens (marking matching regions), a weight lens (gated dwell reward), and unlensed 32B scale.
AI.result: The text lens strongly separates personas but is sensitive to irrelevant profile changes; the pixel lens separates less but resists unrelated attributes; at 4B and 9B, the weight lens generalizes to held-out interests with no extra inference step; the 32B model separates personas with the base prompt alone.
AI.conclusion: Steering VLM gaze simulation involves a trade-off between inference cost, model scale, and robustness to irrelevant persona attributes.

title: Mesh-Free Keypoint Learning for Category-Level 6D Object Pose Estimation
summary: Category-level 6D pose estimation relates partial RGB-D observations of unseen instances to a canonical frame shared across a category. Object-aware reconstruction helps adaptive keypoints retain the geometry of the visible surface. Common reconstruction targets select observed points by their distance to a registered instance surface. We present MORSEPose, which derives this support directly from standard pose and metric-size annotations. We map observed 3D points to normalized object coordinates and retain those inside a tolerancedilated pose-and-size envelope. This construction is consistent across camera frames and metric scales. When the annotated extent bounds the object surface, the envelope conservatively contains the support of a conventional surface-distance selector. We integrate this target with multi-level RGB-D features, adaptive keypoints, and learnable category context. Experiments on REAL275 and HouseCat6D show that the envelope closely matches surface-based supervision at both point and task levels, remains stable under boundary perturbations and viewpoint changes, and supports competitive category-level pose accuracy across benchmarks.

AI.tldr: MORSEPose is a mesh-free keypoint learning method for category-level 6D object pose estimation that derives surface reconstruction targets directly from standard pose and metric-size annotations.
AI.motivation: Object-aware reconstruction helps adaptive keypoints preserve visible surface geometry in category-level 6D pose estimation, but common reconstruction targets require registered instance meshes to compute surface distances.
AI.method: MORSEPose maps observed 3D points to normalized object coordinates and retains points inside a tolerance-dilated pose-and-size envelope, integrating this mesh-free target with multi-level RGB-D features, adaptive keypoints, and learnable category context.
AI.result: Experiments on REAL275 and HouseCat6D show that the envelope closely matches surface-distance supervision at both point and task levels, remains stable under boundary perturbations and viewpoint changes, and achieves competitive category-level pose accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Standard pose and metric-size annotations suffice to construct effective surface reconstruction targets for category-level 6D pose estimation without instance meshes.

title: Multi-View Relighting with Mergeable Radiance Fields
summary: We propose MergeableRF, a method for radiance field relighting through model parameter merging. Given multi-view images of a scene under known basis lights, our goal is to relight the scene by directly combining the parameters of radiance fields trained under these lights. This is motivated by the linearity of light transport: the image under a mixture of lights is the same weighted combination of the images under each light. However, combining the parameters of independently trained radiance fields does not produce the corresponding combination of images. To address this, we represent a scene with shared geometry and a separate appearance network for each basis light. We start these networks from the same initialization and introduce merge-aware training, which teaches their parameter combinations to reproduce the corresponding combinations of images. Given a target HDR environment map, we compute its basis-light coefficients and use them to merge the appearance networks into a single relit model. Our method supports both Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) and 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), without material estimation, additional relighting networks, or target-specific optimization. Unlike image-space blending, it requires only one rendering pass per viewpoint. Experiments on synthetic Neural Gaffer objects and real OLATverse captures demonstrate relighting quality competitive with methods trained on the same multi-light observations.

AI.tldr: MergeableRF enables single-pass scene relighting under arbitrary HDR environment maps by training basis-light appearance networks with shared initialization and merge-aware supervision, then linearly merging their parameters.
AI.motivation: Light transport is linear, but directly merging the parameters of independently trained radiance fields under basis lights does not reproduce the corresponding linear combination of rendered images.
AI.method: MergeableRF represents a scene with shared geometry and per-basis-light appearance networks initialized identically and trained with merge-aware supervision so parameter combinations match image combinations; at test time, basis coefficients from a target HDR map merge the appearance networks into one model for NeRF or 3DGS.
AI.result: On synthetic Neural Gaffer objects and real OLATverse captures, MergeableRF achieves relighting quality competitive with multi-light baselines while requiring only a single rendering pass per viewpoint and no material estimation or target-specific optimization.
AI.conclusion: Merge-aware training aligns radiance field parameter space with light-transport linearity, enabling fast, single-pass relighting via parameter merging.

title: Contrast Where It Matters: Visual Evidence-Guided Decoding for Mitigating Hallucinations in LVLMs
summary: Despite strong multimodal capabilities, large vision-language models (LVLMs) often hallucinate when linguistic priors outweigh visual evidence or when predictions are grounded in irrelevant or misleading image regions. Training-free contrastive decoding mitigates hallucinations by contrasting the original prediction with an auxiliary one that exposes linguistic priors. Yet existing methods focus on altering the auxiliary input or computation and do not ensure that either branch uses query-relevant visual evidence during decoding. We propose Visual Evidence-Guided Decoding (VEGD), a training-free framework that identifies query-relevant visual evidence and guides its use throughout contrastive decoding. VEGD locates this evidence by aggregating localization heads with strong visual responses and coherent spatial structure, then selectively weakens it in the auxiliary image. During generation, VEGD directs visual-carrier heads in both branches toward the same evidence location, strengthening access to intact evidence in the main branch while anchoring the auxiliary branch to its weakened counterpart. An adaptive distribution fusion strategy then combines or contrasts their predictions according to distribution divergence. Experiments across diverse LVLMs and benchmarks demonstrate that VEGD consistently reduces hallucinations.

AI.tldr: Visual Evidence-Guided Decoding (VEGD) is a training-free contrastive decoding framework that locates query-relevant visual evidence and steers visual-carrier heads in both branches to mitigate LVLM hallucinations.
AI.motivation: Existing training-free contrastive decoding methods alter auxiliary inputs or computations to expose linguistic priors, but do not ensure that either branch actually attends to query-relevant visual evidence during decoding.
AI.method: VEGD aggregates localization heads with strong visual responses and coherent spatial structure to locate query-relevant evidence, selectively weakens it in the auxiliary image, directs visual-carrier heads in both branches toward that evidence location, and fuses or contrasts predictions via divergence-adaptive distribution fusion.
AI.result: Experiments across diverse LVLMs and benchmarks show that VEGD consistently reduces hallucinations.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly locating and guiding attention toward query-relevant visual evidence during contrastive decoding effectively curbs LVLM hallucinations without training.

title: Support-Guided Triadic Decoding for Hallucination Mitigation in Multimodal Dialogue with LVLMs
summary: In multimodal multi-turn dialogue, dialogue history plays a dual role: reliable responses provide useful context for subsequent turns, whereas hallucinated responses can propagate errors across turns. Existing training-free methods globally adjust the effect of dialogue history on generation, making it difficult to suppress misleading information without weakening useful context. To address this trade-off, we introduce Support-Guided Triadic Decoding (SGTD), a training-free framework that selectively controls the influence of unreliable history and fuses complementary predictions during decoding. Specifically, Historical Answer Support Estimation measures the visual support of historical responses against type-matched alternatives and identifies low-support content that may mislead later generation. Support-Targeted Attention Intervention then weakens the influence of this content while preserving the surrounding dialogue, producing a support-refined prediction. Triadic Decoding combines this prediction with the full-history prediction and answer-free visual evidence, while the Support-Adaptive Plausibility Constraint filters implausible tokens using visual agreement and historical support. Experiments on MMHalSnowball and VisDiaHalBench across representative LVLMs show that SGTD consistently achieves the highest accuracy under hallucinated histories while preserving the benefits of factual context.

AI.tldr: Support-Guided Triadic Decoding (SGTD) is a training-free framework that mitigates hallucination propagation in multimodal multi-turn dialogue by estimating historical answer support and selectively attenuating unreliable history.
AI.motivation: Global adjustments to dialogue history in multimodal multi-turn conversations cannot suppress hallucinated turns without also weakening useful factual context.
AI.method: SGTD estimates visual support for historical responses against type-matched alternatives, weakens low-support history via Support-Targeted Attention Intervention, fuses the support-refined, full-history, and answer-free visual predictions via Triadic Decoding, and filters tokens with a Support-Adaptive Plausibility Constraint.
AI.result: On MMHalSnowball and VisDiaHalBench across representative LVLMs, SGTD consistently achieves the highest accuracy under hallucinated histories while preserving the benefits of factual context.
AI.conclusion: Fine-grained, support-guided intervention on dialogue history prevents error propagation in multimodal multi-turn dialogue without sacrificing helpful context.

title: Query-Aware vs. Query-Agnostic Training-Free Video Token Pruning in Multimodal LLMs
summary: Video Large Language Models process large numbers of visual tokens, making token pruning important for efficient inference. Training-free pruning methods differ in whether and how they use the user query, and the value of query conditioning remains unclear. We present a controlled study of training-free, pre-LLM video token selection. Using a shared Qwen-3-VL backbone, token budgets, and decoding settings, we compare 21 pruning principles spanning query-agnostic, shallow query-conditioned, structured query-conditioned, and holistic strategies. To instantiate the last two categories, we introduce Structured Query Pruning, which decomposes the question into semantic anchors, and a Pareto variant, which combines anchor relevance with query-agnostic visual diversity. Across Video-MME, MVBench, and LongVideoBench, relevance computed from the raw question embedding is unreliable (8--16 points below the best methods), whereas anchors derived from query decomposition avoid this failure. However, query access is not inherently advantageous: strong query-agnostic coverage methods remain competitive or superior in the full-field comparison. Relative to a redundancy-only baseline, structured selection helps most on evidence-specific and long-context tasks at tight budgets; on broad tasks, the holistic selector improves over either relevance or redundancy alone. Further, pruning reduces cost and memory. These results support a practical design rule: preserve visual coverage by default, and add structured relevance when the task and token budget demand selective evidence retrieval.

AI.tldr: This controlled study compares 21 training-free video token pruning principles on Qwen-3-VL, finding that raw question embeddings are unreliable while query-agnostic coverage remains strong and structured query decomposition helps on evidence-specific tasks.
AI.motivation: Training-free video token pruning methods differ in whether and how they condition on the user query, leaving the actual value of query conditioning unclear.
AI.method: Using a shared Qwen-3-VL backbone, token budgets, and decoding settings, the authors evaluate 21 pruning principles across query-agnostic, shallow query-conditioned, structured query-conditioned (decomposing questions into semantic anchors), and holistic (Pareto anchor-relevance plus visual diversity) strategies.
AI.result: Across Video-MME, MVBench, and LongVideoBench, raw question-embedding relevance drops 8 to 16 points below top methods, whereas decomposed semantic anchors avoid this failure; strong query-agnostic coverage remains competitive or superior overall, structured selection helps most on evidence-specific long-context tasks at tight budgets, and holistic selection improves broad tasks.
AI.conclusion: Video token pruning should preserve visual coverage by default and add structured query relevance only when tight budgets and evidence-specific tasks require selective retrieval.

title: Anchored Inertial Proposals with Objective Verification for Diffusion-Prior Inverse Problems
summary: Training-free diffusion priors are powerful for inverse problems, but measurement guidance during reverse sampling is local: aggressive updates can improve immediate data fit while disrupting later denoising. We introduce an anchored inertial correction rule that separates proposal generation from acceptance. At each corrected step, the denoiser prediction anchors a frozen clean-space objective combining measurement fit with a noise-level-dependent proximal term. Heavy-ball dynamics with step size and momentum computed from the measured curvature generate a clean-state candidate; a separate verifier evaluates it with the same objective, with the denoiser prediction retained as fallback; both stages are derived from one objective for the whole trajectory, considered one step at a time. The accepted clean state is re-noised to continue sampling. The rule applies to pixel and latent diffusion with differentiable measurement operators, requires no retraining, and adds no denoiser calls inside the correction loop. We analyze how objective verification yields local nonincrease and displacement control. Across natural-image benchmarks, the method achieves competitive reconstruction quality. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an anchored inertial correction rule with objective verification for training-free diffusion-prior inverse problems, separating candidate generation from acceptance to prevent measurement guidance from disrupting denoising.
AI.motivation: Local measurement guidance during reverse diffusion sampling can improve immediate data fit at the expense of disrupting subsequent denoising steps.
AI.method: At each corrected step, the denoiser prediction anchors a clean-space objective (measurement fit plus noise-level-dependent proximal term); heavy-ball dynamics with curvature-derived step size and momentum propose a candidate, which a verifier accepts only if it improves the same objective (falling back to the denoiser prediction otherwise) before re-noising.
AI.result: Applicable to pixel and latent diffusion with differentiable measurement operators without retraining or extra denoiser calls in the correction loop, the method provides local nonincrease and displacement control and achieves competitive reconstruction quality across natural-image benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Separating inertial proposal generation from objective-based verification stabilizes measurement guidance in diffusion-prior inverse problems.

title: TwoPass: Draft-Guided Few-Step Video Prediction for Robotic Manipulation
summary: Action-conditioned video prediction lets robots anticipate the visual consequences of their actions for planning and policy evaluation. Existing predictors denoise each future from noise without using their own estimate of it, which limits the quality of the predicted future, in particular of the manipulated objects, and requires many network calls. We present TwoPass, a self-conditioned training-and-inference framework that keeps the standard flow-matching objective. Self-Generated Draft Training supplies a detached clean-video estimate from the shared network as conditioning at the same noisy state. A Refinement-Only Late Adapter applies a dedicated residual transformation when a draft is present. At inference, Draft-Reuse Iterative Refinement obtains both a solver update and the next draft from each velocity prediction, requiring as few as 4 function evaluations (NFE) per video chunk. Training samples discrete solver-query noise levels and updates the pretrained backbone. Extensive experiments on Bridge and Language Table show that TwoPass achieves state-of-the-art results with 4 NFE, far fewer than the 50-59 calls of existing predictors. Code: this https URL.

AI.tldr: TwoPass is a self-conditioned flow-matching framework for action-conditioned video prediction in robotic manipulation that reuses its own clean-video draft to achieve state-of-the-art results in just 4 function evaluations.
AI.motivation: Existing action-conditioned video predictors denoise each future from scratch without using their own intermediate estimates, limiting object prediction quality and requiring 50 to 59 network evaluations.
AI.method: TwoPass keeps the standard flow-matching objective and adds Self-Generated Draft Training (conditioning on a detached clean-video estimate at the same noisy state), a Refinement-Only Late Adapter, and Draft-Reuse Iterative Refinement at inference to obtain both a solver update and the next draft per velocity prediction.
AI.result: On Bridge and Language Table, TwoPass achieves state-of-the-art video prediction quality with 4 function evaluations (NFE) per video chunk, far fewer than the 50 to 59 calls of existing predictors.
AI.conclusion: Self-conditioned draft reuse enables fast, few-step action-conditioned video prediction for robotic manipulation without sacrificing visual quality.

title: UniReFP: Robust Unified Fingerprinting for Vision Models against Cross-Task Repurposing Attacks
summary: We identify, for the first time, a new model modification attack--the cross-task model repurposing attack--that can render fingerprints generated by existing model fingerprinting approaches inapplicable. To address this challenge, we propose UniReFP--a novel unified model fingerprinting framework applicable to diverse vision models across different tasks--that utilizes ownership evidence in a shared class-level semantic space rather than original task-specific output space, enabling effective ownership verification when a protected model is repurposed across tasks with heterogeneous output formats. Specifically, UniReFP constructs a surrogate classifier by repurposing the protected model, enabling fingerprints to be generated independently of the original task-dependent output space of the protected model. Moreover, it optimizes grouped fingerprints to encode ownership evidence: fingerprints within the same group are encouraged to induce consistent semantic responses and intermediate representations on the surrogate classifier, while producing dispersed responses on independently trained reference classifiers. During verification, UniReFP uses a task-aware semantic projection mechanism to map heterogeneous suspect-model outputs into unified semantic-presence vectors, and determines ownership by measuring inner-group consistency. Extensive experimental results validate the effectiveness of UniReFP, consistently showing superior performance under cross-task repurposing attacks, commonly studied model modification attacks, and even their combinations.

AI.tldr: UniReFP is a unified model fingerprinting framework that verifies vision model ownership in a shared class-level semantic space, defending against cross-task model repurposing attacks.
AI.motivation: Cross-task model repurposing attacks alter a protected vision model's output format, rendering existing task-specific model fingerprinting methods inapplicable.
AI.method: UniReFP constructs a surrogate classifier by repurposing the protected model, optimizes grouped fingerprints to elicit consistent semantic responses and intermediate features on the surrogate while dispersing responses on reference classifiers, and uses a task-aware semantic projection during verification to measure inner-group consistency.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show that UniReFP consistently outperforms baselines under cross-task repurposing attacks, standard model modification attacks, and their combinations.
AI.conclusion: Anchoring ownership verification in a shared class-level semantic space rather than task-specific output spaces enables robust fingerprinting across repurposed vision models.

title: Online Mistake Detection in Instruction-Conditioned Procedural Video
summary: An assistant monitoring a person performing a procedure is most useful when it can detect mistakes while there is still time to recover. This requires judging actions against task instructions as the video unfolds, identifying the attempted step, locating it in time, and assessing its execution. Existing online detectors do not use the instruction text, while instruction-conditioned methods operate offline. In this paper, we study online, instruction-conditioned mistake detection in egocentric videos. Using only observed video, task instructions, and prior predictions, our model identifies and localizes completed action attempts and classifies them as correct, modified, slip, corrections, or additions; omitted steps are determined after the video ends. We compare a modular pipeline, with separate step identification, temporal localization, and execution verification, to a joint model that predicts all outputs in a single step. To support supervised learning from mistakes, we repartition EgoPER to include erroneous videos in all splits. The approaches achieve similar step-segmentation F1@0.5 (93.6% and 92.1%), while the joint model achieves higher binary mistake-detection F1@0.5 (84.1% vs. 80.7%), with its largest gain on slips (56.4% vs. 37.5%). Component-level analysis suggests that error propagation between stages contributes to the modular approach's lower detection score. On test videos containing mistakes, both designs outperform released AEM and ESTANet checkpoints under our evaluation protocol.

AI.tldr: This paper studies online, instruction-conditioned mistake detection in egocentric procedural videos, showing that a joint prediction model outperforms a modular pipeline by avoiding stage-to-stage error propagation.
AI.motivation: Existing online mistake detectors ignore task instructions, while instruction-conditioned methods operate offline, preventing real-time intervention while a user can still recover.
AI.method: Using only observed video, task instructions, and prior predictions, the authors compare a modular pipeline (separate step identification, localization, and execution verification) against a joint model on a repartitioned EgoPER dataset containing erroneous videos in all splits.
AI.result: Both models achieve similar step-segmentation F1@0.5 (93.6% and 92.1%), but the joint model achieves higher binary mistake-detection F1@0.5 (84.1% vs. 80.7%), especially on slips (56.4% vs. 37.5%), and both outperform released AEM and ESTANet checkpoints on mistake-containing test videos.
AI.conclusion: Jointly predicting step identity, localization, and execution status reduces error propagation and improves online instruction-conditioned mistake detection.

title: VidToC: Rethinking Video Token Compression for Multimodal Large Language Models
summary: Extending multimodal large language models (MLLMs) from images to videos faces substantial memory and latency challenges due to the massive number of visual tokens. These challenges have driven the development of numerous visual token compression methods and more efficient LLM architectures. However, existing compression methods are often evaluated with different training setups, tasks, and models, making fair comparison difficult. Meanwhile, the growing use of hybrid Mamba-Transformer architectures raises questions about whether compression strategies transfer across backbones. We present VidToC, a controlled evaluation framework for representative compression algorithms, LLM backbones, and time encoding strategies, covering training-free and fine-tuned settings on three complementary video understanding tasks. Our results reveal task-dependent compression behavior and characterize the effects of compression placement, time encoding, and backbone choice. These findings provide empirical guidance for designing and selecting video token compression strategies across tasks and training settings.

AI.tldr: VidToC is a controlled evaluation framework for video token compression across representative algorithms, LLM backbones (including hybrid Mamba-Transformer), and time encodings, revealing task-dependent compression behavior.
AI.motivation: Existing video token compression methods are evaluated under inconsistent training setups, tasks, and backbones, making fair comparison and transferability to hybrid Mamba-Transformer architectures unclear.
AI.method: VidToC benchmarks representative compression algorithms, LLM backbones, and time encoding strategies across both training-free and fine-tuned settings on three complementary video understanding tasks.
AI.result: Experiments reveal task-dependent compression behavior and characterize how compression placement, time encoding, and backbone choice affect performance.
AI.conclusion: VidToC provides empirical guidelines for selecting and designing video token compression strategies tailored to specific tasks, backbones, and training regimes.

title: QFT-Based Hybrid PointNet-Quantum Neural Networks for LiDAR Point-Cloud Classification
summary: Hybrid quantum-classical learning architectures provide a promising framework for integrating quantum feature transformations into complex data-processing tasks. Among these transformations, the Quantum Fourier Transform (QFT) offers a structured approach to feature processing, motivating an investigation of how its circuit configuration influences predictive performance, quantum resource requirements, and noise robustness. We present a hybrid PointNet-quantum neural network architecture for LiDAR point-cloud classification, combining classical feature extraction, amplitude encoding, and a variational quantum circuit. Five Fourier-processing configurations are systematically evaluated: No-QFT, Full-QFT-After, QFT-no-swap, IQFT-After, and Trainable-QFT. Experiments on KITTI, nuScenes, and PandaSet across three random seeds assess classification performance, class-level behavior, circuit complexity, and sensitivity to the IBM FakeManilaV2 noise model. Under ideal simulation, IQFT-After achieves the highest weighted F1-score on KITTI (0.857 $\pm$ 0.033), compared with 0.838 $\pm$ 0.023 for No-QFT. Removing the final SWAP gates in the QFT circuit reduces circuit complexity while preserving the Pauli-Z measurement features up to a fixed permutation that can be absorbed by the classification head. Under quantum noise, the circuit ranking changes, with IQFT-After exhibiting greater performance degradation and No-QFT and Trainable-QFT showing stronger robustness. Per-class analysis further identifies dataset-dependent differences in minority-class performance. These results demonstrate that Fourier-processing configuration influences both classification behavior and noise sensitivity, highlighting the role of circuit structure and hardware-aware evaluation in hybrid quantum learning for three-dimensional point-cloud data.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a hybrid PointNet-quantum neural network for LiDAR point-cloud classification and evaluates five Quantum Fourier Transform (QFT) circuit configurations under ideal simulation and quantum noise.
AI.motivation: Understanding how QFT circuit structure affects predictive performance, quantum resource requirements, and noise robustness in hybrid quantum-classical learning for 3D point clouds remains underexplored.
AI.method: The architecture combines classical PointNet feature extraction, amplitude encoding, and a variational quantum circuit, systematically comparing five configurations: No-QFT, Full-QFT-After, QFT-no-swap, IQFT-After, and Trainable-QFT.
AI.result: On KITTI, nuScenes, and PandaSet across three random seeds, IQFT-After achieves the highest ideal weighted F1-score on KITTI (0.857 +/- 0.033 vs. 0.838 +/- 0.023 for No-QFT), removing final SWAP gates reduces complexity while preserving Pauli-Z features up to a permutation, and under the IBM FakeManilaV2 noise model, No-QFT and Trainable-QFT show stronger robustness while IQFT-After degrades more.
AI.conclusion: Fourier-processing configuration significantly impacts both classification accuracy and noise sensitivity, underscoring the need for hardware-aware evaluation in hybrid quantum 3D point-cloud learning.

title: Characterizing Age-Conditioned Affective Reasoning in Vision-Language Models
summary: An age prompt can change how a vision-language model (VLM) rates the emotion evoked by an image. Does the change predict how people of different ages rate that same image? We evaluate 17 VLMs on 900 OASIS images using young-, middle-, and older-adult prompts and estimate image-specific age differences from ratings by 822 participants. Without an age cue, models closely track average human valence (median Pearson $r=0.891$). Under an older-adult prompt, 16 of 17 models assign lower valence on average than under a young-adult prompt. Yet after adjusting for image pleasantness, correlations between model and human age effects range from $-0.030$ to $0.093$, against an estimated ceiling of $0.595$. The discrepancy is clearest on 54 sensitive images rated as pleasant. Across models, the older prompt reduces valence by $0.845$ points on average, while older participants rate these images $0.443$ points higher than younger participants. Providing human ratings from other images improves agreement on the direction of age differences, although image-specific fidelity remains modest on 600 held-out images ($r_{\mathrm{part}}=0.105$). These results show why evaluations of demographic personalization in foundation models need human comparisons at the level of individual stimuli. Project page available at this https URL

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates whether age-conditioned prompts in vision-language models (VLMs) accurately predict how humans of different ages rate the emotion evoked by individual images.
AI.motivation: Age prompts shift VLM valence ratings, but it is unclear whether these shifts reflect true human age differences at the level of individual stimuli.
AI.method: The authors evaluate 17 VLMs on 900 OASIS images using young-, middle-, and older-adult prompts and compare them against image-specific age differences estimated from 822 human participants.
AI.result: Without age cues, models track average human valence (median Pearson r = 0.891), and 16 of 17 models assign lower valence under older-adult prompts; however, after adjusting for image pleasantness, model-human age-effect correlations range from -0.030 to 0.093 (versus a 0.595 ceiling), and on 54 sensitive pleasant images, older prompts reduce valence by 0.845 points while older humans rate them 0.443 points higher.
AI.conclusion: Evaluations of demographic personalization in foundation models must include stimulus-level human comparisons rather than relying on average rating shifts.

title: LoopedWAM: Looped World Action Models for Elastic Inference
summary: World action models (WAMs) couple generative video modeling with robotic action prediction but typically require large video and action transformers, limiting deployment efficiency. We present LoopedWAM, a compact WAM that recurrently applies a shared six-block core in each expert, executing 30 transformer layers while storing only 12 blocks per expert. To account for their asymmetric inference costs, the video and action experts can operate at different depths: visual features are computed once per query, whereas action computation repeats at every sampling step. We further propose elastic self-distillation, which trains a single elastic checkpoint, LoopedWAM-E, across action-depth and sampling-step budgets. With only 0.58B policy parameters and no robot pretraining, LoopedWAM achieves 96.1% success on LIBERO, 91.9% on RoboTwin 2.0, and 52.2% on RoboCasaGR1, while using $7.4\times$ less peak GPU memory than Fast-WAM under matched inference measurements. On LIBERO, LoopedWAM-E achieves 96.0% success in 27.6 ms or 95.2% in 24.7 ms on an H100, providing multiple accuracy-latency operating points from a single checkpoint; with two sampling steps and four action loops, it stays within 0.5 points of LoopedWAM on all three benchmarks. Ablations demonstrate that weight-shared depth preserves competitive performance, while aggressive action-depth reduction requires explicit budget-aware training. On a real AgileX PiPER arm, LoopedWAM succeeds in 71.3% of 80 trials across four tasks.

AI.tldr: This paper presents LoopedWAM, a compact world action model that uses weight-shared looped transformer blocks and elastic self-distillation for efficient, budget-adaptive robotic control.
AI.motivation: World action models couple video generation with action prediction but typically rely on large transformers that limit deployment efficiency.
AI.method: LoopedWAM recurrently applies a shared six-block core in each expert (executing 30 layers while storing 12 blocks per expert), runs video features once per query while looping action computation at each sampling step, and uses elastic self-distillation (LoopedWAM-E) to support multiple action-depth and sampling-step budgets from one checkpoint.
AI.result: With 0.58B policy parameters and no robot pretraining, LoopedWAM achieves 96.1% success on LIBERO, 91.9% on RoboTwin 2.0, and 52.2% on RoboCasaGR1 using 7.4x less peak GPU memory than Fast-WAM; LoopedWAM-E reaches 96.0% in 27.6 ms or 95.2% in 24.7 ms on an H100, and succeeds in 71.3% of 80 real AgileX PiPER arm trials.
AI.conclusion: Weight-shared looping and elastic self-distillation enable compact world action models with flexible accuracy-latency trade-offs for real-world robotics.

title: CaT-Movie: Balancing Global Planning and Local Rendering for Long Multi-Shot Video Generation
summary: Current multi-shot video generators render only limited durations per pass, requiring long movies to be stitched from local segments across which narrative progression and visual identity drift. To synthesize long-horizon movies with Coherence across Time, we present CaT-Movie, a multi-shot generation system consisting of a global story planner and a local window renderer. The planner expands user requests via a large language model to preserve, infer, and complete story details, while deterministic code maintains the resulting storyboard across shots to compile self-contained shot prompts and index reference frames from generated history. To execute this guidance, the renderer applies reference-routed sparse self-attention and shot-wise cross-attention to route identities from the indexed frames while isolating per-shot textual conditions. Given the scarcity of high-quality open-source multi-shot data, we construct a dataset of over 350K film shots annotated with semantic state transitions, entity grounding, and multi-granularity requests. We further build CaT-MBench, a benchmark on held-out films with the same annotations. It gives every baseline its native format and counts cross-shot consistency only when a cut opens a new camera setup, preventing repeated framing from passing as consistency. On CaT-MBench, CaT-Movie attains the highest average score and the most consistent characters among all methods. The project page is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces CaT-Movie, a multi-shot video generation system combining a global LLM story planner with a local window renderer, alongside a 350K-shot dataset and the CaT-MBench benchmark.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-shot video generators only render short durations per pass, causing narrative drift and visual identity loss when stitching long movies.
AI.method: An LLM-based global planner expands user requests into a deterministic storyboard that compiles self-contained shot prompts and indexes reference frames, while the local renderer uses reference-routed sparse self-attention and shot-wise cross-attention to maintain identity and isolate per-shot text conditions.
AI.result: Evaluated on CaT-MBench (which counts cross-shot consistency only across new camera setups), CaT-Movie achieves the highest average score and the most consistent characters among all compared methods.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling global story planning from reference-routed local rendering enables coherent long-horizon multi-shot video generation.

title: DAWN: Robust Neural Blind Deconvolution via Alternating Wiener Guidance
summary: Blind image deconvolution (BID) is an ill-posed inverse problem that aims to jointly recover a sharp image and blur kernel from a single degraded observation. Under nontrivial and high noise, which is common in photography and scientific imaging such as microscopy, BID remains particularly challenging, as existing methods suffer from noise overfitting and inaccurate kernel estimation. Existing training-data-free learning methods for BID, such as those based on the deep image prior (DIP), often utilize external guidance by including model-based estimates as additional loss terms, which underexploits the information these estimates carry especially under nontrivial noise. To address these challenges, we propose DAWN, a training-data-free DIP framework that alternates between injecting model-based estimates directly into the model input and refining this imperfect estimate with the network's own prior. To provide more reliable kernel estimates for these injections, we apply autoencoding regularization to both the image and kernel networks. On natural and scientific images under varying levels of Gaussian and Poisson noise, DAWN outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both image and kernel quality (achieving up to +4.5 dB over the next best baseline on the Levin dataset at $\sigma = 0.1$). Without any training images, DAWN remains highly competitive with a state-of-the-art diffusion model on FFHQ, despite the latter being trained on a massive number of in-distribution images.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes DAWN, a training-data-free deep image prior (DIP) framework for blind image deconvolution that alternates between injecting model-based Wiener estimates and refining them with autoencoding-regularized networks.
AI.motivation: Existing training-data-free blind deconvolution methods suffer from noise overfitting and inaccurate kernel estimation under nontrivial noise, as using model-based estimates only as loss terms underexploits their guidance.
AI.method: DAWN alternates between directly injecting model-based estimates into the network input and refining them with the network's prior, while applying autoencoding regularization to both the image and kernel networks.
AI.result: Under Gaussian and Poisson noise on natural and scientific images, DAWN outperforms state-of-the-art methods in image and kernel quality (up to +4.5 dB over the next best baseline on Levin at sigma = 0.1) and remains competitive with a trained diffusion model on FFHQ without training images.
AI.conclusion: Alternating Wiener guidance with autoencoding regularization makes training-data-free blind deconvolution substantially more robust to high noise.

title: Physical Laws without Physics Loss? Probing Learned Dynamics in Video World Models through Forced Response
summary: Do video world models learn physical laws without a physics loss, or merely imitate motion? Overall motion and appearance scores cannot settle it. We investigate this through nonlinear forced response: an excitation shakes the support of a suspended object. We introduce dual visual-numeric conditioning and adapt six image-to-video backbones to predict this motion using only the flow-matching loss. Wan predicts motion accurately and generalizes to unseen excitations, objects, poses, and scenes. Counterfactual tests suggest capabilities beyond replaying training videos. But what laws have they learned? We design three tiers of tests using Taylor expansions of the dynamics and geometry.
