All six reproduce the linear response, including resonance; five capture higher-order dynamics, including nonlinear softening. Remarkably, softening is barely present in training: only 0.74% of the swing's squared displacement. Extensions to a double pendulum and a rocking block show sustained dynamics are learned more faithfully than brief impacts. Yet learned dynamics may fail to appear when state estimation or propagation goes wrong. We turn these tests and findings into strategies to improve video training and generation.

AI.tldr: This paper probes whether video world models learn physical laws without a physics loss by testing six image-to-video backbones on nonlinear forced-response dynamics.
AI.motivation: Standard motion and appearance metrics cannot determine whether video world models genuinely learn physical laws or merely imitate training motion.
AI.method: The authors introduce dual visual-numeric conditioning to adapt six image-to-video backbones using only flow-matching loss, and design three tiers of tests based on Taylor expansions of dynamics and geometry, plus counterfactual, double-pendulum, and rocking-block experiments.
AI.result: All six models reproduce linear response including resonance, and five capture higher-order nonlinear softening despite softening accounting for only 0.74% of squared displacement in training; Wan generalizes to unseen excitations, objects, poses, and scenes, while sustained dynamics are learned more faithfully than brief impacts.
AI.conclusion: Video world models trained solely with flow-matching can internalize underlying physical laws, though failures in state estimation or propagation can mask them.

title: RelGeo: Pair-Conditioned Relational Calibration for Frozen Diffusion Correspondence
summary: Frozen diffusion descriptors retrieve strong semantic correspondence candidates, yet cosine nearest-neighbor matching can select incorrect locations despite valid high-ranking alternatives. Across DIFT-SD2.1 and DiTF-FLUX on SPair-71k, AP-10K, and SOCO (CC, SOC, Cross-SOC), 41-69% of Top-1 errors retain a PCK@0.10-valid match among the original Top-5 spatial peaks, revealing a persistent candidate-selection bottleneck. We find that descriptor rankings and current-pair relational evidence can favor different candidates: reciprocal diffusion Query/Key associations and pretrained RoMa transport exhibit distinct, partly complementary preferences. To incorporate this evidence into matching decisions, we introduce RelGeo, a Pair-Conditioned Relational Calibration framework expressing heterogeneous relations as shared source-target coordinates. Spectral Relational Coordinates (SRC) encode reciprocal diffusion affinities, while Warp Identity Coordinates (WIC) encode reliability-weighted bidirectional transport endpoints. Their inner products augment frozen descriptor similarity while preserving full-domain cosine nearest-neighbor matching without additional semantic-correspondence training. RelGeo improves all ten evaluations by an average of 5.51 PCK@0.10 points; fixed-candidate reranking and pair-misalignment controls corroborate improved selection and dependence on current-pair relational alignment.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces RelGeo, a training-free relational calibration framework that improves semantic correspondence in frozen diffusion descriptors by incorporating reciprocal diffusion and transport relations.
AI.motivation: Across DIFT-SD2.1 and DiTF-FLUX, 41-69% of Top-1 cosine nearest-neighbor errors still contain a valid PCK@0.10 match in the Top-5 spatial peaks, showing a candidate-selection bottleneck.
AI.method: RelGeo expresses reciprocal diffusion Query/Key affinities as Spectral Relational Coordinates (SRC) and pretrained RoMa bidirectional transport endpoints as Warp Identity Coordinates (WIC), augmenting frozen descriptor similarity via inner products without additional semantic-correspondence training.
AI.result: Across ten evaluations on SPair-71k, AP-10K, and SOCO, RelGeo improves PCK@0.10 by an average of 5.51 points, with reranking and misalignment controls confirming better candidate selection.
AI.conclusion: Pair-conditioned relational calibration effectively resolves candidate-selection ambiguity in frozen diffusion correspondence.

title: What One Sample Cannot See: Why Fewer Denoising Steps Can Score Higher on Physics Benchmarks
summary: When a storm can head north or south, a forecast down the middle may score better under squared error than either plausible path. The same paradox appears when video generators are tested as world models: fewer denoising steps can raise physics scores even as videos blur or stop moving early. Why? Physics-IQ compares each generated video with one recording, although a scene can have multiple valid futures. An exact decomposition shows its scores can reward reduced variation among generated futures, even when their distribution becomes less accurate. We introduce Kernel Physics-IQ to remove this incentive in expectation, needing only two independent samples per condition. Two-step sampling lowers Kernel Physics-IQ in all five image-to-video models. For CogVideoX, the official score rises by 0.055 while ours falls by 0.131. Changing the sampling schedule reveals further differences official scores miss. In controlled physical systems with known outcome probabilities, our metric favors the true distribution over collapsed predictions. In short, a world model should be judged not only by how closely one video matches what happened, but by how faithfully its predictions represent what could have happened.

AI.tldr: This paper diagnoses why fewer denoising steps can artificially inflate Physics-IQ scores in video world models and introduces Kernel Physics-IQ to fix this bias.
AI.motivation: Physics-IQ compares each generated video against a single ground-truth recording, which rewards collapsed, low-variance predictions (such as blurry or static videos from few denoising steps) even when the predicted distribution is less accurate.
AI.method: The authors provide an exact decomposition of this bias and propose Kernel Physics-IQ, an unbiased metric requiring only two independent samples per condition.
AI.result: With two-step sampling across five image-to-video models, Kernel Physics-IQ decreases in all five (e.g., for CogVideoX, the official score rises by 0.055 while Kernel Physics-IQ drops by 0.131), and in controlled physical systems it favors true distributions over collapsed ones.
AI.conclusion: Evaluating video world models requires distribution-aware metrics like Kernel Physics-IQ that account for multiple valid physical futures.

title: AesDistill: Distilling Generative Aesthetics for Image Color Enhancement
summary: Image color enhancement aims to improve visual appeal, but previous methods often learn to reproduce ground-truth expert targets. These targets reflect the preferences of a few experts and cover a limited range of aesthetic choices. Matching them does not ensure stronger aesthetic quality across different tastes and scenes. By contrast, large generative models learn rich visual knowledge from large image collections and often produce vivid, appealing image edits. However, direct generation can change the source image's semantic structure along with its colors. In this paper, we introduce AesDistill, a framework for distilling generative aesthetics into image color enhancement. We use 4 leading open-source large generative models to produce 64,644 edited images as teacher targets at a cost of about 3,360 H100 GPU-hours, forming the AesDistill Dataset. AesDistill also includes AesDistill Student, a 1.13M-parameter model that learns teacher color changes through confidence-weighted supervision while preserving the source image's semantic structure. We evaluate AesDistill with 12 aesthetic and 4 image-quality assessment models. Every teacher's targets rank above the FiveK and PPR10K expert target means in the joint assessment. Across both datasets, AesDistill Student outperforms all 20 baseline methods and ranks directly behind the 4 teachers. These results demonstrate that distilling aesthetics from generative models enables a compact student to outperform methods trained on expert targets.

AI.tldr: This paper presents AesDistill, a framework that distills aesthetic color enhancement from large generative models into a compact 1.13M-parameter student model while preserving semantic structure.
AI.motivation: Training color enhancement models on expert-retouched datasets limits aesthetic diversity, whereas direct edits from large generative models can alter image semantics.
AI.method: The authors use four open-source generative models to create 64,644 edited target images (AesDistill Dataset) and train AesDistill Student (1.13M parameters) with confidence-weighted supervision to learn color changes without structural drift.
AI.result: Evaluated across 12 aesthetic and 4 image-quality models, every teacher outperforms FiveK and PPR10K expert means, and AesDistill Student outperforms all 20 baseline methods on both datasets, ranking directly behind the four teachers.
AI.conclusion: Distilling generative aesthetics into a lightweight student yields stronger, more diverse color enhancement than learning from limited expert targets.

title: LG-FiLM: Local-Global Mixture-of-Experts Modulation for RAW-to-RGB Reconstruction
summary: An image signal processor does more than reconstruct an image. It also has to decide how strongly to denoise, how to balance color, and which tone curve maps the scene onto the display, and these settings depend on the scene itself, the curve that suits a backlit sky is not the one that suits an indoor portrait. Most neural ISPs learn a single fixed transformation and apply it to every scene. We instead make the adaptation an explicit part of the network. Our model, LG FiLM, keeps one shared encoder decoder and places a small mixture of affine experts at its bottleneck; the experts scales, shifts, and mixing weights are predicted from local neighborhood evidence together with a global scene descriptor. Reconstruction stays in a single shared pathway and only the processing mode is switched. We evaluate LG FiLM on three datasets, Fujifilm UltraISP, Zurich RAW to RGB, and a COCO derived benchmark built with an inverse ISP. The model reaches the best reconstruction fidelity of the compared entries on the primary benchmark and transfers to the other two.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes LG-FiLM, a neural ISP that uses a local-global mixture of affine experts at its bottleneck to adapt denoising, color balance, and tone mapping to each scene.
AI.motivation: Most neural ISPs apply a single fixed transformation to all images, whereas optimal ISP processing depends on scene-specific lighting and content.
AI.method: LG-FiLM keeps a shared encoder-decoder and inserts a small mixture of affine experts at the bottleneck whose scales, shifts, and mixing weights are predicted from local neighborhood features and a global scene descriptor.
AI.result: Evaluated on Fujifilm UltraISP, Zurich RAW to RGB, and a COCO-derived inverse-ISP benchmark, LG-FiLM achieves the best reconstruction fidelity on the primary benchmark and transfers well to the other two.
AI.conclusion: Explicit local-global affine modulation enables a single neural ISP backbone to adaptively switch processing modes across diverse scenes.

title: TRACE: Attribute Execution for Sequential Image Editing
summary: Given an image and successive user instructions, sequential image editing should return an updated image that satisfies each new request and preserves earlier requirements that remain active. This lets users develop a result without repeatedly restating or repairing their decisions. The difficulty is that a retrieved image can contain a valid color on an obsolete surface, while the current image may lack the newly requested material. Neither reference selection nor a precise object mask alone specifies how to reconcile attributes occupying the same region. We present TRACE, which separates the continuing attribute from its visual carrier and prioritizes local appearance operations under complete-request checks. Active-goal binding identifies what should persist, carrier selection supplies suitable current or newly generated pixels, and tonal calibration reduces tinting near highlights and shadows. Experiments across frozen editors, independent visual readers, new source images, and complete sequential benchmarks support joint color-material recovery and show how local execution preserves the surrounding scene.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces TRACE, a framework for sequential image editing that separates persistent attributes from their visual carriers to apply local edits without losing prior requirements.
AI.motivation: Sequential image editing struggles when retrieved references have valid colors on obsolete surfaces or when current images lack requested materials, as neither reference selection nor object masks alone reconcile overlapping attributes.
AI.method: TRACE uses active-goal binding to track persistent requirements, carrier selection to supply appropriate current or generated pixels, and tonal calibration to reduce tinting near highlights and shadows under complete-request checks.
AI.result: Experiments across frozen editors, independent visual readers, new source images, and sequential benchmarks demonstrate effective joint color-material recovery and preservation of surrounding regions.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling attributes from visual carriers enables reliable, locally-scoped sequential image editing.

title: Minimal Memory for Correctable Visual Continuation
summary: Given past images and known actions, visual continuation generates future frames from one evolving scene state. Keeping this state revisable matters when an object reappears or a later view changes an earlier interpretation. Once past images cannot be replayed, a summary sufficient for current rendering can lose candidates needed after correction. We establish matching sparse and dense bounds on the bits needed for later correction under stable observations and bounded disagreement. For static streams at the stated smoothness and margin scales, correction incurs at least logarithmic overhead in one dimension and polynomial overhead in higher dimensions. Coherent Archive Memory (CAM) stores geometric summaries with exact updates under clipped expansion and coordinate assignments, then uses historical existence constraints to select one state for all requested frames. Exhaustive photographic tests show strict worst-truth image-risk gains from joint witnesses, while controlled neural continuations recover positions hidden in the current view.

AI.tldr: This paper establishes information-theoretic bounds on memory needed for revisable visual continuation and proposes Coherent Archive Memory (CAM) for consistent scene-state updates.
AI.motivation: When past images cannot be replayed in visual continuation, compact summaries sufficient for current rendering may discard candidates needed to correct earlier interpretations when objects reappear or viewpoints change.
AI.method: The authors prove sparse and dense bit bounds for correction overhead (logarithmic in 1D, polynomial in higher dimensions) and introduce CAM, which stores geometric summaries with exact updates and uses historical existence constraints to select one state across all requested frames.
AI.result: Exhaustive photographic tests show strict worst-truth image-risk gains from joint witnesses, and controlled neural continuations recover positions hidden in the current view.
AI.conclusion: Maintaining bounded geometric archives with historical constraints enables correctable visual continuation without storing full frame histories.

title: Beyond Entity Recognition: Vision-Centric Knowledge Visual Question Answering
summary: We propose VC-VQA, a large-scale benchmark for vision-centric knowledge reasoning, aiming to systematically evaluate the capabilities of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) in fine-grained visual knowledge acquisition and complex multi-stage reasoning. Unlike existing benchmarks that primarily treat visual information as entity recognition and rely on text-based external knowledge, VC-VQA explicitly models the role of visual information by considering both its source (internal vs. external images) and stage of involvement (pre-retrieval vs. post-retrieval). Specifically, VC-VQA requires models to retrieve external visual evidence, identify visual clues before retrieval, and localize, verify, or match retrieved knowledge against the internal image. We further construct a controlled multimodal knowledge base with traceable textual and visual evidence for each sample. We evaluate 21 representative MLLMs under four settings: no external knowledge, with provided evidence, knowledge base retrieval, and open-web search. Experimental results lead to three key findings: current models still struggle with vision-centric knowledge reasoning; fine-grained visual knowledge acquisition remains the primary bottleneck; and agentic retrieval highlights the value of multi-step planning and cross-modal knowledge integration. Overall, VC-VQA provides a more challenging benchmark for evaluating vision-centric knowledge reasoning in MLLMs. Our code and dataset are available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces VC-VQA, a large-scale benchmark and controlled multimodal knowledge base for evaluating vision-centric knowledge reasoning in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs).
AI.motivation: Existing knowledge VQA benchmarks mostly reduce vision to entity recognition and rely on text-based external knowledge, leaving multi-stage visual evidence retrieval and verification untested.
AI.method: VC-VQA models both knowledge source (internal vs. external images) and involvement stage (pre-retrieval vs. post-retrieval), requiring models to identify visual clues, retrieve external visual evidence, and verify it against the internal image using a traceable multimodal knowledge base.
AI.result: Evaluating 21 MLLMs across four settings (no knowledge, provided evidence, KB retrieval, open-web search) shows that models struggle with vision-centric reasoning, fine-grained visual knowledge acquisition is the main bottleneck, and agentic retrieval aids multi-step cross-modal integration.
AI.conclusion: VC-VQA exposes key limitations in current MLLMs' visual knowledge acquisition and highlights the need for multi-step agentic visual reasoning.

title: D3-Cache: Accelerating Diffusion Models with Dynamic Mode Decomposition
summary: Diffusion Transformers generate high-quality images and videos, but every sampling step requires a full network evaluation. Training-free caching reduces this cost by reusing or forecasting network outputs across steps, but common approaches use per-model calibrated skip criteria or maintain per-layer prediction histories. We present D3-Cache, which applies Dynamic Mode Decomposition (DMD) to Diffusion sampling: it fits DMD to a short history of exact velocities and forecasts only the velocity that the scheduler consumes. A horizon-aware gate decides when to skip: whenever the network is evaluated, its output is compared with the forecast for that step, and the larger the error, the sooner the network is evaluated again, up to a cap on consecutive skipped steps. D3-Cache requires no training or per-model offline calibration curve and adds negligible memory. It shares one history length and risk tolerance across the four evaluated models. On four state-of-the-art image and video models, D3-Cache achieves speedups of 2.6-3.8x with high fidelity to the base model output.

AI.tldr: This paper presents D3-Cache, a training-free caching method that accelerates Diffusion Transformers using Dynamic Mode Decomposition (DMD) and a horizon-aware skip gate.
AI.motivation: Diffusion Transformers require costly full network evaluations at every sampling step, while existing caching methods often need per-model offline calibration or large per-layer histories.
AI.method: D3-Cache fits DMD to a short history of exact velocities to forecast only the scheduler-consumed velocity, using a horizon-aware gate that schedules the next full evaluation based on forecast error up to a consecutive skip cap.
AI.result: Using a single shared history length and risk tolerance across four state-of-the-art image and video models, D3-Cache achieves 2.6x to 3.8x speedups with high fidelity to base model outputs and negligible memory overhead.
AI.conclusion: Forecasting scheduler velocities with DMD provides a simple, generalizable, training-free way to accelerate diffusion sampling.

title: LIFT: Lifting Language-Controlled Image Fusion to Free-Viewpoint 3D Scenes
summary: Multimodal image fusion traditionally generates a single fused image from paired observations at a specific viewpoint, limiting comprehensive scene perception and adaptability to diverse perceptual objectives. To overcome these limitations, we present LIFT, a novel framework for our proposed language-controlled 3D image fusion (L3D-IF) paradigm that extends multimodal image fusion from 2D images to free-viewpoint 3D scenes, enabling language-guided fusion tailored to diverse perceptual objectives. First, LIFT formulates Semantic Modality Binding (SMB), which interprets language instructions to identify semantic targets and their associated modality preferences and grounds these targets in corresponding regions of a shared Gaussian scene, establishing persistent semantic-to-spatial correspondences for consistent fusion control across viewpoints. Second, Language-Conditioned Gaussian Appearance (LCGA) is developed to achieve scene-wide multimodal appearance modeling by combining adaptive multimodal blending with language- and viewpoint-conditioned appearance refinement, enabling spatially adaptive realization of diverse fusion appearances while preserving source fidelity at pure-modality endpoints. Finally, we construct a Multi-View Language-Supervision (MVLS) dataset that associates language instructions and calibrated viewpoints with modulated fused images, providing effective supervision for learning instruction-dependent fusion from finite multi-view observations. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LIFT achieves coherent multimodal fusion across continuous viewpoints, accurate semantic target localization, and consistent regional fusion control under diverse language instructions.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces LIFT, a framework for language-controlled 3D image fusion (L3D-IF) that extends multimodal image fusion from 2D views to free-viewpoint 3D Gaussian scenes.
AI.motivation: Traditional multimodal image fusion produces a single 2D fused image from a fixed viewpoint, limiting 3D scene perception and flexible adaptation to diverse user goals.
AI.method: LIFT uses Semantic Modality Binding (SMB) to ground language-specified targets and modality preferences in a shared 3D Gaussian scene, Language-Conditioned Gaussian Appearance (LCGA) for spatially adaptive multimodal blending, and a new Multi-View Language-Supervision (MVLS) dataset.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show that LIFT achieves coherent multimodal fusion across continuous viewpoints, accurate semantic target localization, and consistent regional fusion control under diverse language instructions.
AI.conclusion: LIFT establishes a practical paradigm for instruction-guided, free-viewpoint 3D multimodal scene fusion.

title: Slide2PPT: Native PowerPoint Reconstruction with Localization-Guided Refinement
summary: Image-to-slide reconstruction must recover both visual appearance and native object structure for subsequent editing. Yet visually faithful charts and tables may lack editable series and cells, and direct code generation couples content prediction to rendering implementation. We present Slide2PPT, a model-agnostic, training-free framework that equips both open- and closed-source vision-language models with native PowerPoint reconstruction capabilities. Through a unified typed interface, the model predicts object records while a fixed renderer materializes their native properties, enabling integration with different backbones without task-specific training or architectural changes. Localization-guided refinement then connects visual discrepancies to object records for correction. Regional updates preserve unselected records, while whole-slide updates address cross-region relationships. Record refinement and targeted object editing support structural and attribute-level changes, with rendered feedback governing iterative acceptance. To evaluate this framework across diverse reconstruction demands, we introduce Slide2PPT-Bench, covering controlled elements, real slides, and scientific figures. Evaluation separately measures file production, rendered agreement, and native-object availability. Experiments across open- and closed-source backbones demonstrate substantially more reliable PPTX generation than direct code generation, improved layout and text recovery on scientific figures, and native chart and table interfaces beyond geometric primitives.

AI.tldr: This paper presents Slide2PPT, a training-free framework for reconstructing native, editable PowerPoint slides from images, along with the Slide2PPT-Bench evaluation suite.
AI.motivation: Direct code generation for image-to-slide reconstruction couples content prediction to rendering and often produces charts or tables that lack native editable series and cells.
AI.method: Slide2PPT uses a unified typed interface where VLMs predict object records materialized by a fixed renderer, followed by localization-guided refinement that updates regional or whole-slide records using rendered visual feedback.
AI.result: On Slide2PPT-Bench (covering controlled elements, real slides, and scientific figures), Slide2PPT outperforms direct code generation in PPTX reliability, scientific figure layout/text recovery, and native chart and table editability across open- and closed-source backbones.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling typed object prediction from rendering with localization-guided refinement enables reliable native slide reconstruction.

title: Calibrate in Context: Efficient Data-Free Quantization from Small Synthetic Pools
comment: 21 pages, 5 main figures. Supplementary material included
summary: We enable accurate low-bit recovery from small synthetic pools by improving both image synthesis and student preparation. A grid with lower local response error can incur greater error in the student's block context. Functional Grid Calibration (FGC) selects activation scales and integer offsets against full-precision responses constructed from the student's current block input. With weights fixed during calibration, FGC evaluates candidates only at their consuming operators, bringing block context to calibration at nearly local-scoring cost. For DeiT and ViT, progressive inversion updates the same images through increasingly deep teacher prefixes. With 1,000 images, the complete pipeline exceeds MimiQ's reported accuracy in all 18 W4A4/W5A5 settings across nine backbones. With 256 images, DeiT-S and ViT-S reach 68.20% and 66.90% ImageNet top-1 accuracy at W4A4 in 26-27 minutes on one RTX 5090. The pipeline outperforms strengthened 1K-image MimiQ by 13.03 and 24.36 percentage points at lower preparation cost and the same recovery-update count. The same low-budget checkpoints retain their advantage on ImageNetV2.

AI.tldr: This paper improves low-bit data-free quantization from small synthetic image pools using Functional Grid Calibration (FGC) and progressive inversion for vision transformers.
AI.motivation: Quantization grids with low local response error can still incur high error in the student's block context, degrading data-free quantization when only small synthetic pools are available.
AI.method: FGC selects activation scales and integer offsets against full-precision responses from the student's current block input by evaluating candidates only at consuming operators, while progressive inversion updates DeiT and ViT images through increasingly deep teacher prefixes.
AI.result: With 1,000 images, the pipeline beats MimiQ across all 18 W4A4/W5A5 settings on nine backbones; with 256 images, DeiT-S and ViT-S reach 68.20% and 66.90% ImageNet top-1 accuracy at W4A4 in 26-27 minutes on one RTX 5090, outperforming 1K-image MimiQ by 13.03 and 24.36 percentage points and retaining gains on ImageNetV2.
AI.conclusion: Block-context-aware grid calibration and progressive inversion enable fast, accurate data-free quantization from small synthetic pools.

title: SkillLens: Action-Guided Dense Visual Dynamics for Proficiency Estimation
comment: 6 pages, 4 figures, 6 tables, Project page: this https URL
summary: Human proficiency estimation is challenging because skill is a high-level and often subjective property that is not captured by action identity alone. Existing approaches leverage multimodal observations such as ego-exo video, gaze, pose, and inertial signals, but the gap between sensor-level evidence and abstract proficiency labels remains difficult to bridge. We present SkillLens, a proficiency estimation framework that uses atomic action descriptions as temporal guidance, rather than direct semantic supervision, to localize proficiency-relevant windows for dense visual-dynamics extraction. Each window is summarized into an action-dynamics feature and scored by a high-low prototype margin against higher- and lower-proficiency executions from the same activity-action category. Fusing these ego/exo PDM cues with a global ego-exo-gaze baseline through CORAL ordinal calibration, our method achieves 0.542 accuracy on Ego-Exo4D. Our project page is available at this https URL

AI.tldr: This paper introduces SkillLens, a proficiency estimation framework that uses atomic action descriptions as temporal guidance to extract dense visual dynamics for skill scoring.
AI.motivation: Human skill is a high-level property not captured by action identity alone, making it hard to bridge sensor-level multimodal observations and abstract proficiency labels.
AI.method: SkillLens uses atomic action descriptions to localize proficiency-relevant windows, summarizes each into an action-dynamics feature scored by a high-low prototype margin within the same activity-action category, and fuses ego/exo cues with a global ego-exo-gaze baseline via CORAL ordinal calibration.
AI.result: On the Ego-Exo4D benchmark, SkillLens achieves 0.542 proficiency estimation accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Using atomic actions as temporal guidance for prototype-margin scoring effectively bridges low-level visual dynamics and high-level skill assessment.

title: Interpreting DeepStack-Style Vision-Language Models: Do Input or Deeper-Layer Visual Tokens Drive Answers?
comment: Includes the supplementary material. Code and numerical results: this https URL
summary: DeepStack-style vision-language models feed visual tokens to the language model at its input, and again at deeper layers. We call these the main entry and the later entries. What do the later entries add when the model already has the image? We give the entries versions that differ in one object's color and see which one the answer follows. On photographs, the original DeepStack follows the later entries, while Qwen3-VL-8B/32B follow the main entry. Does weakening the main entry give the later features more influence? On synthetic images, we keep this conflict and reduce color saturation at the main entry only. The unchanged later features gain a stronger effect on the relative scores of the two colors, in all four models, including Granite Vision. This holds even under mild desaturation, when accuracy without the conflict stays at 100%. To test whether later features can also correct errors, we degrade both entries and restore only the later ones. The same blur costs both Qwen models 50 percentage points of accuracy on stripe orientation. The 32B model recovers 48 points and the 8B model only 8. Accuracy with one clean entry predicted which entry each model can lose, and five of six tested predictions held on new GQA attribute questions. With the other entry zeroed, Qwen3-VL-8B loses only 0.3 points on its main entry alone, and DeepStack at most 3.45 points on either entry alone. In split inference on these questions, DeepStack can then send only its main-entry features at higher precision. This takes 49% fewer bytes than all entries at a shared precision, at similar accuracy.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how DeepStack-style vision-language models use visual tokens injected at the input (main entry) versus deeper layers (later entries) through color-conflict and degradation experiments.
AI.motivation: It is unclear what deeper-layer visual token injections contribute when a VLM already receives the image at its input.
AI.method: The authors feed conflicting object-color versions to the main and later entries across four models (including DeepStack, Qwen3-VL-8B/32B, and Granite Vision), test main-entry desaturation and blur restoration, and evaluate split-inference compression.
AI.result: On photographs, DeepStack follows later entries while Qwen3-VL follows the main entry; weakening the main entry increases later-entry influence across all four models, Qwen3-VL-32B recovers 48 of 50 blur-lost points from later entries (vs. 8 for 8B), and DeepStack can send only main-entry features at higher precision using 49% fewer bytes at similar GQA accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Both input and deeper-layer visual entries carry distinct, model-dependent roles that can be exploited for robustness analysis and efficient split inference.

title: SteerTrace: Tracing How Target Attacks Steer World Action Models
summary: World action models (WAMs) predict future videos and actions with one backbone, and their imagined future is often seen as a safety signal. We introduce SteerTrace, a targeted universal attack on WAMs that also traces its effect inside the model. One $\ell_\infty$-bounded (4/255) perturbation per model, shared across frames, tasks, and camera views, pushes the executed action toward an attacker-chosen target. On eight WAMs from four families (FastWAM, Faster-WAM, OpenWAM and LingBot-VA) on LIBERO and RoboTwin, it drives task success close to zero and moves the attacked action toward the target. Same-budget noise and BadWAM produce little action shift in the target direction. We use the signed targeted effect to measure how much of the effect each intervention removes or reproduces. Under the standard attack, restoring future tokens removes 61-94% of the targeted effect in the five models whose action experts attend to them. When the attack is constrained to keep the predicted future close to the clean prediction, the targeted effect can become more dependent on current-frame tokens. In three of these five models, restoring current-frame tokens removes 87-99% of the effect, compared with 9-15% for future tokens. In six models, restoring just 0.36% of the FFN neurons in layers 10-29 of the video expert removes 72-96% of the targeted effect. Residual directions 2-16 hold only 11-18% of the shift energy, yet removing them cancels most of the targeted effect.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces SteerTrace, a universal targeted attack on World Action Models (WAMs), and uses causal interventions to trace how perturbations steer actions inside the model.
AI.motivation: While WAMs are increasingly used in robotics, how adversarial perturbations propagate through their coupled video and action experts to steer executed actions is not understood.
AI.method: SteerTrace crafts a single l_infinity-bounded (4/255) perturbation per model shared across frames, tasks, and views, and measures signed targeted effects when restoring future tokens, current-frame tokens, FFN neurons, or residual directions.
AI.result: Across eight WAMs from four families on LIBERO and RoboTwin, SteerTrace drives task success near zero and shifts actions toward the target; restoring future tokens removes 61-94% of the effect in standard attacks, whereas under future-preserving constraints, restoring current-frame tokens removes 87-99% in three models, and restoring 0.36% of FFN neurons in video layers 10-29 removes 72-96% in six models.
AI.conclusion: Targeted attacks on WAMs operate through sparse, traceable internal pathways that shift between future and current-frame tokens depending on attack constraints.

title: DACA: Dual-Anchor Collaborative Agent for Zero-Shot 3D Visual Grounding
summary: 3D visual grounding (3D-VG) is a task that bridges the natural language and 3D space, serving as a foundational capability for embodied intelligence and human-computer interaction. Although recent 3D-VG agents overcome the reliance on pre-processed 3D point clouds, they essentially employ a unidirectional, pipeline-style tool-calling architecture. This architecture separates semantic understanding from geometric reconstruction, leading to error accumulation and an inability to autonomously recover from failures. To address this flaw, this paper proposes the Dual-Anchor Collaborative Agent (DACA), which reinterprets 3D-VG as a semantic-geometric dual-anchor collaborative reasoning paradigm. DACA comprises two complementary specialized tools: the semantic anchor tool holds the visual semantic features of the target and achieves efficient target tracking via optical flow and VLM local verification; the geometric anchor tool holds the 3D spatial geometric features of the target and performs global spatial reasoning via voxelization and multi-keypoint projection. The two components exchange information bidirectionally via a standardized tool call protocol, autonomously deciding on the next perception-action step to form a closed-loop optimization. Experiments on the ScanRefer and Nr3D benchmarks demonstrate that zero-shot DACA achieves an overall Acc@0.25 of 73.6\% on ScanRefer and 70.4\% overall accuracy on Nr3D, far surpassing the latest zero-shot 3D-VG methods. The code and models are available at this https URL

AI.tldr: This paper proposes DACA, a Dual-Anchor Collaborative Agent for zero-shot 3D visual grounding that couples semantic and geometric reasoning in a closed loop.
AI.motivation: Existing zero-shot 3D visual grounding agents use unidirectional pipelines that separate semantic understanding from geometric reconstruction, causing error accumulation and no recovery from failures.
AI.method: DACA pairs a semantic anchor tool (using optical flow and VLM local verification) with a geometric anchor tool (using voxelization and multi-keypoint projection) that exchange information bidirectionally via a standardized tool-call protocol.
AI.result: On ScanRefer and Nr3D, zero-shot DACA achieves 73.6% overall Acc@0.25 and 70.4% overall accuracy, respectively, substantially outperforming prior zero-shot 3D-VG methods.
AI.conclusion: Bidirectional collaboration between semantic and geometric anchors enables self-correcting, high-accuracy zero-shot 3D visual grounding.

title: Verifying Before Enhancing: Target Evidence Chain Verification for Infrared Small Target Detection
summary: Infrared small target detection is essential for early warning, surveillance, remote sensing, and space-based target perception. However, infrared small targets are typically tiny, weakly textured, and boundary-blurred, making them difficult to distinguish from complex backgrounds. Moreover, target-like background structures can produce salient responses across multiple scales, making response strength alone insufficient for reliable target discrimination. To address this challenge, we propose VBE-UNet, a Target Evidence Chain Verification Network that assesses candidate reliability beyond response magnitude through complementary evidence cues. Specifically, counterfactual background explanation models local target evidence, while joint evidence verification integrates cross-scale support and perturbation-based contribution verification to guide feature recomposition. The resulting reliability estimates guide selective feature refinement, promoting target-relevant responses while reducing unsupported background activations. Extensive experiments on IRSTD-1K, NUDT-SIRST, and NUAA-SIRST demonstrate that VBE-UNet achieves superior detection accuracy and lower false-alarm rates compared with state-of-the-art methods. Ablation studies and evidence reliability analysis further validate the effectiveness of the proposed verification framework.

AI.tldr: This paper presents VBE-UNet, an infrared small target detection network that verifies candidate target evidence before selective feature enhancement.
AI.motivation: Infrared small targets are tiny and weakly textured, while background clutter can trigger strong multi-scale responses, making response magnitude alone unreliable for target discrimination.
AI.method: VBE-UNet uses counterfactual background explanation for local target evidence and joint evidence verification (combining cross-scale support and perturbation-based contribution) to estimate candidate reliability and guide selective feature refinement.
AI.result: On IRSTD-1K, NUDT-SIRST, and NUAA-SIRST, VBE-UNet achieves superior detection accuracy and lower false-alarm rates compared to state-of-the-art methods, supported by ablations and reliability analyses.
AI.conclusion: Verifying candidate evidence chains before feature refinement reduces false alarms and improves infrared small target detection.

title: What's in the box? Revealing Object Layouts Inside Opaque Boxes via Contactless Vibration Excitation and Sensing
summary: Can we reveal what is inside an opaque box by observing its surface vibrations? Objects inside a box alter its mechanical response, providing cues about their hidden locations. We introduce a method that uses these cues to predict a box's 2D occupancy layout entirely remotely. A nearby speaker excites vibrations, which we measure on one visible wall using a grid of laser points and a camera measuring each point's speckle-pattern shifts. Our model, WhisperBox, learns to encode these vibrations into a latent representation and decode it into an occupancy map of the box's contents. The method requires no physical contact to excite or sense vibrations. We demonstrate layout recovery across various boxes and single- and multiple-object scenes, with generalization to unseen object instances, positions, orientations, and weights, as well as changes in laser placement and excitation source. Our analysis reveals that informative frequency bands need not coincide with the box's resonances and that the learned latent space captures object placement and supports arithmetic operations. These results demonstrate the potential of remote vibration sensing to infer spatial layouts hidden from view.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces WhisperBox, a contactless system that infers 2D object layouts inside opaque boxes by exciting surface vibrations with sound and sensing laser speckle shifts.
AI.motivation: Seeing inside opaque containers without physical contact or penetrating radiation is challenging, yet internal objects alter a box's mechanical vibration response.
AI.method: A speaker excites box vibrations while a camera tracks speckle-pattern shifts across a grid of laser points on one visible wall; WhisperBox encodes these vibrations into a latent space and decodes a 2D occupancy map.
AI.result: WhisperBox recovers single- and multi-object layouts across different boxes and generalizes to unseen object instances, positions, orientations, weights, laser placements, and excitation sources, with a latent space that supports arithmetic operations.
AI.conclusion: Remote acoustic excitation and laser-speckle sensing provide a viable non-contact modality for inferring hidden spatial layouts.

title: CGM: Chaos-Guided Graph Attention and Expert Routing for Autism Stereotypy Detection
summary: Skeleton graph attention for autism video analysis weights joints by content alone, giving an erratic wrist the same standing as a still one. Stereotypy, however, is defined by how unpredictably movement unfolds rather than how much of it occurs: in our cohort, every amplitude-based kinematic descriptor falls in stereotyped clips, while windowed Sample Entropy of angular velocity alone rises (Hedges' g = +1.05). We compute this irregularity as a per-joint, per-frame tensor that structurally drives computation. The proposed chaos-guided graph attention and mixture-of-experts model (CGM) couples two mechanisms. First, a learned pairwise term added to the graph-attention logit concentrates attention on irregular joints and re-ranks the remaining edge weight toward jointly irregular pairs; its unconstrained coefficient neither vanishes nor inverts, and zeroing the tensor realigns attention in 94% of clips. Second, a gate conditioned on the same signal routes each frame to two of four experts, whose weights track frame-level irregularity. Under subject-grouped five-fold cross-validation on 116 clips, CGM reaches 0.930 balanced accuracy, exceeding the graph-attention baseline by +0.187; the component ordering replicates on the public MMASD dataset, and on held-out Panoptic Studio sessions, CGM keeps 0.86 specificity without retraining, against at most 0.35 for chaos-free baselines. In ablation, routing without irregularity yields no reliable gain, whereas chaos modulation alone contributes +0.132. A severity index from the same tensor reaches 0.87 split-half reliability, separates the cohorts with Hedges' g = +1.08, and stays consistent within children across therapy recordings, supporting video-only monitoring of stereotypy during intervention.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes CGM, a chaos-guided graph attention and mixture-of-experts model for autism stereotypy detection from skeleton video.
AI.motivation: Standard skeleton graph attention weights joints by content alone, whereas stereotypy is characterized by movement irregularity rather than amplitude.
AI.method: CGM computes a per-joint, per-frame tensor of windowed Sample Entropy of angular velocity to both modulate graph-attention logits toward irregular joints/pairs and route each frame to two of four experts.
AI.result: Under subject-grouped five-fold cross-validation on 116 clips, CGM reaches 0.930 balanced accuracy (+0.187 over graph-attention baseline), replicates on MMASD, retains 0.86 specificity without retraining on held-out Panoptic Studio sessions (vs. at most 0.35 for chaos-free baselines), and yields a severity index with 0.87 split-half reliability (Hedges' g = +1.08).
AI.conclusion: Explicitly driving graph attention and expert routing with movement irregularity enables accurate, generalizable, video-only stereotypy detection and severity monitoring.

title: Towards High-Fidelity Learned Video Compression
summary: Professional video workflows operate at qualities that learned video codecs do not reach. We measure how much of a professional quality range a codec covers, from the lowest quality of the standard test conditions, VVC at QP 37, to the highest 4:2:2 grade of the production codec ProRes. To compare inter-frame coding alone, every codec receives original frames as references at the intra positions. On 10-bit YCbCr 4:2:2 test sequences, four recent learned codecs cover 24 to 38% of this range. Their encoders are feed-forward networks with a fixed latent capacity, the number of latent values per sample, of at most 0.25, and removing their quantization raises the quality by at most 1 dB. We propose a learned inter-frame codec whose encoder searches, as the encoders of conventional codecs do. It searches block motion, which a learned network refines, and it searches among learned block transforms whose latent capacity ranges up to 1, selecting the partition, the skip decisions, and the quantized coefficients by a rate-distortion cost. Our codec reaches the upper end of the range on all six sequences. With all residual blocks fixed to 16x16, whose latent capacity is 0.25, the same codec covers 55% of the range, with or without quantization.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a search-based learned inter-frame video codec that bridges the quality gap between existing learned codecs and professional production formats like ProRes.
AI.motivation: On 10-bit YCbCr 4:2:2 sequences, recent feed-forward learned video codecs cover only 24-38% of the professional quality range (VVC QP 37 to ProRes) due to fixed latent capacity (at most 0.25 values per sample).
AI.method: Unlike feed-forward encoders, the proposed codec's encoder searches block motion (refined by a network) and selects among learned block transforms with latent capacity up to 1, choosing partitions, skip decisions, and quantized coefficients via rate-distortion cost.
AI.result: The proposed codec reaches the upper end of the professional quality range on all six 10-bit 4:2:2 test sequences, and even with blocks fixed to 16x16 (0.25 capacity) it covers 55% of the range.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating encoder-side rate-distortion search over variable-capacity learned transforms unlocks high-fidelity learned video compression for professional workflows.

title: SAM 3 Sees More Than It Detects: Promptable Concept Maps Beyond Categories
summary: Promptable segmenters answer what a thing is. Dense prediction tasks also ask class-agnostic questions, such as what stands out or hides, how light is blocked, transmitted or reflected, and where structure lies. Robots, surveillance systems and image editors build on their answers. We study promptable concept maps (PCM), which extend SAM 3's promptable concept segmentation from noun instances to maps of concepts named by short noun phrases such as `"transparent object", with "none" as an answer. PCM-Bench groups the standard test sets of seven such tasks by the question they ask. On it, we find that SAM 3 sees more than it detects. Its semantic path responds to many of these concepts, yet a low image-level presence score can block every detection of its instance path. We present UNVEIL, which trains a copy of SAM 3's semantic path for these maps, with LoRA on copies of its last blocks. A separate presence decoder learns from verified negatives whether a concept occurs. With one text phrase per query, UNVEIL maps region concepts such as salient and camouflaged objects, shadows, transparent objects and mirrors. The same weights map thin structures such as edges and skeletons as well as object categories. Run next to SAM 3, it leaves SAM 3's own outputs unchanged. On each of the seven tasks, UNVEIL reaches the highest score among the compared promptable models, including SAM 3's official fine-tuning and pipelines built on multimodal LLMs. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces UNVEIL and PCM-Bench to extend SAM 3 from noun-instance segmentation to promptable concept maps for class-agnostic dense prediction tasks.
AI.motivation: SAM 3's semantic path responds to class-agnostic concepts (e.g., shadows, camouflage, transparency), but low image-level presence scores often block its instance path from detecting them.
AI.method: UNVEIL trains a LoRA-adapted copy of SAM 3's semantic path alongside a separate presence decoder trained with verified negatives to map short noun-phrase concepts, leaving SAM 3's original weights and outputs intact.
AI.result: Across all seven tasks in PCM-Bench (covering salient/camouflaged objects, shadows, transparent objects, mirrors, edges, and skeletons), UNVEIL achieves the highest score among promptable models, outperforming official SAM 3 fine-tuning and MLLM pipelines.
AI.conclusion: Unlocking SAM 3's semantic path with a dedicated presence decoder enables unified, promptable concept mapping beyond object categories.

title: AdaptReg: Skip-level FiLM Adapter for Task-Specific Adaptation of a Frozen Registration Foundation Model
comment: 9 pages, 2 figures, 3 tables. Paper for the Learn2Reg 2026 PSMAReg challenge (PSMA-PET/CT longitudinal registration), 4th place among 16 teams on the hidden test set
summary: Longitudinal PSMA-PET/CT registration is a key step in assessing treatment response in prostate cancer, and it requires more than generic alignment accuracy: the deformation must preserve lesion volume, so that measured changes in metabolic tumor volume (MTV) and total lesion glycolysis (TLG) reflect treatment response rather than registration artifacts. We propose AdaptReg, which adapts a frozen registration foundation model to such task-specific requirements through a lightweight trainable adapter branch with identity-preserving initialization. Keeping uniGradICON fully frozen, we apply FiLM-style per-voxel affine modulation ($\gamma$, $\beta$) to its decoder skip connections; the modulation is generated from anatomical semantic features of a frozen TotalSegmentator encoder and supervised by a lesion volume-preservation loss. On the official Codabench validation set (20 pairs), AdaptReg achieves DSC 0.7585, HD95 6.33 mm, MTV/TLG errors of 1.68%/2.11%, and 0.0022% non-diffeomorphic voxels, improving on the uniGradICON + instance optimization baseline by $+0.05$ DSC and reducing the MTV/TLG errors by 70.9%/67.7%. On the hidden official test set (160 pairs), AdaptReg achieves CT DSC 0.816, PET DSC 0.598, and MTV/TLG errors of 4.02%/3.46%, ranking fourth among 16 teams in the final PSMAReg evaluation. Code: this https URL

AI.tldr: This paper proposes AdaptReg, a skip-level FiLM adapter that adapts the frozen uniGradICON registration foundation model for lesion-volume-preserving longitudinal PSMA-PET/CT registration.
AI.motivation: Longitudinal PSMA-PET/CT registration for prostate cancer treatment assessment requires preserving lesion volume so that metabolic tumor volume (MTV) and total lesion glycolysis (TLG) reflect true response rather than registration artifacts.
AI.method: AdaptReg keeps uniGradICON frozen and applies identity-initialized FiLM affine modulation to its decoder skip connections, driven by anatomical features from a frozen TotalSegmentator encoder and supervised by a lesion volume-preservation loss.
AI.result: On the Codabench validation set (20 pairs), AdaptReg achieves 0.7585 DSC, 6.33 mm HD95, and 1.68%/2.11% MTV/TLG errors (reducing errors by 70.9%/67.7% over uniGradICON + instance optimization); on the 160-pair hidden test set, it reaches 0.816 CT DSC and 0.598 PET DSC, ranking fourth among 16 teams.
AI.conclusion: Lightweight skip-level FiLM adaptation with anatomical priors effectively specializes frozen registration foundation models for clinical volume-preserving tasks.

title: Driver Gaze Target Identification via Gaze Estimation and Structured Driving Scene Understanding
summary: Identifying a driver's gaze target provides object-level information for visual attention monitoring in intelligent vehicles. Gaze-zone classification and continuous attention localization provide limited information about the identity of the attended scene target. This paper proposes a modular framework that identifies object- or region-level gaze targets from synchronized in-cabin driver images and forward-view road images. The framework comprises four components: MFGaze, which combines a Vision Transformer pretrained with a masked autoencoder (MAE) and head-pose conditioning through feature-wise linear modulation (FiLM); panoptic scene understanding, which constructs a structured candidate set; polynomial ridge regression, which maps gaze features to 2D scene-image coordinates through individualized calibration; and entropy-driven target inference, which adaptively fuses boundary-distance geometry with class-level semantic priors. Experiments evaluate the framework using three public gaze datasets, a laboratory test using Cityscapes road scenes and self-collected gaze data, and the Look Both Ways (LBW) dataset. The complete framework achieves an overall Top-1 gaze target identification accuracy of 96.27% in the laboratory experiment. After sequence-specific calibration, it achieves Top-1 accuracies of 79.92% for task-relevant objects and 85.58% for the road class on LBW. MFGaze achieves the lowest mean angular errors among the compared methods, with 4.06$^\circ$, 4.23$^\circ$, and 10.52$^\circ$ on MPIIFaceGaze, ETH-XGaze, and Gaze360, respectively, and demonstrates strong cross-dataset generalization. Sensitivity analyses show stable performance under hyperparameter perturbations. These results support the framework as a source of object-level gaze information for driver monitoring.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a modular framework for identifying object- and region-level driver gaze targets from synchronized in-cabin and forward-view road images.
AI.motivation: Existing gaze-zone classification and continuous attention localization methods do not identify the specific scene object a driver is looking at.
AI.method: The framework combines MFGaze (an MAE-pretrained ViT with FiLM head-pose conditioning), panoptic scene understanding for candidate objects, polynomial ridge regression for individualized 2D calibration, and entropy-driven inference fusing boundary distance with semantic priors.
AI.result: The framework achieves 96.27% Top-1 gaze target identification accuracy in laboratory tests, 79.92% (task-relevant objects) and 85.58% (road) on Look Both Ways after calibration, and lowest mean angular errors on MPIIFaceGaze (4.06 deg), ETH-XGaze (4.23 deg), and Gaze360 (10.52 deg).
AI.conclusion: Combining calibrated gaze estimation with panoptic scene priors provides accurate object-level driver attention monitoring.

title: Suppressing the Shortcut Hidden Behind the Gains of VideoLLM Fine-Tuning
summary: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is the stage in which Video Large Language Models (VideoLLMs) advance their capability to reason over video. However, the VideoLLM also learns to answer from textual regularities of its training data, a shortcut that bypasses the video. The regularities behind the shortcut are hard to define at the data level, and the shortcut forms regardless of training epoch, data size, or backbone. The shortcut is hidden behind a rise in accuracy within the training distribution, yet it is not required for the rise and even costs SFT the gain the video offers under distribution shift. We therefore propose Video-Evidence Training via Orthogonal projection (VETO), which intervenes on the fine-tuning update where the shortcut is written rather than on the data. VETO calibrates the subspace that the text alone occupies in the activations of the base model and projects the update onto its orthogonal complement. The VideoLLM is thus left to ground its answer in the full input, with the shortcut suppressed as it forms and never defined. Across seven VideoLLMs, VETO preserves the gain of SFT on the training distribution and suppresses the shortcut. On six benchmarks under shift it gains more than SFT and answers from the full input rather than the shortcut. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes VETO, a fine-tuning intervention that suppresses textual shortcuts in VideoLLMs by projecting parameter updates orthogonally to the text-only activation subspace.
AI.motivation: During supervised fine-tuning (SFT), VideoLLMs learn hidden textual shortcuts that boost in-distribution accuracy but hurt generalization under distribution shift, and these shortcuts are hard to define at the data level.
AI.method: Video-Evidence Training via Orthogonal projection (VETO) calibrates the subspace occupied by text-only inputs in the base model's activations and projects SFT updates onto its orthogonal complement.
AI.result: Across seven VideoLLMs, VETO preserves SFT's in-distribution gains while suppressing shortcuts, and outperforms SFT across six benchmarks under distribution shift by grounding answers in the full multimodal input.
AI.conclusion: Orthogonalizing fine-tuning updates against text-only subspaces prevents shortcut learning in VideoLLMs without requiring data-level shortcut definitions.

title: GeoPillars: A Large-Kernel Pillar Detector for Single-Sweep LiDAR Under Point Sparsity, and a Decomposition of Its Gain
summary: GeoPillars is a pillar-based 3D detector for single-sweep LiDAR under a hard budget of eight points per 0.4 m pillar, a budget that discards 46.6% of in-range points. It adds geometric pillar features, grouped vector attention within each pillar, a learned absolute positional prior on the bird's-eye-view (BEV) grid, a large-kernel backbone, auxiliary surface-normal supervision and a full-resolution detection head. Trained on 123k synthetic CARLA scans and evaluated on cars, it reaches 81.33 BEV AP@0.7, 13.76 points above CenterPoint at the same input budget and 1.91 points above CenterPoint at its native, denser budget. These are in-distribution figures, because the validation split is per-frame rather than scene-disjoint. A rung-by-rung decomposition shows that the new components explain little of the gain. Raising the detection-head resolution alone recovers 10.19 of the 13.76 points, the joint change of encoder, backbone, neck and positional prior adds 3.37, and the normal-supervision branch adds 0.20, which is within run-to-run variation. With heading reversals folded out, orientation error is similar for all seven models, although GeoPillars reverses headings about half as often as a resolution-matched baseline. It is also the slowest of the seven models. Evaluated zero-shot on 6,743 real nuScenes keyframes, no model transfers, and each retains 3.7% to 12.2% of its CARLA accuracy. A collection defect left LiDAR intensity constant, so every model learned from geometry alone. Code and checkpoints are publicly available.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces GeoPillars, a single-sweep LiDAR 3D detector for sparse point budgets, and decomposes its accuracy gains to show that detection-head resolution drives most of the improvement.
AI.motivation: Under a strict budget of eight points per 0.4 m pillar (discarding 46.6% of points), pillar-based 3D detectors lose accuracy, and it is unclear which architectural additions actually matter.
AI.method: GeoPillars combines geometric pillar features, grouped vector attention, a learned BEV positional prior, a large-kernel backbone, auxiliary surface-normal supervision, and a full-resolution detection head, evaluated via rung-by-rung ablation on 123k CARLA scans and zero-shot on nuScenes.
AI.result: On CARLA cars, GeoPillars reaches 81.33 BEV AP@0.7 (+13.76 over CenterPoint at the same budget), but raising head resolution alone accounts for 10.19 of the 13.76 points; GeoPillars is the slowest of seven tested models, and all models retain only 3.7% to 12.2% of CARLA accuracy zero-shot on nuScenes.
AI.conclusion: Full-resolution detection heads dominate accuracy gains under sparse pillar budgets, while complex architectural additions add limited benefit and sim-to-real transfer remains poor.

title: Fast and Accurate Body Estimation in Pixels, World Space and Scenes
comment: 28 pages, 9 pages of main text. 16 figures
summary: We present FAB (Fast and Accurate Body estimation), a human body estimator that jointly improves inference efficiency and body-recovery fidelity. Rather than predicting only parametric mesh-model parameters, FAB directly predicts human skeleton joints and dense surface points. In images, it predicts dense 2D and 3D body points alongside a parametric Momentum Human Rig (MHR) head, then fits SMPL in one learned pass followed by two Gauss-Newton steps. Its ViT-L student, FAB-L, distilled from a fine-tuned SAM 3D Body, runs in real time for one person on an RTX 4070 Ti SUPER, from detection to a fitted body, at 4.6x the speed of SAM 3D Body's eager-PyTorch body-only path, while improving accuracy on most camera-space benchmarks. The same network predicts heel, toe, hand, and knee contacts, which connect the body to the scene. FAB also estimates world-space motion, fuses static-scene depth around the visible person, and aligns body and scene using predicted contacts. For human-to-humanoid real-to-sim transfer, an in-model G1 head and FAB-Retarget, a motion-level retargeter that reads dense points or the fitted mesh, map motion to a Unitree G1. FAB-Retarget produces references that follow the person more closely than specialized retargeters including SOMA, GMR, UMR, and OmniRetarget, and substantially more closely than Fast SAM 3D Body retargeted with our sequence IK. Project page: this https URL.

AI.tldr: This paper presents FAB, a fast human body estimator that predicts skeleton joints, dense surface points, and scene contacts for camera-space, world-space, and humanoid-retargeting tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing parametric mesh estimators can be slow or lack direct dense surface and contact predictions needed for scene alignment and robot retargeting.
AI.method: FAB predicts dense 2D/3D body points, a Momentum Human Rig (MHR) head, and heel/toe/hand/knee contacts, fitting SMPL in one learned pass plus two Gauss-Newton steps; FAB-L (ViT-L) is distilled from fine-tuned SAM 3D Body, paired with depth fusion and an in-model Unitree G1 head / FAB-Retarget.
AI.result: FAB-L runs in real time on an RTX 4070 Ti SUPER at 4.6x the speed of SAM 3D Body's eager-PyTorch path while improving accuracy on most camera-space benchmarks, and FAB-Retarget tracks human motion more closely than SOMA, GMR, UMR, and OmniRetarget.
AI.conclusion: Jointly predicting dense surface points, contacts, and fast parametric fits enables real-time, scene-grounded body estimation and accurate human-to-humanoid retargeting.

title: World-delta: Continually Integrating Observations for Incremental 3D Scene Generation
summary: Existing 3D generation methods synthesize visually compelling scenes from fixed inputs, yet struggle to continually expand and revise a 3D world as new observations arrive. Iterative approaches often fuse real observations and generated content into a single representation, treating generated content as established structure rather than revisable predictions. Consequently, early generation errors can persist and accumulate despite new evidence. We propose World-delta, an incremental 3D scene generation framework combining uncertainty-aware persistent world modeling with delta-guided diffusion for continual scene expansion and correction. Our framework comprises three components: 1) Visual Evidence Encoding integrates geometric and semantic cues from incoming images into unified world tokens. 2) Observation-Calibrated World Modeling maintains a persistent latent world state that distinguishes observation-supported content from provisional completion hypotheses. New evidence drives selective world deltas to revise conflicting hypotheses while preserving well-supported content. 3) Incremental World Diffusion Generation uses delta-derived masks to restrict diffusion to regions requiring updates, freezing unchanged regions. Only affected 3D chunks are decoded and integrated into the existing scene. Together, these components enable continual world expansion and revision while reducing redundant generation and preserving scene consistency. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of World-delta in incremental 3D scene generation, observation-driven correction, scene consistency, and update efficiency over successive scene updates.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes World-delta, an incremental 3D scene generation framework that separates observed evidence from provisional hypotheses to continually expand and correct 3D worlds.
AI.motivation: Iterative 3D generation methods fuse observations and generated content into one representation, treating generated regions as fixed truth and causing early errors to accumulate as new views arrive.
AI.method: World-delta encodes incoming images into world tokens, maintains an observation-calibrated latent world state that computes selective world deltas for conflicting hypotheses, and uses delta-derived masks to restrict diffusion and 3D chunk decoding to affected regions.
AI.result: Experiments demonstrate improved incremental 3D scene generation, observation-driven error correction, scene consistency, and update efficiency over successive updates.
AI.conclusion: Distinguishing observation-supported content from revisable hypotheses enables consistent, efficient continual 3D scene generation.

title: What Places an Action Boundary? Structure-Aware Attribution for Temporal Action Localization
summary: Temporal action localization (TAL) detectors must identify actions and estimate their temporal boundaries, but localization remains a major source of detection errors. While understanding what determines boundary placement requires faithful attribution of temporal evidence, existing attribution methods have not sufficiently addressed the temporal structure of TAL or the need to tailor attribution to boundary localization. We introduce a structure-aware attribution framework that averages contributions across random evidence-restoration orders following the Shapley-Shubik principle. We make it tractable by using the detector's receptive field to limit which time steps are ordered individually, and by approximating each order with a soft gradient path. For boundary predictions, we further introduce cell-structured restoration orders and boundary-anchored references that selectively remove adjacent evidence. We also adapt faithfulness evaluation to assess the joint effects of contiguous temporal evidence and the direction of boundary displacement. Experiments on THUMOS14 and EPIC-KITCHENS-100 with TriDet and ActionFormer demonstrate improved attribution faithfulness over existing methods. Attribution analysis and controlled interventions further reveal that class-score changes do not reliably track boundary displacement, providing input-level evidence that classification relies on content less informative about boundary placement. Code and evaluation artifacts will be publicly released.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a structure-aware attribution framework for temporal action localization (TAL) that reveals what temporal evidence drives boundary placement.
AI.motivation: Boundary localization is a major source of TAL errors, yet existing attribution methods ignore TAL's temporal structure and fail to isolate boundary-specific evidence.
AI.method: The framework averages contributions over random evidence-restoration orders via the Shapley-Shubik principle, made tractable using the detector's receptive field and soft gradient paths, and introduces cell-structured orders and boundary-anchored references.
AI.result: On THUMOS14 and EPIC-KITCHENS-100 with TriDet and ActionFormer, the method improves attribution faithfulness over baselines and shows that class-score changes do not reliably track boundary displacement.
AI.conclusion: Structure-aware temporal attribution provides faithful explanations of boundary placement and shows that action classification and boundary localization rely on distinct temporal cues.

title: SCCV-6D: Sparse Canonical Coordinate Voting for Holistic Multi-View RGB-D 6D Pose Estimation in Robotic Bin Picking
comment: to appear in Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Winter Conference on Applications of Computer Vision (WACV), 2027
summary: Industrial bin picking requires pose estimates that are accurate under clutter, partial occlusion, and the reflective, texture-less nature of manufactured parts. Most recent approaches to 6D pose estimation follow multi-stage pipelines. These achieve high accuracy, but incur memory and runtime footprints that do not cope with the operational constraints of many real-world industrial deployments. Holistic pipelines estimate poses in a single pass, with cost controlled through indiscriminate subsampling or lowered resolution. Continuing this line, we present SCCV-6D, a fully sparse multi-view RGB-D estimator. We reconstruct the 3D space at millimeter precision, prune background via a staged heatmap mechanism, and predict class, translation offset and rotation at highest resolution for an arbitrary number of objects simultaneously. Rotation is formulated as canonical coordinate voting. Points vote for their canonical object coordinates with an associated confidence, enabling closed-form pose recovery with a symmetry-aware weighted Procrustes solve. Along an in-cluster point recovery induced by offset votes, this removes time-consuming post-processing stages. We reuse the task-supervised attention priors from the heatmap formulation for a novel attention-gated distillation objective that reweights teacher-student feature alignment. On the IPD test split we report competitive 0.826 AP at 1.13 s per scene, significantly faster than the leading entries. On MV-YCB our approach reaches 96.1 ADD-S, and remains competitive even on the densely packed bins of ROBI.

AI.tldr: This paper presents SCCV-6D, a fully sparse multi-view RGB-D 6D pose estimator for robotic bin picking that uses canonical coordinate voting and attention-gated distillation.
AI.motivation: Multi-stage 6D pose pipelines are too slow and memory-heavy for industrial bin picking, while single-pass holistic methods often sacrifice resolution through indiscriminate subsampling.
AI.method: SCCV-6D reconstructs 3D space at millimeter precision, prunes background via staged heatmaps, predicts class, offset, and canonical object coordinates for all objects simultaneously, recovers poses in closed form via symmetry-aware weighted Procrustes, and uses heatmap attention priors for teacher-student distillation.
AI.result: SCCV-6D achieves 0.826 AP at 1.13 s per scene on the IPD test split, 96.1 ADD-S on MV-YCB, and competitive performance on densely packed ROBI bins.
AI.conclusion: Sparse canonical coordinate voting with closed-form Procrustes solving enables fast, high-resolution multi-object 6D pose estimation in cluttered industrial bins.

title: Limits of local curvature for constructing search subspaces in segmentation models
comment: 10 pages, 3 figures, 4 tables. Includes an appendix
summary: We examine how well subspaces constructed from local curvature represent the change in the gradient update field after a finite step in semantic segmentation models. The local response is the action of the curvature operator on the actual input displacement. In a study of 50 images and two models, we measure the ratio of the loss increase attained in a fixed subspace to that attained in the full space. This ratio decreases as the search radius increases. On ten images from the same sample, we compare the one-dimensional subspace spanned by the initial gradient with two rank-16 subspaces for both models. The two equal-rank subspaces are assessed at the same initial states, using the same actual steps and measured vectors. Adding generalised Gauss-Newton directions to the initial gradient reduces the mean relative error in representing the field change from 0.922 to 0.874 for the first model and from 0.819 to 0.763 for the second. At the same rank, including the response direction for the initial gradient nearly eliminates the error in representing the local response. The mean error in representing the field change does not decrease. A decomposition with fixed pixel weights shows that the finite-step remainder is comparable in norm to the field change and makes the largest diagonal contribution to the squared projection error of the field after the step. Evaluation of a search subspace should measure how accurately it represents the field change and the local response.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes how well local-curvature subspaces represent finite-step gradient field changes in semantic segmentation models.
AI.motivation: Optimization and adversarial methods often build search subspaces from local curvature, but their accuracy over finite steps in segmentation models is unclear.
AI.method: Across 50 images and two segmentation models, the authors measure loss-increase ratios in fixed subspaces versus full space, and on 10 images compare a 1D initial-gradient subspace against two rank-16 subspaces (adding generalized Gauss-Newton directions or the initial-gradient response direction).
AI.result: Loss-increase ratios decrease with larger search radii; adding generalized Gauss-Newton directions lowers mean field-change representation error from 0.922 to 0.874 and 0.819 to 0.763, whereas adding the response direction eliminates local-response error without reducing field-change error, as the finite-step remainder dominates projection error.
AI.conclusion: Search subspaces should be evaluated on both finite-step field-change representation and local response rather than local curvature alone.

title: Fusing Multimodal CNN Features with Structurally-Masked Transformers for Hierarchical Sub-Pixel Tree Species Mapping
summary: Precise forest species mapping using spaceborne hyperspectral data is challenging due to high spectral similarity and the inherent sub-pixel heterogeneity of natural forest stands. While traditional deep learning models exploit spatial context through convolutional architectures, these approaches can introduce noise in fragmented or mixed-species forests. In this paper, we propose a hierarchy-aware, multimodal deep learning framework to resolve sub-pixel forest composition by integrating PRISMA (PRecursore IperSpettrale della Missione Applicativa) hyperspectral imagery, high-resolution panchromatic data, and digital elevation models. The architecture features a multi-branch encoder combining an EfficientNetV2-based one-dimensional convolutional neural network (CNN) for spectral signatures and twin two-dimensional CNNs for spatial and topographic features, coupled with a novel structurally-masked Transformer. By using a binary transition tensor to condition the Transformer slot embeddings and constrain inference, the model enforces taxonomic consistency between broad forest categories and fine-grained species distributions. The framework is validated across three diverse Italian biogeographical regions (the Alps and the Central and Southern Apennines) using field-surveyed plots. The proposed method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art multi-label and ranking-based paradigms, particularly in identifying subordinate species and their relative dominance. The bidirectional learning mechanism allows sub-pixel compositional features to refine macroscopic forest type predictions, while the integration of topographic priors effectively resolves spectral ambiguities in complex terrains. This knowledge-driven method supports regional-scale biodiversity monitoring and forest characterization within the evaluated PRISMA scenarios.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a hierarchy-aware multimodal deep learning framework combining CNNs and a structurally-masked Transformer for sub-pixel tree species mapping from spaceborne hyperspectral data.
AI.motivation: High spectral similarity and sub-pixel heterogeneity in mixed forests make species mapping difficult, and standard CNNs can introduce noise in fragmented stands.
AI.method: The model fuses PRISMA hyperspectral imagery, panchromatic data, and digital elevation models using a 1D EfficientNetV2 CNN for spectra and twin 2D CNNs for spatial/topographic features, feeding a structurally-masked Transformer conditioned by a binary transition tensor to enforce taxonomic consistency.
AI.result: Validated against field surveys across three Italian biogeographical regions (Alps, Central and Southern Apennines), the framework consistently outperforms state-of-the-art multi-label and ranking-based methods, especially for subordinate species and relative dominance.
