AI.conclusion: Enforcing taxonomic structure in multimodal CNN-Transformer architectures improves sub-pixel forest composition mapping across complex terrains.

title: Rank2Replace: VLM-Ranked Slot Replacement for Out-of-Distribution Generalization
summary: Spurious correlations can give image predictors high in-distribution accuracy but poor generalization under distribution shift. We introduce $\textbf{Rank2Replace}$, which transfers knowledge of task-relevant evidence from pretrained vision--language models (VLMs) to small predictors through training-time augmentation for out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization. The VLM ranks object-centric slots by task relevance and guides rank-dependent replacement with same-rank slot embeddings from another image. This augmentation retains the original image's label, encouraging reliance on preserved task evidence as incidental cues change, and supports combination with existing OOD methods. Across four datasets and six splits under shared frozen slot embeddings, the default cross-entropy configuration reaches macro-averaged average-group and worst-group accuracies of $80.43\%$ and $65.28\%$ without environment labels or dataset-specific replacement tuning. Slot corruption improves both macro-averaged metrics for all fourteen OOD training methods. Combining it with slot ranking and IRM reaches $81.96\%$ and $72.68\%$. Controlled ablations support the ranking and replacement design, with gains across five ranking VLMs and six extractor--predictor combinations. Permutation-invariant predictors further improve both macro-averaged metrics over their unaugmented counterparts while using VLM guidance only during training for efficient inference.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Rank2Replace, a training-time augmentation that uses VLM-ranked object-centric slots to improve out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization in small predictors.
AI.motivation: Image predictors often rely on spurious correlations that yield high in-distribution accuracy but fail under distribution shift.
AI.method: A pretrained VLM ranks object-centric slots by task relevance, guiding rank-dependent replacement of same-rank slot embeddings from other images while preserving the original label, without requiring VLM guidance at inference time.
AI.result: Across four datasets and six splits, default cross-entropy training with Rank2Replace reaches 80.43% average-group and 65.28% worst-group accuracy without environment labels; slot corruption improves all 14 tested OOD methods, and combining it with slot ranking and IRM reaches 81.96% and 72.68%.
AI.conclusion: Transferring VLM relevance knowledge via training-time slot replacement offers an inference-free, plug-and-play boost for OOD generalization.

title: Harnessing Medical Visual-Language Models with Agentic Evidence Management
comment: 22 pages, 3 figures. Qiming Huang, Hanze Dong, and Jipeng Zhang contributed equally
summary: Medical vision-language agents increasingly rely on segmentation tools, and recent work has focused on acquiring the right mask, often treating a good mask as the end point of tool use. But do these agents use the resulting evidence effectively? To answer this question, we need a benchmark that separates evidence use from segmentation quality, spans multiple medical image types, and allows the same mask to be presented in different ways. Existing medical VQA datasets do not jointly provide these properties. We therefore construct Mask-Evidence MedVQA, a 2.5K-example benchmark spanning four image types, where each question is paired with an answer-relevant ground-truth mask and multiple possible renderings. Our study reveals two limitations of direct tool use. First, evidence presentation matters. Different renderings of the same fixed mask can substantially change model behavior. Second, masks introduce an evidence trade-off. Highlighting a relevant region can expose diagnostic evidence the model previously missed, but the added visual cue can also induce incorrect associations. As a result, even a ground-truth mask can correct some answers while turning initially correct ones into incorrect ones. Together, these findings show that acquiring the right mask is not enough. An agent must also decide how to present the evidence and whether it should change the answer. We therefore introduce TUNE (Tool Use is Not Enough), an evidence-management harness that explicitly manages what evidence to acquire, how to present it, and whether to accept the resulting answer update. Across three public medical VQA benchmarks, evidence management improves the fine-tuned Qwen3.5-9B backbone's mean accuracy by 4.0 percentage points. Full TUNE improves over direct tool use by 9.1 points on average across seven benchmarks and achieves competitive results against existing medical VLMs and agents.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the Mask-Evidence MedVQA benchmark and the TUNE harness to address how medical vision-language agents use segmentation masks.
AI.motivation: Medical VQA agents often treat acquiring a good segmentation mask as the end goal, without verifying whether different mask renderings or the mask itself actually improve diagnostic answers.
AI.method: The authors build Mask-Evidence MedVQA (2.5K examples across four image types with ground-truth masks and multiple renderings) and propose TUNE (Tool Use is Not Enough), an evidence-management harness that controls evidence acquisition, presentation, and whether to accept answer updates.
AI.result: The benchmark reveals that mask rendering alters behavior and ground-truth masks can both fix errors and induce new ones; TUNE improves a fine-tuned Qwen3.5-9B backbone by 4.0 points on three public benchmarks and outperforms direct tool use by 9.1 points on average across seven benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Effective medical VLM tool use requires explicit evidence management over how masks are presented and integrated, not just accurate segmentation.

title: TrajCal: Trajectory-Calibrated Time Schedules for Few-Step Flow Sampling
summary: Flow matching enables high-quality image and video generation, but its iterative sampling process requires repeated evaluations of large neural networks. Existing few-step methods can distort the output and reduce its agreement with a many-step reference. We propose TrajCal, a training-free calibration framework for few-step sampling. Based on scatter search, a well-established metaheuristic for difficult optimization problems, TrajCal starts with diverse seed schedules, deforms and combines these candidates, and selects one fixed schedule by final output fidelity for reuse on new inputs. For both image and video generation, TrajCal achieves higher reference fidelity than all compared baselines at low evaluation budgets while maintaining competitive visual quality. The search is effective even with randomly generated seeds, while trajectory-based seeds further improve fidelity. For cross-style generalization, photography-calibrated schedules also improve fidelity on unseen image styles.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes TrajCal, a training-free scatter-search framework that calibrates fixed time schedules for few-step flow-matching generation.
AI.motivation: Few-step sampling in flow-matching models often distorts outputs and reduces agreement with many-step reference trajectories.
AI.method: Using scatter search, TrajCal starts from diverse seed schedules, deforms and combines candidates, and selects a single fixed schedule maximizing final output fidelity for reuse on new inputs.
AI.result: For both image and video generation at low evaluation budgets, TrajCal achieves higher reference fidelity than all compared baselines while maintaining competitive visual quality, and photography-calibrated schedules generalize to unseen image styles.
AI.conclusion: Metaheuristic calibration of sampling time schedules provides a simple, training-free way to improve few-step flow-matching fidelity.

title: EgoWitness: Benchmarking Instance-Level Spatial Memory and Reasoning in Egocentric Video Streams
comment: 43 pages, including supplementary material. Zhengru Fang and Zehao Liu contributed equally. Project page: this https URL ; Code: this https URL
summary: Recalling where and when an object was last seen and who saw it requires recognizing it across days and people. Existing long-video benchmarks focus on events, object categories, or relative locations, leaving instance-level spatial memory largely untested in multimodal models. To address this gap, we present EgoWitness, a benchmark for instance-level spatial memory and reasoning in egocentric video. Its 8,453 human-verified questions span approximately 324 hours of week-long and short-horizon recordings and test seven abilities, from recognizing an object or room to recalling who saw it and reasoning about room visits. Over one million reviewed masks of 34 registered landmarks and 21 movable-object labels are linked through room timelines. Among twelve direct vision-language models (VLMs), open-weight models reach at most 46.97% accuracy, and none exceeds 35% on identifying who saw an object last. We therefore propose EgoClue, a spatial-memory agent that retrieves candidate intervals, verifies instance identity, and computes spatial and temporal relations with five tools. Two-stage training with supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) raises its 4B controller from 23.64% to 72.65% accuracy on 1,320 held-out questions. Evidence-trace synthesis matches the best direct VLM at 74.85% on week-long questions and achieves 80.56% in environments excluded from training.

AI.tldr: This paper presents EgoWitness, a benchmark for instance-level spatial memory in egocentric video, and EgoClue, a tool-using spatial-memory agent trained with SFT and GRPO.
AI.motivation: Existing long-video benchmarks focus on events or object categories, leaving instance-level spatial memory (where and when an object was last seen, and by whom) largely untested.
AI.method: EgoWitness provides 8,453 human-verified questions over 324 hours of egocentric video with over one million masks; EgoClue retrieves candidate intervals, verifies instance identity, and computes spatiotemporal relations using five tools, trained via two-stage SFT and GRPO.
AI.result: Twelve direct VLMs reach at most 46.97% accuracy (and under 35% on who last saw an object), whereas two-stage training raises EgoClue's 4B controller from 23.64% to 72.65% on 1,320 held-out questions, reaching 74.85% on week-long questions and 80.56% in unseen environments.
AI.conclusion: Tool-augmented spatial-memory agents trained with SFT and GRPO substantially outperform direct VLMs on long-horizon instance-level egocentric reasoning.

title: Thinking in Streams: Proactive Spatial Reasoning with Vision-Language Models
summary: Recognizing when a requested spatial condition holds in streaming video can require maintaining and updating spatial knowledge across changing viewpoints. We study this capability through proactive spatial reasoning, where a model receives a query in advance and determines whether and when to respond as the stream unfolds. We introduce ProSpace-Bench, comprising nine tasks across object, camera, and scene reasoning, and ProSpace-Train for supervised training. To support spatial decisions, we propose ProSpace-VLM, which injects explicit geometric encodings estimated causally from incoming frames into intermediate VLM layers, using the existing KV cache as spatial memory and spatial token selection for efficient streaming. Experiments reveal a substantial gap between VLMs and humans, while ProSpace-VLM improves timely responses and correct abstention over fine-tuned baselines. Analyses examine how ProSpace-VLM represents previously observed spatial information across changing viewpoints.

AI.tldr: This paper formalizes proactive spatial reasoning in streaming video and introduces ProSpace-Bench, ProSpace-Train, and ProSpace-VLM, which injects causal geometric encodings into intermediate VLM layers to improve timely responses and abstention.
AI.motivation: Recognizing when a spatial condition holds in streaming video requires maintaining and updating spatial knowledge across changing viewpoints, which existing VLMs struggle to do proactively.
AI.method: The authors introduce ProSpace-Bench with nine tasks across object, camera, and scene reasoning, ProSpace-Train for supervised training, and ProSpace-VLM, which causally estimates geometric encodings from incoming frames, injects them into intermediate VLM layers, and uses the existing KV cache as spatial memory with spatial token selection.
AI.result: Experiments show a substantial gap between VLMs and humans, while ProSpace-VLM improves timely responses and correct abstention over fine-tuned baselines.
AI.conclusion: Explicit causal geometric encodings and KV-cache spatial memory enable more reliable proactive spatial reasoning in streaming video, though significant headroom remains compared to human performance.

title: WHU-Road3D: A dataset and benchmark towards fine-grained road surface mapping
summary: Accurately extracting and mapping road surface elements is crucial for applications such as high-definition maps, road asset management, and intelligent transportation systems. This study first provides a comprehensive review of the benchmark datasets for extracting and mapping road elements, encompassing overhead-to-perspective data, large-to-local scales, and coarse-to-fine details. Subsequently, we thoroughly review the relevant approaches for extracting road surface elements. However, we argue that existing datasets still require enhancements in semantic richness, data modality diversity, and scenario complexity. To bridge these gaps, this paper presents WHU-Road3D, a large-scale multimodal dataset for fine-grained road surface mapping to address these shortcomings. WHU-Road3D provides approximately 100 km of diverse Chinese highways and urban streets. It features a rich combination of MLS point clouds, associated panoramic images, vehicle trajectories, detailed vectorized annotations, and pointwise instance annotations for road surface elements. The dataset carefully annotates 15 distinct categories of road elements, including common markings like road boundaries, zebra crossings, lane dividers, stop lines, as well as 10 types of direction symbols. To our knowledge, WHU-Road3D stands as the first multimodal dataset for mapping such a comprehensive range of road surface elements, designed to facilitate cutting-edge research in instance segmentation, full-element extraction and mapping on road surfaces. Beyond these immediate applications, WHU-Road3D also provides a valuable source for hierarchical road topology reasoning, map updating, and street scene generation. The dataset, along with the code for our benchmark methods, will be made publicly available at \href{this https URL}{this https URL}.

AI.tldr: This paper presents WHU-Road3D, a large-scale multimodal dataset and benchmark covering approximately 100 km of Chinese highways and urban streets for fine-grained road surface mapping.
AI.motivation: Existing road surface mapping datasets lack sufficient semantic richness, data modality diversity, and scenario complexity for fine-grained element extraction and mapping.
AI.method: The authors construct WHU-Road3D using MLS point clouds, panoramic images, vehicle trajectories, vectorized annotations, and pointwise instance annotations across 15 road element categories, including road boundaries, zebra crossings, lane dividers, stop lines, and 10 direction symbol types.
AI.result: WHU-Road3D provides approximately 100 km of annotated multimodal data and benchmark code to support instance segmentation, full-element extraction, and road surface mapping.
AI.conclusion: WHU-Road3D establishes a comprehensive multimodal resource for advancing fine-grained road surface mapping, hierarchical road topology reasoning, map updating, and street scene generation.

title: EvoMem: Self-Evolving Skills for Time-Aware Long Video Memory Agents
summary: Although memory-augmented architectures have expanded the ability of large vision-language models (LVLMs) to process long videos, existing retrieval processes still largely rely on global semantic matching and lack state-driven temporal control, often returning fragmented or redundant evidence and failing to maintain a coherent evidence chain. To address this challenge, we propose EvoMem, a time-aware long-video memory agent guided by self-evolving retrieval skills. EvoMem constructs a hierarchical time-indexed memory, where different types of evidence are aligned onto a unified video timeline; during retrieval, temporal cues from acquired evidence are further converted into explicit signals that constrain subsequent memory access. To address recurring procedural errors in long-video question answering, such as unclear retrieval targets, improper memory access paths, or premature stopping, EvoMem introduces retrieval skills to provide process-level guidance, enabling the agent to dynamically adjust retrieval content, memory operations, and target temporal ranges according to the current evidence state, while deciding when to stop. Furthermore, inspired by reinforcement learning, we formulate skill evolution as a reward-guided policy improvement process. Each candidate skill is treated as an external policy patch, and rewards are assigned according to answer-correctness state transitions on the validation set. In this way, effective skills are accepted and low-quality skills are rejected without updating model parameters. Experiments on four long-video question answering benchmarks show that EvoMem significantly outperforms existing baselines, achieving an average accuracy of 60.1% and an average improvement of 8.6 percentage points over the previous best methods, demonstrating its effectiveness for long-video reasoning.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes EvoMem, a time-aware long-video memory agent that uses hierarchical time-indexed memory and reward-guided self-evolving retrieval skills to achieve 60.1% average accuracy on four long-video QA benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing memory-augmented LVLMs rely on global semantic matching without state-driven temporal control, leading to fragmented or redundant evidence and recurring procedural errors in long-video question answering.
AI.method: EvoMem builds a hierarchical time-indexed memory aligned to a unified video timeline, converts temporal cues into explicit access constraints, and introduces retrieval skills evolved as external policy patches via reward-guided policy improvement on validation answer-correctness transitions without updating model parameters.
AI.result: Across four long-video question answering benchmarks, EvoMem achieves an average accuracy of 60.1%, outperforming previous best methods by an average of 8.6 percentage points.
AI.conclusion: Formulating retrieval guidance as parameter-free, self-evolving skills over time-indexed memory substantially improves evidence coherence and reasoning accuracy in long-video QA.

title: Does It Depend on the Split? Frozen Satellite Features vs. Fine-Tuned CNNs for Tree Species Mapping
summary: Self-supervised foundation models are often said to need fewer labels than supervised training. We test this on a forestry task: classifying 20 tree species classes in 0.2 m aerial images from the TreeSatAI dataset. We compare a frozen DINOv3 model pretrained on 493 million satellite images, with only a linear classifier trained on top, against an ImageNet ResNet-50 that is fine-tuned end to end. On the official split, fine-tuning wins clearly (macro F1 0.764 vs. 0.685). However, 28.8% of the official test patches overlap a training or validation patch, and copying the label of the nearest such patch is correct for 83.6% of them. We therefore build a spatial split that holds out whole 2 km squares with a 200 m buffer. On this split the comparison becomes inconclusive (0.648 vs. 0.640, paired 95% CI of the difference [-0.054, 0.016]), and the learning curves of the two models overlap at every label budget from 343 to 33,126 training patches. On the five rarest classes, the frozen model achieves a higher mean F1 (0.566 vs. 0.445), although the confidence interval for this difference includes zero ([-0.05, 0.23]). Diagnostics show that the frozen features mainly miss differences between closely related species, such as the two native oaks. Choosing the input size and layer on validation data (224 px, block 16) raises the frozen model to 0.662 on the spatial split. A comparison that looks decisive on the official split is thus inconclusive under geographically separated evaluation. We release the spatial split and our code.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that while end-to-end fine-tuning of ResNet-50 outperforms a frozen DINOv3 linear probe on the official TreeSatAI split, the comparison becomes inconclusive on a geographically separated spatial split.
AI.motivation: Self-supervised foundation models are often claimed to need fewer labels than supervised models, but standard dataset splits with spatial overlap between training and test patches may bias comparisons.
AI.method: The authors compare a frozen DINOv3 model pretrained on 493 million satellite images with a linear classifier against an end-to-end fine-tuned ImageNet ResNet-50 on 20 tree species in 0.2 m aerial images from TreeSatAI, evaluating both the official split and a new spatial split holding out 2 km squares with a 200 m buffer.
AI.result: On the official split, fine-tuning wins (macro F1 0.764 vs. 0.685), but 28.8% of test patches overlap training or validation patches; on the spatial split, the difference is inconclusive (0.648 vs. 0.640, 95% CI [-0.054, 0.016]), and tuning input size and layer (224 px, block 16) raises the frozen model to 0.662.
AI.conclusion: Geographically separated evaluation reveals that apparent advantages of fine-tuned CNNs over frozen satellite foundation models on overlapping splits do not necessarily hold under spatial generalization.

title: SpatialMem: Building Quantitative Spatial Reasoning Agents with Hierarchical Memory
summary: Vision Language Models (VLMs) have shown remarkable capabilities in qualitative spatial reasoning, but remain limited in quantitative spatial reasoning. Current work leverages the VLM agent to invoke external vision tools to perform computation. However, these methods usually bind each functional requirement to a single predefined vision specialist, implicitly resulting in fixed and rigid tool pipelines. In practice, addressing diverse spatial scenarios and tasks demands a broader diversity in pipeline orchestration and vision specialist selection to achieve robust spatial reasoning. However, such diversity leads to a combinatorial execution space, making it challenging for the agent to orchestrate the optimal pipelines and specialists for different scenarios. In this work, we propose SpatialMem, a memory framework that enables a VLM agent to accumulate tool-use experience and leverage that memory to orchestrate vision specialists to solve the spatial reasoning problem. SpatialMem builds a two-level memory structure, with task memory capturing tool orchestration and scene memory capturing tool selection. It further introduces a dual-state trajectory optimization process to preserve successful tool experiences and refine suboptimal ones. Moreover, existing spatial reasoning benchmarks suffer from quality issues and limited coverage of scene types and tasks. To address these gap, we propose MetricBench, a benchmark covering both indoor and outdoor scenes and three quantitative spatial reasoning tasks. Our method achieves state-of-the-art results on MetricBench, Q-Spatial, and SpatilRGPT-Bench, outperforming best VLM baselines by 32% on MetricBench. Additionally, the memory design yields a 9.1% absolute gain over a memory-free agent on MetricBench.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes SpatialMem, a hierarchical memory framework for VLM agents to orchestrate vision specialists, and MetricBench, a quantitative spatial reasoning benchmark, achieving state-of-the-art results.
AI.motivation: Existing VLM agents for quantitative spatial reasoning bind functional requirements to rigid, predefined vision tool pipelines, and existing benchmarks suffer from quality issues and limited scene and task coverage.
AI.method: SpatialMem builds a two-level memory structure with task memory for tool orchestration and scene memory for tool selection, paired with dual-state trajectory optimization; the authors also introduce MetricBench covering indoor and outdoor scenes across three quantitative spatial reasoning tasks.
AI.result: SpatialMem achieves state-of-the-art performance on MetricBench, Q-Spatial, and SpatilRGPT-Bench, outperforming the best VLM baselines by 32% on MetricBench, with the memory design yielding a 9.1% absolute gain over a memory-free agent.
AI.conclusion: Accumulating and refining tool-use experience in hierarchical task and scene memory enables more flexible and accurate quantitative spatial reasoning in VLM agents.

title: Why Flat Drafts Stay Flat: Region-Mean Latents Govern Texture in Flow-Based Image Generation
summary: Flat color-block drafts specify layout and regional color while leaving interior detail unspecified, yet pretrained flow-based generators can preserve their flat appearance even under photorealistic prompts. We trace this behavior to a cross-scale mechanism linking fine pixel variation to regional means in variational autoencoder (VAE) latent space. Flattening photo regions systematically shifts their latent means, with offsets concentrated along a shared channel direction within each backbone. Controlled field exchanges in FLUX.1-dev and Qwen-Image establish the effect of this displacement on texture generation: adding the photo-derived regional mean field to a flat latent restores texture, whereas adding its complementary field alone largely preserves flatness. A second-order encoding expansion explains how encoder curvature can convert zero-mean perturbations into mean shifts. An analytically solvable conditional Gaussian flow shows how regional noise averaging enables near-unit endpoint sensitivity at high signal-to-noise ratios. This mechanism motivates training-free rendering through pixel dither before encoding, mean-field scaling, and early boundary holding. Paired low-rank adaptation (LoRA) with draft conditioning improves content recovery and produces photo-like regional means under the standard velocity objective. Explicit regional mean guidance remains effective after adaptation, continuously controlling texture and improving color fidelity. These findings connect encoding shifts to persistent generation behavior and support interventions evaluated for texture, spatial fidelity, and semantic recovery.

AI.tldr: This paper explains why flow-based image generators preserve flat color-block drafts as a cross-scale VAE latent mean shift and introduces training-free and LoRA-based interventions to control texture and fidelity.
AI.motivation: Pretrained flow-based generators often preserve the flat appearance of color-block drafts even under photorealistic prompts, and the underlying mechanism in latent space was unclear.
AI.method: The authors analyze VAE latent shifts in FLUX.1-dev and Qwen-Image via controlled field exchanges, a second-order encoding expansion, and an analytically solvable conditional Gaussian flow, motivating training-free pixel dithering, mean-field scaling, early boundary holding, and paired LoRA adaptation with regional mean guidance.
AI.result: Controlled field exchanges confirm that adding photo-derived regional mean fields to flat latents restores texture while complementary fields preserve flatness, and the proposed training-free and LoRA interventions improve texture, spatial fidelity, and color fidelity.
AI.conclusion: Connecting VAE encoding mean shifts to flow-model endpoint sensitivity provides a principled basis for controlling texture generation from flat drafts.

title: TwinD: Generalizing Deepfake Detection from Blending to Entire Face Synthesis
summary: Facial deepfake detectors are usually trained on blending fakes, where a generated face is pasted back into a real frame. Recent generators synthesize the entire face and leave no traces of blending. On a benchmark of 19 datasets released from 2019 to 2026, the best prior facial deepfake detector reaches a mean AUROC of 96.2% on ten blending datasets, but none exceeds 78.1% on five datasets of entire face synthesis (EFS). AI-generated content (AIGC) detectors do not close this gap. We propose TwinD, a detector trained on FaceForensics++ fakes and two kinds of twins: fakes made from a real frame. A reconstruction twin is a real frame reconstructed by an autoencoder, with the real pixels put back in a random region. It targets the neural traces of a decoder. A blob twin blends an altered copy of a real frame with the frame itself, targeting blending artifacts. It needs no generator and no face-shaped mask. Together, these twins provide two complementary forensic cues that generalize to unseen manipulations. TwinDreaches a mean AUROC of 96.3%, 8.9 points above the prior state-of-the-art, with 98.1% on the blending datasets and 95.6% on the EFS datasets. Trained on twins alone, without a deepfake dataset, single models still reach 94.3% on average over three seeds. For reproducibility, the code, trained model, and training data are at: this https URL

AI.tldr: This paper proposes TwinD, a deepfake detector trained on FaceForensics++ and two synthetic "twin" transformations of real frames, achieving 96.3% mean AUROC across 19 blending and entire-face-synthesis datasets.
AI.motivation: Prior facial deepfake detectors trained on blending fakes achieve high accuracy on blending datasets (96.2% AUROC) but fail to generalize to entire face synthesis (EFS) datasets (at most 78.1% AUROC).
AI.method: TwinD trains on FaceForensics++ alongside reconstruction twins (real frames reconstructed by an autoencoder with real pixels restored in a random region) and blob twins (real frames blended with altered copies of themselves without face masks or generators).
AI.result: Across 19 datasets, TwinD achieves 96.3% mean AUROC (8.9 points above prior state-of-the-art), reaching 98.1% on blending datasets and 95.6% on EFS datasets, while models trained on twins alone still reach 94.3% average AUROC.
AI.conclusion: Combining complementary decoder-trace and blending-artifact twin cues enables strong generalization from blending deepfakes to unseen entire-face-synthesis manipulations.

title: Point Dynamics as Proxy for Robotic World Models
comment: 24 pages, 7 figures, 11 tables. Project page: this https URL
summary: Robotic world models predict future video frames from the current observation and a sequence of robot actions. While recent models follow the given actions closely, manipulated objects often collapse or move inconsistently with the action. We attribute this to the conditioning: an action, or a rendering of the robot, specifies where the robot goes but not how the scene responds, leaving a single video model to infer the interaction dynamics implicitly while also rendering appearance. We therefore separate dynamics prediction from visual rendering, with 3D point dynamics as the proxy between them. Specifically, we lift the first frame into 3D points, simulate how they respond to the robot's motion with a learned point dynamics model, and render the simulated points back into pixel-aligned videos that any video model can read. In controlled experiments on the DROID dataset with two video renderers of different architectures, this point dynamics proxy reduces object motion error by 8.6% and 6.2% without degrading image quality, and by 8.1% on a real bimanual robot. Moreover, the video follows the simulation: more accurate dynamics yield more accurate object motion, and editing the points steers the video. This suggests that advances in dynamics modeling can translate into more faithful robotic world models.

AI.tldr: This paper decouples dynamics prediction from visual rendering in robotic world models using 3D point dynamics as a proxy, reducing object motion error by up to 8.6% on DROID and 8.1% on a real bimanual robot.
AI.motivation: Existing robotic world models condition a single video generator directly on robot actions, forcing it to implicitly infer interaction dynamics while rendering appearance, which often causes manipulated objects to collapse or move inconsistently.
AI.method: The authors lift the first frame into 3D points, simulate scene responses to robot actions with a learned point dynamics model, and render the simulated points into pixel-aligned videos as conditioning for video renderers.
AI.result: On the DROID dataset across two video renderer architectures, the point dynamics proxy reduces object motion error by 8.6% and 6.2% without degrading image quality, and reduces error by 8.1% on a real bimanual robot.
AI.conclusion: Separating 3D point dynamics simulation from video rendering allows improvements in physical dynamics modeling to translate directly into more faithful robotic world models.

title: MorphTwin: Enriching Deformable Material Responses from Videos for Morphable and Interactive Physical Twins
summary: Reconstructing interactive physical twins from video requires accurately capturing how objects deform while maintaining efficient simulation. We observe that reproducing motion in a video does not guarantee correct responses to new forces when the physical representation restricts how an object can deform. In spring-based twins, coupling between volume and shape responses creates such a limitation. We present MorphTwin, which enriches local deformation modes to capture and independently control these responses while retaining standard spring forces and explicit simulation. To support interpretable material editing and transfer, we use offline calibration to map shared relative response changes to stiffness updates on each reconstructed graph. Under identical inverse settings on synthetic scenes, MorphTwin reduces the mean absolute error of Poisson's ratio by 75.8% and the mean relative error of Young's modulus by 22.1% compared to PhysTwin. We introduce an egocentric stereo and RGB-D benchmark covering interactions with objects of varying stiffness. Real-world experiments demonstrate improved reconstruction accuracy and up to 14.4% lower future tracking error than PhysTwin at interactive speeds.

AI.tldr: This paper presents MorphTwin, a physical twin reconstruction method that decouples volume and shape deformation responses in spring-based models, reducing material parameter errors and future tracking error over PhysTwin.
AI.motivation: Existing spring-based physical twins couple volume and shape responses, which restricts how reconstructed objects deform and prevents accurate responses to novel forces.
AI.method: MorphTwin enriches local deformation modes to independently capture and control volume and shape responses while retaining standard spring forces and explicit simulation, and uses offline calibration to map relative response changes to graph stiffness updates.
AI.result: On synthetic scenes, MorphTwin reduces Poisson's ratio MAE by 75.8% and Young's modulus MRE by 22.1% compared to PhysTwin, and achieves up to 14.4% lower future tracking error at interactive speeds on a new egocentric stereo and RGB-D benchmark.
AI.conclusion: Enriching local deformation modes with calibrated stiffness mapping enables accurate, interactive, and editable physical twins from video.

title: Sample-efficient end-to-end Optical Music Recognition through Active Learning
summary: End-to-end approaches to Optical Music Recognition (OMR) have recently shown promising results, but their performance often degrades on unseen data. A common solution is to pretrain and fine-tune models with annotated samples from the target domain, improving adaptation to new distributions. However, this process typically requires extensive manual annotation to yield competitive models, making it costly and time-consuming. In this work, we explore Active Learning to reduce this burden by selecting informative samples for labeling in low-resource scenarios, where the amount of manual annotation that can be performed is limited. We evaluate both uncertainty- and diversity-based sampling strategies on staff-level and full-page corpora. Results show that confidence-based sampling performs comparably to oracle selection (based on true error), and that each scenario benefits from a tailored strategy.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates Active Learning for end-to-end Optical Music Recognition (OMR) in low-resource domain adaptation scenarios, finding that confidence-based sampling matches oracle selection.
AI.motivation: Adapting end-to-end OMR models to unseen target domains requires extensive manual annotation, which is costly and time-consuming.
AI.method: The authors evaluate uncertainty-based and diversity-based active learning sampling strategies on both staff-level and full-page OMR corpora under limited annotation budgets.
AI.result: Confidence-based sampling performs comparably to oracle selection based on true error, with staff-level and full-page scenarios each benefiting from tailored sampling strategies.
AI.conclusion: Active learning provides a sample-efficient path to adapting end-to-end OMR models to new domains with minimal manual labeling.

title: Multi-View Transformer with Geometry-Guided Multi-Modal ControlNet for 3D Virtual Try-On
summary: Editing a 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) capture of a person so that they wear a new garment requires every rendered view to agree on the same garment details. Existing 3D virtual try-on (VTON) pipelines, however, edit training views largely independently and fuse them with hand-designed heuristics such as manually chosen reference views and fixed attention-blending weights. The resulting inconsistencies are baked into the 3D representation and surface as texture drift, blurred prints, and implausible geometry in novel views. We present GS-VTON-MVT, a three-stage framework that combines implicit and explicit 3D reasoning for consistent 3DGS try-on. (i) A multi-view inpainting transformer jointly edits a set of training views with full cross-view self-attention, so that cross-view correspondence is learned rather than imposed. (ii) A geometry-guided multi-modal ControlNet conditions the diffusion editor on the garment image together with depth and surface normals rendered from the current 3DGS state, supplying explicit structure where visual evidence is weakest. (iii) A pose-adaptive persona-aware attention replaces the fixed blending weight between current-view and reference-view features with weights derived from camera-pose proximity. On the 3D-VTONBench benchmark, GS-VTON-MVT improves FID, KID, LPIPS-based cross-view consistency, and user preference over general-purpose 3D editors and prior 3D try-on methods.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes GS-VTON-MVT, a three-stage 3D virtual try-on framework combining a multi-view inpainting transformer, geometry-guided ControlNet, and pose-adaptive attention to improve cross-view consistency.
AI.motivation: Existing 3D Gaussian Splatting virtual try-on pipelines edit views independently and fuse them with heuristics, causing texture drift, blurred prints, and implausible geometry in novel views.
AI.method: GS-VTON-MVT uses a multi-view inpainting transformer with full cross-view self-attention, a multi-modal ControlNet conditioned on garment images plus rendered 3DGS depth and normals, and pose-adaptive persona-aware attention weighted by camera-pose proximity.
AI.result: On 3D-VTONBench, GS-VTON-MVT improves FID, KID, LPIPS-based cross-view consistency, and user preference compared to general-purpose 3D editors and prior 3D try-on methods.
AI.conclusion: Integrating learned cross-view attention with explicit 3D geometric conditioning and pose-adaptive feature blending produces consistent, high-fidelity 3DGS virtual try-on.

title: Fixing the Twin, Not the Detector: Sim-to-Real Roadside LiDAR Detection from Digital-Twin Data
comment: 8 pages, 1 figure, 5 tables. Accepted to the IEEE BigData 2026 Cup (UCF UrbanTwin Sim2Real LiDAR Challenge); first place, LUMPI track. Code: this https URL
summary: Roadside LiDAR detectors are expensive to train on real labels, and digital twins promise to replace these labels, but a detector trained on a twin meets a different sensor, different objects and different annotation conventions on the real site. We describe the pipeline that placed first in the LUMPI track of the UrbanTwin Sim2Real LiDAR Challenge (IEEE BigData 2026 Cup, 0.5541 combined score) and fifth on its V2X-Real track (0.8102). Every detector is a CenterPoint model trained only on synthetic data, on a single 8 GB laptop GPU. Most of the gain came from correcting differences between the twin and the real site rather than from the detector. We align the twin's coordinates, point density and box convention with the test sensor, generate the pedestrians and riders that the twins lack, plus street clutter as unlabeled negatives, and rebuild twin objects at real size and real point density. A non-learned resampling to the per-cell point density of unlabeled real frames lifts LUMPI realism from 0.589 to 0.947, against 0.949 between real frames. Label-free post-processing then exploits what a fixed roadside sensor guarantees: static structures recur in every frame, and real objects have characteristic point statistics. Reporting the validation and test gain of each component side by side, we find that corrections of systematic sim-to-real differences transfer to the test set, typically keeping a quarter to three quarters of their validation gain, while choices that fit the few objects of a validation set do not.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a sim-to-real roadside LiDAR detection pipeline that aligns digital-twin data with real sensor and scene properties, winning first place on the LUMPI track of the UrbanTwin Sim2Real LiDAR Challenge.
AI.motivation: Roadside LiDAR detectors trained on digital twins face severe domain shift due to differences in sensors, missing object classes, and annotation conventions at real sites.
AI.method: Using a CenterPoint model trained solely on synthetic data on an 8 GB GPU, the authors align coordinates, point density, and box conventions, synthesize missing pedestrians, riders, and street clutter, resample to real per-cell point densities, and apply label-free static-structure post-processing.
AI.result: The pipeline placed first on the LUMPI track (0.5541 combined score) and fifth on the V2X-Real track (0.8102), with per-cell resampling lifting LUMPI realism from 0.589 to 0.947 (vs. 0.949 between real frames).
AI.conclusion: Correcting systematic sim-to-real discrepancies in digital-twin data transfers reliably to test performance and matters more than modifying the detector architecture.

title: Streaming-AAA: Streaming AAA Game Video Generation at High Resolution, High Frame Rate, and Low Latency
summary: Controllable streaming video generation offers a promising route toward interactive game simulation, yet existing methods remain far from practical gameplay. They often fail to jointly achieve high visual fidelity, high frame rates, and low interaction latency, resulting in poor responsiveness and degraded user experience. We present Streaming-AAA, a new paradigm for controllable infinite generation of AAA-quality game videos. Our system generates 1080p gameplay videos at 43 FPS with 198 ms end-to-end latency interaction on merely NVIDIA A800 GPUs, while supporting long-horizon play without severe temporal degradation or collapse. Streaming-AAA is built upon three key designs. First, we redesign the VAE architecture for efficient high-resolution decoding, enabling real-time synthesis at 1080p. Second, we pretrain the diffusion model using diffusion forcing and significantly extend the temporal training horizon, allowing the model to capture long-term dependencies and maintain persistent memory. Third, we perform post-training distillation and memory compression to improve inference efficiency while retaining visual quality and temporal consistency. Experiments show that Streaming-AAA substantially improves visual fidelity, frame rate, latency, and long-term stability over prior controllable video generation approaches, enabling a significantly more playable experience for interactive AAA game video generation.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Streaming-AAA, a controllable streaming game video generation system that generates 1080p gameplay at 43 FPS with 198 ms end-to-end latency on A800 GPUs.
AI.motivation: Existing controllable video generation methods fail to simultaneously achieve high visual fidelity, high frame rates, low interaction latency, and long-horizon stability required for playable AAA game simulation.
AI.method: Streaming-AAA redesigns the VAE for fast 1080p decoding, pretrains the diffusion model with diffusion forcing over extended temporal horizons, and applies post-training distillation and memory compression.
AI.result: The system achieves 1080p generation at 43 FPS and 198 ms end-to-end latency on NVIDIA A800 GPUs while substantially improving visual fidelity and long-term stability over prior controllable video generation methods.
AI.conclusion: Combining efficient high-resolution VAE decoding, extended-horizon diffusion forcing, and distillation makes real-time, interactive AAA-quality game video streaming practical.

title: PaveSplat: Resolution-Robust Feed-Forward Gaussian Splatting with Residually Corrected Surface-Aligned Covariances
comment: Accepted to ACCV 2026. 16 pages, 4 figures, 4 tables. Project page: this https URL ; code: this https URL
summary: We present PaveSplat, a feed-forward Gaussian splatting method that adds a learned residual to the analytic surface-aligned covariance, keeping surfels paving the visible surface across rendering resolutions. Pixel-aligned feed-forward Gaussian splatting predicts one primitive per pixel from a few images in a single pass, and its rendering quality depends on how well these primitives cover the surface. Recent surfel-based methods compute the surface-aligned covariance analytically from predicted depth. However, this covariance has no way to correct the surfel orientation where the depth-derived frame is ill-posed. The surfels then cover the surface loosely; at the training resolution each surfel's one-pixel minimum footprint covers the gaps, but they show up as holes when the same prediction is re-rendered at a higher resolution. To address this, we keep the analytic covariance as an initialization, with its axes aligned to the surface tangents, and add an identity-initialized unit-quaternion residual that reorients a surfel only where this improves rendering, turning surfels that the analytic frame mis-aims back onto the surface. On RealEstate10K, PaveSplat achieves the best PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS among single-Gaussian-per-pixel methods at every scale (1x-8x). The native-resolution gain is small; the benefit appears when the same prediction is rendered at higher display resolutions without re-running the network. On zero-shot DL3DV, it leads PSNR within this group at every scale and ranks first or second on SSIM/LPIPS. A coverage-hole analysis shows fewer uncovered pixels than both baselines under high-resolution re-rendering.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes PaveSplat, a feed-forward Gaussian splatting method that adds a learned unit-quaternion residual to analytic surface-aligned covariances, eliminating holes during high-resolution re-rendering.
AI.motivation: Pixel-aligned feed-forward surfel methods compute covariance analytically from predicted depth, which mis-orients surfels where depth is ill-posed and causes visible holes when re-rendered at higher resolutions.
AI.method: PaveSplat initializes surface-aligned covariances analytically and adds an identity-initialized unit-quaternion residual that reorients surfels only where it improves rendering.
AI.result: On RealEstate10K and zero-shot DL3DV, PaveSplat achieves the best PSNR among single-Gaussian-per-pixel methods across 1x to 8x scales, with fewer uncovered pixels under high-resolution re-rendering.
AI.conclusion: Residually correcting analytic surface-aligned covariances preserves surface coverage across rendering resolutions without re-running the feed-forward network.

title: Less Than Meets the Eye: Action-Set Identifiability and Principled Abstention for 3D Physical Geometry
summary: A corridor, its mirror reflection, and its image on a display can look identical, yet their physical surfaces lie at different depths. We test whether bounded camera motions distinguish these explanations. Intervene3D takes an image and an initial geometry estimate, predicts the view under each hypothesis and candidate motion, and selects a motion by maximin separability. It reports the mechanism and first physical surface only if the available motions separate the hypotheses still in contention. Otherwise it abstains. An adequacy test also rejects observations that no hypothesis explains. On a matched synthetic benchmark with exact landmarks, disabling abstention gives confident answers on 76.4% of unresolvable scenes. With abstention, none receives a confident answer under exact or noisy landmarks. At 100% accuracy on answered scenes, maximin selection answers 61.0% of scenes and summed selection 43.1%. The adequacy test lowers wrong answers on strongly curved mirror scenes from 56.8% to 12.4%. Real display experiments compare two hypotheses using one frozen depth-network estimate. The second image supplies photometric evidence and is never passed through the depth network. One executed motion reduces the pooled median surface error of twelve networks by 31.5%. These networks have larger error inside the annotated panel than outside on 33.4% of illusion-benchmark images. They place the first physical surface behind the glass on 36.9% of Mirror3D frames.

AI.tldr: This paper presents Intervene3D, an active geometry framework that selects bounded camera motions by maximin separability and abstains when physical surfaces (corridors, mirrors, displays) remain unidentifiable.
AI.motivation: Corridors, mirror reflections, and display images can appear identical from a single view despite having different physical surface depths, and single-view depth networks often fail silently on these illusions.
AI.method: Intervene3D predicts views under competing hypotheses and candidate camera motions, selects a motion via maximin separability, reports the mechanism and first physical surface only when hypotheses separate, and uses an adequacy test to reject unexplained observations.
AI.result: On a synthetic benchmark, abstention eliminates confident wrong answers on unresolvable scenes (down from 76.4% to 0%) while maximin selection answers 61.0% of scenes at 100% accuracy; on real displays, one executed motion reduces pooled median surface error of twelve depth networks by 31.5%.
AI.conclusion: Principled action-set identifiability and abstention prevent overconfident depth errors on optical illusions and improve physical surface localization with minimal camera motion.

title: One-to-Many: Diverse and Bidirectional Image-to-Image Translation via Rectified Flow
comment: 12 pages, 13 figures, 4 tables. Includes supplementary material
summary: Many paired image-to-image translation tasks admit multiple valid target appearances, while training provides only one target per source. We propose One-to-Many Flow (O2MFlow), a latent-conditioned Rectified Flow (RF) model for one-to-many generation and backward translation (target$\rightarrow$source) within a single transport framework. Conditioning the RF dynamics on an appearance latent turns transport into a family of latent-indexed bijections: a fixed latent gives a mapping that is inverted by time-reversed integration, and sampled latents produce diverse outputs for the same input. We formalize reusable appearance variations as Shared Latent Transport and show that Kullback--Leibler (KL) regularization directly controls the source--latent distribution gap between training and generation. Across three benchmarks, O2MFlow offers dataset-dependent forward diversity--fidelity trade-offs and the lowest backward LPIPS-Dist among evaluated methods, with the lowest backward FID on two benchmarks.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes O2MFlow, a latent-conditioned Rectified Flow model for diverse one-to-many forward and bidirectional image-to-image translation within a single transport framework.
AI.motivation: Paired image-to-image translation datasets provide only one target per source even though multiple valid target appearances exist.
AI.method: O2MFlow conditions Rectified Flow dynamics on an appearance latent, creating a family of latent-indexed bijections inverted by time-reversed integration, and uses KL regularization under Shared Latent Transport to control the source-latent distribution gap.
AI.result: Across three benchmarks, O2MFlow demonstrates dataset-dependent forward diversity-fidelity trade-offs, achieves the lowest backward LPIPS-Dist among evaluated methods, and achieves the lowest backward FID on two benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Latent-conditioned Rectified Flow with Shared Latent Transport enables unified diverse forward generation and accurate backward inversion in image-to-image translation.

title: Domain-Aware Conformal Prediction for Trustworthy Spacecraft Pose Estimation under Sim-to-Real Shift
summary: Autonomous rendezvous and proximity operations require not only an accurate estimate of the pose of the target spacecraft, but also a reliable indication of when this estimate can be trusted. Conformal prediction provides such an indication with a formal guarantee, by producing pose uncertainty sets that contain the true pose with a specified probability. Such a guarantee, however, assumes that calibration and test data follow the same distribution, an assumption that is violated in orbital perception, where labelled calibration images are available only from synthetic renderings while operational images are real. In this work, we show on the SPEED+ dataset that conformal pose estimation calibrated on synthetic images loses its coverage guarantee on real images, and that many of the resulting failures are silent: the predicted pose set appears valid but excludes the true pose. To address this, we calibrate on synthetic images translated to the appearance of real images. Since translation alters appearance while preserving geometry, the synthetic pose labels remain valid and no labelled real images are required. Experiments with two translation models show that this calibration restores coverage above the specified level for miscoverage levels of 0.1 and above, and reduces silent failures from up to 43.5% to at most 3.3% of the test images, bringing conformal pose estimation a step closer to trustworthy deployment in space.

AI.tldr: This paper restores conformal prediction coverage guarantees for spacecraft pose estimation under sim-to-real shift by calibrating on synthetic images translated to real appearance.
AI.motivation: Conformal pose estimation calibrated on synthetic orbital renderings loses its coverage guarantee on real images, causing silent failures where predicted pose sets appear valid but exclude the true pose.
AI.method: The authors translate synthetic calibration images to real-image appearance using two translation models, preserving geometry and synthetic pose labels without requiring labelled real images.
AI.result: On the SPEED+ dataset, calibrating on translated images restores coverage above the specified level for miscoverage levels of 0.1 and above, reducing silent failures from up to 43.5% to at most 3.3%.
AI.conclusion: Appearance-only image translation enables label-free conformal calibration that makes spacecraft pose uncertainty sets trustworthy under sim-to-real shift.

title: DfD-GS: Defocus Image Prior for Metric-Scale Single-View Depth Estimation and View Synthesis
summary: Recovering metric-scale geometry from observations at a single viewpoint remains fundamentally ill-posed, limiting the reliability of novel view synthesis. Recent methods rely on learned monocular depth priors, which provide strong structural estimates but can suffer from scale ambiguity and dataset-dependent biases. We propose DfD-GS, a feed-forward framework that predicts a metric-scale 3D Gaussian scene representation from a single-view all-in-focus--defocused image pair. The key idea is to exploit defocus blur as a physical metric depth cue. DfD-GS first estimates a defocus-based metric disparity map from the all-in-focus--defocused image pair and the corresponding defocus strength. This estimate is used to align and refine a monocular depth prior to metric scale. Visible and hidden 3D Gaussians are then predicted for occlusion-aware novel view synthesis. Experiments on synthetic-defocus datasets constructed from Booster and Middlebury show that DfD-GS outperforms single-image baselines in metric depth estimation and novel view synthesis. On WildRGB-D, DfD-GS achieves lower AbsRel and LPIPS but higher depth RMSE than the single-image baselines. Additional analyses show that DfD-GS maintains a more stable metric scale under field-of-view changes. Qualitative results on a real dataset show recovery of the main scene structure under optical defocus.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces DfD-GS, a feed-forward framework that uses an all-in-focus and defocused image pair as a physical metric depth cue to predict metric-scale 3D Gaussians for single-view depth estimation and view synthesis.
AI.motivation: Single-view depth estimation and novel view synthesis suffer from scale ambiguity and dataset-dependent biases when relying solely on learned monocular depth priors.
AI.method: DfD-GS estimates a defocus-based metric disparity map from an all-in-focus and defocused image pair, uses it to align and refine a monocular depth prior to metric scale, and predicts visible and hidden 3D Gaussians for occlusion-aware view synthesis.
AI.result: On synthetic-defocus Booster and Middlebury datasets, DfD-GS outperforms single-image baselines in metric depth and novel view synthesis; on WildRGB-D, it achieves lower AbsRel and LPIPS (though higher depth RMSE) and maintains more stable metric scale under field-of-view changes.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating optical defocus blur as a physical metric cue resolves scale ambiguity in single-view 3D Gaussian scene reconstruction.

title: Frequency-Synchronized Boundary Coupling for Training-Free Multi-Prompt Long Video Generation
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. Project page: this https URL
summary: Text-to-video generation has made remarkable progress with diffusion models and transformer-based video architectures, yet generating coherent long videos from evolving textual descriptions remains challenging. Training long-video models from scratch requires substantial computation and large-scale multi-event data, while training-free multi-prompt generation must activate new prompt semantics without breaking temporal continuity. We identify a frequency-agnostic boundary coupling problem in existing transition strategies: weak coupling causes abrupt changes, flicker, and background jumps, whereas overly strong or coarse coupling may over-preserve source semantics and produce ghosting or duplicated subjects around prompt boundaries. To address this problem, we propose FreqSync, a training-free framework that formulates prompt transitions as frequency-selective boundary coupling. FreqSync combines Frequency-Synchronized Source-Conditioned Attention (FS-SCA) with Residual-Clipped Spectral Stitching (RCSS), enabling adjacent segments to share stable low- and mid-frequency structure and motion cues while keeping high-frequency prompt-specific details target-dominant under explicit residual constraints. Extensive experiments show that FreqSync achieves state-of-the-art transition smoothness and prompt alignment while maintaining strong perceptual video quality, demonstrating its effectiveness for coherent multi-prompt long video generation.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes FreqSync, a training-free framework for multi-prompt long video generation that formulates prompt transitions as frequency-selective boundary coupling.
AI.motivation: Existing training-free multi-prompt video transition strategies suffer from frequency-agnostic coupling, causing either abrupt flicker and background jumps when weak or ghosting and duplicated subjects when overly strong.
AI.method: FreqSync combines Frequency-Synchronized Source-Conditioned Attention (FS-SCA) with Residual-Clipped Spectral Stitching (RCSS) so adjacent segments share low- and mid-frequency structure and motion while keeping high-frequency prompt details target-dominant.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show that FreqSync achieves state-of-the-art transition smoothness and prompt alignment while maintaining strong perceptual video quality.
AI.conclusion: Frequency-selective boundary coupling resolves the trade-off between temporal continuity and semantic responsiveness in training-free multi-prompt video generation.

title: HiUni: Harmonizing Understanding and Generation in Shared Visual Space
summary: Unified multimodal models aim to support visual understanding and generation within a single framework. However, prevailing approaches often separate their visual representations or backbone computation to accommodate the different requirements of these two tasks, which limits the degree of unification. In this paper, we present HiUni, which revisits this design choice and explores whether a pretrained vision language model can be directly extended into a unified model with extensive parameter sharing. Specifically, HiUni reuses the same language-aligned ViT and dense Transformer backbone for both capabilities, while confining task-specific computation to the output side. Yet such a design introduces two key challenges. Generation in pixel space is difficult to optimize, and semantic abstraction in pretrained ViT discards fine spatial details required for synthesis. To address these challenges, HiUni introduces a \emph{Pixel Diffusion Head} tailored to direct pixel-space optimization and a lightweight \emph{HiGate} pathway that provides fine-grained spatial details near the output stage. Extensive experiments show that HiUni achieves a similar average understanding score to the pretrained VLM while attaining competitive performance on image generation and editing. Controlled comparisons and analyses further demonstrate that a single dense backbone can effectively support both capabilities without task-specific backbone computation, highlighting a simpler path toward unified multimodal modeling.

AI.tldr: This paper presents HiUni, a unified multimodal model that extends a pretrained VLM to both visual understanding and image generation using a shared ViT and dense Transformer backbone.
AI.motivation: Prevailing unified multimodal models separate visual representations or backbone computation for understanding and generation, limiting true parameter sharing.
AI.method: HiUni reuses the same language-aligned ViT and dense Transformer backbone for both tasks, adding a Pixel Diffusion Head for direct pixel-space optimization and a lightweight HiGate pathway to supply fine spatial details near the output stage.
AI.result: HiUni matches the average understanding score of the pretrained VLM while achieving competitive performance on image generation and editing.
AI.conclusion: A single dense backbone with minimal output-side specialization can effectively support both visual understanding and pixel-space generation.

title: Learning Reconstruction Errors as Spatiotemporal Evidence for AI-Generated Video Detection
summary: The proliferation of AI-generated videos has raised growing concerns about misinformation, fraud, and potential societal risks, creating an urgent need for detection. Reconstruction-error-based methods have shown strong empirical performance for AI-generated image detection by exploiting discrepancies between an input and its reconstructed version. Their extension to video detection, however, faces two challenges: (i) a fixed reconstructor is not optimized for the detection objective and may yield weak discriminative signals; and (ii) an additional raw-video feature stream is often introduced to model temporal dependencies, increasing architectural overhead. To address these challenges, we develop a detector that learns and exploits reconstruction errors as a unified source of spatiotemporal evidence. First, we jointly optimize a reconstructor and the downstream classifier to produce reconstruction errors that are more informative for detecting AI-generated videos. Second, we show that consecutive reconstruction errors alone carry temporal evidence, and thus a 3D convolution over them captures spatiotemporal evidence without a raw-video stream. Extensive experiments on over 30 existing AI-video generators demonstrate competitive performance against baselines.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an AI-generated video detector that jointly optimizes a reconstructor and classifier and applies 3D convolutions directly to consecutive reconstruction errors without a raw-video stream.
AI.motivation: Extending reconstruction-error-based image detectors to video is limited by fixed reconstructors that yield weak discriminative signals and the overhead of adding a raw-video feature stream for temporal modeling.
AI.method: The authors jointly train the reconstructor and downstream classifier to produce informative reconstruction errors, and apply 3D convolutions over consecutive reconstruction errors alone to capture spatiotemporal evidence.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across more than 30 AI-video generators demonstrate competitive detection performance against existing baselines.
AI.conclusion: Jointly learned reconstruction errors carry sufficient spatiotemporal evidence for AI-generated video detection without requiring a separate raw-video stream.

title: Better Retrieval, Not Better Binding: Pretraining Exposure in Egocentric Video Retrieval
summary: Video-language models (VLMs) achieve strong performance on video-text retrieval and are increasingly used for egocentric video understanding. Yet, despite gains in zero-shot retrieval, they have shown limitations in compositional understanding, and it remains unclear whether they understand compositional relationships between verbs and nouns. In this work, we introduce Ego-ExBind, a compositional diagnostic protocol for analyzing pretraining exposure and verb-noun binding in egocentric video-text retrieval. Ego-ExBind consists of an Exposure Ledger built from the EgoClip pretraining corpus used by EgoVLPv2, which defines Seen Composition, Unseen Composition, and Unseen Atom splits for EPIC-KITCHENS-100 multi-instance retrieval (MIR). We further probe noun and verb binding channels through controlled noun-swap and verb-swap negatives. We find that zero-shot retrieval is positively associated with pair exposure within seen compositions, even after controlling for the marginal frequencies of verbs and nouns. However, higher pair exposure is associated with larger noun-swap margins and slightly smaller verb-swap margins. This asymmetry motivates us to test whether exposure reweighting can improve retrieval with little change in the measured swap margins. To isolate the effect of exposure input, we keep the trained checkpoint fixed and replace only the exposure input at inference. We demonstrate that this exposure reweighting can improve video-text retrieval without stronger verb-noun compositional understanding, and that the gain depends on the correct sample-level exposure correspondence. By separating exposure-driven retrieval gains from verb-noun binding, Ego-ExBind provides a diagnostic framework for evaluating whether future improvements in egocentric MIR reflect compositional understanding rather than pretraining familiarity.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Ego-ExBind, a diagnostic protocol for egocentric video-text retrieval, showing that pretraining exposure drives retrieval gains without improving verb-noun compositional binding.
AI.motivation: Video-language models achieve strong zero-shot retrieval on egocentric video, but it remains unclear whether these gains reflect true verb-noun compositional understanding or mere pretraining familiarity.
AI.method: Ego-ExBind builds an Exposure Ledger from EgoClip for EPIC-KITCHENS-100 multi-instance retrieval (Seen Composition, Unseen Composition, Unseen Atom splits) and probes binding using controlled noun-swap and verb-swap negatives plus inference-time exposure reweighting.
AI.result: Zero-shot retrieval correlates positively with pair exposure in seen compositions, while higher exposure increases noun-swap margins and slightly decreases verb-swap margins; inference-time exposure reweighting improves retrieval without strengthening verb-noun binding.
AI.conclusion: Separating exposure-driven familiarity from compositional binding reveals that current egocentric retrieval gains can occur without genuine verb-noun understanding.

title: CryoGaussian: Heterogeneous Cryo-EM Reconstruction Made Explicit with Gaussian Splatting
summary: Single-particle cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) determines macromolecular structures from noisy particle images. However, rare, transient compositional states and subtle, continuous conformational variation are difficult to resolve. We present CryoGaussian, a Gaussian splatting method for heterogeneous cryo-EM reconstruction that fits an explicit Gaussian density representation directly to the particle images through a differentiable rasterizer rendering orthographic line integrals modulated by the contrast transfer function. The Gaussians are initialized randomly, with their number derived from the estimated spatial support of the molecular density and their minimum size bounded by the Nyquist frequency of the particle images. To capture the compositional and conformational variation across particle images, we learn particle-image and per-Gaussian latents that jointly modulate the base position, amplitude, and scale of each Gaussian. Each structural state is then reconstructed by fitting the Gaussians conditioned on its inferred latent. On CryoBench, CryoGaussian achieves state-of-the-art reconstruction accuracy for both compositional and conformational heterogeneity. On experimental data, it resolves a rare compositional state of the 50S ribosomal subunit (class C4, 1.3% of particles) with rRNA helix 68 docked in the absence of the central protuberance, and continuous conformational motion of the SF3b and helicase subcomplexes of the pre-catalytic spliceosome. We further optimize the rasterizer for additive cryo-EM projection, reducing training time by 12.8-28.0$\times$.

AI.tldr: This paper presents CryoGaussian, an explicit Gaussian splatting method for heterogeneous cryo-EM reconstruction that achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on CryoBench and 12.8-28.0x faster training.
AI.motivation: Resolving rare, transient compositional states and subtle continuous conformational variations in single-particle cryo-EM remains challenging for existing reconstruction methods.
AI.method: CryoGaussian fits an explicit Gaussian density representation directly to particle images via a differentiable orthographic rasterizer modulated by the contrast transfer function, using particle-image and per-Gaussian latents to modulate position, amplitude, and scale.
AI.result: On CryoBench, CryoGaussian achieves state-of-the-art accuracy for compositional and conformational heterogeneity; on experimental data, it resolves a rare 50S ribosomal state (1.3% of particles) and continuous spliceosome motion while reducing training time by 12.8-28.0x.
AI.conclusion: Explicit Gaussian splatting with latent modulation provides a fast, accurate framework for resolving both discrete and continuous structural heterogeneity in cryo-EM.

title: When Foundation Models Disagree: Representational Heterogeneity for Calibrated Uncertainty in Whole-Slide Image Classification
summary: Pathology foundation models supply strong representations for whole-slide image classification, yet the confidence attached to their predictions remains hard to trust. Prevailing uncertainty estimators act within a single feature space and thereby overlook the uncertainty that the choice of foundation-model representation itself induces. This work introduces CALIFUSE, a calibration-oriented framework that fuses several pathology foundation models for the specific purpose of uncertainty estimation. Departing from accuracy-driven fusion, CALIFUSE reads representational heterogeneity across encoders as an explicit confidence cue. Slide-level decision consensus is coupled with chunk-level evidence agreement quantified through Jensen-Shannon divergence, so that both prediction stability and fine-grained evidence consistency inform the estimate. Foundation-model encoders stay frozen. A task-specific nnMIL classifier is still trained for each FM; CALIFUSE then estimates confidence at inference without training an extra fusion module. Evaluated on seven WSI classification tasks under several foundation-model combinations, the framework sharpens calibration, misclassification detection, and selective prediction relative to both the strongest single-encoder baseline and naive ensemble averaging, all while preserving competitive balanced accuracy.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces CALIFUSE, a calibration-oriented framework that fuses frozen pathology foundation models using decision consensus and chunk-level Jensen-Shannon divergence to improve uncertainty estimation in whole-slide image classification.
AI.motivation: Existing uncertainty estimators for whole-slide image classification operate within a single foundation-model feature space and ignore uncertainty arising from the choice of foundation model itself.
AI.method: CALIFUSE keeps foundation-model encoders frozen, trains a task-specific nnMIL classifier per encoder, and estimates inference confidence by combining slide-level decision consensus with chunk-level evidence agreement measured via Jensen-Shannon divergence without an extra fusion module.
AI.result: Across seven WSI classification tasks and multiple foundation-model combinations, CALIFUSE improves calibration, misclassification detection, and selective prediction over the strongest single-encoder baseline and naive ensemble averaging while maintaining competitive balanced accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Reading representational heterogeneity across frozen pathology foundation models provides an effective, training-free confidence cue for trustworthy WSI classification.

title: MultiBinder: Preventing Multi-Subject Identity Leakage in Personalized Video Generation
summary: Personalized video generation faces a significant scalability challenge: as the number of custom subjects increases, existing methods suffer from severe identity leakage and semantic entanglement, resulting in videos with blended attributes and incoherent narratives. We identify that this stems from a lack of explicit binding between textual entity phrases and their corresponding visual patterns prior to fusion in diffusion models. To address this, we propose MultiBinder, a novel framework built on a ``bind-then-narrate'' paradigm. Our approach introduces a two-stage conditioning process before video diffusion. First, Cross-modal Entity Binding devises an entity-aware Q-Former to extract identity-centric features from each subject's reference image and tightly align them with its unique entity phrase, yielding disentangled ``identity tokens.'' Second, a Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) acts as a ``narrative director'' in the Narrative-Aware Subject Arrangement stage, capturing the action of each subject from the text prompt and synthesizes contextualized subject features that encapsulate ``who is doing what'' and preserve role-specific distinctions. These features are then injected into a video diffusion model via dedicated conditioning pathways, ensuring precise attribute allocation. Extensive experiments on both general and newly curated multi-subject benchmarks show that MultiBinder significantly outperforms existing methods in multi-subject identity fidelity.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes MultiBinder, a "bind-then-narrate" framework that prevents multi-subject identity leakage in personalized video generation using an entity-aware Q-Former and an MLLM narrative director.
AI.motivation: As the number of custom subjects increases in personalized video generation, existing methods suffer from identity leakage and semantic entanglement due to lacking explicit entity-to-visual binding before diffusion fusion.
AI.method: MultiBinder uses Cross-modal Entity Binding with an entity-aware Q-Former to align each subject's reference image with its entity phrase into disentangled identity tokens, followed by an MLLM narrative director that synthesizes role-specific contextualized features for dedicated diffusion conditioning pathways.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on general and newly curated multi-subject benchmarks show that MultiBinder significantly outperforms existing methods in multi-subject identity fidelity.
AI.conclusion: Explicit cross-modal entity binding and narrative-aware subject arrangement effectively eliminate attribute blending in multi-subject personalized video generation.

title: StreamEgo: Streaming Exocentric-to-Egocentric Video Generation
summary: Exocentric-to-egocentric (Exo2Ego) video generation transforms third-person recordings into first-person viewpoints, unlocking immersive AR/VR experiences and scalable demonstration synthesis for embodied robotics. Extending it to a streaming setting is expected to further enable live applications. However, existing methods suffer from degraded manipulation regions, overfitting and confinement to fixed-length clips with prohibitive latency. To address these limitations, we present StreamEgo, a real-time framework for unbounded, generalizable Exo2Ego video generation. To resolve intricate manipulation dynamics while supporting the streaming pipeline, a streaming dual-branch prior provides pixel-aligned guidance for translating appearance and skeletal kinematics. We also introduce a region-aware loss curriculum to improve generalization and stabilize multi-objective diffusion training. Furthermore, we distill the model into a chunk-wise autoregressive model, augmented with a region-aware corruption mechanism and a first-chunk curriculum, enabling high-quality, generalizable real-time streaming Exo2Ego generation at 24.3 FPS on a single H100 GPU.

AI.tldr: This paper presents StreamEgo, a real-time streaming exocentric-to-egocentric video generation framework that runs at 24.3 FPS on a single H100 GPU.
AI.motivation: Existing exocentric-to-egocentric video generation methods are confined to fixed-length clips with high latency and suffer from degraded manipulation regions and overfitting.
AI.method: StreamEgo uses a streaming dual-branch prior for pixel-aligned appearance and skeletal kinematics guidance, a region-aware loss curriculum, and distillation into a chunk-wise autoregressive model with region-aware corruption and a first-chunk curriculum.
